question: A 43-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset chest pain, dyspnea, and fatigue. Physical exam is notable for a murmur heard at the cardiac apex that radiates to the axilla during systole. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Mitral regurgitation (MR) is a valvular heart disease characterized by the abnormal leaking of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. MR can range from mild to severe based on the amount of blood regurgitating back into the left atrium. Mitral valve prolapse is the most common cause, and other causes are rheumatic heart disease, ischemic heart disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, endocarditis, and congenital heart defects. Also, acute MR occurs following rupture of the chordae tendinae or papillary muscles.

Patients may present with dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, pulmonary edema, and even cardiogenic shock. Physical examination reveals a holosystolic (or pansystolic) murmur heard best at the cardiac apex and radiating to the axilla, although the radiation can vary somewhat in acute MR and depends on the direction of the jet. The apical impulse may also be displaced laterally if significant ventricular dilation is present. The diagnostic test of choice is echocardiography. Medical management includes diuretics to reduce symptoms of congestion, vasodilators for acute MR, and beta-blockers or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors for heart failure symptoms. If needed, valve replacement is definitive therapy.



Aortic regurgitation (A) presents with a diastolic murmur heard along the left sternal border at the third or fourth rib space (Erb point) or second right intercostal space if the cause is aortic root dilation. Other exam findings in more severe cases may include head bobbing (De Musset sign), water hammer pulses (Corrigan pulse), fingernail pulsations (Quincke sign), and wide pulse pressure.

Aortic stenosis (B) presents with a systolic murmur heard in the right second rib space near the right sternal border with radiation to the carotids with a reduction in the murmur with the Valsalva maneuver. Patients may present with dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, and reduced exercise tolerance.

Tricuspid regurgitation (D) is a pansystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border. Jugular venous distension and a pulsatile and enlarged liver may be noted on exam.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis presents with a diastolic murmur that is described as rumbling with radiation to the cardiac apex?

Reveal Answer:
Mitral stenosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mitral Regurgitation

History
Acute: ischemic heart disease, endocarditis, MI, trauma
Chronic: rheumatic heart disease, degenerative mitral valve disease
Presentation
Acute Sx: dyspnea, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic edema
Chronic Sx: asymptomatic until CHF onset, S3
PE
Acute: unique, harsh, midsystolic murmur best heard at apex that radiates to the base or axilla
Chronic: blowing holosystolic murmur best heard at apex with radiation to axilla
Dx
Echocardiogram
Tx
Acute: nitroprusside, dobutamine, intra-aortic balloon pump, emergency surgery
Chronic: CHF Rx, valve repair or replacement

question: A 62-year-old man with a history of tuberculosis presents to the ED with progressive dyspnea. Vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, jugular venous distension is noted. A pericardial knock is heard on cardiac auscultation. Echocardiography reveals a thickened, calcified pericardium with abnormal ventricular filling. Which of the following additional physical examination findings is likely to be found in this patient, based on the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Constrictive pericarditis is caused by a rigid, noncompliant pericardium (often from tuberculosis, prior cardiac surgery, or radiation). The hallmark physical exam finding is Kussmaul sign, a paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure (JVP) during inspiration. Normally, JVP falls on inspiration, but in constrictive pericarditis, the right ventricle cannot accommodate increased venous return, so JVP paradoxically rises.

Other classic findings include a pericardial knock (an early diastolic sound) and a prominent y descent in the JVP waveform. Differentiation from tamponade is crucial: tamponade presents with pulsus paradoxus and absent y descent, not Kussmaul sign, and this patient’s presentation and echocardiogram findings suggest constrictive pericarditis, not cardiac tamponade.



Mid-diastolic rumble at the apex (B) is a feature of mitral stenosis produced by turbulent flow across the narrowed mitral valve, not a rigid pericardium.

Opening snap (C) is also associated with mitral stenosis, not pericardial disease. It is caused by the abrupt halting of the stenotic mitral valve leaflets.

Pulsus paradoxus (D) is a classic finding in cardiac tamponade but is rare in constrictive pericarditis. It represents an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure. When present in those with constrictive pericarditis, it presents with an associated echocardiographic effusion that was not seen on this patient's imaging.

Wide fixed splitting of S2 (E) is characteristic of atrial septal defect due to prolonged right ventricular systole and is unrelated to constrictive pericarditis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Dressler syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
It is a late post-myocardial infarction pericarditis caused by an autoimmune reaction, presenting weeks after the infarction.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Constrictive Pericarditis

Caused by thickening and scarring of the pericardium
Risk factors: history of viral or idiopathic pericarditis, prior radiation therapy or cardiac surgery, prior infection (e.g., tuberculosis), autoimmune conditions, malignancy
PE: increased JVP, pericardial knock, Kussmaul sign, pulsus paradoxus (rare)
Tx options (depending on whether early or chronic disease) include anti-inflammatory agents, Tx of the underlying cause, pericardiectomy

question: Which of the following differentiates unstable angina from non-ST segment myocardial infarction?

options.text: Presence of ST segment depression on ECG

englishExplanation:
Unstable angina and non-ST segment myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) are often initially indistinguishable as both present with symptoms of chest pain or pressure, dyspnea, diaphoresis, and nausea. Unstable angina is defined as angina that is new in onset, occurring at rest or with minimal exertion, worsening in frequency or duration from a previously stable pattern, resistant to previously effective doses of nitroglycerin, or precipitated by decreased levels of exertion.

The ECG may show evidence of myocardial ischemia, such as ST segment depression or new T wave inversions, or it may be unchanged from previous ECGs or even normal. Patients with unstable angina have a normal troponin level, while those with NSTEMI have an elevated troponin, indicating myocardial damage.



The duration of chest pain (A) does not differentiate between unstable angina and NSTEMI. The duration of pain can help to differentiate cardiac pain (often 5–20 minutes in duration) and noncardiac pain (seconds or hours). However, the duration of symptoms alone is not enough to rule out acute coronary syndrome.

The onset of pain at rest (C) can be seen with both unstable angina and NSTEMI.

The presence of ST segment depression (D) can not be used to diagnose or rule out unstable angina or NSTEMI. Serial ECGs should be performed in patients presenting with signs and symptoms concerning for acute coronary syndromes, as patients with unstable angina or NSTEMI may evolve and develop ST segment elevation requiring more aggressive care.

One Step Further
Question:
What ECG changes are indicative of a right ventricular infarct?

Reveal Answer:
ST segment elevation in lead V1 in the setting of an inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction, as well as ST segment elevation in leads V3R–V6R.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Angina

Chest pain or pressure with exertion or stress that is relieved by rest
Consider noncardiac causes
Diagnosis is made by stress test
Tx: lifestyle modifications, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, nitrates

question: An 86-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents with syncope while taking out the garbage. On examination, he has a narrow pulse pressure with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates to his carotids. His ECG does not show any acute ST-T wave changes. Based on his findings, which of the following will most likely be seen on echocardiogram?

options.text: Regurgitant flow through the aortic valve

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with symptoms and exam findings of aortic stenosis, an abnormality of the heart valve that prevents left ventricular outflow. It is most commonly seen in older patients with a history of coronary artery disease and hypertension. It can be seen in younger patients as well who have a bicuspid aortic valve. Symptoms of aortic stenosis progress slowly, often starting with dyspnea followed by angina, before developing exertional syncope and congestive heart failure.

Exam findings include a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids as well as an S4 gallop. Carotid pulses may be delayed and diminished, and a narrowed pulse pressure is typically present. The normal aortic valve area is 3 cm2 or greater, with obstruction and resulting symptoms occurring when the valve area is reduced by greater than 50%. A valve area of 0.8 cm2 or less is seen in critical aortic stenosis. Other findings on echocardiogram consistent with aortic stenosis include a pressure gradient across the valve of greater than 50 mm Hg and left ventricular hypertrophy. Although patients may be asymptomatic for a long period of time, once symptoms develop mortality increases significantly. Because patients with critical aortic stenosis are preload dependent, vasodilators and diuretics should be avoided as they can cause significant hypotension. Definitive treatment is aortic valve replacement.



A flail mitral leaflet (B) may be seen in acute mitral regurgitation. Occurring in the setting of recent myocardial infarction or infectious endocarditis, patients present with acute onset of pulmonary edema and shock. A harsh, midsystolic murmur that radiates to the base may be heard.

Findings of regurgitant flow through the aortic valve (C) are consistent with aortic regurgitation, often the result of rheumatic heart disease, endocarditis, or bicuspid aortic valve. Patients with chronic aortic regurgitation will have a widened pulse pressure and a high-pitched, blowing diastolic murmur.

Right ventricular hypertrophy (D) can be seen in the setting of mitral stenosis. Patients present with dyspnea on exertion and exercise intolerance and will have a low-pitched rumbling apical diastolic murmur.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common complication of mitral stenosis?

Reveal Answer:
Atrial fibrillation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aortic Stenosis

Risk factors: advancing age, diabetes, hypertension
Sx: dyspnea, chest pain, syncope
PE: crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids, paradoxically split S2, S4 gallop
Murmur decreases with Valsalva
Most commonly caused by degenerative calcification
Treatment: aortic valve replacement
Complications:
Anemia
Thromboembolism
Chronic kidney disease
Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis + acquired von Willebrand syndrome type 2A + gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasia)

question: A 66-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the emergency department with chest pain that started 2 hours ago while he was mowing the lawn. An ECG demonstrates a left bundle branch block and additional findings suggestive of a myocardial infarction. Which of the following is likely present on this patient’s ECG that meets the diagnostic criteria for an ST elevation myocardial infarction in the setting of a left bundle branch block?

options.text: Discordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in any lead
ST segment elevation > 2 mm in leads V2–V3
ST segment elevation ≥ 1 mm concordant with the QRS complex in any lead
ST segment elevation ≥ 3 mm discordant with the QRS complex in any lead
T wave inversion ≥ 5 mm in any lead

correctAnswer: ST segment elevation ≥ 1 mm concordant with the QRS complex in any lead
englishExplanation:
The Sgarbossa ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) criteria were created to help clinicians more accurately diagnose STEMI in patients with a baseline conduction delay. Three independent ECG predictors of myocardial infarction are used in the presence of a conduction delay like a left bundle branch block (LBBB). ST segment elevation of at least 1 mm that is concordant with the QRS complex in any lead meets one of the criteria for STEMI. Concordant means that the ST segment and QRS complex have the same direction.

The two other criteria for STEMI include concordant ST segment depression of at least 1 mm in lead V1, V2, or V3 and ST segment elevation of at least 5 mm that is discordant with the QRS complex. However, this latter criterion is based on the original Sgarbossa criteria and has been replaced in the modified Sgarbossa criteria with excessive discordance, defined by an ST/S ratio > 0.25. The original Sgarbossa criteria assigned weighted scores to determine the likelihood of STEMI. However, in the modified Sgarbossa criteria, meeting any single criterion yields increased sensitivity without significant loss of specificity in the diagnosis of STEMI in the setting of a conduction delay.



According to the modified Sgarbossa criteria, worrisome ST depressions should be concordant, not discordant (A).

ST segment elevation > 2 mm in leads V2–V3 (B) is part of the standard criteria for diagnosing STEMI in patients without LBBB. There is no mention of concordance. Thus, this criterion does not apply to the modified Sgarbossa criteria.

While discordant ST elevation is part of the original Sgarbossa criteria, the correct threshold for ST segment elevation is ≥ 5 mm, not ≥ 3 mm (D).

T wave inversion (E) is not part of the modified Sgarbossa criteria for diagnosing STEMI in the setting of LBBB.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the time frame for urgent fibrinolysis in patients with ECG findings of ST elevation myocardial infarction who are not located in a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) center and are not able to meet PCI recommended goals?

Reveal Answer:
30 minutes.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Modified Sgarbossa Criteria

Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in any lead with a positive QRS complex
Concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1, V2, or V3
Excessive discordant ST elevation ≥ 25% of the depth of the preceding S wave

question: A 23-year-old man presents with syncope while playing basketball. He is currently awake and alert and reports no symptoms. His vital signs are within normal limits and he has a midsystolic murmur on auscultation. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following medications, if given, could worsen his condition?
englishExplanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant condition that results in left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of other causes such as hypertension or aortic stenosis. Many patients have minimal to no symptoms and are diagnosed only through family screening, detection of a harsh, systolic crescendo-decrescendo heart murmur on routine examination or abnormal electrocardiogram findings. Symptomatic patients may present with dyspnea (the most common symptom), chest pain, palpitations, syncope or near-syncope, or dysrhythmias. Sudden cardiac death is the most ominous presentation. Diagnosis is aided by electrocardiogram findings, which vary and may include deep, narrow Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads with tall R waves in leads V1–V2, large amplitude QRS complexes, P wave abnormalities, deeply inverted T waves in the mid-precordials in patient with the apical variant. Echocardiography will show left ventricular hypertrophy, most often asymmetrically affecting the septal wall, left ventricular outflow tract narrowing, and a small left ventricular cavity. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, long-term beta-blocker therapy is the treatment of choice. Beta-blockers are negative inotropes that work by prolonging diastole, which allows for increased ventricular filling and reduces left ventricular outflow obstruction. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine), nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin), and diuretics should be avoided as they can worsen outflow obstruction.



Disopyramide (A) is an antidysrhythmic medication with negative inotropic effects. It is considered a second-line medication in the treatment of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Beta-blockers, such as nadolol (B), and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as verapamil (D), are both recommended as treatment options in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Verapamil works by decreasing contractility, improving diastolic relaxation, and reducing blood pressure and heart rate which decreases myocardial oxygen demand.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment of choice for patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with risk factors for sudden cardiac death?

Reveal Answer:
Automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillator placement.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant, first-degree relatives
May present as sudden death in a young athlete
Sx: dyspnea on exertion (most common), syncope, orthopnea, chest pain, palpitations
PE: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that increases in intensity with Valsalva maneuver and decreases with squatting
Dx
ECG: repolarization changes, large-amplitude QRS, narrow deep Q waves inferior and lateral
Echocardiography: LVH with septal hypertrophy
Tx: refrain from vigorous physical activity, ICD for high-risk patients
Options for symptomatic patients: beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, myosin inhibitors (second-line)

question: A 68-year-old man with a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and abdominal aortic aneurysm last measured at 5.5 cm presents for evaluation after an episode of syncope just prior to arrival. He reports 4 hours of abdominal pain and right flank pain. Vital signs include a BP of 76/48 mm Hg, HR of 125 bpm, RR of 20/min, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. His exam demonstrates periumbilical and right flank ecchymosis. Which imaging modality is optimal for evaluating the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms?

options.text: Bedside ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
CT of the chest with contrast
MRI of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast

correctAnswer: Bedside ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
englishExplanation:
Abdominal aortic aneurysms are defined by an aortic diameter > 3 cm. Indications for surgical intervention include a diameter > 5–5.5 cm (depending on the source text) or a size increase of > 0.5 cm/yr. Risk factors include age > 60 years, male sex, and smoking. Smoking is the most important risk factor and places patients at risk of accelerated aneurysm growth and rupture. Clinical features include abdominal or back pain that is typically severe and sudden in onset and described as ripping or tearing. A pulsatile abdominal mass may be present, depending on the aneurysm diameter and the patient’s body habitus. The presence of hypotension, syncope, and flank or umbilical ecchymosis should raise suspicion for aneurysmal rupture secondary to the massive, rapid blood loss. Imaging for diagnosis is guided by hemodynamic stability. In patients who are hemodynamically stable, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast is warranted. In hemodynamically unstable patients, a focused bedside ultrasound of the abdominal aorta should be pursued. When clinical suspicion is high, imaging should not delay operative intervention (e.g., open or endovascular repair). Temporizing measures in the emergency department should include blood product transfusion and permissive hypotension (e.g., systolic BP 80–100 mm Hg).



Anterior-posterior abdominal X-rays (A) may reveal aortic widening easily seen in patients with a heavily calcified aorta. But they are less sensitive than ultrasonography for diagnosing aortic aneurysm, rupture, and dissection.

Bedside echocardiogram (B) allows for the evaluation of underlying cardiac function, valvular function, pericardial disease, and clues to a patient’s volume status. In patients with known thoracic aortic disease, such as proximal aortic dissection, echocardiography may help rule out associated tamponade. However, it will not diagnose an abdominal aneurysm.

CT of the chest with contrast (D) would reveal thoracic aortic disease but provides insufficient information regarding the patient’s abdominal aorta.

MRI of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast (E) would be an appropriate imaging modality in hemodynamically stable patients with contraindications to CT, but CT is still preferred given its widespread availability and decreased time to complete.

One Step Further
Question:
What feared complication after abdominal aortic surgery might present with hemorrhagic shock secondary to gastrointestinal bleeding?

Reveal Answer:
Aortoenteric fistula.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)

Risk factors: male sex, older age, smoking, HTN
Sx: often asymptomatic but may present with abdominal pain
PE: pulsatile abdominal mass
If ruptured: hypotension
If arteriovenous fistula formation: abdominal bruit, signs of fluid overload and heart failure
Dx: U/S (consider CT if symptomatic and hemodynamically stable)
Tx
Monitor progression (Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines)
4.0–4.9 cm: U/S annually
5.0–5.4 cm: U/S every 6 months
Can also use CT or MRI (MRI is preferred over time due to less radiation)
Surgical repair indicated for
Symptomatic aneurysms
Asymptomatic aneurysms with a diameter ≥ 5.5 cm (some sources consider the threshold ≥ 5 cm in female patients) or with a rapid rate of expansion
The USPSTF recommends one-time screening for AAA by ultrasonography in men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked

question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the ED concerned about high blood pressure. She has been working on a big project at work and developed a slight bitemporal headache today. She decided to check her blood pressure and found it to be 188/116 mm Hg. She reports no other medical history and takes no medications. She reports no other symptoms aside from the headache, which has now improved. Vital signs show HR 76 bpm, BP 178/104 mm Hg, RR 12/min, and T 98.6°F (37°C). Which of the following tests would be the most useful in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with asymptomatic hypertension. Current emergency medicine literature does not give definitive advice about which patients with asymptomatic elevated blood pressure should receive screening tests. Literature supports that ED patients with asymptomatic severe hypertension do not require any routine screening for acute organ injury. However, of the choices listed, a serum creatinine (or BMP) may be useful to identify a small subset of patients who have acute kidney injury in the setting of severe hypertension and may help establish a baseline creatinine value to more comfortably initiate certain antihypertensive therapy. Other laboratory testing and imaging are not useful.



A chest X-ray (B) can help evaluate for cardiomegaly or pulmonary edema. However, in a patient with asymptomatic elevated blood pressure, a chest X-ray has not been shown to change management.

Although this patient reported a bitemporal headache when her blood pressure was elevated, she did not present with signs and symptoms characteristic of a hypertensive emergency. Elevated blood pressure, headache, and focal neurologic deficits are associated with the hypertensive emergencies of ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. A CT scan of the head (C) would be indicated in such a scenario but not in this patient whose headache is resolved and is not associated with neurologic concerns.

Similar to a chest X-ray, an ECG (D) can help evaluate for left ventricular hypertrophy or cardiac ischemia, but in a patient without chest pain or cardiac symptoms, there is little utility in this diagnostic test.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the target blood pressure before treatment for patients with ischemic stroke who are candidates for thrombolysis?

Reveal Answer:
Blood pressure ≤ 185/110 mm Hg.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Asymptomatic Hypertension

Most common causes of BP elevation: pain, anxiety
Diagnostic workup in the ED:
Controversial recommendations as yield of routine testing is low; testing should be guided by severity of HTN, history and medication adherence, and PE
Highest yield is BMP to check creatinine and electrolytes, especially if starting antihypertensive treatment
Outpatient follow-up

question: A 66-year-old man presents to the ED reporting palpitations and feeling lightheaded. He has a history of hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, and myocardial infarction 4 years prior. In the ED, his vital signs are BP 88/62 mm Hg, HR 170 bpm, RR 18/min, and SpO2 94% on room air. An ECG is obtained as seen above. Which of the following is the next step in management?
englishExplanation:
This patient has ventricular tachycardia. Patients may present with palpitations, hypotension, or syncope. Patients are generally > 50 years of age and usually have a history of myocardial infarction, structural heart disease, or heart failure. In a patient with previous myocardial infarction, a wide complex tachycardia is almost always ventricular tachycardia. It is recognized on ECG by more than three ectopic ventricular beats. Ventricular tachycardia can be grouped into monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (ectopic beats are morphologically the same) and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (QRS complexes have many different shapes). The most well-known polymorphic ventricular tachycardia is torsades de pointes. Ventricular tachycardia is characterized by a regular rhythm. Hemodynamically unstable patients (hypotension, respiratory distress, chest pain, diaphoresis) with ventricular tachycardia should undergo immediate synchronized cardioversion. If time permits, patients should receive sedation and analgesia prior to cardioversion.



Amiodarone (B), procainamide (C), or lidocaine are antidysrhythmics that are used in patients with hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia. Adenosine (A) is an ultra-short-acting atrioventricular-nodal blocker that is commonly used in the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia, not unstable ventricular tachycardia.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a quick way to decide whether a tachycardic rhythm is supraventricular or ventricular in origin?

Reveal Answer:
Supraventricular rhythms usually have a narrow QRS complex and ventricular rhythms have a wide QRS complex.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ventricular Tachycardia

More than three consecutive ectopic ventricular beats
Monomorphic, polymorphic
Wide complexes
Bidirectional: digoxin toxicity
Brugada criteria can help differentiate ventricular tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy
If unsure about the rhythm, manage all wide complex tachycardias as ventricular tachycardia

question: An 18-year-old woman presents with palpitations and near syncope. Her vital signs are T 98.7°F (37.1°C), HR 199 bpm, BP 113/66 mm Hg, RR 32/min, and SpO2 94%. Her ECG is shown above. What treatment is indicated?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with near syncope in the setting of atrial fibrillation with aberrant conduction, most likely secondary to Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, and should be chemically or electrically cardioverted. WPW syndrome refers to the presence of an accessory pathway between the atria and the ventricles. This accessory pathway has a shortened refractory period and can bypass normal conduction down the atrioventricular (AV) node. Because of the shortened refractory time, the accessory pathway in WPW can conduct atrial impulses much faster than the AV node, allowing for a ventricular rate between 150 and 300 bpm. Any tachycardia > 200 bpm in an adult or older adolescent should raise suspicion for an accessory pathway.

Patients with WPW can be asymptomatic or may present with severe tachydysrhythmias. The most common presenting dysrhythmia is reentrant tachycardia (70–80%), and the second is atrial fibrillation (10–30%). In these tachydysrhythmias, the patient can conduct orthodromically (down the AV node and back up the accessory pathway), antidromically (down the accessory pathway and up the AV node), or in both directions. Patients who have any antidromic conduction will present with wide complex tachycardias. In patients with irregularly irregular wide complex tachycardias, atrial fibrillation with WPW is the most common diagnosis. If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, electrical cardioversion should be pursued immediately, as these patients run the risk of degrading into ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. If the patient is hemodynamically stable, procainamide can be administered for chemical cardioversion. Procainamide is a class IA antidysrhythmic agent. The dose of procainamide is 17 mg/kg, administered at a rate of 20–30 mg/min.



Antidysrhythmic agents that block the AV node are contraindicated in patients with a wide complex rhythm with WPW, especially in those with atrial fibrillation. Blocking the AV node causes unopposed electrical conduction down the accessory pathway, which can lead to ventricular dysrhythmias. Additionally, the accessory pathway in WPW responds paradoxically to AV nodal-blocking agents by further decreasing its refractory time. Adenosine (A), calcium channel blockers (B), beta-blockers (C), and digoxin all block the AV node and are not recommended in this patient.

question: What is the appropriate IV medication to use for the treatment of wide complex atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response in a patient with a history of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
englishExplanation:
Accessory pathways are abnormal myocardial conduction pathways that link the atria to the ventricles and bypass the normal atrioventricular (AV) node. They can be potentially dangerous because they are not governed by the natural rate limits of the AV node, and this can lead to reentrant tachycardia and rapid ventricular rates. Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is the most common accessory pathway syndrome. It is characterized by a short PR interval (< 0.12 sec), QRS duration > 0.1 sec, and delta wave (slurred upstroke to the QRS complex).

When accessory pathways are present, they can form a reentry circuit with the AV nodal pathway and produce tachydysrhythmias. When the AV node is being used for anterograde conduction to the ventricles and the accessory pathway is used for retrograde conduction, this is referred to as orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT). The QRS complex is usually narrow, and the ventricular rate is governed by the AV node. However, when the accessory pathway is used for anterograde conduction and the AV node is used for retrograde conduction, this is referred to as antidromic AVRT. The QRS complex is typically wide, and ventricular rates can be very rapid, at times > 200 bpm.

An orthodromic (or narrow complex) rhythm is treated the same as AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (commonly referred to as supraventricular tachycardia, though this term encompasses other tachydysrhythmias as well). Initial treatment is with vagal maneuvers, and adenosine can be used if these fail. Second-line agents include calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers. Synchronized cardioversion can be considered if the patient is hemodynamically unstable.

Because retrograde conduction is through the AV node in antidromic (or wide complex) rhythms, administration of AV nodal blocking agents is contraindicated. Procainamide is the first-line therapy in these cases. Synchronized cardioversion should be considered if there is any question about the diagnosis or if the patient is clinically unstable.



Adenosine (A) is an AV nodal blocker that is unlikely to convert atrial fibrillation (Afib). It has a short half-life but may precipitate ventricular fibrillation (Vfib) in a patient with wide complex Afib and WPW. It is contraindicated in this situation.

Diltiazem (B) and metoprolol (C) and other beta-blockers are also AV nodal blocking agents. In antidromic AV reciprocating tachycardia, the accessory pathway is the anterograde limb of the circuit and the AV node is the retrograde limb. Blocking the AV node in this scenario can lead to Vfib.

Verapamil (E) is an AV nodal blocker that lengthens the refractory period of the AV node. It does not affect the accessory pathway. There have been reports of Vfib in patients who have received IV verapamil for the treatment of wide complex Afib in the setting of WPW syndrome.

Reveal Answer:
An accessory pathway disease, similar to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, with a short PR interval, normal QRS complex, and no delta wave.

question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with an ongoing seizure that began 10 minutes ago while sleeping. He has no history of seizures and was well when put down for a nap 2 hours ago. He was given one dose of intranasal midazolam by EMS en route. On exam, his temperature is 37.1°C. There is a thready but palpable pulse, but the oscillometric sphygmomanometer cannot determine his blood pressure and his capillary perfusion is delayed. He is actively seizing with generalized tonic-clonic movements. Intraosseous access is obtained, and bag-mask ventilation is provided with good chest rise. His blood glucose level is 39 mg/dL, and a rhythm strip is pictured above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with a potential beta-blocker overdose. Beta-adrenergic antagonist overdoses can cause some of the most challenging resuscitations due to the multiple life-threatening problems that present at once. In particular, propranolol overdoses in children can present with profound hypoglycemia, seizures, coma, and dysrhythmia, as seen in this patient. Not all children with a propranolol overdose become symptomatic, and those who do typically develop symptoms within 4–6 hours. The profound bradycardia and hypotension are due to impaired atrioventricular conduction, which can manifest on ECG as a long PR interval and a widened QRS complex. This patient’s QRS complex is beginning to widen. However, bradycardia and hypotension are not requisite for children to develop seizures when they overdose on propranolol.

The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends that for children with bradycardia and a pulse, the initial treatment is to assist breathing and identify the rhythm. Children with hypotension, shock, or abnormal mental status caused by profound bradycardia who do not respond when adequate oxygenation is provided should be treated with chest compressions when their heart rate is < 60 bpm. Additional treatment for bradycardia resulting in shock or hypotension consists of epinephrine, atropine, and then transthoracic pacing.

Seizures in children with a beta-adrenergic antagonist overdose are best treated by working to restore circulation, not with anticonvulsant medications. For those with mild symptoms of beta-adrenergic antagonist overdose, treatment is stepwise with IV fluids, atropine, glucagon, calcium, high-dose insulin with dextrose, vasopressors, and finally lipid emulsion therapy. A stepwise approach is not possible in critically ill patients like this one. These measures should be initiated but performed simultaneously when possible, and if they fail to produce the desired result, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation should be considered.



Intravenous atropine (A) is recommended as an early measure for children with a beta-adrenergic antagonist overdose. However, those who do not have adequate circulation must first be treated with chest compressions while the medication is being drawn up.

Intravenous dextrose (B) is an appropriate treatment for children with severe hypoglycemia, and in the real-world setting would seem like the best next step. However, in the setting of insufficient circulation, chest compressions are recommended while this is being drawn up. It is important to follow the stepwise process created by the AHA. Additionally, when a beta-blocker overdose is suspected, one of the recommended medications is glucagon, which is an antihypoglycemic agent that also augments cardiac contractility. It has been used successfully to treat these types of overdoses and acts within minutes, but it may become ineffective over time. Consider starting with glucagon instead of intravenous dextrose in these cases.

EXAM TIP: It can be challenging to answer questions about a resuscitation where many steps are performed at the same time. It's important to follow the algorithm when choosing your answer choice. Airway and breathing come before CPR, and CPR comes before medications in this algorithm. ABEM likes to ask these types of questions, so remember your algorithm.

Blood pressure is an extremely important vital sign to obtain, but sometimes emergency clinicians must act on partial information. Oscillometric sphygmomanometers rely on sound to estimate blood pressure and are less reliable at lower blood pressures and in noisy environments. Instead of letting the machine cycle or using critical moments to obtain a manual blood pressure (D), it is better to act based on other signs of severe hypotension, such as altered mental status or shock and begin treatment with chest compressions.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 72-year-old man presents with chest heaviness associated with diaphoresis and shortness of breath. Acute occlusion of which of the following coronary arteries is most likely to cause transient complete heart block with a narrow QRS complex?
englishExplanation:
A branch off of the right coronary artery (RCA) is responsible for the blood supply of the AV node in 70%-80% of the population. This is often referred to as being “right dominant.” In the remaining portion of the population, the left coronary artery provides flow to the AV node. In complete heart block, there is no communication between the atrium and ventricle because of interruption of electrical flow through the AV node in the setting of acute ischemia to the node. Occlusion of the RCA (causing an inferior infarct) can cause complete heart block as it supplies the AV node. This block is usually transient and asymptomatic with a narrow QRS complex, and does not often require pacing.



In contrast, occlusion of the left anterior descending artery (A) causes a block below the AV node resulting in a high-grade block (Mobitz II or complete heart block) that is more often abrupt in onset, persistent, and symptomatic. While conduction disturbances are more frequent with RCA occlusions, they are often more severe when associated with LAD occlusions. The left circumflex artery (B) provides flow to the lateral portion of the left ventricle not involving any of the electrical nodes. The left coronary artery (C) does provide flow in a minority of people to the AV node as mentioned above.

question: A 59-year-old man presents to the ED for severe foot pain. He reports no preceding trauma and states he has been feeling well recently until this morning when his foot pain began. His medical history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism, for which he takes amlodipine and levothyroxine daily. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is notable for an irregular heart rate on cardiac auscultation and a foot that seems somewhat dusky and pale compared to the other foot. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Acute limb ischemia is characterized by a rapid reduction in extremity perfusion with associated symptoms of new or worsening ischemia. In the absence of known or suspected peripheral arterial disease, acute limb ischemia is most likely caused by an acute arterial thromboembolism. Acute arterial thromboemboli account for roughly 50% of cases of acute arterial occlusion, with the remainder resulting from in situ thrombosis. They most commonly occur due to cardiac thrombi resulting from recent myocardial infarction or concomitant atrial fibrillation, the latter suggested by this patient’s irregular heart rate on examination.

Clinically, acute arterial thromboemboli can often be differentiated from acute-on-chronic arterial thrombosis by the timing of symptom onset and the presence of preceding symptoms or known peripheral arterial disease. Acute arterial thromboembolism and arterial thrombosis present with some variation of the six Ps (i.e., pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia), but patients with arterial thrombosis typically have a history of peripheral arterial disease or a recent clinical history to suggest it (e.g., claudication). Conversely, patients with acute limb ischemia due to arterial thromboembolism generally have otherwise normal vasculature but may have a comorbid condition that increases their risk of a cardiac thrombus that may embolize. These patients typically have a more rapid onset of symptoms in minutes to hours, while those with in situ thrombosis typically develop symptoms in hours to days. This patient’s sudden-onset foot pain associated with foot pallor and suspected atrial fibrillation are highly suspicious for acute arterial thromboembolism.

Acute arterial thromboembolism represents a surgical emergency, and treatment should be initiated on clinical suspicion alone. IV heparin should be started to minimize further clot propagation while awaiting vascular surgery consultation. Patients whose clinical course clearly suggests acute embolism rather than in situ thrombosis may undergo catheter-based embolectomy without prior vascular imaging, while CT angiography of the involved extremity should be obtained in uncertain cases. Those with acute emboli usually show minimal degrees of atherosclerosis compared to those with arterial thrombi. The likelihood of limb salvage begins to decrease at 4–6 hours after symptom onset. If not adequately treated, acute arterial embolism may ultimately result in inviability of the involved limb.



As described, patients with acute limb ischemia due to in situ arterial thrombosis (B) usually have either a known history of peripheral arterial disease or clinical symptoms such as claudication to suggest it.

Compartment syndrome (C) shares some clinical features of acute arterial thromboembolism, such as pain and neuromuscular symptoms. However, no risk factor like trauma has been presented for this patient, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Deep vein thrombosis (D) typically presents with acute, unilateral lower extremity swelling in patients with risk factors for venous thromboembolism, none of which are present in this patient.

Iatrogenic or traumatic popliteal arterial dissection (E) may result in limb ischemia, but this patient has none of the preceding circumstances (e.g., trauma) to cause this complication.

One Step Further
Question:
What sequelae of an infectious disorder can result in acute limb ischemia?

Reveal Answer:
Septic emboli, most commonly due to bacterial endocarditis.

question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease presents to the ED with chest pain and shortness of breath. Vital signs are BP 70/40 mm Hg, HR 160 bpm, RR 12/min, and SpO2 100%. Her ECG is shown above. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Procainamide 17 mg/kg at a rate of 30–50 mg/min IV

englishExplanation:
This patient has unstable ventricular tachycardia. Her ECG demonstrates a monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia. Regardless of the etiology (underlying bundle branch block, supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy), the patient is unstable (hypotensive). Unstable patients demonstrate signs related to organ hypoperfusion including hypotension, altered sensorium, syncope, shortness of breath, and chest pain consistent with myocardial ischemia.

When the dysrhythmia is unstable, the patient requires synchronized cardioversion. The etiologies of ventricular tachycardia include ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, coronary artery disease (acute myocardial infarction or scar tissue from previous infarction), electrolyte abnormalities, or medications.



For hemodynamically stable patients with ventricular tachycardia, medical therapy with amiodarone 150 mg IV (A) or procainamide 17 mg/kg IV at a rate of 30–50 mg/min (C) are both potential options. Both of these agents may medically cardiovert the patient into a stable rhythm. Amiodarone does not typically cause hemodynamic instability when administered. Procainamide may cause hypotension and widening of the QRS complex over the course of its infusion. If either of these occurs, the infusion should be held.

Defibrillation (B) is indicated for the treatment of a wide complex tachycardia without a pulse.

Reveal Answer:
A supraventricular and a ventricular impulse coincide to produce a hybrid complex called a fusion beat. Indicates two foci of pacemaker cells firing spontaneously.

question: A 74-year-old man is having a pre-operative ECG performed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Atrial fibrillation is an irregularly irregular rhythm due to uncoordinated atrial activation and random occurrence of ventricular depolarization. The atria are not contracting but they do discharge electrical impulses to the ventricles. However, no single impulse depolarizes the atria completely, so only an occasional impulse gets through the atrioventricular node. It is the most common sustained dysrhythmia in clinical practice.



Atrial flutter (B) is a rapid atrial rhythm but due to nodal delay and the ventricular response rate is slower. Therefore, atrial flutter typically occurs with some sort of atrioventricular block so that not all impulses are conducted. The resulting block is often variable (2:1, 3:1, 4:1). P waves have a characteristic sawtooth pattern.

In normal sinus rhythm (C) and sinus tachycardia (D) the sinoatrial node is the pacemaker that causes the atria to depolarize regularly and, thus, the ventricles to depolarize regularly. Therefore, the ECGs for both of these rhythms have P waves and QRS complexes that occur regularly. The difference between these two rhythms is the rate. The rate of sinus rhythm is 60–100 bpm. The rate of sinus tachycardia is > 100 bpm.

question: A 27-year-old gravida 2 para 1 woman at 36 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath and leg swelling. Her vital signs are BP 186/109 mm Hg, HR 113 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 92%, and T 37.2°C. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrates bilateral B-lines, left ventricular dilation, hypokinesia, reduced ejection fraction, and a plethoric inferior vena cava. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to treat this patient’s underlying condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s symptoms are most consistent with hypertensive acute heart failure due to peripartum cardiomyopathy. Acute congestive heart failure can be de novo, as in this patient, or an acute decompensation of chronic heart failure. Most commonly, patients present with shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, jugular venous distention, pulmonary congestion, and peripheral edema. Less often, patients present in cardiogenic shock and demonstrate signs of end-organ damage due to inadequate perfusion. Point-of-care ultrasound can help evaluate volume status, the presence of pulmonary edema, and the ejection fraction. Treatment of acute heart failure should be guided by fluid status and hemodynamics. This patient has signs and symptoms of congestion without evidence of hypoperfusion, so management should focus on oxygen support and vasodilatory therapy. Supplemental oxygen can be administered via nasal cannula or nonrebreather mask, but the presence of respiratory distress should prompt the use of noninvasive positive pressure ventilation or intubation if indicated. For patients who are hypertensive with a systolic blood pressure ≥ 150 mm Hg, the use of vasodilators is indicated. Nitroglycerin is both a venodilator and arteriodilator and thus reduces preload and afterload to improve stroke volume. Patients with acute heart failure and severe hypertension usually have pulmonary edema due to volume redistribution rather than hypervolemia, so treatment should focus on vasodilation rather than diuresis. If there is a concern for hypervolemia, loop diuretics such as furosemide may be used but should only be given after vasodilatory therapy. In addition to initial management, the precipitating cause should be identified. Common causes of acute heart failure include acute coronary syndrome (most common), thromboembolic events, infection, uncontrolled hypertension, dysrhythmias, substance use, and medication nonadherence. The etiology of this patient’s acute heart failure is postpartum dilated cardiomyopathy. It can occur in the last month of pregnancy or in the first 5 months of the postpartum period. Treatment does not differ significantly from standard management of acute heart failure, although angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and nitroprusside should be avoided during pregnancy and lactation.



Heparin (A) should be considered for acute coronary syndrome or pulmonary embolism. These are less likely as this patient’s ECG and ultrasound are not consistent with ischemia or right ventricular strain. However, anticoagulation should be considered for pregnant patients after the initial stabilization due to the increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Magnesium (B) should be given for preeclampsia. Preeclampsia should be considered for peripartum patients with hypertension and proteinuria. Severe preeclampsia can present with pulmonary edema but does not present with left ventricular dilation, reduced ejection fraction, or hypocontractility. Nitroprusside (D), a nitrate, has vasodilatory effects similar to nitroglycerin. But it is less commonly used due to the risk of cyanide toxicity and reduction of coronary blood flow. Additionally, nitroprusside is relatively contraindicated in pregnancy. Tissue plasminogen activator (E) may be considered if a thromboembolic event is thought to be the precipitating factor of acute heart failure. However, this is not consistent with the patient’s presentation.

Reveal Answer:
Sublingual tablet or spray, topical paste, or intravenous.

question: A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a cough and shortness of breath. He reports no bloody stools, syncope, or focal weakness. His brother died unexpectedly at the age of 30 years from an unknown cause. His vital signs are T 100.2ºF (37.9ºC), HR 175 bpm, RR 20/minute, BP 125/75 mm Hg, and SpO2 93% on room air. A chest X-ray demonstrates a right lower lobe opacity. His rhythm strip is shown above. Which of the following should be administered at this time?
englishExplanation:
Adenosine 6 mg IV is the first-line agent for the management of narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). This is identified by the absence of definable P waves, narrow QRS complexes (< 100 msec), and a heart rate > 100 bpm (often > 170 bpm). SVT is most commonly caused by the reentrance of electrical currents through the atrioventricular node but may also result from an atrial focus other than the sinoatrial node. Adenosine exerts its therapeutic effects by binding to adenosine receptors and inhibiting adenylate cyclase, impeding calcium ion influx at the atrioventricular node. It also acts at the sinoatrial node to activate acetylcholine currents and decrease depolarization. Vagal maneuvers, such as Valsalva, should be attempted first in patients with a stable narrow complex SVT. When these measures fail, adenosine is the agent of choice for converting the rhythm back to sinus rhythm.



Azithromycin 500 mg PO (B) is appropriate management for community-acquired pneumonia. However, in patients with cardiac dysrhythmias, management of the dysrhythmia takes precedence over that of the underlying condition. Attempts should be made to convert the rhythm back to sinus rhythm.

A normal saline 30 mL/kg IV bolus (C) is recommended for fluid resuscitation in patients with evidence of sepsis. However, this patient has normal blood pressure and minimal fever making sepsis less likely. Intravenous fluids alone are unlikely to convert SVT to sinus rhythm in this case.

Synchronized cardioversion at 200 joules (D) may be delivered to patients with SVT who do not respond to medical therapy. Additionally, it is generally recommended in hemodynamically unstable patients (including altered mental status, hypotension, ischemic chest discomfort, or evidence of acute heart failure or shock). However, hemodynamic instability is rare in patients with SVT, and some experts recommend that if rapid IV access is established, adenosine can be given first to break the dysrhythmia.

One Step Further
Question:

Reveal Answer:
12 mg IV, which may be repeated once.

question: A 2-year-old boy presents from home after he was discovered in his crib unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. Bystander CPR was immediately initiated. His initial rhythm strip upon arrival to the emergency department is as shown above. CPR is continued. What is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Asystole is the most common rhythm identified in pediatric cardiac arrest, with respiratory etiologies (e.g., respiratory failure, drowning, asphyxiation) representing the most common antecedents. The resuscitation of these patients should be focussed on maintaining ventilation and oxygenation, as well as perfusion via high-quality chest compressions, which is key for improving the likelihood of return of spontaneous circulation. The hand encircling technique is preferred for infants, while two-hand compressions are preferred in older children. Compressions should be performed at a rate of 100–120 bpm. The rate of chest compressions to breaths, as suggested in the 2025 American Heart Association guidelines, is 15 compressions to 2 ventilations. Placement of an advanced airway (i.e., supraglottic airway or endotracheal tube) may be attempted, but bag-mask ventilation is an appropriate alternative, and the available evidence demonstrates no difference in survival to hospital discharge. If an advanced airway is established, ventilation should occur at a rate of one breath every 2–3 seconds. Nonshockable rhythms, such as asystole, should be treated with early administration of epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg every 3–5 minutes. The duration of resuscitation efforts varies by clinical scenario, but in general, those requiring > 30 minutes are unlikely to result in favorable outcomes.



Empiric administration of calcium chloride 20 mg/kg (A) is associated with worse outcomes and should be reserved for specific indications, such as hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and calcium channel blocker overdose.

Defibrillation at 2 J/kg (B) is indicated for the treatment of ventricular tachycardia without a pulse or ventricular fibrillation but has not demonstrated benefit in asystole or pulseless electrical activity.

Similarly to calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg (D) administration is associated with worse outcomes. However, it can be considered for etiologies suspected to benefit from its use, including hyperkalemia and tricyclic antidepressant overdose.

One Step Further
Question:
How might a child’s weight be estimated?

Reveal Answer:
Parental estimates, a Broselow-Luten tape measure, or upper extremity circumference (i.e., using a Mercy TAPE).

question: A 32-year-old man presents after a syncopal episode. He was running on the track when he developed shortness of breath followed by witnessed syncope. He was not post-ictal and had no seizure activity. He reports that his father’s brother died while playing basketball. Physical examination is notable for a midsystolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an autosomal dominant disease causing mutations in the cardiac sarcomere protein. This leads to abnormal muscle protein development and compensatory hypertrophy of the left ventricle. Most commonly, there is asymmetric hypertrophy with significant enlargement of the anterior interventricular septum. During exertion, patients may experience syncope associated with shortness of breath, chest pain, or palpitations. In a large percentage of patients, the presenting symptom is sudden death. The ECG is abnormal in 90% of cases and abnormalities include left ventricular hypertrophy, “dagger-like” Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads, and nonspecific ST segment changes. The diagnosis is made by echocardiogram. Treatment and prevention of symptoms is aimed at maintaining adequate left ventricular filling and increasing diastolic time for filling.



Aortic stenosis (A) can also be associated with exertional syncope and causes a crescendo-decrescendo murmur. However, these patients are typically older and often have other symptoms such as progressive dyspnea with exertion and angina.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (dysplasia) (B) is another leading cause of sudden death in young athletes. Cardiomyopathy develops as the right ventricle is replaced by fat tissue. The ECG may demonstrate epsilon waves in 50% of people. This is a small positive deflection at the end of the QRS complex. The S wave upstroke may also be prolonged in leads V1–V3. The physical examination will not reveal a cardiac murmur.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (D) is one of several pre-excitation syndromes that predispose patients to dysrhythmia. In Wolff-Parkinson-White, an abnormal accessory pathway exists between the atria and ventricles. Sudden cardiac death is rare in patients with this syndrome. Classic ECG findings include a short PR interval with an associated delta wave (upsloping of the QRS complex).

One Step Further
Question:
What is the mainstay of treatment for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

Reveal Answer:
Long-term beta-blocker therapy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant, first-degree relatives
May present as sudden death in a young athlete
Sx: dyspnea on exertion (most common), syncope, orthopnea, chest pain, palpitations
PE: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that increases in intensity with Valsalva maneuver and decreases with squatting
Dx
ECG: repolarization changes, large-amplitude QRS, narrow deep Q waves inferior and lateral
Echocardiography: LVH with septal hypertrophy
Tx: refrain from vigorous physical activity, ICD for high-risk patients
Options for symptomatic patients: beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, myosin inhibitors (second-line)

question: A 45-year-old man with a history of idiopathic cardiomyopathy presents with 3 days of progressive shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. His HR is 110 bpm, BP is 110/60 mm Hg, RR is 22/min, and SpO2 is 91% on room air. An ECG shows sinus dysrhythmia with frequent premature ventricular contractions. Normal sensitivity troponin I level is 0.12 ng/mL. Chest X-ray shows bilateral pleural effusions and moderate cardiomegaly. An echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% and cardiomegaly. Which of the following in this patient is an indication for implanted cardioverter placement?
englishExplanation:
Implanted cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) are indicated for patients with conditions that have a high likelihood of causing sudden cardiac death secondary to ventricular fibrillation (VF) or ventricular tachycardia (VT).

There are a number of primary indications for ICD placement. The first criterion is sudden arrest resulting from VF or VT in the setting of ischemic heart disease. The second criterion is unexplained syncope with induced monomorphic VT demonstrated on an electrophysiologic study in the setting of ischemic heart disease. Depressed left ventricular function 40 days following myocardial infarction (MI) or 90 days after revascularization with heart failure symptoms and inducible VF or VT during an electrophysiology study in the setting of prior MI make up criteria three and four, respectively. The fifth criterion is nonischemic cardiomyopathy with depressed left ventricular function. Finally, ICD placement is indicated with sudden arrest or sustained ventricular dysrhythmia in the setting of right ventricular dysplasia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, sarcoidosis, neuromuscular disorders, channelopathies, Brugada syndrome, early repolarization, short QT syndrome, idiopathic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, congenital heart disease, and symptomatic long QT syndrome refractory to beta-blocker therapy.

This patient meets the fifth criterion based on his history of idiopathic cardiomyopathy and ejection fraction of 30% compared to a baseline normal range of 55–70%.



Cardiomegaly (A) is not an indication in and of itself for ICD placement. It must be accompanied by decreased left ventricular function or dysrhythmia.

Pleural effusion (C) is a sign of heart failure and could be an indication for ICD placement in the setting of ischemic cardiomyopathy, but not in this patient with nonischemic cardiomyopathy.

There are multiple causes of premature ventricular contractions (D) and troponin elevation (E). These may be present in the setting of cardiomyopathy but are not indications for ICD placement.

One Step Further
Question:
What effect does magnet placement over an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator pulse generator have?

Reveal Answer:
Disables defibrillation and antidysrhythmic pacing functions.

Rapid Review

Improved survival over pharmacologic treatment in those with risks for sudden cardiac death (VT, Vfib)
All ICDs are also ventricular pacemakers
Some have cardiac resynchronization therapy-defibrillator (CRT-D) that combines biventricular pacing with the ability to deliver a shock
Indications (abbreviated) if survival expected > 1 year:
Ischemic heart disease and cardiac arrest from VF or VT
Ischemic heart disease and unexplained syncope and induced VT during electrophysiology study
Depressed left ventricular function at least 40 days after MI and at least 90 days after revascularization and persistent heart failure symptoms
Nonsustained VT due to prior MI with depressed left-sided systolic function and inducible VT or VF during electrophysiology study
Nonischemic cardiomyopathy and depressed left ventricular function
Sudden cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular dysrhythmias from other underlying heart conditions
Complications
Infection
Device malfunction
Placing a magnet over the device turns off the defibrillator function

question: A 17-year-old boy presents after an episode of syncope. He felt palpitations and then lost consciousness. He is currently asymptomatic with normal vital signs. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following may be found by history or physical examination?

options.text: A family member with sudden death
Systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva

correctAnswer: A family member with sudden death
englishExplanation:
Brugada syndrome is an autosomal dominant inherited channelopathy. It most commonly presents in male patients in young adulthood. The syndrome predisposes individuals to ventricular dysrhythmia and either syncope or sudden death. There are two ECG manifestations of Brugada syndrome: a downward sloping ST segment or saddleback ST segment in the high precordial leads (V1–V3). In patients who have a syncopal episode from ventricular dysrhythmia and an ECG suggestive of Brugada, admission is recommended for cardiology evaluation. Given the autosomal dominant nature of inheritance, there may be a family history of sudden death.



Brugada syndrome does not cause any structural heart disease or ventricular hypertrophy. As a result, there is no displaced point of maximal impulse (B) on physical examination unless there is another diagnosis.

Quinolone antibiotic use (C) has been linked with prolongation of the QTc, which is another risk factor for sudden death or ventricular dysrhythmia causing syncope.

A systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva (D) is characteristic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an autosomal dominant defect leads to overgrowth of the left ventricle, which disproportionately affects the interventricular septum. The murmur is accentuated with the Valsalva maneuver.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for Brugada syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Placement of an automatic implantable cardiac defibrillator.

ECG with RBBB-like pattern

Type 2: saddleback ST elevation > 2 mm followed by upright or biphasic T wave
Type 3: coved or saddleback ST elevation < 2 mm
Type 2 and 3 changes are nondiagnostic and require further workup

question: A 47-year-old man with a history of HIV, who takes his antiretroviral therapies, reports progressively worsening shortness of breath, pedal edema, and orthopnea over the past 2 weeks. Vital signs include an HR of 100 bpm, BP 156/94 mm Hg, RR 24/min, and T 37.6°C. On physical examination, he has mild jugular venous distention and rales on lung auscultation. He has 2+ pitting edema in his lower legs. What will be the most likely findings visualized on echocardiography based on this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Dilation and impaired contraction of both ventricles
Increased interventricular septal wall thickness and diastolic dysfunction
Nondilated and nonhypertrophied ventricles with impaired ventricular filling
Right ventricular free wall replacement with fibrofatty tissue and right ventricle dyskinesis

correctAnswer: Dilation and impaired contraction of both ventricles
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of heart failure. Taking into consideration his young age, lack of previous cardiac history, and history of HIV, his symptoms are most likely due to an underlying cardiomyopathy. Cardiomyopathy is broadly defined as a group of diseases associated with an altered cardiac structure, impaired myocardial function, and dysfunctional electrical properties in the absence of underlying coronary artery disease and hypertension. Primary cardiomyopathies are genetic, whereas secondary cardiomyopathies are related to other underlying illnesses, toxins, or infections. Cardiomyopathies are further divided based on the underlying anatomy and physiology of the heart muscle, generally falling into one of the following categories: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, arrhythmogenic right ventricular, and unclassified. The patient in this question has HIV, and the clinician should recall that HIV and antiretroviral therapies, such as zidovudine, didanosine, and zalcitabine, can cause dilated cardiomyopathy. Additionally, this patient’s signs and symptoms are most suggestive of both systolic and diastolic cardiac dysfunction that is leading to congestive heart failure. Therefore, echocardiographic findings will most likely be dilation and impaired contraction of both ventricles. Other more well-known causes of dilated cardiomyopathy include stress-induced disease (also known as takotsubo cardiomyopathy), Chagas disease, Lyme disease, chronic alcohol use, and other viral infections, such as coxsackievirus or influenza virus. Dilated cardiomyopathy is a major cause of heart failure and the need for cardiac transplantation in the United States. Treatment includes general heart failure therapies, including diuretics, beta-blockers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. Depending on the severity of the disease, patients may also benefit from an implantable defibrillator.



Increased interventricular septal wall thickness and diastolic dysfunction (B) are echocardiographic findings in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is genetic and is the leading cause of sudden death in athletes. Nondilated and nonhypertrophied ventricles with impaired ventricular filling (C) are characteristic of a restrictive cardiomyopathy. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is much less common than both dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies since it is usually related to infiltrative disorders such as scleroderma or amyloidosis. Right ventricle free wall replacement with fibrofatty tissue and right ventricle dyskinesis (D) are the findings in patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. This is a less common genetic cardiomyopathy.

One Step Further

What is the cause of Chagas disease, the leading cause of dilated cardiomyopathy in Central and South America?

Reveal Answer:
A protozoan infection with Trypanosoma cruzi.

PE will show an S3 gallop on auscultation
Echocardiogram will show four dilated chambers (ventricles > atria)
Management includes abstaining from alcohol
Rx options: ACE inhibitors and diuretics
For refractory disease to maximum medical therapy, consider cardiac transplantation or LVAD (for those who are not candidates for transplantation)

question: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department at the instruction of his coach for palpitations during exercise. His exam and vital signs are normal. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most correct interpretation of this patient’s ECG?
englishExplanation:
The atria and ventricles are normally electrically isolated, connected by the atrioventricular (AV) node, which creates a brief delay in conduction to allow the atria to completely empty before the ventricles begin to contract. This delay is seen on the ECG as the PR interval. Patients with an extra or accessory pathway through this electrical isolation allow for early excitation of the myocardium. This preexcitation is often seen on ECG as the electrical signal traveling from the atrium to the ventricle along this accessory pathway causing early contraction of part of the ventricle, which is seen as a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex called a delta wave in a Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern. But sometimes, this pathway only conducts in one direction, so patients with WPW may have a normal ECG when the pathway only conducts from the ventricles to the atria.

Patients with WPW are at risk of supraventricular tachycardia, which can be perpetuated normally through the AV node and retrograde across the accessory pathway (orthodromic) or from atrium to ventricle across the accessory pathway and then retrograde through the AV node (antidromic). Antidromic tachycardia usually results in a wider QRS complex and has greater potential for ventricular fibrillation. Another type of tachycardia common in adolescents with WPW and associated with exercise is AV nodal reentrant tachycardia in which two pathways within the AV node perpetuate the tachycardia. Most patients with a WPW pattern have no symptoms, and the pattern can be discovered when they receive an ECG for a different reason. When patients with a WPW pattern develop a dysrhythmia, it tends to be a tachydysrhythmia such as orthodromic or antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia, and they present with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, chest pain, or sudden cardiac arrest. The definitive treatment for recurrent episodes of tachydysrhythmia in patients with WPW is catheter ablation of the accessory pathway. The most favorable medical treatments are flecainide or propafenone.



Long QT syndrome (A) is diagnosed on ECG with a QTc > 460 milliseconds before puberty and > 470 and 480 milliseconds in postpubertal male patients and female patients, respectively, although these specific thresholds can vary slightly based on the reference textbook.

WPW can easily be mistaken for normal sinus rhythm (B) but can be distinguished by the short PR interval and delta wave seen on the ECG of this patient.

Sinus dysrhythmia (C) occurs when there is variation in the P-wave to P-wave interval, frequently due to respiration, which is not seen in this patient.

One Step Further
Question:
Which medication is preferred in patients to stop a tachydysrhythmia due to Wolff-Parkinson-White?

Reveal Answer:
Procainamide.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome

Most commonly caused by an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) connecting atria to ventricles, bypassing AV node
ECG will show short PR interval, delta wave, wide QRS
Acute treatment
Orthodromic (narrow complex): vagal maneuvers, AV nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker)
Antidromic (wide complex): procainamide
Synchronized cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable patients
Definitive treatment is radiofrequency ablation

question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of chest pressure and shortness of breath that occurred while shoveling snow. His symptoms resolved after he sat down and rested. His vital signs are within normal limits and he is currently asymptomatic. His ECG is shown above. What is the most appropriate care plan for this patient?

options.text: Admit to an observation unit for serial troponins and exercise stress testing
Discharge home if his 3-hour troponin is normal

englishExplanation:
Wellens syndrome is highly specific for critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery. Without intervention, these patients are at high risk for extensive myocardial infarction in days to weeks. Patients present with a history of concerning chest pain due to transient occlusion of the left anterior descending artery. Spontaneous reperfusion results in resolution of symptoms. The most common ECG finding is deeply and symmetrically inverted T waves in the anterior precordial leads. Biphasic T waves are seen in 25% of cases. The classic ECG findings are present when the patient is pain free. Cardiac markers are often normal or only mildly elevated. Given the high risk of imminent infarction, patients should be treated with aspirin and heparin and admitted for urgent cardiac catheterization.



Activation of the cardiac catheterization lab (A) would be appropriate for symptomatic patients who present with evidence of acute ST segment myocardial infarction (i.e., new ST segment elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads, Sgarbossa criteria).

Admission to an observation unit for serial troponins and exercise stress testing (C) would be appropriate for a patient with anginal-type symptoms who is at moderate risk for coronary artery disease.

Discharging home if a 3-hour troponin is normal (D) would be an appropriate plan for a patient with low-risk criteria for coronary artery disease.

One Step Further
Question:
What is seen on this ECG?

Reveal Answer:
Considered a STEMI equivalent seen with acute left anterior descending artery occlusion, this shows the de Winter pattern with ST depression and peaked T waves in the precordial leads.

Rapid Review
Wellens Syndrome

Highly specific for critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery
ECG: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–3
May be pain-free
Normal or minimally elevated troponin
Tx: urgent percutaneous coronary intervention

question: A 27-year-old man presents with palpitations that began while he was sitting at work. He reports no chest pain, shortness of breath, or syncope. His ECG is seen above. Which of the following agents is the most appropriate therapy?
englishExplanation:
The electrocardiogram shows a wide complex tachycardia concerning for Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW). WPW is caused by the presence of an accessory electrical pathway that bypasses the atrioventricular (AV) node. Patients with an accessory pathway are at risk for developing reentrant tachycardia, during which there are high ventricular rates. WPW has three characteristic findings on ECG: short PR interval (< 120 msec), QRS > 120 msec, and the delta wave (a slurred upstroke to the QRS complex). All three features may not be present on the ECG. There are two possibilities for conduction in a reentrant tachycardia depending on the direction of flow through the accessory pathway and AV node. In orthodromic AV-reentrant tachycardia, the electrical impulse passes anterograde through the AV node and retrograde through the accessory pathway. In this case, the QRS complex is narrow and usual nodal agents are safe in the treatment of tachydysrhythmias. In antidromic AV-reentrant tachycardia, the electrical impulse passes anterograde through the accessory pathway and retrograde through the AV node. In this situation, the QRS complex is wide and ventricular rates are much higher due to faster conduction through the accessory pathway. Medications that act as AV nodal blockers are contraindicated in these patients because conduction will preferentially pass through the accessory pathway and can lead to ventricular fibrillation. As a result, procainamide is the preferred pharmacologic agent in the treatment of wide-complex dysrhythmias in patients with WPW.



Adenosine (A) is a common agent used to block the AV node in cases of supraventricular tachycardia. Because of its direct inhibition on the AV node, in cases of antidromic conduction, this could lead to degeneration of the rhythm into ventricular fibrillation because of sole conduction through the accessory pathway.

Diltiazem (B) and verapamil (D) are calcium channel blockers with activity at the AV node and should not be used in the treatment of WPW with antidromic conduction. Because in most cases of wide complex tachydysrhythmias, it is not definitively known if the patient has WPW, it is safer to assume the rhythm to be ventricular tachycardia and avoid AV nodal blocking agents.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment of an unstable tachydysrhythmia in the setting of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Cardioversion.
