question: A 16-year-old boy who uses IV drugs and was recently diagnosed with influenza by a nearby urgent care presents to the ED with a fever and chest pain that has gradually worsened over the last week. He appears ill but alert. His temperature is 38.9°C, heart rate is 120 bpm, respiratory rate is 22/minute, blood pressure is 94/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. His lungs are clear to auscultation, and he has a 3/6 harsh systolic murmur. You find injection marks over his arms as well as several tender skin lesions. Which of the following tests is associated with a major criterion for the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Bacterial endocarditis can be difficult to distinguish from other illnesses and is often missed on the first visit. It usually presents in those with an underlying heart defect but can be seen in those with structurally normal hearts, especially in those who use IV drugs. A new heart murmur is universal, fever is common, and skin manifestations occur occasionally. Skin lesions are rare, with petechiae being more commonly seen on mucosal surfaces or conjunctivae.

Diagnosis of infective endocarditis requires two major Duke criteria, one major and three minor criteria, or five minor criteria to be present. The two major Duke criteria to diagnose infective endocarditis are a persistently positive blood culture and positive echocardiographic findings. Organisms that commonly cause infective endocarditis include Streptococcus viridans (think dental procedures), enterococci (think genitourinary or GI procedures), and Staphylococcus aureus (think those who use IV drugs).



A complete blood cell count (C) should be obtained in this patient, but it will not help make the diagnosis of endocarditis.

A chest X-ray (B) may reveal opacifications, which can be due to septic emboli, which is one of the minor criteria.

An electrocardiogram (D) is also a reasonable test in this patient but will not confirm the diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What are Roth spots?

Reveal Answer:
Retinal hemorrhages.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bacterial Endocarditis in Children

Risk factors: valvular heart disease, congenital heart disease, central venous catheter
Sx: fever, rash, cough, and myalgias
PE: fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, murmur, Janeway lesions, anemia, nailbed hemorrhages, emboli (FROM JANE), hematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts
Dx: blood culture, echocardiography, Duke criteria
Cause: Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci (neonates, catheter)
Tx: antibiotics for 4–6 weeks
Dental prophylaxis in some cases

question: A healthy 21-year-old man presents to the ED after a syncopal episode. The patient was walking to class when he felt a short duration of palpitations and syncopized. He reports previous episodes of palpitations that self-resolved and he has never sought medical attention for these symptoms. He is well appearing on exam with a normal cardiopulmonary exam and normal range vital signs. His triage ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This clinical scenario and ECG are consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. This syndrome is most commonly seen in young (20–29-year-old) male patients. It is caused by an aberrant atrioventricular cardiac pathway that allows pre-excitation and bypass of the atrioventricular (AV) node. Bypass of the AV node allows faster propagation of electrical impulses and increases the risk of severe dysrhythmias. The diagnosis is made by ECG, with pathognomonic findings of a delta wave, a slurred upstroke of the QRS caused by depolarization from the accessory pathway, as well as a shortened PR interval.

The most common associated dysrhythmia is AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and these patients often present for palpitations or syncope. Patients with associated tachydysrhythmias require acute treatment in the ED (e.g., cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable patients; vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or procainamide for hemodynamically stable patients). The patient above, with delta waves and shortened PR interval but normal vital signs and mentation, would not require emergent treatment. Definitive treatment is utilized to prevent sudden cardiac arrest and symptomatic dysrhythmias and includes catheter-directed ablation or antidysrhythmics such as amiodarone if ablation is not an option.



Brugada syndrome (A) could present with a similar presentation, but ECG findings would show the saddle-back deformity or the coved-type ST segment in the anterior leads. This is due to a sodium channelopathy and is treated with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (B) can present with syncope in young adults but typically occurs with exertion. ECG findings would show left ventricular hypertrophy, left axis deviation, atrial enlargement, and abnormal Q waves.

Orthostatic syncope (C) would occur shortly after standing, typically without palpitations or ECG findings, and can be caused by dehydration, certain drugs, or autonomic instability.

One Step Further
Question:
What nonpharmacologic measures can be attempted to terminate supraventricular tachycardia?

Reveal Answer:
Vagal maneuvers such as forced expiration, Valsalva, cold water application, or carotid massage.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome

Most commonly caused by an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) connecting atria to ventricles, bypassing AV node
ECG will show short PR interval, delta wave, wide QRS
Acute treatment
Orthodromic (narrow complex): vagal maneuvers, AV nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker)
Antidromic (wide complex): procainamide
Synchronized cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable patients
Definitive treatment is radiofrequency ablation

question: A 14-year-old boy is brought in by his parent after experiencing a syncopal episode. His uncle died suddenly at age 15. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient's ECG shows the presence of an epsilon wave, a terminal notch in the QRS complex due to slowed intraventricular conduction. It also shows a T wave inversion and a prolonged upstroke of the S wave in the anterior leads. This ECG pattern is seen in patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). About 50% of patients with ARVC have a noticeable epsilon wave.

ARVC results from a genetic abnormality in cardiac desmosomes, leading to fatty infiltration of the ventricular tissue followed by fibrofatty replacement of the cardiac muscle. ARVC affects the right ventricular wall and may be seen as hypokinesis on an echocardiogram. The fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular wall leads to ventricular dysrhythmias, which can present as syncope or sudden cardiac arrest. Approximately 30–50% of cases of ARVC are familial in nature, and these are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Treatment of ARVC includes the initiation of a beta-blocker and implantation of a cardioverter-defibrillator. Severe cases may require heart transplantation.



The presence of an accessory tract (A) describes the pathogenesis of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (WPW). In this condition, an accessory tract connects the ventricles directly to the atria, thereby bypassing the atrioventricular node, increasing the risk of reentrant atrial tachycardias. ECG findings consistent with WPW include the presence of a delta wave, a shortened PR interval, and QRS widening.

Septal hypertrophy (C) describes the pathogenesis of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, in which hypertrophy of the interventricular septum and ventricular walls results in subaortic outflow obstruction.

Brugada syndrome is a genetic sodium channelopathy (D) characterized by the presence of ST segment changes with a right bundle block pattern in leads V1–V3. Patients with Brugada syndrome have an increased risk for both ventricular dysrhythmias as well as reentrant atrial tachycardias.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common ECG abnormality in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy?

Reveal Answer:
T wave inversions in leads V1–V3.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant inheritance (most common)
Etiology: fibrofatty replacement of right ventricle myocardium
Clinical: syncope or sudden death from dysrhythmia
Dx: ECG shows epsilon wave (positive deflection buried in the terminal QRS complex), T wave inversion V1–V3, prolonged S wave upstroke
Tx: activity restrictions, beta-blockers to prevent dysrhythmia, implantable cardiac defibrillator

question: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treating a patient with this ECG and a blood pressure of 68/32 mm Hg?
englishExplanation:
This ECG shows a regular, wide complex tachycardia with RS complexes > 100 ms in the precordial leads, which is diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia (VT). VT originates within or below the bundle of His and is categorized as nonsustained if the duration is < 30 seconds or sustained if > 30 seconds. It is most commonly caused by reentry pathways that develop in patients with underlying heart disease, particularly ischemic and nonischemic cardiomyopathy. It should be suspected in patients presenting with regular, wide complex tachycardia, though other rhythms may present similarly, especially supraventricular tachycardias with aberrant conduction, such as atrial flutter and atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia.

Initial management of VT depends upon hemodynamic stability, with pharmacotherapy indicated in cases of stable VT, while electrical cardioversion is required in unstable VT. This patient’s marked hypotension classifies them as unstable and warrants synchronized cardioversion at 100 J as the first step in treatment. If initial cardioversion is unsuccessful, escalating doses up to 200 J should be used. Cardiology should be consulted for all patients with VT, regardless of hemodynamic stability. First-line pharmacotherapy is an IV amiodarone bolus followed by a continuous infusion, with procainamide and lidocaine available as second-line agents.



IV adenosine (A) is used in patients with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias who are hemodynamically stable. It would not be appropriate in the treatment of unstable ventricular tachycardia.

Amiodarone given IV as a continuous infusion (C) and single bolus (B) are components of the first-line pharmacotherapy for patients with VT who are hemodynamically stable. Electrical cardioversion should be used as initial treatment for patients who are unstable with hypotension, mental status changes, or significant chest pain.

Defibrillation (D) is appropriate for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless VT but is not used in patients with VT who have a palpable pulse.

One Step Further
Question:
What antidysrhythmic agents have been shown to reduce mortality in patients with a history of sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia?

Reveal Answer:
Beta-blockers.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ventricular Tachycardia

More than three consecutive ectopic ventricular beats
Monomorphic, polymorphic
Wide complexes
Bidirectional: digoxin toxicity
Brugada criteria can help differentiate ventricular tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy
If unsure about the rhythm, manage all wide complex tachycardias as ventricular tachycardia
Tx
Pulseless: immediate defibrillation
Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
Stable: procainamide, amiodarone, synchronized cardioversion (especially if refractory)

question: A 67-year-old man with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes-related nephropathy presents to the ED via EMS after the sudden onset of left-sided chest pain radiating to his neck and mandible. His pain slightly improved with nitroglycerin prior to arrival but has returned and is worsening. He appears diaphoretic. He has no murmurs on exam, clear breath sounds, and no jugular venous distension. His extremities are warm, and his capillary refill is < 2 seconds. No lower extremity edema is present. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Occlusive myocardial infarction occurs secondary to unstable coronary artery stenosis or coronary artery disease with associated plaque rupture. A posterior myocardial infarction demonstrates ST segment depression in anterior leads (e.g., V1–V2, possibly V3–V4) and sometimes ST segment elevation in aVR. A posterior ECG can aid in the diagnosis. An inferior myocardial infarction, which often occurs in conjunction with a posterior myocardial infarction, demonstrates ST segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the mainstay of treatment. Outside of occlusive myocardial infarction, patients with hemodynamic instability, development of dysrhythmia, a new bifascicular block, or refractory chest pain should be considered for urgent PCI.



An electrolyte disturbance (A) could lead to shortening or prolongation of ECG intervals, ST segment abnormalities, and changes in T waves. Contiguous ST depression consistent with an anatomic territory is unlikely to be related to a systemic pathology such as an electrolyte derangement.

An inherited cation channel mutation (B), such as Brugada syndrome, is expected to manifest with characteristic ECG changes. Leads V1–V3 should demonstrate QRS widening, concave (i.e., type I pattern) or saddleback (i.e., type II pattern) ST segment elevation, and inverted T waves.

ECG changes are typically diffuse and reversible with non-occlusive myocardial ischemia (C). This is typically seen in patients with existing coronary vessel narrowing and superimposed noncardiac systemic pathologies such as increased metabolic demand, hypotension (e.g., dehydration, hemorrhage), anemia, and high-output states.

Viral pericarditis (E) should be suspected in a patient with recent respiratory symptoms and associated pleuritic chest pain, with diffuse rather than isolated PR interval depression and ST segment elevation on ECG.

One Step Further
Question:
What rhythm is a strong indicator of reperfusion following percutaneous coronary intervention?

Reveal Answer:
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)

Patient presents with substernal chest pain that radiates to the neck and arm
Lab tests will show elevated troponin I or troponin T and CK, ST segment elevations > 1 mm in two or more contiguous leads
In anterior leads (V2 and V3), ST segment elevation should be ≥ 1.5 mm in female patients, ≥ 2.0 mm in male patients ≥ 40 years, and ≥ 2.5 mm in male patients < 40 years
Treatment
Percutaneous coronary intervention: gold standard
Thrombolytic therapy
Aspirin
P2Y12 receptor blocker
Beta-blocker
Anticoagulation
Anterior wall ST elevation in leads V1 through V4
Inferior wall ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
Lateral wall ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6
Posterior wall ST depressions in leads V1 through V3 and elevations in leads V8 and V9

question: A 23-year-old man is admitted for a femur fracture. An admission ECG is shown above. What management is indicated?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s ECG shows a first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, a normal variant finding in 2% of the population that requires no specific management. First-degree AV block is defined as prolonged conduction of atrial impulses. The PR interval is > 0.20 seconds (200 msec) and there is no loss of any atrial impulse. All impulses result in a ventricular response. Although it can be a normal variant, it can be seen in pathologic conditions like Lyme disease and should be followed up. However, no specific management is needed. Nodal depressing agents should be avoided or used with caution.



Atropine (A) is required for patients with symptomatic bradycardia.

Beta-blockers (B) are AV nodal blockers and should be used with caution in patients with first-degree AV blocks.

Transvenous pacing (D) is required for higher-degree AV blocks (second-degree type II and third-degree heart block).

One Step Further
Question:
How does carotid massage affect second-degree type I and type II heart blocks?

Reveal Answer:
Carotid massage will typically worsen second-degree type I block and improve second-degree type II block.

Rapid Review
First‐Degree Heart Block

Delayed AV node conduction
Associated with aging, digitalis, ischemia, inflammation, cardiomyopathies
Rhythm will be regular
PR interval will be > 0.20 s (200 msec) and constant

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use presents to the emergency department for evaluation of dark stools. He reports that he has been having frequent dark, tarry stools for the last 24 hours. On arrival, he had a large, dark maroon, liquid stool. He has a history of abdominal aorta surgery but does not recall exactly what surgery he had. Physical exam reveals an ill-appearing, pale person with a well-healed midline surgical scar on the abdomen but no tenderness to palpation. His initial BP is 65/30 mm Hg, HR is 115 bpm, and T is 98.9°F (37.2°C). After a rapid transfusion of one unit of uncross-matched blood, the patient’s BP is 95/55 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfusion of a second unit of uncross-matched blood

englishExplanation:
This patient is experiencing life-threatening GI bleeding due to an aortoenteric fistula (AEF). He needs emergent vascular surgery consultation to repair the underlying cause of his bleeding, which is due to an abnormal connection between his previously repaired aortic aneurysm and the GI tract. AEFs can occur as a rare complication of prior aortic surgery, aortic aneurysms, postinfectious aortitis, trauma, and tumor invasion. This patient’s prior abdominal surgery and midline surgical scar indicate that he has had prior surgical repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). The third and fourth portions of the duodenum are the most common sites of AEFs. An AEF occurs in < 1.5% of patients with a prior endovascular repair or aortoiliac surgery. However, the incidence may be underestimated due to the high mortality rate associated with delayed or undiagnosed bleeds. Patients will often have a mild sentinel hemorrhage followed by massive hemorrhage with rapid exsanguination.

Approximately half of patients will have associated abdominal or back pain. If a patient has an unrepaired AAA, they may have a palpable pulsatile mass at any point in the midline abdomen. The classic triad of GI bleeding, abdominal pain, and a pulsatile abdominal mass occurs in < 15% of patients. To further complicate matters, the absence of bleeding does not exclude the presence of an AEF. Patients with a known AAA (repaired or unrepaired) presenting with massive bleeding and hemodynamic instability should be taken directly to the operating room for definitive diagnosis and repair. Bedside ultrasound may identify the presence of a AAA but will not identify an AEF. In hemodynamically stable patients, CT angiography is the noninvasive imaging modality of choice. Extravasation of contrast into the bowel lumen, ectopic gas adjacent to or within the aorta, focal bowel wall thickening, and discontinuity of the aortic wall are all CT findings that strongly correlate with the presence of an AEF. Additionally, any evidence of perigraft infection on CT should raise concern for the presence of an AEF. The mortality of an unrecognized fistula is 100%, while the mortality of a recognized fistula is 30%.



Abdominal ultrasound (A) is the appropriate imaging modality for surveillance of AAAs, but it is not the appropriate test for a patient with hypotension and GI bleeding due to an AEF. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis is the preferred imaging study in a hemodynamically stable patient in whom the diagnosis of AEF is suspected. GI consultation (B) is typically appropriate in a patient with acute GI bleeding requiring a transfusion of blood products. However, in the case of a suspected AEF, vascular surgery consultation is more appropriate since they will be able to definitively manage the source of the patient’s bleeding. If an endoscopy were to be performed on a patient with a secondary AEF, aortic graft material may be seen protruding into the bowel lumen. The patient will likely require ongoing transfusion of blood products (C), but allowing for permissive hypotension, the patient is more stable with a systolic blood pressure > 80 mm Hg, and the priority at this point should be definitively managing the source of the bleeding. Given the risk for rapid loss of a large volume of blood, the patient may ultimately need a massive transfusion of blood products that should be readily available in the case of worsening hemodynamic status.

One Step Further
Question:
What sexually transmitted infection may be associated with postinfectious aortitis?

Reveal Answer:
Syphilis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aortoenteric Fistula

Abnormal connection between aorta and GI tract
History of AAA, aortic repair, aortic graft replacement
Presents with rectal bleeding
PE: signs of shock, sepsis
Management includes blood transfusion or resuscitation and emergent surgical consultation

question: A 58-year-old man with a left ventricular assist device collapses at home and is brought to the ED by EMS. He is unresponsive and apneic. He is already intubated with confirmed tube placement and receiving mechanical ventilation. There is no palpable pulse, and auscultation reveals no heart sounds. Which of the following, if additionally found in this patient, would immediately indicate device failure and the need for chest compressions?

options.text: Flat pulse oximetry waveform despite adequate ventilation
Mean arterial pressure of 60 mm Hg

englishExplanation:
In a patient with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD), the absence of a palpable pulse and inability to obtain a standard blood pressure can make recognition of cardiac arrest challenging, as most devices provide continuous rather than pulsatile flow. Modern guidance supports initiating compressions in an unresponsive patient with an LVAD and without signs of life when the characteristic “hum” is not heard. However, sometimes resuscitation rooms are loud and clinicians must rely on alternative indicators of perfusion such as mental status, skin perfusion, Doppler mean arterial pressure, and capnography. In an unresponsive, intubated patient with an LVAD, an end-tidal carbon dioxide < 20 mm Hg despite proper ventilation is a strong indicator of inadequate cardiac output, most often due to cardiac arrest or LVAD failure.

Low end-tidal carbon dioxide reflects reduced pulmonary blood flow and, consequently, reduced carbon dioxide delivery to the lungs. This finding should prompt immediate initiation of chest compressions while simultaneously assessing LVAD function, checking power sources and connections, and evaluating for reversible causes such as hypovolemia, pump thrombosis, tamponade, right ventricular failure, and major dysrhythmias. Given the unique physiology of patients with LVADs, resuscitation efforts should be coordinated with advanced heart failure or mechanical circulatory support specialists as soon as possible.



Pulse oximetry depends on pulsatile flow and is frequently unreliable in patients with an LVAD. A flat waveform (B) may reflect the device’s physiology rather than true perfusion failure. While it should prompt further evaluation, it does not reliably discriminate between adequate and inadequate systemic flow. In this patient, end-tidal carbon dioxide measurement is a superior method to evaluate systemic perfusion.

Mean arterial pressure (C) can be misleading in patients with LVADs and requires Doppler or arterial line confirmation. A low Doppler mean arterial pressure can indicate a need for chest compressions, but the threshold for initiating compressions is 50 mm Hg, not 60 mm Hg.

Systolic blood pressure measurement is often unreliable in patients with LVADs because many have continuous-flow devices and minimal pulse pressure. An unobtainable systolic blood pressure (D) is not a reliable marker of arrest in this patient population.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a suction event in patients with a left ventricular assist device?

Reveal Answer:
It occurs when excessive pump speed or low preload causes the left ventricular wall or septum to collapse toward the inflow cannula, reducing flow and potentially triggering low-flow alarms.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD)

Continuous left ventricle flow
Patient has absent pulses
Anticoagulation required
Complications include hemolysis and bleeding, pump thrombosis, embolic events, right heart failure, infection (driveline), technical problems

question: A 55-year-old man presents 2 weeks after a myocardial infarction. He had transient right-sided chest pain without any associated symptoms. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Left ventricular aneurysm occurs when a region of the left ventricle bulges during systole. Aneurysms may develop spontaneously but are more common in areas of the myocardium injured in a previous infarction, most commonly the anterior wall. This area of weakened tissue swells into a bubble-like aneurysm when blood fills the chamber. On ECG, it causes ST elevations that are difficult to distinguish from an acute myocardial infarction. The ST elevation may be either concave up or down and may or may not be associated with Q or QS waves. Additionally, in ventricular aneurysms, reciprocal changes are not present.



Patients with acute stent thrombosis (A) have symptoms consistent with a myocardial infarction. This patient had transient right-sided chest pain that had no associated symptoms. Additionally, acute stent thrombosis will typically cause marked ST elevations with the associated reciprocal changes of an acute injury pattern.

Acute myocardial infarction is sometimes associated with heart block (B) due to ischemia of the atrioventricular (AV) node. However, there is no evidence of heart block in this ECG. The PR interval is < 200 msec, there is no lengthening of the PR with a dropped QRS complex, and there is no AV dissociation.

Pericarditis (C) is another potential cause of ST elevations. However, the findings are most commonly diffuse across the entire ECG and also associated with PR depression. It is possible to develop pericarditis after an acute myocardial infarction. This is called Dressler syndrome.

One Step Further
Question:
In an anterior wall ST elevation myocardial infarction, what decreases the rate of aneurysm development?

Reveal Answer:
Time to revascularization.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Left Ventricular Aneurysm

Persistent ST elevation > 2 weeks following myocardial infarction
Most commonly seen in precordial leads
Q or QS waves
T waves small relative to QRS
Reciprocal changes absent

question: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance for altered mental status. Over the past week, he has been increasingly fatigued with intermittent chills. Today, he woke up and was unsure of where he was for several minutes. He has a history of ischemic cardiomyopathy, for which a left-ventricular-assist device was implanted 3 weeks ago. He has had no other new symptoms since the surgery. His HR is 80 bpm, and MAP is 66 mm Hg based on brachial artery Doppler ultrasound. Peripheral SpO2 cannot be calculated. Physical examination shows a patient in no acute distress with normal rate and work of breathing, 1-second capillary refill, equal strength in all four extremities, an absence of cranial nerve deficits, and a small patch of erythema without expressible discharge at the site of the left ventricular assist device drive line. Which of the following tests is most likely to reveal the etiology of this patient’s symptoms?

options.text: CT scan of the chest and abdomen with contrast
CT scan of the head followed by MRI of the brain
Serum basic metabolic panel, magnesium, and ionized calcium
Serum hemoglobin, haptoglobin, and lactate dehydrogenase

correctAnswer: CT scan of the chest and abdomen with contrast
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with multiple vague symptoms in the setting of a recent left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation. LVADs are complex devices that place patients at risk of multiple direct and indirect complications. Some of the most common complications are infection, cerebrovascular accident, dysrhythmia, valvular disease, cardiogenic shock (due to device failure), and secondary right ventricular failure. This patient’s rapid capillary refill, drive-line erythema, fatigue, and decreased oral intake are all suggestive of an infection. Patients with an LVAD are at the greatest risk of infection in the first 30 days after device implantation. These infections may not present with any of the symptoms, signs, or laboratory findings typically seen in patients with moderate to severe infections. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen with contrast is the best diagnostic modality in these patients and would show inflammatory and infectious changes around the device or driveline. Infection is a common trigger for other LVAD complications such as stroke, thrombosis, and bleeding. A full neurological examination, full-surface skin examination, and diffuse panel of lab tests, including blood gas, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), haptoglobin, INR, B-type natriuretic peptide, troponin, and ECG, should be routinely obtained in these patients, regardless of their reason for presentation. All patients with an LVAD will also have a phone number on the LVAD controller for a device specialist who can provide additional details on the device itself and that particular patient’s LVAD settings. These specialists can provide critical details regarding pump errors and the best next steps if initial steps in treatment do not stabilize the patient.



An arterial blood gas (A) could be useful in this patient due to the inability to obtain a peripheral SpO2. However, it is not likely to reveal an underlying infection in this patient. A CT scan of the head followed by an MRI of the brain (C) would be helpful to reveal a hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke, or another form of intracranial bleeding. However, this patient’s symptoms are more consistent with a surgical site infection. A serum basic metabolic panel, magnesium, and ionized calcium (D) could reveal a significant electrolyte abnormality or metabolic cause of the patient’s symptoms. An infection is more likely in this patient, given his short amount of time since surgery. Serum hemoglobin, haptoglobin, and lactate dehydrogenase (E) would reveal significant hemolysis but is not specific for infection complications.

One Step Further
Question:
What cardiac dynamic change is most likely to lead to low flow, speed, and power on a left ventricular assist device controller?

Reveal Answer:
Significantly low preload.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD)

Continuous left ventricle flow
Patient has absent pulses
Anticoagulation required
Complications include hemolysis and bleeding, pump thrombosis, embolic events, right heart failure, infection (driveline), technical problems

question: A 72-year-old man presents to the ED with a 2-month history of a painless, pulsatile mass in his right groin. He also reports occasional thigh discomfort when walking long distances. On examination, there is a firm, pulsatile swelling in the right femoral triangle with a bruit on auscultation. Distal pulses are palpable. His bedside vascular ultrasound is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Given the thickened wall appearance and eccentric turbulent flow pattern, this ultrasound represents a femoral artery aneurysm with partial thrombus. Peripheral arterial aneurysms rarely rupture but are more often complicated by thrombosis or embolism, which can threaten distal tissues. Their cause varies by location. Lower extremity aneurysms are most often due to atherosclerosis, upper extremity aneurysms usually result from local trauma, and visceral aneurysms are linked to abnormal hemodynamics, atherosclerosis, and infections.

Femoral and popliteal artery aneurysms almost always affect male patients > 65 years with advanced atherosclerosis. About one-fourth present with distal atheroembolism or thromboembolism, while another 15% develop complete occlusion from in situ thrombosis. Popliteal aneurysms are the most common peripheral type, bilateral in 60% of cases, and they are strongly associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm. Symptoms include claudication, thromboembolic or atheroembolic events, gangrene, and sometimes venous compression causing deep vein thrombosis. Femoral aneurysms are the second most common peripheral aneurysms and can also compress the femoral nerve, causing anterior thigh pain and weakness.

Diagnosis is often made by palpating a pulsatile mass, with plain radiographs showing calcifications and ultrasonography or CTA confirming the finding. Asymptomatic cases may undergo elective excision with end-to-end anastomosis or grafting, often alongside repair of coexisting aneurysms. Limb-threatening thromboembolism is treated initially with Fogarty catheter embolectomy before definitive repair.



Arteriovenous fistula (A) produces a continuous thrill and bruit, with Doppler showing high-velocity, low-resistance arterial flow and arterialized venous flow. It does not cause isolated arterial dilation with mural thrombus.

Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm (C) is caused by arterial wall disruption with blood contained by surrounding tissues, often after catheterization or trauma. Ultrasound reveals a sac connected to the artery by a narrow neck with “to-and-fro” Doppler flow, not uniform arterial dilation.

Femoral vein thrombosis (D) presents with swelling, tenderness, and a noncompressible vein on ultrasound. It would not produce a pulsatile mass or a turbulent arterial Doppler signal.

Inguinal hernia (E) presents as a groin bulge that may be reducible, is nonpulsatile, and lacks arterial Doppler flow.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the criteria of Buerger disease?

Reveal Answer:
Distal extremity ischemia in a patient < 50 years old who uses tobacco, with infrapopliteal arterial occlusion, upper limb involvement or migratory superficial thrombophlebitis, and no other atherosclerotic risk factors.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Peripheral and Nonaortic Arterial Aneurysms

Etiology by location
Lower extremity: mostly atherosclerosis
Popliteal (most common)
Femoral: can compress femoral nerve → anterior thigh pain and weakness
Upper extremity: usually local trauma
Visceral: abnormal hemodynamics, atherosclerosis, infections
Signs: palpable pulsatile mass
Dx: U/S, CTA, angiography → confirms diagnosis
Tx
Asymptomatic: observation vs elective excision based on size
Symptomatic or limb-threatening ischemia: consider catheter embolectomy or surgical repair

question: A 9-month-old girl presents to the ED with signs of progressive dyspnea. The patient’s parent reports upper respiratory infection symptoms that have been present for 2 weeks. Over the previous 24 hours, the patient has been increasingly fussy, noted to be sweaty with feeds, and has become increasingly dyspneic. Her vital signs are T 100.9°F (38.3°C), HR 180 bpm, RR 38/min, SpO2 93%, and BP 55/35 mm Hg. On examination, you note rales at the lung bases. Her heart rhythm is irregular with an S3 gallop, and the liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapeutic intervention?
englishExplanation:
This patient has acute myocarditis. Myocarditis is an inflammatory condition typically caused by viral infections or postviral inflammatory processes. A common scenario involves a child who seems to have a prolonged viral illness that worsens and then develops signs of heart failure (diaphoresis with feeds, dyspnea, hepatomegaly, and tachycardia).

The treatment for pediatric heart failure is aimed at improving cardiac inotropy and chronotropy. Epinephrine (norepinephrine could be an alternative) is a first-line vasopressor for pediatric patients with shock, including cardiogenic shock associated with hypotension, as is evident in this patient. However, dobutamine can be added to augment cardiac function.



The other choices presented here would not address this patient’s problem. Intubation (B) can improve oxygenation, but this patient’s primary issue is acute pump failure. Therefore, the most important immediate intervention is to increase cardiac function by using vasopressors such as dobutamine and norepinephrine.

A bolus of normal saline (C), although generally the best first measure to treat hypotension, could worsen this patient’s cardiogenic shock, especially since the patient has evidence of pulmonary edema (rales on exam).

Propranolol (D), a nonselective beta-blocker, is not recommended for acute heart failure. Administration can lead to cardiovascular collapse.

Transcutaneous pacing (E) is generally reserved for patients with complete heart block and bradycardia resulting in inadequate perfusion. There is no role for pacing in this patient at this time.

One Step Further
Question:
What are common viral causes of myocarditis in children in the United States?

Reveal Answer:
Coxsackievirus B and enteroviruses.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Myocarditis

Causes: infectious (e.g., parvovirus B19, coxsackievirus, influenza, adenovirus, coronavirus), autoimmune, toxins, MIS-C
Sx: viral prodrome (fatigue, fever, chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations)
Can present with symptoms of fulminant heart failure
PE: tachycardia disproportionate to fever, hepatomegaly, pulmonary edema, jugular venous distention
Dx: ECG, inflammatory markers, echocardiogram
Echocardiogram will show decreased ventricular ejection fraction with hypokinesis and wall motion abnormalities
Cardiac MRI, endomyocardial biopsy (gold standard)
Tx: diuretics, afterload reduction, inotropes
VADs, ECMO may be required for severe disease

question: A 67-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator presents to the ED after experiencing four shocks at home. He is alert and anxious and reports palpitations between shocks. ECG performed between shocks shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 170 bpm. His BP is 122/78 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?
englishExplanation:
Multiple implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) shocks in a short period, known as ICD storm or electrical storm, often result from recurrent ventricular tachycardia (VT) or ventricular fibrillation. This is a medical emergency due to the high risk of myocardial injury, hemodynamic collapse, and increased mortality if not promptly controlled. In a hemodynamically stable patient with monomorphic VT, the primary goal is to suppress the dysrhythmia and prevent further shocks, as repeated ICD discharges can exacerbate myocardial irritability and trigger additional dysrhythmias.

First-line therapy is IV amiodarone, given as a bolus followed by continuous infusion (150 mg bolus, followed by an infusion of 1 mg/min for 6 hours, then 0.5 mg/min for 18 hours). Amiodarone reduces ventricular ectopy, stabilizes myocardial excitability by blocking multiple ion channels, and decreases ICD discharges. If monomorphic VT persists or recurs, adjunctive beta-blockers (e.g., IV metoprolol, propranolol, or esmolol) are recommended to blunt adrenergic drive, which is often a key trigger during storm episodes.

Additional considerations include correcting electrolyte abnormalities (especially potassium and magnesium), reviewing recent device interrogation to confirm dysrhythmia diagnosis, and ruling out reversible triggers such as myocardial ischemia, heart failure decompensation, hypoxia, or medication toxicity. Sedation may help reduce the sympathetic surge in patients experiencing repeated shocks. If dysrhythmia remains refractory, advanced interventions like catheter ablation or stellate ganglion blockade can be considered in consultation with cardiology and electrophysiology.



Magnesium sulfate (B) is indicated for torsades de pointes or polymorphic VT, not for stable monomorphic VT. Using it here would not address the underlying dysrhythmia effectively.

A magnet (C) can temporarily suspend ICD shocks, useful for inappropriate shocks due to oversensing or lead malfunction. In this case, shocks are appropriate for true VT found on the ECG, and disabling therapy would leave the patient unprotected from degeneration into ventricular fibrillation.

Unsynchronized cardioversion (D) is reserved for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation, when synchronization is impossible. This patient is hemodynamically stable, perfusing, and in organized monomorphic VT, so unsynchronized shocks are not indicated.

One Step Further
Question:
Which pad position is used in the defibrillation of a patient with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD)?

Reveal Answer:
Place defibrillation pads in an anteroposterior position or ≥ 8 cm away from the ICD generator, avoiding placement directly over the device.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ventricular Tachycardia

More than three consecutive ectopic ventricular beats
Monomorphic, polymorphic
Wide complexes
Bidirectional: digoxin toxicity
Brugada criteria can help differentiate ventricular tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy
If unsure about the rhythm, manage all wide complex tachycardias as ventricular tachycardia
Tx
Pulseless: immediate defibrillation
Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
Stable: procainamide, amiodarone, synchronized cardioversion (especially if refractory)

question: A 46-year-old woman with a history of untreated hypertension, migraines, and hyperlipidemia presents for evaluation of a right frontotemporal headache with associated right neck pain that began 2 days ago. She does not recall trauma to the head or neck. She has no history of easy bleeding or venous thromboembolism. Her neurologic exam is significant for ptosis and miosis on the right side but is otherwise unremarkable. Magnetic resonance imaging with angiography of the head and neck is performed expeditiously and is shown above. Lab tests show a hemoglobin of 14.5 g/dL, platelet count of 380,000/µL, prothrombin time of 12 sec, and activated partial thromboplastin time of 28 sec. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Carotid artery dissection is an important cause of stroke in up to 20% of young and middle-aged adults. Neck manipulation (e.g., chiropractic adjustments) and direct trauma are common causes. Other risk factors for spontaneous carotid artery dissection include hypertension, previous large-vessel arteriopathies, connective tissue disease, and a migraine history. Patients often have a headache, neck pain, and neurologic deficits (e.g., Horner syndrome with miosis and ptosis, focal weakness, or focal sensory abnormalities). Cranial nerve palsies may be present in up to 12% of cases. The diagnosis is made by CT with angiography of the head and neck or MRI with magnetic resonance angiography, depending on availability. Management involves intravenous thrombolysis for patients within the appropriate time window, which may range from 3–4.5 hours, depending on the institution and the presenting symptoms. Endovascular therapy should also be considered. Patients who are not candidates for thrombolytics should be started on anticoagulation (heparin) or antiplatelet therapy.



Consultation for thrombectomy (A) should be considered in patients presenting with acute stroke-like symptoms thought to be secondary to complete proximal internal carotid artery or middle cerebral artery occlusion, as well as other indications (e.g., within 6 hours of symptom onset, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] ≤ 6, modified Rankin scale < 2). Intravenous ketorolac, prochlorperazine, and diphenhydramine (C) are appropriate for the treatment of migraines. Migraines may be preceded by an aura, followed by moderate to severe, pulsating, unilateral pain, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The presence of red flag signs and symptoms, such as neck pain, neurologic deficits, fever, abrupt onset, older age, or a history of malignancy or immunosuppression, should prompt further evaluation before the diagnosis of migraine is made. Intravenous thrombolytics (D) are indicated in several scenarios, such as acute ischemic stroke, high-risk pulmonary embolism, and myocardial infarction, in which delayed percutaneous coronary intervention is anticipated. This patient may appear to have stroke-like symptoms, but she is outside the treatment window for thrombolytics and her symptoms are minor. Oral warfarin therapy (E) for anticoagulation may be considered in the plan for the long-term management of carotid artery dissection. Given its prolonged onset of action of 5–6 days, a faster acting anticoagulant (e.g., heparin) is indicated in the acute phase of treatment.

One Step Further
Question:
What anatomic head and neck features in children predispose them to traumatic cervical spine injuries related to anterior-posterior vertebral movement?

Reveal Answer:
Larger head to body ratio, anatomic fulcrum at C2-C3, ligamentous laxity, and shallow facets.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Carotid Artery Dissection

Most common cause of stroke in patients < 45 years
Etiologies: connective tissue disorders, neck trauma
Presentation: abrupt unilateral neck pain or headache around the eye and frontal area, partial ipsilateral Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis)
Dx: CT with CTA, MRI with MRA
Tx
Anticoagulation or antiplatelet medication if no evidence of acute ischemic stroke
Thrombolytic therapy (if no contraindications) if evidence of acute ischemic stroke

question: A 78 year-old-woman with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of shortness of breath. Four days earlier, she reported an episode of heartburn and nausea. On physical examination, she is tachycardic and hypotensive. She has inspiratory rales and a holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex with radiation to the left axilla. Her ECG reveals Q waves in II, III, and aVF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Papillary muscle rupture is one of three catastrophic complications of acute myocardial infarction along with left ventricular wall rupture and interventricular septum rupture. It tends to occur several days following myocardial infarction. Papillary muscle rupture results in acute mitral regurgitation, pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. Mitral regurgitation is recognized on physical exam by a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex with radiation to the left axilla. The only blood supply of the posteromedial papillary muscle comes from the posterior descending artery. Occlusion of this artery results in an inferior myocardial infarction (MI) pattern on ECG. This patient had symptoms of an MI 4 days ago and now has Q waves on ECG which are consistent with old inferior wall MI. Emergent surgical intervention is often necessary, with mitral valve repair or valve replacement along with percutaneous revascularization.



Aortic stenosis (A)presents on physical exam with a systolic ejection murmur heard best at the right second intercostal space with radiation to the carotids. Undiagnosed aortic stenosis is often discovered following a syncopal episode.

Cardiac tamponade (B)may present on physical exam as decreased or “muffled” heart sounds, jugular venous distension and hypotension. Low QRS voltage, tachycardia or electrical alternans may be seen on ECG.

Mitral valve prolapse (C) is often asymptomatic and is associated with a mid-systolic click heard best at the apex.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Beck triad?

Reveal Answer:
Muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension, and hypotension.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mitral Regurgitation

History
Acute: ischemic heart disease, endocarditis, MI, trauma
Chronic: rheumatic heart disease, degenerative mitral valve disease
Presentation
Acute Sx: dyspnea, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic edema
Chronic Sx: asymptomatic until CHF onset, S3
PE
Acute: unique, harsh, midsystolic murmur best heard at apex that radiates to the base or axilla
Chronic: blowing holosystolic murmur best heard at apex with radiation to axilla
Dx
Echocardiogram
Tx
Acute: nitroprusside, dobutamine, intra-aortic balloon pump, emergency surgery
Chronic: CHF Rx, valve repair or replacement

question: A 2-year-old boy presents to the emergency department in respiratory arrest. His heart rate is 80 bpm, but he is unresponsive and limp. He has pinpoint pupils but does not respond to naloxone administration. The first attempt at endotracheal intubation is successful. What respiratory rate is most appropriate for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Many children with a toxic ingestion of narcotics will not present with a history of swallowing the medication. So long as hypoxia is avoided by providing respiratory support, many of these children can have good outcomes. Unfortunately, due to the nature of the ingestion, these children often experience severe hypoxia or death before being brought to medical attention. When an advanced airway is necessary and in place, the appropriate respiratory rate should be relatively close to the patient’s normal respiratory rate to provide adequate oxygenation and ventilation. A respiratory rate of 30–60 breaths/min is best for children < 6 months, 24–30 breaths/min for children 6 months to 1 year, 20–30 breaths/min for 1–5 years, and 12–20 breaths/min for > 5 years old. Overventilation is common even with an advanced airway when breathing is manually supported with a bag due to the stressful nature of the situation.

Some texts still support the use of 12–20 breaths/min when there is isolated respiratory arrest, like this patient. The more recent 2025 American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines recommend closer to 20–30 breaths/min. This is the same rate they recommend for children receiving chest compressions with an advanced airway. Take care to provide just enough support to see appropriate chest rise and to support adequate oxygenation and ventilation.



Older AHA recommendations emphasized the use of 12–20 breaths/min (A) for children needing cardiopulmonary resuscitation who had an advanced airway. More recent evidence supports faster rates even in the setting of chest compressions.

Newly born infants with an advanced airway should be given 40 breaths/min (C) to 60 breaths/min (D) due to their naturally higher baseline respiratory rates.

One Step Further
Question:
Which medication is sometimes mixed with nonmedically used narcotics, with overdose cases presenting as opiate ingestion unresponsive to naloxone?

Reveal Answer:
Xylazine.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pediatric Advanced Life Support: Pulseless Arrest

CPR + bag-mask ventilation
Chest compressions
15:2 (prepuberty) and 30:2 (postpuberty) if no advanced airway
100–120/min
At least one-third chest wall depth
Use thumb-encircling hands technique
Advanced airway: continuous chest compressions, breath every 2–3 seconds
Shockable rhythm: 2 J/kg, 4 J/kg, epinephrine every 3–5 minutes, amiodarone, lidocaine
Nonshockable rhythm: CPR and epinephrine ASAP, then every 3–5 minutes

question: Which of the following diagnoses is most strongly suggested by this ECG?
englishExplanation:
T wave inversions on ECG are a notable, though nonspecific, finding in patients in whom there is concern for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, given the significant variability in normal T wave patterns for each patient, coupled with the fairly broad differential diagnosis for new T wave abnormalities, accurate interpretation of T wave inversions can prove difficult. In patients presenting with chest pain or other anginal equivalents in whom ACS is a concern, proper interpretation of which T wave inversions are more likely to be coronary in origin versus those that are likely not aids in risk stratification of patients both in the ED and for disposition.

This ECG shows deep T wave inversions in multiple precordial leads (V3–V6), which is also referred to as Wellens pattern or coronary T waves due to the high likelihood that they are coronary in origin. This particular T wave morphology and distribution is usually associated with high-grade stenosis of the left anterior descending artery and carries a high risk of recurrent anginal symptoms and myocardial infarction. While this pattern is a classic example of ischemic T wave changes, other more subtle findings exist as well. For instance, T wave inversions in any two contiguous leads (i.e., I and aVL) in the context of anginal symptoms should prompt suspicion of ischemic heart disease. Additionally, pseudonormalization of T waves can occur in patients with T wave inversions at baseline that paradoxically become upright in the setting of acute transmural ischemia.

The disposition for patients with an ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is fairly straightforward, given the need for expeditious reperfusion therapy. T wave inversions are much less specific and do not carry an indication for immediate reperfusion. Thus, disposition from the ED in cases of normal cardiac enzymes is more nuanced. The HEART score is a clinical decision-making tool that is often applied to these patients and takes into account features from the ECG, clinical history, and troponin levels to determine the risk of a major adverse cardiac event resulting in their presentation.



Acute pericarditis (B) classically causes diffuse ST elevation and PR depression rather than localized T wave inversions seen here.

The most common ECG abnormality of pulmonary embolism (C) is sinus tachycardia, while the S1Q3T3 pattern has also been described. The T wave inversions seen here are not typically caused by pulmonary embolism.

Signs of pulmonary hypertension (D) on ECG include right axis deviation, right bundle branch block, and P wave amplitude > 2 mm in lead II.

One Step Further
Question:
What ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST depression in at least two leads of V2–V6 with tall, symmetric T waves?

Reveal Answer:
De Winter sign. This may represent left anterior descending artery occlusion or other coronary artery occlusions.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wellens Syndrome

Highly specific for critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery
ECG: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–3
May be pain-free
Normal or minimally elevated troponin
Tx: urgent percutaneous coronary intervention

question: A 70-year-old man with a medical history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents with left leg pain that started acutely 2 hours prior to arrival with no preceding trauma. His vital signs are unremarkable. On physical exam, the left lower extremity is cool to the touch, and there are no palpable posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis pulses. Strength and sensory exams are intact, and there is no swelling or focal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient, who presents with acute onset of extremity pain, absent pulses, and a history of atrial fibrillation, most likely has an acute arterial occlusion due to an embolic event. Acute arterial occlusion results in an abrupt decrease in blood flow to an extremity and may result in acute limb ischemia and tissue loss. The most common cause is thrombosis at the site of an atherosclerotic plaque followed by embolic occlusion. Most emboli originate from the heart, with atrial fibrillation being the most common risk factor. Other etiologies include arterial dissection (spontaneous, iatrogenic, or traumatic), thrombosis of a peripheral arterial aneurysm, and vasospasm. Patient presentation varies based on the etiology and the presence of underlying peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Patients with preexisting PAD often have collateral circulation, allowing for residual perfusion to the extremity despite thrombotic occlusion. Symptoms may progress over hours to days and often include new or worsening claudication. Pain at rest in a patient with prior exertional symptoms is concerning for irreversible ischemia. Patients with an embolic etiology, especially if there is no preexisting vascular disease, present more dramatically with acute onset of severe pain and rapidly progressing symptoms. The signs and symptoms of acute limb ischemia can be remembered by the six Ps mnemonic: pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paresthesias, and paralysis. Pain is usually the first symptom, whereas sensory and motor changes are late findings indicative of limb-threatening ischemia. Patients with a thrombotic cause often have signs of PAD, including decreased or absent pulses on the contralateral limb, hair loss, and shiny skin. The lack of these findings suggests an embolic occlusion.

Acute arterial occlusion is a limb-threatening surgical emergency. All patients should be started on heparin, and vascular surgery should be consulted. Patients with limb-threatening ischemia (sensory or motor changes), regardless of the etiology, and all patients with suspected embolisms require emergent revascularization. Diagnostic imaging should not delay definitive management. The vascular surgeon will determine treatment, which may include catheter or open embolectomy, catheter-directed thrombolysis, angioplasty or stenting, and bypass grafting. If the diagnosis or etiology (thrombotic versus embolic) is unclear and there are no findings of limb-threatening ischemia, arterial ultrasound, CT angiography, or conventional angiography can help further evaluate the arterial anatomy prior to intervention. Thrombotic occlusion that is not acutely limb-threatening is often managed medically.



Compartment syndrome (B) can result in limb ischemia, as elevated compartment pressures cause decreased arterial flow. Patients with acute arterial occlusion can also develop compartment syndrome due to muscle breakdown and reperfusion injury. However, patients with primary compartment syndrome usually have significant extremity swelling and pain with muscle palpation and passive stretch. Deep vein thrombosis (C) rarely causes limb ischemia except in cases of extensive disease when venous pressures are high enough to cause decreased arterial perfusion, a syndrome known as phlegmasia cerulea dolens. Patients with phlegmasia cerulea dolens have marked asymmetric edema and mottling due to venous congestion, which is not present in this patient. Peripheral neuropathy (D) can cause extremity pain and mimic findings of chronic limb ischemia. However, it is less likely to start acutely, and unless there is underlying PAD, it should not present with pulselessness.

One Step Further
Question:
What does an ankle-brachial index > 1.4 indicate?

Reveal Answer:
Vascular calcification.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Wellens Syndrome

Highly specific for critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery
ECG: deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–3
May be pain-free
Normal or minimally elevated troponin
Tx: urgent percutaneous coronary intervention

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the ED with an expansive mood, increased energy, and aggression. His blood pressure is 177/118 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 bpm, and respiratory rate is 24/min. Physical exam shows hyperhidrosis and mydriasis. The patient is calmer after administration of benzodiazepines, but his blood pressure remains significantly elevated. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient’s hypertension?
englishExplanation:
Cocaine is a sympathomimetic that leads to symptoms of increased energy, aggression, tachycardia, hypertension, tremulousness, hyperhidrosis, and mydriasis. Typically, the management of cocaine intoxication involves observation, supportive therapy, and sedation, which can include the administration of benzodiazepines.

In patients presenting with hypertension, management can include blood pressure control, which typically requires administration of an alpha-blocker rather than a beta-blocker, secondary to the theoretical concern of precipitating a hypertensive crisis with the administration of a beta-blocker. Alpha-blocking medications include drugs such as phentolamine, which can be used as initial treatment of hypertension in these patients.



Hydralazine (A) can be used to treat hypertension, but it also carries the risk of causing a reflex tachycardia, which can be detrimental in those with cocaine intoxication. Hydralazine works as a direct-acting vasodilator that preferentially relaxes the smooth muscles of arteries, which can lead to a precipitous drop in blood pressure and tachycardia. Thus, it is not a preferred agent in this situation. Furthermore, hydralazine has a delayed and unpredictable blood pressure-lowering effect, and it can be difficult to titrate.

Nitroprusside (B) is a potent medication (also acting via nitric oxide) for lowering blood pressure. However, it carries a risk of causing a significant reflex tachycardia. It is typically administered after administration of a beta-blocker for this reason (though not in cocaine intoxication for the aforementioned reason).

Sodium bicarbonate (D) does not have any effect on blood pressure but is recommended in patients with QRS prolongation associated with cocaine intoxication.

One Step Further
Question:
What toxicity is associated with high doses of nitroprusside?

Reveal Answer:
Cyanide toxicity.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Sympathomimetic Toxidrome

Cocaine, amphetamines, stimulants: may be mixed with other agents
PE: hypertension, tachypnea, tachycardia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, altered mental status, increased bowel sounds (anticholinergic toxicity is decreased bowel sounds)
Supportive care, benzodiazepines
Consider phentolamine for uncontrolled hypertension

question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presents to the ED reporting fever, fatigue, and dyspnea for the past 3 days. She also notes intermittent palpitations and a recent unexplained weight loss. In the ED, vital signs are a BP of 126/82 mm Hg, HR of 90 bpm, RR of 16/min, SpO2 of 99% on room air, and T of 101.6°F (38.7°C). On exam, a murmur is noted. Transesophageal echocardiography is ordered. Which of the following valvular anomalies is most likely?
englishExplanation:
This patient most likely has bacterial endocarditis. Endocarditis is more common in patients with valvular abnormalities, individuals with prosthetic valves, and people who use intravenous drugs. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus and viridans group streptococci. Of note, viridans streptococci endocarditis commonly presents after dental work. Endocarditis presents most commonly with fever and malaise, but other signs and symptoms may be present. Although the classic triad is fever, anemia, and a heart murmur, this rarely presents clinically. People who use intravenous drugs usually have right-sided endocarditis, most commonly affecting the tricuspid valve. The murmur noted on the exam is usually tricuspid regurgitation.

Lab tests should be ordered for individuals with suspected endocarditis, as leukocytosis, anemia, an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and an increased C-reactive protein would be expected. Three blood cultures from three separate venipuncture sites should be taken, with the first and last draw occurring at least 1 hour apart. The most useful diagnostic imaging is an echocardiogram, especially a transesophageal echocardiogram, demonstrating vegetations. The Duke criteria are the most widely used and accepted criteria to clinically diagnose bacterial endocarditis. Empiric antibiotics should be initiated in patients with suspected or confirmed endocarditis once cultures have been drawn, with antibiotics being altered as needed once the pathogen and susceptibility return.



Left-side valves (aortic, mitral) are most commonly involved in endocarditis outside of people who use intravenous drugs and those with prosthetic valves. The mitral valve is the most commonly affected valve in infective endocarditis (causing mitral regurgitation), but the aortic valve may also be affected. Aortic regurgitation (A) can be acute or chronic and may result from conditions like rheumatic heart disease, congenital valve defects, or aortic dissection. Most patients are asymptomatic from chronic mitral regurgitation until middle age, at which point signs and symptoms of left heart failure become evident. Acute aortic regurgitation can present with severe dyspnea, pulmonary edema, and acute heart failure.

Mitral stenosis (B) is typically caused by rheumatic fever, a complication of untreated streptococcal pharyngitis or scarlet fever, which leads to inflammation and scarring of the valve. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, palpitations, and swelling in the ankles and legs. Over time, mitral stenosis can lead to complications such as atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, and heart failure. It is rare for infective endocarditis to cause mitral stenosis, but it may worsen existing stenosis.

Pulmonic regurgitation (C) is present only rarely in infective endocarditis, as only about 10% of cases of right-sided native valve endocarditis involve the pulmonic valve. Pulmonic regurgitation is often mild and asymptomatic, commonly resulting from pulmonary hypertension or congenital heart defects. In more severe cases, symptoms might include fatigue, shortness of breath, heart palpitations, and swelling in the abdomen or legs.

Tricuspid stenosis (E) is rarely caused by infective endocarditis. It is often caused by rheumatic fever, but carcinoid syndrome and prosthetic valve degeneration are the most common causes in the United States. Symptoms may include fatigue, abdominal swelling, and generalized swelling due to fluid retention. Rheumatic tricuspid stenosis almost never occurs alone, and it is often associated with tricuspid regurgitation and mitral valve disease. It may also be associated with aortic valve disease.

question: A 39-year-old man presents to the ED, reporting general weakness. He has signs of an upper respiratory infection on exam. His rhythm strip is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer 325 mg aspirin and check a troponin

englishExplanation:
The ECG shows first-degree atrioventricular (AV) heart block. This is due to prolonged conduction of atrial impulses without the loss of any single impulse. On the ECG, the PR interval will be > 200 msec. This type of block is often a normal variant without clinical significance, occurring in close to 2% of healthy young adults, and it does not require specific treatment. Although the block is benign, in some patients, it may be associated with beta-adrenergic blocker therapy, endocarditis, myocarditis, inferior wall myocardial infarction, hyperkalemia, and hypothermia. Treatment for the patient in this case is supportive, and he can be sent home.



Aspirin (A) is administered to patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome and is not necessary for this patient.

First-degree heart block does not progress to more advanced conduction blocks that would require the application of a transcutaneous pacemaker (B).

Since this block is benign, cardiology (C) does not need to be consulted.

In the context of a first-degree AV block with associated symptoms and signs of an upper respiratory infection, symptomatic care and evaluation of his acute symptoms are prioritized before considering long-term monitoring strategies like Holter monitoring (D).

question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fatigue, weakness, and severe shortness of breath. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, and congestive heart failure. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 225/130 mm Hg, HR is 99 bpm, RR is 35/min, and SpO2 is 80% on room air. Physical exam reveals bilateral pulmonary crackles. A chest radiograph is performed as above. Which of the following combinations represents the most appropriate management of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Nitroglycerin, furosemide, and positive pressure ventilation

correctAnswer: Nitroglycerin, furosemide, and positive pressure ventilation
englishExplanation:
A hypertensive emergency is defined as hypertension causing end-organ dysfunction. Isolated severe hypertension does not define a hypertensive emergency. Kidney dysfunction, blurry vision, myocardial infarction, encephalopathy, stroke, and pulmonary edema are all possible end-organ manifestations of a hypertensive emergency.

When a hypertensive emergency causes pulmonary edema (as suggested by this patient’s presentation and chest X-ray), management is first centered on stabilizing the patient’s respiratory status and ruling out a myocardial infarction. Further management of pulmonary edema should include early administration of diuretics (e.g., furosemide), a nitroglycerin drip to reduce preload and afterload, and positive pressure ventilation. Generally, blood pressure should not be reduced by more than 20% acutely. Patients whose status does not improve with positive pressure ventilation should be intubated. Patients with a hypertensive emergency should be admitted to the intensive care unit for a higher level of care.



Blood cultures, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin (A) comprise the appropriate management for patients with community-acquired pneumonia, which can lead to sepsis. Early antibiotic administration reduces mortality in sepsis. Community-acquired pneumonia may present with hypoxia but more commonly with a lobar consolidation on chest X-ray.

The combination of intubation, nicardipine, and torsemide (B) is not the best initial care plan for this patient. Intubation can be avoided by providing aggressive early treatment with positive pressure ventilation and nitroglycerin. While nicardipine will address elevated blood pressure, the preload reduction of nitroglycerin makes it a preferred agent.

Morphine, aspirin, nitroglycerin, and furosemide (C) would not be an appropriate treatment regimen for this patient. Morphine is no longer used in acute pulmonary edema, as it may be associated with higher mortality. Aspirin is reasonable if acute coronary syndrome is suspected as a possible underlying cause. Nitroglycerin and furosemide are appropriate treatment options, but this patient will also benefit from positive pressure ventilation to prevent the need for mechanical ventilation.

Reveal Answer:

A 54-year-old woman presents to the ED with progressive shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance over the past several months. She reports occasional episodes of palpitations but reports no chest pain or syncope. Her medical history is unremarkable, and she takes no daily medications. Vital signs show a BP of 142/80 mm Hg, HR of 100 bpm, RR of 18/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. Physical exam reveals small crackles on lung exam and bilateral lower extremity edema. Her heart sound is presented above. Which of the following dysrhythmias is most likely responsible for this patient’s episodes of palpitations?
englishExplanation:
This patient most likely has mitral stenosis (MS), which leads to left atrial enlargement and predisposes patients to atrial fibrillation (AF). AF worsens symptoms by eliminating atrial contraction (atrial kick) and creating rapid, irregular ventricular rates. This further impairs left ventricular filling and raises left atrial pressures, causing pulmonary congestion and dyspnea. A patient with classic AF symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnea, and fatigue may arrive in the ED after spontaneously converting back to sinus rhythm. This can make diagnosis challenging unless the dysrhythmia is captured on telemetry, an event monitor, or during the ED stay.

The most common cause of MS worldwide is rheumatic heart disease, a late consequence of acute rheumatic fever and valvulitis, while in resource-rich countries, the leading etiology is degenerative mitral annular calcification in patients > 65 years old. Rarely, it may be congenital. Stenosis becomes clinically significant when the valve area falls to < 1.5 cm2, producing impaired left atrial emptying, decreased cardiac output, and elevated left atrial pressures that drive pulmonary congestion. With progression, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right-sided heart failure develop.

Symptoms usually begin with exertional dyspnea and reduced exercise tolerance, and progress to orthopnea and edema. Classic but less common findings include hemoptysis from bronchial vein rupture and hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression. Examination often reveals a loud S1, an opening snap, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. A chest X-ray may show pulmonary congestion or left atrial enlargement. ECG often demonstrates AF, and echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and severity. Emergency care focuses on treating triggers, initiating diuresis for congestion, and starting medications for heart rate control if AF is present. Definitive therapy for severe symptomatic disease includes percutaneous balloon valvotomy when anatomy is suitable or surgical valve replacement, depending on comorbidities and valve characteristics.



Junctional tachycardia (B) originates from automaticity in the atrioventricular (AV) junction and is most often seen in the setting of digitalis toxicity, post-cardiac surgery, or myocardial ischemia. It is not typically associated with structural valvular disease such as MS.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (C) is classically seen in patients with COPD and manifests with at least three distinct P wave morphologies. It is not associated with MS.

Supraventricular tachycardia (D) refers to a group of paroxysmal tachycardias involving reentrant circuits, most commonly AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. These are usually seen in younger patients without structural heart disease and present with abrupt-onset palpitations. The progressive exertional dyspnea, lower extremity edema, and murmur in this patient indicate underlying valvular disease.

Ventricular tachycardia (E) is typically associated with ischemic cardiomyopathy, structural heart disease from prior myocardial infarction, or electrolyte disturbances. It presents with wide complex tachycardia on ECG and often causes syncope, chest pain, or hemodynamic instability, none of which are found in this patient. Furthermore, this patient has no history of coronary artery disease or prior infarction.

Reveal Answer:
Bioprosthetic valves generally avoid the need for long-term anticoagulation, making them preferred in patients planning pregnancy despite their shorter durability (typically 10–15 years).

question: A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department unresponsive. He was brought to the hospital by private vehicle and slumped to the ground while walking into the waiting room. Emergency department staff have wheeled him into the resuscitation bay. The patient is unresponsive and pulseless, so you initiate CPR. No other history is obtainable now, as the family is still in the car. The patient is receiving oxygen via a bag-valve mask. When CPR is stopped briefly for a pulse check, you notice the above rhythm on the monitor. What is the most likely diagnosis for this presenting rhythm?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting in cardiac arrest with ventricular tachycardia. Both inside and outside the hospital, sudden cardiac arrest in an adult is attributable to primary cardiac disease in the majority of cases. Among the cardiac causes of arrest, acute coronary syndromes are the most common. Cardiac arrest due to acute coronary syndromes is most commonly present in those with ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation due to the direct ischemic effects on the myocardium. Management of cardiac arrest begins with assessing the airway, breathing, and circulation of the patient and initiating CPR. In this patient presenting with cardiac arrest due to ventricular tachycardia, along with CPR, defibrillation is indicated. Although different drugs are still indicated according to advanced cardiac life support guidelines for cardiac arrest, more emphasis should be placed on high-quality CPR and defibrillation. There is little evidence that pharmacological interventions impact long-term survival in patients with cardiac arrest.



Among noncardiac causes of arrest, hypoxia (B) is the most common. Other frequent causes include pulmonary embolism (C), tension pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, severe sepsis (D), and hypovolemia. Pulseless electrical activity is the most common presenting rhythm for patients with noncardiac causes of arrest. Asystole is the end rhythm for all causes of cardiac arrest, regardless of etiology. This patient is presenting with ventricular tachycardia and is most likely to have a cardiac rather than a noncardiac cause for arrest.

What is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in pediatric patients?

Reveal Answer:
Hypoxia.
