question: A 16-year old boy presents to the emergency department after passing out. He collapsed without warning while sitting in class at school. A friend prevented him from hitting his head. There were no shaking movements or postictal period to suggest a seizure. He has had no ill symptoms but did feel palpitations and chest pain prior to his collapse. He reports plenty of intake during the day and has normal orthostatic vital signs. His father died unexpectedly in his sleep. His ECG is above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activity restrictions and outpatient cardiology follow-up
Outpatient Holter monitor placed in the ED

englishExplanation:
Brugada syndrome is usually caused by an autosomal dominant cardiac sodium channel disorder that can cause spontaneous ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in otherwise well patients. It is more common in men and usually diagnosed in adulthood. Dysrhythmias from Brugada syndrome generally occur at night and these patients commonly have a pattern of nocturnal agonal respiration thought to be aborted cardiac dysrhythmias.

Cardiac dysrhythmia in patients with Brugada syndrome can be triggered by a fever, cocaine abuse, or overdose of a neuroleptic. Brugada syndrome is uncommonly diagnosed in children and many of these patients have a history of unexplained syncope.

A normal ECG does not rule out Brugada syndrome since the ECG findings can be transient. Stress testing, echocardiogram, and even cardiac MRI often reveal no abnormalities. When discovered, a Brugada ECG pattern appears as a pseudo-right bundle branch block with an ST segment elevation that descends with upward convexity into an inverted T wave (i.e., “coved type”) or ST segment elevation that begins to descend toward the baseline before rising again to an upright T-wave (i.e., “saddleback”). Symptomatic patients (e.g., syncope) with a Brugada pattern on their ECG are suspected to have a recent life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmia. As such they should be admitted to the hospital on continuous cardiac telemetry for consultation and workup by a cardiac electrophysiologist.



Activity restrictions and outpatient cardiology follow-up (A) is generally recommended for patients with syncope during exercise that have a normal ECG while in the emergency department.

An outpatient Holter monitor placed in the ED (C) is most appropriate for patients with frequent palpitations, syncope, near syncope, or dizziness, not those with suspected life-threatening dysrhythmia.

Reassurance and discharge (D) is most appropriate in patients with vasovagal syncope and a normal ECG, not for patients with Brugada syndrome.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 64-year-old woman presents to the ED with chest pain and dyspnea. The patient has a medical history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, and a recent diagnosis of breast cancer. She states her symptoms started abruptly 2 hours prior to arrival. She describes the chest pain as sharp, and her symptoms are worsened with deep inspiration. Vital signs are remarkable for HR 120 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 110/85 mm Hg, and SpO2 92%. Physical examination is unremarkable other than conversational dyspnea. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with T wave inversions in leads V2–V4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when material, which is most commonly a thrombus, causes obstruction of the pulmonary trunk or one of its branches. A PE is classified into one of three categories. A massive PE, also called a hemodynamically unstable PE, results in a systolic blood pressure of < 90 mm Hg or a drop of ≥ 40 mm Hg in baseline systolic BP. Hemodynamically stable PEs are classified as submassive or low-risk. A submassive PE is defined as a PE that does not result in hypotension (or hypotension, if present, is fluid responsive) but does have right ventricular dysfunction, right ventricular dilation, elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (> 500 pg/mL), elevated troponin I (> 0.4 ng/mL), elevated troponin T (> 0.1 ng/mL), or new ECG changes (right bundle branch block, anteroseptal ST elevation or depression or anterolateral T wave inversion). A low-risk PE has no features of right heart strain and also does not have hemodynamic compromise. Risk factors for PE include coagulopathies (inherited or acquired), active cancer, recent surgery, hormonal therapies (estrogen), trauma, immobilization, and heavy cigarette smoking.

Clinical features for PE range from being asymptomatic to shock or sudden death. Most commonly, patients present with dyspnea, chest pain that can be pleuritic, cough, and features concerning for deep venous thrombosis. Hemoptysis is uncommon as is shock, dysrhythmia, or syncope. The recommended diagnostic approach for hemodynamically stable patients suspected of having a PE is to combine clinical and pretest probability assessment, D-dimer values (if appropriate), and diagnostic testing. An ECG should also be performed as part of the workup. There are no specific findings on ECG that suggest PE. However, signs of right heart strain may be present and suggest a submassive or massive PE. The classic S1Q3T3 is an ECG finding that may be present in a PE causing right heart strain. However, this pattern may be present in other causes of right heart strain such as severe pulmonary hypertension. Other ECG findings that have been shown to be more likely in patients with PE are both sinus tachycardia and T wave inversions in leads V2–V4. The pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria, or PERC, and the Wells criteria help stratify patients who are thought to be at risk for PE. Patients who are found to be low-risk and PERC-negative require no additional workup for PE. Patients who are PERC-positive but low-risk should be evaluated with the use of a D-dimer. Currently, if the D-dimer is < 500 ng/mL or less than the age-adjusted value (10 x age), then the patient requires no additional evaluation. However, if the D-dimer is greater than the thresholds noted above or the patient is moderate- or high-risk, then further evaluation with a CT angiogram of the chest or a ventilation-perfusion scan should be obtained. Patients found to be too unstable or unsafe to have advanced imaging performed should have a bedside echocardiogram and venous compression of the lower extremities to obtain a presumptive diagnosis. Treatment for PE starts with categorizing the patient into one of the three categories listed above. Patients found to be hemodynamically stable without contraindications to anticoagulation should be treated with anticoagulants as soon as possible.

Outpatient follow-up is imperative as these patients will require anticoagulation for typically 3 months but 6–12 months in specific cases. Currently, fibrinolytic therapy for submassive PE is not warranted on a routine basis but can be given on a case-by-case basis when the benefit outweighs the risk. The following situations for submassive PE may warrant the administration of fibrinolytic therapy: severe or worsening right ventricular strain, cardiopulmonary arrest due to PE with a BP > 90 mm Hg after resuscitation, extensive clot burden, or free-floating right atrial thrombus or ventricular thrombus. For patients found to be hemodynamically unstable and without contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy, the recommendation is to administer fibrinolytic therapy and then subsequently start anticoagulation. If thrombolysis is contraindicated or unsuccessful, embolectomy is an alternative therapy.



Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (A) is on the continuum of acute coronary syndromes and resides between stable angina and ST elevation myocardial infarction. Unstable angina occurs when a patient starts experiencing angina at rest, which is usually > 20 minutes in duration, new onset of angina that markedly limits physical activity, or increasing angina that is more frequent, longer in duration, or occurs with less exertion than previous angina. Unstable angina and acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) differ primarily in whether the ischemia is severe enough to cause sufficient myocardial damage to release detectable quantities of a marker of myocardial injury measured with cardiac troponins. The ECG may be normal or have nonspecific findings.

ST elevation myocardial infarction (C) is characterized by ST segment elevation defined as approximately 1 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF), 2 mm in the precordial leads, or 0.5 mm depression in leads V1 and V2 for a posterior MI. Reciprocal depression is typically noted in leads opposite to the elevation. Chest pain is the main symptom. However, atypical symptoms such as shortness of breath, weakness, lightheadedness, syncope, and palpitations are also frequently reported. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention with stenting is the first-line and preferred therapy. In this case, the ECG is not demonstrating changes consistent with an ST elevation myocardial infarction.

Wellens syndrome (D) represents a high-grade stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. Its natural progression often leads to anterior wall myocardial infarction. Patients present classically with chest pain or pressure that resolves on its own before or during initial evaluation, or after the patient receives nitroglycerin or pain medications. The initial ECG may not demonstrate the classic finding as it will most often become evident when the patient becomes pain-free. Classically, Wellens sign is described as biphasic T wave inversion or deep symmetric T waves in leads V2–V4. ECG will be without Q waves, significant ST segment elevation, and normal precordial R wave progression. Cardiac enzymes are normal or minimally elevated. Medical management alone is not enough to stop the natural progression. Understanding and recognizing Wellens syndrome is of paramount importance as ST elevation may not be present and cardiac enzymes may also be negative. If a patient is diagnosed with unstable angina and subjected to a stress test for further cardiac evaluation, the patient may have sudden decompensation due to complete LAD occlusion and demonstrate an anterior ST elevated myocardial infarction. Treatment of patients with Wellens syndrome includes aspirin therapy, heparinization, and urgent cardiac catheterization to evaluate the need for angioplasty or coronary artery bypass surgery.

One Step Further
Question:
When is fibrinolytic therapy recommended for patients with a ST elevation myocardial infarction?

Reveal Answer:
In patients with symptom onset within 12 hours who cannot receive primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Patients should have the infusion started within 30 minutes of arrival.

question: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency department in full cardiac arrest. Paramedics note that he was found unconscious at home in cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. He has received three rounds of compressions and epinephrine twice. You confirm a lack of carotid pulse and see normal sinus rhythm with narrow QRS complexes on the cardiac monitor. Based on his presenting rhythm, which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s cardiac arrest?

options.text: Myocardial infarction with acute pump failure

englishExplanation:
Outcomes from cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA) have very poor outcomes. It has been proposed that outcomes could be improved if the differential diagnosis of PEA arrest could be focused to allow better cause-specific treatments than the cumbersome list of Hs and Ts (hypoxia, hydrogen ions, hypovolemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, coronary thrombosis, pulmonary thromboembolism, trauma) that could cause PEA. As such, there is a new classification of PEA that is based on the initial electrocardiographic findings. Narrow-complex rhythms are usually secondary to mechanical causes and usually result in pseudo-PEA, a severe shock state in which the heart continues to pump but does not create a palpable pulse. Narrow-complex PEA is most often associated with mechanical problems causing right ventricular inflow or outflow obstruction, including cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and pulmonary embolism. These etiologies are often identifiable on ultrasonography and are managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation as well as cause-specific treatments including pericardiocentesis, needle decompression, and thrombolysis, respectively. On the other hand, wide-complex PEA tends to be true electromechanical dissociation (i.e., true PEA) secondary to metabolic problems like hyperkalemia and sodium channel blocker toxicity, in addition to acute myocardial infarction with pump failure. Treatment for wide-complex PEA should include IV calcium chloride as well as sodium bicarbonate. While there is no outcome data to prove this theory, it does provide a good physiologic background to the difference between true- and pseudo-PEA and highlights the importance of early ultrasonography in the identification of the etiology of PEA arrest.



Hyperkalemia (A) causes a number of ECG abnormalities, progressing from peaked T waves to flattening of P waves, bradycardia, prolongation of the QRS complex, conduction blocks, and asystole. When severe hyperkalemia causes PEA arrest, the QRS complex is usually wide and it would be highly atypical to see normal sinus rhythm with a narrow QRS complex on the cardiac monitor. Treatment is with IV calcium chloride. Myocardial infarction with acute pump failure (B) is also more likely to cause true PEA with a wide complex secondary to disruption of the His-Purkinje system and a hypokinetic heart on ultrasound secondary to the infarction. Myocardial infarction typically will cause cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia. However, PEA can happen and has a very poor prognosis. Sodium channel blockade (D) will present with a widened QRS complex secondary to the flattening of phase zero of the cardiac action potential. It is treated with sodium bicarbonate to overcome the sodium channel blockade.

question: A 63-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope. He reports that he has been feeling well except for occasional dizziness and mildly decreased exercise tolerance. On physical examination, a systolic murmur is noted at the right second intercostal space which radiates to the carotids. Which of the following is the imaging modality of choice to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: CT of the chest with contrast

englishExplanation:
The classic triad of aortic stenosis is chest pain, dyspnea, and syncope. Typically, patients experience a long asymptomatic period followed by a stepwise onset of symptoms starting with dyspnea, ensued by chest pain, then syncope, and finally overt signs of heart failure. Decreased exercise tolerance and exertional dyspnea or dizziness may not be noticed or reported by the patient for some time prior to the onset of more ominous symptoms. Mortality increases significantly after the onset of symptoms.

Classic physical examination findings include a late-peaking systolic murmur at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids, a single or paradoxically split S2, an S4 gallop, and a diminished carotid pulse with a delayed upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus). Another important clinical finding is a narrowed pulse pressure, which may occur with or without hypotension.

Patients with aortic stenosis typically have diastolic dysfunction and depend on preload from atrial contraction to maintain cardiac output. It is important to remember that cardiac output can drop dramatically, especially if the patient is given nitroglycerin to treat chest pain or dyspnea. Nitrates, vasodilators, diuretics, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers are poorly tolerated in patients with symptomatic aortic stenosis and may cause significant and sudden hypotension. Positive-pressure ventilation may be necessary.

Transthoracic echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and determines the severity, and thus remains the first-line imaging modality of choice. Most patients with newly symptomatic aortic stenosis will require admission. Without surgery, nearly 50% of patients with classic symptoms die within one year. Any discharged patient should avoid all vigorous physical activity and be seen promptly by a cardiologist.



Cardiac magnetic resonance tomography (A), despite the limited availability in most centers, provides the gold-standard assessment of left ventricular volumes and ejection fraction, can quantify the aortic regurgitant volume and provide detailed assessment of the hypertrophic response, and is therefore an excellent imaging modality in aortic regurgitation. However, myocardial hypertrophic response is only weakly correlated with the hemodynamic severity of aortic stenosis and is less suited for its assessment.

A CT of the chest with contrast (B) may confirm a diagnosis of aortic dissection leading to acute aortic regurgitation, rapid onset dyspnea, and sudden-onset tearing chest or interscapular pain. Aortic regurgitation is associated with a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur heard immediately after S2 in the second or third intercostal space at the left sternal border. Electrographically gated non-contrast CT can accurately quantify the calcium burden in aortic stenosis as an alternative measure of disease severity.

ECG (C) findings lack sensitivity and specificity in patients with aortic stenosis. The ECG usually demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy, and a left or right bundle-branch block may be present.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in the United States?

Reveal Answer:
Degenerative calcification.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aortic Stenosis

Risk factors: advancing age, diabetes, hypertension
Sx: dyspnea, chest pain, syncope
PE: crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates to the carotids, paradoxically split S2, S4 gallop
Murmur decreases with Valsalva
Most commonly caused by degenerative calcification
Treatment: aortic valve replacement
Complications:
Anemia
Thromboembolism
Chronic kidney disease
Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis + acquired von Willebrand syndrome type 2A + gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasia)

question: A 71-year-old man with a history of hypertension, diabetes, and tobacco use presents to the emergency department for evaluation of left leg pain. He has been having progressively worsening leg pain for the past 2 days. Physical exam reveals a pale-colored left foot that is cool to the touch. There is no associated swelling or redness of the leg. The patient is able to range the digits of his left foot but reports associated pain. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulses are unable to be palpated or found on Doppler ultrasound. The right leg is normal in appearance, with dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis pulses found on Doppler. The patient’s BP is 155/75 mm Hg, HR is 99 bpm, SpO2 is 95%, and T is 98.9°F (37.2°C). Which of the following is likely to be the earliest finding or symptom in this case?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms of acute limb ischemia due to arterial occlusion. Paresthesias are often an early symptom of limb ischemia, along with pain, pallor, decreased skin temperature regulation (poikilothermia), diminished or absent pulses, and muscle weakness (paralysis). These findings are commonly referred to as the six Ps of acute limb ischemia. Not all findings will be present, and the lack of one or more symptoms does not exclude the diagnosis. Limb ischemia is most often due to acute thrombosis of a diseased artery, but it can also be due to thrombosis of a stent or graft, artery dissection, trauma, or embolus from a proximal source. Limb ischemia is considered acute if symptoms have been present < 2 weeks.

Risk factors include tobacco use, diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. The most frequently diseased arteries resulting in limb ischemia are femoropopliteal, followed by tibial, aortoiliac, and brachiocephalic vessels. Pain in the limb distal to the site of occlusion is the most common initial symptom. As the ischemic injury progresses, anesthesia and paralysis develop and may indicate a lack of limb viability. An acutely ischemic limb is an emergent condition, and surgical consultation is appropriate as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, even while obtaining diagnostic imaging. If there are still pulses on Doppler ultrasound, ankle-brachial indexes (ABIs) can be measured to risk-stratify the patient. An ABI < 0.9 is suggestive of peripheral artery disease. An ABI ≤ 0.4 suggests severe disease and the need for emergent management. Ultrasound can detect an arterial obstruction, but sensitivity declines for localization below the calf level. Emergency physicians may use point-of-care ultrasound to expedite the diagnosis and management. CT angiography is often the most readily available study in the emergency department and has a sensitivity and specificity of 95%. Once the diagnosis is established or strongly suspected based on the clinical history and exam findings, therapy with unfractionated heparin should be initiated and vascular surgery consulted.



Complete loss of motor function (A) is a late finding in acute limb ischemia. Paralysis is a poor prognostic indicator and suggests the limb may no longer be viable. Pallor is typically the first skin finding and may progress to cyanosis, mottling, and blistering (B) later in the disease process. Skin necrosis is a late-stage finding. Pain is often the first symptom of limb ischemia, starting distally and progressing more proximally as the limb becomes more ischemic. Decreased pain (C) is a late finding that may develop due to ischemic sensory loss.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the term for the cramping pain associated with chronic peripheral arterial disease that occurs with exertion and is relieved by rest?

Reveal Answer:
Claudication.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Arterial Embolism and Thrombosis

Embolism
Most common source is left heart; most common site is femoral artery bifurcation
Risks: recent MI or atrial fibrillation (usually lack of peripheral atherosclerosis)
Sx: sudden onset of pallor, paresthesias, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, and pain out of proportion to exam (6 Ps)
Thrombosis
Risks: atherosclerosis (lack of atrial fibrillation)
Sx: previous claudication, pain, diminished pulses
Tx: anticoagulation (heparin), restore flow (embolectomy, thrombolysis, bypass, angioplasty)

question: A 73-year-old man presents to the ED with progressive shortness of breath for 2 days without chest pain. The patient has a history of hypertension controlled with hydrochlorothiazide but has been nonadherent with his medications. In the ED, his vital signs are BP 186/102 mm Hg, HR 108 bpm, RR 34/min, and SpO2 90% on room air. On exam, the patient has pulmonary crackles midway up both lung fields, jugular venous distension, and pitting edema of his lower extremities. A chest X-ray depicts increased interstitial markings and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Give the patient aspirin and activate the cath lab

englishExplanation:
This patient has acute heart failure with pulmonary edema. The clinical presentation of heart failure includes shortness of breath, jugular venous distension, crackles and rales, peripheral edema, S3 gallop, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. A chest X-ray may show an enlarged cardiac silhouette, Kerley B lines suggesting pulmonary edema, and pulmonary vessel cephalization. Lab studies may show an elevated plasma brain natriuretic peptide (BNP).

Management of heart failure with acute pulmonary edema begins with addressing the ABCs. Noninvasive respiratory therapy, such as bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP) or continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the most appropriate next step in care. Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation increases oxygenation, decreases the work of breathing, and decreases preload and afterload. In addition to BPAP, adjunctive medications include nitrates, diuretics, and positioning the patient sitting up. Nitrates act as venous and arterial vasodilators and help to reduce preload and afterload. Morphine sulfate is thought to decrease oxygen consumption by decreasing catecholamine release, decreasing preload from mild vasodilatory effects, and decreasing pain and anxiety. However, there are some studies that link the use of morphine sulfate to increased mortality. Furosemide can be used in patients with evidence of fluid retention (jugular venous distention, extremity edema).



Pulmonary edema secondary to heart failure usually responds well to preload and afterload reduction with noninvasive ventilation and nitroglycerin. If the patient continues to deteriorate, intubation (C) may be necessary.

A myocardial infarction is less likely given the lack of chest pain and ECG that does not reveal ST segment elevations. Therefore, activation of the cath lab (B) is unnecessary.

Hydrochlorothiazide (D) has no role in the acute management of pulmonary edema. Once stabilized, the patient can resume his daily medications.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?

Reveal Answer:
Left-sided heart failure.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Decompensated Heart Failure

Sx: exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
PE: crackles, pitting edema, S3 heart sound
Labs: ↑ BNP
CXR: cardiomegaly, cephalization, Kerley B lines, effusions
Dx: ECHO (most useful study)
Tx
NIPPV: ↑ oxygenation, ↓ work of breathing, ↓ preload, afterload
Nitroglycerin: ↓ preload, afterload
Furosemide: diuresis
Hypotension without signs of shock: dobutamine (but may worsen hypotension)
Severe hypotension with signs of shock: norepinephrine (↑ systemic vascular resistance, ↑ HR, ↑ BP, ↑ myocardial oxygen demand)

question: A 53-year-old man presents with dyspnea on exertion and near syncope. His blood pressure is 110/62 mm Hg. His ECG is shown above. What is the best management of this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with symptomatic third-degree heart block and should be admitted for permanent pacemaker placement. Third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block (or complete heart block) is defined as an absence of conduction of atrial impulses accompanied by an escape rhythm. The morphology and rate of the escape rhythm depend on the site of the pacemaker. If the pacemaker is above the bundle of His, the rhythm will have a narrow complex QRS with a rate of 40–60 bpm. If the pacemaker is below the bundle of His, the QRS will be wide and the rate will be slower (20–40 bpm). Analysis of the ECG in a complete heart block will reveal AV dissociation or the lack of an electrocardiographic relationship between atrial and ventricular activity. Patients with third-degree heart block are often unresponsive to atropine and may require transcutaneous or transvenous pacemakers if unstable as a bridge to permanent pacemaker placement.



Aspirin, heparin, and telemetry admission (B) is appropriate for a patient with possible acute coronary syndrome but inappropriate for a patient with a symptomatic third-degree heart block.

Norepinephrine (D) is an agent that can temporarily be used in the setting of complete heart block while awaiting transcutaneous, transvenous, or permanent pacemaker placement. It is a vasoconstrictive agent used to increase blood pressure. It has less effect on the heart rate, while epinephrine could be used instead to increase the heart rate. Neither agent would be the first action in this hemodynamically stable patient.

Thrombolytics (C) are useful in the treatment of ST elevation myocardial infarction, not complete heart block.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the most common identified causes of premature ventricular contractions?

Reveal Answer:
Myocardial infarction or ischemia, drug toxicity, and electrolyte imbalance.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Third-Degree Heart Block (Complete Heart Block)

Adult risks: aging, inferior or anterior infarction, digitalis
Pediatric risks: congenital, autoantibodies from autoimmune disease in the mother, infection, trauma, surgery
Rhythm will be
P-P regular
R-R regular
Notable feature: the independent beating of the atria and ventricles
Treatment
Asymptomatic: admission for cardiology evaluation
Symptomatic: atropine, isoproterenol, epinephrine, transcutaneous or transvenous pacing
Permanent: pacemaker

question: A 53-year-old man presents to the ED with shortness of breath. He has bibasilar crackles and peripheral edema. A segment from a point-of-care echocardiogram is shown above. Which of the following, if present, is most likely to have contributed to this patient’s current clinical presentation?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s clinical features and echocardiogram suggest decompensated heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy, which is characterized by ventricular dilation and impaired cardiac contractility due to a wide variety of causative factors. As many as one-third of cases result from mutations in genes that encode proteins of sarcomeres, cytoskeletal components, or the nuclear envelopes. However, most cases have nongenetic origins, and ischemic cardiomyopathy secondary to coronary artery disease is the most common noninherited cause. Other common etiologies include alcohol, cocaine, and anthracycline chemotherapy.

Symptoms of heart failure are the most common clinical manifestation of dilated cardiomyopathy, including this patient’s peripheral edema and crackles on lung exam. Dyspnea, chest pain, and syncope are common subjective concerns, and dysrhythmias and sudden death can also occur. The diagnosis is made via echocardiography, which shows left ventricular (LV) dilation, reduced LV ejection fraction, and variable wall motion abnormalities. A variety of nonspecific ECG findings may be present, including poor R wave progression, intraventricular conduction delays, left bundle branch block, and LV hypertrophy. Chest X-ray may show cardiomegaly or pulmonary vascular congestion, and troponin or B-type natriuretic peptide are often elevated.

ED treatment of patients with dilated cardiomyopathy is supportive, aimed at restoring euvolemia and addressing any rhythm disturbances or conduction abnormalities that may be present. Loop diuretics (i.e., furosemide, bumetanide) are the mainstay for diuresis to achieve euvolemia. Vasodilators and positive pressure ventilation may also be used to reduce preload and improve respiratory function in the setting of pulmonary edema. Long-term management of dilated cardiomyopathy and consequent heart failure typically includes medications that promote beneficial myocardial remodeling, including angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. Patients with LV ejection fraction < 35% should have an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator placed.



Uremia (A) can produce pericarditis, effusion, and tamponade but is not associated with the development of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Infiltrative diseases affecting the myocardium (C), such as sarcoidosis or amyloidosis, can produce a variety of conditions, including conductive disease, but they are far more likely to cause restrictive rather than dilated cardiomyopathy.

Prior radiation therapy (D) and rheumatoid arthritis (E) may contribute to the development of pericarditis but are not commonly associated with dilated cardiomyopathy.

One Step Further
Question:
What sarcomere protein is commonly mutated in genetic cases of dilated cardiomyopathy?

Reveal Answer:
Titan.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Dilated Cardiomyopathy

Common causes: ischemic heart disease, toxins, infiltrative processes
Sx: dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
PE will show an S3 gallop on auscultation
Echocardiogram will show four dilated chambers (ventricles > atria)
Management includes abstaining from alcohol
Rx options: ACE inhibitors and diuretics
For refractory disease to maximum medical therapy, consider cardiac transplantation or LVAD (for those who are not candidates for transplantation)
Most common cardiomyopathy

question: A 27-year-old man with no medical problems presents to the ED with fever and worsening weakness since past week. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 95/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 127 bpm, respirations are 19/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Physical exam is notable for a holosystolic murmur heard best over the left lower sternal border, track marks on both of the patient’s forearms, and dry, flushed skin. The patient is given 2 L of IV fluids and his repeat blood pressure is 111/58 mm Hg and heart rate is 96 bpm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms suggestive of bacterial endocarditis. Bacterial endocarditis presents with a fever and a new cardiac murmur typically in a patient with risk factors such as prosthetic valves or IV drug misuse. Findings in bacterial endocarditis can include petechiae, subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes (tender subcutaneous nodules on the digits), Janeway lesions (nontender maculae on the palms and soles), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages), embolic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and CNS microabscesses. Other less specific findings include splenomegaly, gallops, dysrhythmias, pericardial rubs, and pleural friction rubs.

Any patient with a fever and a new cardiac murmur with risk factors should have blood cultures drawn and be assessed with an ultrasound searching for cardiac vegetations. After blood cultures are drawn, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered with possible regimens including vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam or vancomycin and gentamicin. Micafungin can be added empirically until a fungal etiology is also ruled out. Surgical removal of the vegetations may be necessary for source control of the infection.



Pericarditis (B) presents with chest pain worse when the patient is lying back and relieved when they sit up or lean forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG.

Septic shock (C) presents with hypotension and tachycardia in the setting of infection that does not respond to fluid resuscitation. This patient responded to initial fluid resuscitation.

Sympathomimetic overdose (D)presents with adrenergic symptoms including hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, and diaphoresis. This patient presents with dry, flushed skin, likely secondary to dehydration.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient who uses IV drugs and has a new-onset early diastolic murmur, fever, and new-onset atrioventricular block?

Reveal Answer:
Perivalvular abscess (disrupts the conduction system).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bacterial Endocarditis

Risk factors: injection drug use, valvular heart disease
Sx & syndromes:
Mild and nonspecific febrile illness - fever, rash, cough, and myalgias
Acute heart failure
Focal neurological deficit from septic cerebral embolus
Altered mental status
Axial spine pain from osteomyelitis
Pneumonia from septic pulmonary emboli
PE: fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, murmur, Janeway lesions, anemia, nailbed hemorrhages, emboli (FROM JANE)
Dx: echocardiography and Duke criteria
Most commonly caused by:
IVDA: Staphylococcus aureus, tricuspid
Native valve: Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci (most common in previously diseased), mitral
GI malignancy: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis)
Tx: antibiotics
Dental prophylaxis indicated in some cases

question: A 32-year-old previously healthy woman presents to the ED with a sudden onset of heart palpitations. Her vital signs are BP 124/88 mm Hg, HR 172 bpm, RR 16/min, and SpO2 99% on room air. Her rhythm strip is seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s diagnosis is paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). Patients are generally young and healthy, presenting with palpitations, sudden tachycardia (~120–200 bpm), and sometimes chest pain or shortness of breath. An ECG demonstrates a narrow-complex tachycardia, a regular rhythm, and P waves hidden within the preceding T wave. PSVT is most frequently caused by a reentry abnormality through the atrioventricular (AV) node. Accessory pathways may also cause PSVT, such as seen in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. For hemodynamically stable patients, treatment begins with interventions to increase vagal tone, such as carotid massage or Valsalva maneuvers. If these are not successful, adenosine should be administered. Adenosine acts to transiently inhibit conduction through the AV node. It is metabolized within seconds, so it is quite safe. Calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers, and type 1A or 1C antidysrhythmics are alternative agents. If the patient remains in PSVT, cardioversion is performed.



Atrial flutter (A) is caused by the rapid firing of ectopic atrial foci and presents with a sawtooth pattern on the ECG. It is treated similarly to atrial fibrillation, with rate control in stable patients and cardioversion in unstable patients.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (B) is an irregular tachydysrhythmia characterized by more than three different P wave morphologies on the ECG. It is commonly associated with COPD. The treatment is to treat the underlying condition, such as with bronchodilators and steroids for an acute COPD exacerbation.

Ventricular tachycardia (D) is characterized by a wide complex tachycardia. Stable patients can be treated with antidysrhythmics such as procainamide or amiodarone. Unstable patients should undergo immediate synchronized cardioversion.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the management of incidental, occasional premature ventricular contractions?

Reveal Answer:
No treatment is indicated.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) or Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT)

Common types include
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT)
Atrial tachycardia
Most commonly caused by a reentrant pathway in the atrioventricular node
Clinical
Infants: poor feeding, fussiness, irritability
Older children: palpitations, chest pain, fatigue
Adults: palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath
PE: abrupt onset of tachycardia
Ventricular rate often 160–220 bpm in adults
HR > 180–220 bpm in children
HR up to 300 bpm in infants
Dx: ECG shows regular narrow complex tachycardia (P waves can be obscured at high HRs)
Stress testing or ambulatory monitoring may be needed
Tx: vagal maneuvers, drug therapy (adenosine), cardioversion
Can be associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

question: A 68-year-old man with a history of complete heart block and permanent pacemaker placement presents to the ED with progressive lower extremity swelling, abdominal distension, and fatigue. He reports no chest pain or exertional angina. His vital signs are within normal limits. On exam, he has elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, and bilateral pitting edema, and a faint murmur of a diastolic rumble is heard over the left lower sternal border. A chest X-ray shows right atrial enlargement and a pacemaker lead in place. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Tricuspid stenosis is most often caused by rheumatic heart disease. Other important causes include carcinoid syndrome, congenital malformations, lupus, and prior infective endocarditis. However, in the US, it is increasingly recognized in association with pacemaker or defibrillator leads, which can damage the tricuspid valve. Injury and stenosis lead to right atrial enlargement and systemic venous congestion, producing signs of right-sided heart failure, including ascites, hepatomegaly, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), and peripheral edema. This patient’s history of pacemaker implantation with new right heart failure symptoms suggests tricuspid stenosis.

Diagnosis is usually established with echocardiography, which demonstrates thickened or immobile leaflets, reduced valve orifice area, and elevated diastolic gradients across the tricuspid valve. Doppler imaging helps quantify severity and assess for concomitant regurgitation or pulmonary hypertension.

Treatment focuses initially on treating any systemic congestion with sodium restriction and diuretics, but definitive therapy for tricuspid stenosis is surgical or transcatheter intervention. Surgical tricuspid valve repair or replacement is considered in severe, symptomatic cases, while percutaneous balloon valvotomy has been used in select rheumatic cases. Removal or repositioning of pacemaker leads may also be necessary if they contribute to valve dysfunction.



Constrictive pericarditis (A) causes systemic venous congestion and ascites but is associated with a pericardial knock, calcified pericardium, and Kussmaul sign. Chest X-ray may show pericardial calcification, not specifically valve-related right atrial enlargement with a pacemaker lead.

Pulmonary hypertension (B) causes right heart strain and failure but is associated with a loud P2, right ventricular heave, and pulmonary vascular changes. Pacemaker placement does not predispose to pulmonary hypertension, but it does predispose to tricuspid stenosis.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy (C) causes diastolic dysfunction and right-sided heart failure, often seen with amyloidosis or hemochromatosis. There is no clear link to pacemaker leads and no isolated right atrial enlargement from valve obstruction.

Right ventricular infarction (D) presents with hypotension, clear lungs, and elevated JVP, not chronic progressive systemic congestion with a history of pacing lead placement.

One Step Further
Question:
Why do carcinoid tumors cause tricuspid stenosis?

Reveal Answer:
Serotonin and other vasoactive substances induce fibrous plaque deposition on right-sided heart valves, leading to thickening and narrowing.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tricuspid Stenosis

Most common cause: rheumatic heart disease
Almost always occurs with mitral stenosis (MS)
Murmur
Diastolic murmur along left sternal border
Louder than MS during inspiration
PE: JVP (giant A waves), hepatomegaly, ascites, LE edema

question: A 58-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents to the ED with fever, chills, and worsening abdominal pain for 2 weeks. His T is 102.8°F (39.3°C), BP is 108/70 mm Hg, and HR is 125 bpm. On exam, the patient appears ill and has tenderness in the mid abdomen with an audible bruit. Laboratory studies reveal leukocytosis. CT angiography demonstrates an aortic aneurysm near the bifurcation of the superior mesenteric artery with surrounding inflammatory changes. Which of the following is the most likely associated finding in this patient?

options.text: Calcified hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiography
Positive blood cultures for Candida albicans
Splenomegaly with spherocytes on peripheral smear
Vegetation on the cardiac valve seen on echocardiography

correctAnswer: Vegetation on the cardiac valve seen on echocardiography
englishExplanation:
This patient most likely has a rare diagnosis of mycotic aneurysm caused by septic embolization from infective endocarditis. The hallmark associated finding is a valvular vegetation on echocardiography, which serves as the embolic source. In infective endocarditis, septic emboli can occlude the vasa vasorum or vessel lumen, leading to vascular wall infection and mycotic aneurysm formation.

Embolism can occur in 25–50% of patients, but only rarely do patients develop symptomatic aneurysms. They are often multiple but may be solitary, and spontaneous resolution with antibiotics has been reported, making the true prevalence uncertain. Common sites affected include intracranial arteries, visceral and limb arteries, usually at bifurcations, and rare involvement of the coronary arteries.

Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion in those with possible endocarditis and focal signs of infection. Imaging further supports the diagnosis with CT angiography showing a saccular outpouching with perivascular soft tissue inflammatory changes or contrast extravasation.

Treatment includes prolonged intravenous antibiotics targeting endocarditis pathogens, such as vancomycin plus cefepime or ceftriaxone for empiric coverage (with adjustments for culture results), and surgical or endovascular repair if rupture, rapid enlargement, or high-risk anatomy is present.



Calcified hilar lymphadenopathy (A) is seen in sarcoidosis or prior tuberculosis, and it is not associated with septic embolization or aneurysms. Patients with sarcoidosis present with cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and weight loss, sometimes with associated skin lesions.

Fungal infections like Candida albicans (B) are much less common causes of mycotic aneurysms than bacterial causes. Despite its name, a mycotic aneurysm has no connection to fungal infections, which makes the terminology a source of confusion.

Splenomegaly with spherocytes (C) represents hereditary spherocytosis, a congenital hemolytic anemia unrelated to aneurysm or embolic infection.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common peripheral aneurysm?

Reveal Answer:
Popliteal artery aneurysm.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Infected (Mycotic) Aneurysm

Most commonly due to Streptococcus viridans group, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella spp
Fungal association is misnomer
True description of "mycotic aneurysm" is infected aneurysm resulting from bacterial endocarditis rather than infection of atherosclerotic vessels, infection of existing aneurysm, or post-traumatic infected pseudoaneurysm
Most often occurs at vessel bifurcations
Risks: endocarditis, advanced age, immunocompromised, trauma
Sx: painful, palpable, pulsatile mass with signs of infection (fever); back or abdominal pain if aorta involved
Dx: CTA
Tx: antibiotics, surgery vs endovascular treatment based on surgical risks

question: A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after several episodes of syncope. Her vital signs include a blood pressure of 136/88 mm Hg, heart rate of 58 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, and temperature of 99.1°F. Her rhythm strip is shown above. Which of the following heart blocks is present?

options.text: Second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block
Second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block

correctAnswer: Second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular block
englishExplanation:
The patient has a second-degree Mobitz type I atrioventricular (AV) block. A first-degree AV block refers to slowed conduction through the AV node, resulting in a prolonged PR interval, with preserved conduction of each sinus-generated impulse. In second-degree AV block, there is intermittent conduction through the AV node in which some atrial impulses are conducted through to the ventricles while others are blocked. There are two types of second-degree block: Mobitz type I and type II.

In second-degree Mobitz type I block, also referred to as Wenckebach, there is a progressive delay in each AV conduction until AV conduction is finally blocked. On electrocardiogram, this appears as progressive lengthening of each PR interval until a QRS complex is eventually dropped and the cycle repeats. Grouped beating, or clustering of QRS complexes separated by a pause from the dropped beat, is characteristic of second-degree type I AV block. Mobitz type I block is often transient, seen in association with inferior wall myocardial ischemia, medication toxicity, or cardiac surgery. Treatment is usually not necessary unless it is associated with a very slow rate with signs of hypoperfusion. In this case, atropine, which increases the rate of sinus node firing and conduction through the AV node, is usually effective.

The other type of second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II, is more ominous. Type II block is characterized by a constant PR interval with periodic nonconducted impulses, seen as an absence of a QRS complex. Because Mobitz type II blocks are associated with progression to third-degree, or complete heart block, patients should have transcutaneous pacer pads placed in anticipation of possible need. In third-degree AV block, there is no conduction through the AV node, and an escape pacemaker is responsible for the ventricular rate. On electrocardiogram, there is no association of P waves with QRS complexes, and the ventricular rate is 40–60 bpm, depending on whether a junctional or ventricular escape pacemaker takes over. Pacing is usually needed in a complete heart block.



First-degree AV block (A) shows a prolonged PR interval but no dropped beats.

Left anterior fascicular block (B) shows marked left axis deviation, qR pattern in lead aVL, and QRS duration < 120 ms.

Second-degree Mobitz type II AV block (D) is characterized by a constant PR interval with sporadic dropped beats.

Third-degree AV block (E) is characterized by no association between P waves and QRS complexes.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the definitive treatment for third-degree heart block?

Reveal Answer:
Internal pacemaker placement.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Second-Degree Heart Block (Mobitz I, Wenckebach)

Rhythm will be irregular
PR interval will be progressively lengthening
Notable feature: progressive lengthening of the PR interval until QRS complex fails to appear after a P wave (dropped beat)

question: Which of the following has been associated with a reduced rate of incessant or recurrent pericarditis in patients with a first episode of pericarditis?
englishExplanation:
The pericardium is a fibroelastic sac made up of visceral and parietal layers separated by a (potential) space, the pericardial cavity. In healthy individuals, the pericardial cavity contains 20 to 50 mL of an ultrafiltrate of plasma.

The therapy of acute pericarditis should be targeted as much as possible to the underlying etiology. In patients with an identified cause other than viral infection, specific therapy appropriate to the underlying disorder is indicated. However, in resource-rich countries, most cases of acute pericarditis in immunocompetent patients are due to viral infection or are idiopathic.

Because of the relatively benign course associated with the common causes of pericarditis (most cases), it is not necessary to search for the etiology in all patients. As such, most patients are treated for a presumptive viral cause with NSAIDs and colchicine.

Most patients have prompt resolution of symptoms without recurrent pericarditis when treated with NSAIDs alone. However, when used as an adjunct to NSAID therapy, colchicine reduces symptoms, decreases the rate of recurrent pericarditis, and is generally well tolerated.



Aspirin (A) is a first-line agent for symptom relief and inflammation control in acute pericarditis, but it has not been shown to independently reduce recurrence rates. It serves as background anti-inflammatory therapy to which colchicine is added.

Ibuprofen (C) is similarly used as first-line NSAID therapy for acute pericarditis symptoms but lacks evidence for preventing recurrence when used alone. Like aspirin, it is the foundation therapy that colchicine supplements to reduce recurrence.

Prednisone (D) is associated with an increased risk of recurrence and should be avoided in first-episode pericarditis. Corticosteroids are reserved only for patients who are refractory to or have contraindications to NSAIDs and colchicine.

question: In which of the following patients with a hemodynamically stable supraventricular tachycardia is treatment with adenosine contraindicated?

options.text: Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with antidromic conduction
Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with orthodromic conduction

correctAnswer: Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with antidromic conduction
englishExplanation:
Supraventricular tachycardias can be categorized by the site of origin and the regularity of the rhythm. For example, regular atrial rhythms include atrial tachycardia and atrial flutter, and irregular atrial rhythms include atrial fibrillation and multifocal atrial tachycardia. Atrioventricular rhythms tend to be regular and include atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (AVRT) as well as atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT). In AVRT there is an anatomic re-entry circuit created by an accessory pathway outside of the atrioventricular node. Re-entry circuits can form between the atrioventricular node and the accessory pathway in either direction. These circuits are named for the direction of the current through the atrioventricular node: orthodromic refers to anterograde conduction through the node and retrograde conduction through the accessory pathway, and antidromic refers to retrograde conduction through the node and anterograde conduction through the accessory pathway. ECGs of orthodromic AVRT have narrow QRS complexes, as anterograde conduction through the atrioventricular node allows the impulse to pass quickly through the His-Purkinje system, whereas antidromic AVRT produces wide-complex rhythms. In wide-complex antidromic AVRT, the use of adenosine can enhance anterograde conduction through the accessory pathway, leading to degeneration of the rhythm into ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. As such, antidromic AVRT is best treated like other wide-complex tachycardias with procainamide.



Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia (A) is commonly referred to as classic supraventricular tachycardia and is characterized by a functional re-entry circuit within the atrioventricular node that can be triggered by a premature atrial contraction during the refractory period of the slow pathway of the node. Adenosine interrupts this re-entrant circuit within the node to allow normal conduction through the node to resume.

Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with orthodromic conduction (C) produces a narrow-complex regular tachycardia as the anterograde portion of the circuit goes through the atrioventricular node, allowing for a rapid and coordinated impulse through the His-Purkinje system. Treatment is the same as with AVNRT, sequentially using vagal maneuvers and adenosine to slow nodal conduction. Calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers can also be used.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (D) is defined as an irregularly irregular rhythm with more than three distinct P wave morphologies and variable PR intervals. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is independent of the atrioventricular node, so while adenosine will slow conduction through the node, the tachycardia will persist. Adenosine is not contraindicated but is ineffective.

One Step Further
Question:
In what other supraventricular tachycardia, besides atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia with antidromic conduction, associated with an accessory pathway is adenosine contraindicated?

Reveal Answer:
Atrial fibrillation in the setting of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

A 69-year-old woman presents with reduced exercise tolerance and dyspnea on exertion. Vital signs include a BP of 135/85 mm Hg, HR of 86 bpm, RR of 20 breaths/minute, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. On exam, you auscultate a diastolic murmur at the apex, heard in the audio clip above. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The murmur of mitral stenosis includes a loud S1 and an opening snap in early diastole accompanied by a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic apical murmur. Mitral valve stenosis most commonly results from rheumatic heart disease.

Other causes include atrial myxoma, congenital abnormalities, and calcific valve degeneration. The murmur of mitral stenosis occurs from mitral valve narrowing, leading to increasing pressures across the mitral valve with subsequent left atrial hypertrophy and eventual dilation with right heart failure.



The murmur of aortic regurgitation (A) is a blowing diastolic murmur heard best at the sternal border.

The murmur of aortic stenosis (B) is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that radiates to the neck.

The murmur of mitral regurgitation (C) is a loud holosystolic murmur that radiates to the base and is heard best at the apex.

The murmur of pulmonic stenosis (E) is a systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border that may radiate to the posterior lung fields.

question: A 25-year-old man presents to the ED with recurrent syncope. His ECG is shown above. What is the definitive treatment for this condition?
englishExplanation:
Brugada syndrome is a genetic disorder that can lead to life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest in patients with no structural heart disease. It is a disorder of sodium channels and is most commonly diagnosed in men aged 20–60.

There are two common ECG patterns. In a type 1 pattern, the elevated ST segment descends, has an upward convexity and an inverted T wave (like in this patient and seen best in lead V2), and is called the coved type. In a type 2 pattern, the ST segment has a saddleback ST-T wave in which the elevated ST segment descends toward the baseline and then rises again to make a biphasic or upright T wave.

Patients with unexplained syncope and a Brugada pattern on ECG require admission and placement of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). If the Brugada pattern is noted incidentally on ECG, treatment is not well established. These patients are still at increased risk for sudden cardiac death and may benefit from placement of an ICD, so they should be referred to cardiology.



Pharmacologic therapy such as amiodarone (A) is not typically warranted for patients with a high risk for sudden cardiac arrest, like this patient with syncope. However, amiodarone can be used in patients who are not candidates for or who do not want an ICD after a risk-benefit discussion.

Magnesium (C) and defibrillation are the treatments of choice for patients with torsades de pointes, which is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that occurs in the setting of QT prolongation.

Placement of a permanent pacemaker (D) is indicated for patients with symptomatic bradydysrhythmias, tachydysrhythmias, and sinus node dysfunction. A pacemaker will not protect against sudden cardiac death in patients with Brugada syndrome.

Percutaneous coronary intervention (E) is the treatment for patients with coronary artery disease, particularly those presenting with an ST elevation myocardial infarction.

One Step Further

What is the recommended treatment of wide complex tachycardia in the setting of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Procainamide.

Type 1: coved ST elevation > 2 mm in ≥ 1 lead (V1–V3) followed by negative T wave (Brugada sign)

Type 3: coved or saddleback ST elevation < 2 mm
Type 2 and 3 changes are nondiagnostic and require further workup

question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parents after a syncopal episode. The patient is adopted and does not know his biological parents. The patient was in gym class playing tennis when he suddenly lost consciousness. He does not remember anything from the event. His classmates stated he was unresponsive for 30 seconds. During this time, he demonstrated shaking of his upper and lower extremities. The patient remembers everything after waking up and reports no confusion. Physical exam and vital signs are unremarkable and unrevealing. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Consult to cardiology for automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement

correctAnswer: Consult to cardiology for automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement
englishExplanation:
Syncope is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness associated with a loss of postural tone from which recovery is spontaneous. Life-threatening conditions such as hypoglycemia, heat illness, anaphylaxis, cardiac dysrhythmia, or structural cardiac disease are rare but serious causes of syncope. Although these causes account for only 1–2% of syncope in children, they still warrant diagnostic consideration. Cardiac syncope is thought to present with sudden abrupt loss of consciousness without a prodrome and may be associated with chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath.

Brugada Syndrome is a genetic disorder of fast sodium channels causing a right bundle branch block pattern in leads V1–2 with pathognomonic J-point elevation and saddle-shaped or sloped ST segments. Sudden cardiac arrest may be the initial presentation in as many as one-third of patients. Patients may also present with an episode of syncope but palpitations or nocturnal agonal respirations have also been described. Automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD) placement is recommended for patients who have survived sudden cardiac arrest or those with a history of syncope that is felt to be secondary to ventricular tachydysrhythmias.



Emergent cardiac catheterization (B) would be required for ST elevation myocardial infarction characterized by ST segment elevation of approximately 1 mm in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF), 2 mm in the precordial leads or 0.5 mm depression in leads V1 and V2 for a posterior myocardial infarction. Reciprocal depression is typically noted in leads opposite to the elevation. Chest pain is the main symptom. However, atypical symptoms such as shortness of breath, weakness, lightheadedness, syncope, and palpitations are also frequently reported.

Long QT syndrome is characterized by a QT interval of > 440 msec in men and > 460 msec in women, although some sources say > 460 msec in men and > 480 msec in women. This can be acquired or congenital and can lead to an increased risk of torsades de pointes. Acquired causes are commonly associated with medications (antidepressants, antidysrhythmics, antipsychotics, methadone, antibiotics, and ondansetron). Treatment for acquired prolonged QT syndrome involves removing the offending agent as well as close cardiac monitoring and treating associated dysrhythmias as needed. Beta-blockers, such as propranolol (C), are the mainstay of therapy for congenital causes.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a genetically determined heart muscle disease most often caused by mutations in one of several sarcomere genes. The mutation results in left ventricular hypertrophy, commonly of the septum, that results in left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Many patients have no or only minor symptoms. Thus, affected individuals are often diagnosed as a result of family screening, murmur on exam, or abnormal ECG. The abnormal ECG may show voltage criteria consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy or classically deep dagger Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads. On physical examination, patients may have a systolic murmur auscultated along the left sternal border. Patients who present with dyspnea, presyncope, or syncope on exertion, or who have a familial history of sudden cardiac death, warrant evaluation with a STAT echocardiogram (D) evaluating for left ventricular outflow tract obstruction secondary to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Reveal Answer:
Valsalva increases the intensity of the murmur.

question: A 4-month-old previously healthy baby girl presents to the emergency department for irritability for the past 1 hour. The parents say she is refusing to eat, and they tried to lay her down for a nap, but she could not rest. The exam shows an afebrile, crying infant with HR of 233 bpm, RR of 60/min, BP of 83/52 mm Hg, T of 37.6°C, and SpO2 of 100%. The remainder of her exam is normal. In addition to obtaining an ECG, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Chemical cardioversion followed by electrical cardioversion if needed
Sepsis workup to rule out occult infection
Vagal maneuvers followed by chemical cardioversion if needed

correctAnswer: Vagal maneuvers followed by chemical cardioversion if needed
englishExplanation:
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) presents with nonspecific symptoms in infancy and can include rapid breathing, irritability, poor feeding, or failure to thrive. The diagnosis is confirmed based on the heart rate and characteristic ECG findings. Generally accepted heart rate cutoffs depend on age (children’s heart rate > 180 bpm, and infant’s heart rate > 200 bpm). The ECG will show a narrow complex, fast rhythm without appreciable P waves before the QRS complex. Most P waves will be buried in the QRS complexes, but sometimes, retrograde P waves (i.e., occurring after the QRS complex) can be seen.

Initial treatment depends on if the patient is hemodynamically stable or unstable. Treatment of unstable patients with signs of poor perfusion or hypotension should begin with synchronized electrical cardioversion (although adenosine can be used if an IV can be established rapidly). For children, the starting dose is 0.5–1 J/kg. If that is unsuccessful, the energy can be increased to 2 J/kg for all necessary repeated attempts. Treatment in a stable patient should start with vagal maneuvers. For infants, placing an ice pack over the face for 20–30 seconds may be sufficient. This activates the diving reflex, which is an effective way to increase vagal tone. If vagal maneuvers are unsuccessful, chemical cardioversion should be the next step. Adenosine is the agent of choice. Doses start at 0.1 mg/kg and must be pushed as a rapid infusion followed by a normal saline flush. If a second dose is needed, the dose is 0.2 mg/kg. As in adults, a maximum of three doses should be given. Management should also include a careful history and exam to rule out other sources of tachycardia, such as dehydration, sepsis, hyperthyroidism, and acute blood loss.



Pain can elevate the heart rate, but with exam findings showing no source of pain and a higher than expected heart rate, analgesia and ED observation (A) does not aid in treating the underlying pathology.

Chemical cardioversion followed by electrical cardioversion if needed (B) is a possible treatment for PSVT, but vagal maneuvers should be attempted first, especially in this infant who is not in extremis.

Providing reassurance and discharging home (C) should not be done with patients with abnormal vital signs without an appropriate workup.

A sepsis workup (D) is an important consideration in infants with unexplained tachycardia. Lab work, blood cultures, and urinalysis can be ordered if there is a concern for occult infection, but they are not required for all presentations of PSVT. Furthermore, this patient is afebrile and her symptoms are acute.

question: A 40-year-old man with a distant history of hypertension and kidney disease presents to the emergency department reporting high blood pressure today. He has not seen a clinician for years but has been monitoring his blood pressure occasionally. It has been steadily rising over several days and was 204/100 mm Hg today. He has no symptoms. In the emergency department, vital signs show an HR of 86 bpm, BP of 198/104 mm Hg, RR of 12/min, and T of 37ºC. Laboratory studies performed are unremarkable. From the following options, which would be the best antihypertensive to initiate as outpatient therapy for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with asymptomatic hypertension. Although there is no requirement for the emergency clinician to initiate antihypertensive therapy, it is recommended since chronic hypertension leads to cardiac, kidney, and cerebrovascular disease. It is especially recommended to begin outpatient therapy for patients who do not have appropriate outpatient follow-up. There are multiple medication options to treat chronic hypertension and guidelines are established by the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology. The most often recommended initial treatment is with hydrochlorothiazide, a diuretic. Calcium channel blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are included as acceptable first-line alternatives and recommended as add-ons for patients with persistent, poorly controlled blood pressure. In this patient, lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, is recommended for first-line therapy since the patient has been told he has a previous history of kidney disease.



Clonidine (A) is a central alpha-2 agonist that is not recommended as first-line therapy for severe hypertension and is generally not recommended as a treatment for a true hypertensive emergency either. Clonidine therapy for hypertensive emergencies is only indicated for patients who have recently stopped taking the drug.

Hydrochlorothiazide (B), a diuretic, is recommended as first-line therapy for most patients but is not the best option for a patient with potential kidney disease.

Metoprolol (D), a beta-blocker, is not recommended as initial therapy for asymptomatic hypertension and is only used in hypertensive emergencies associated with acute coronary syndromes.

One Step Further

Which antihypertensive agent is recommended in a patient who presents to the emergency department with a hypertensive emergency related to cocaine overdose and intoxication?

Reveal Answer:

question: A 70-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance for the acute onset of severe right arm pain that woke him from sleep. He is unable to provide additional history due to pain. His HR is 140 bpm and irregular, BP is 180/120 mm Hg, and SpO2 is 94% on room air. Physical examination is significant for a cold and pale right upper extremity. Acoustic Doppler of the right upper extremity shows an absent pulse compared to a monophasic pulse in the left upper extremity. Point-of-care ultrasound reveals an irregularly irregular heartbeat but no other cardiac abnormalities. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient’s care?
englishExplanation:
Acute limb ischemia presents with the sudden onset of severe pain in one limb, usually in combination with an obvious perfusion deficit. Other components of the six Ps (pain, pallor, paralysis, pulse deficit, paresthesia, and poikilothermia) may also be present. Atraumatic acute limb ischemia is most commonly due to an embolus that arises from the atria in the setting of atrial fibrillation or thrombosis in a patient with severe peripheral arterial disease. Other etiologies of limb ischemia, such as venous occlusion and aortic dissection, are possible but rare, and patients typically do not present with the classic signs of limb ischemia in isolation. The first-line treatment for patients with acute limb ischemia includes a heparin bolus followed by an infusion. This therapy is traditionally performed even in patients for whom surgical or endovascular treatment is planned.



CT angiography (A) is typically performed after administering heparin to avoid delays in treatment. If aortic dissection or trauma is strongly suspected, angiography may occur before anticoagulation. An esmolol bolus (B) would be appropriate if this patient had an aortic dissection. The absence of chest pain, pericardial effusion, aortic root dilation on cardiac ultrasound, and any significant signs or symptoms outside of the affected limb is reassuring against a diagnosis of dissection. Vascular surgery consultation (C) is critical in all suspected cases of limb ischemia. However, initial treatment with heparin should not be delayed to obtain a consultation. Systemic thrombolytics (D) are not typically used for limb ischemia. In some cases, catheter-directed thrombolysis may be administered. Both systemic and local thrombolysis should only be initiated at the recommendation of a vascular surgeon.

One Step Further
Question:
What laboratory test is used to monitor anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin?

Reveal Answer:
The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT).

Embolism
Most common source is left heart; most common site is femoral artery bifurcation
Risks: recent MI or atrial fibrillation (usually lack of peripheral atherosclerosis)
Sx: sudden onset of pallor, paresthesias, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis, and pain out of proportion to exam (6 Ps)

Risks: atherosclerosis (lack of atrial fibrillation)

question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the ED after experiencing a syncopal episode. She reports that she has congenital long QT syndrome and has intermittent palpitations and shortness of breath. She was recently prescribed an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection, but she is unable to recall the name of it. While examining the patient, she reports recurrent palpitations, and the cardiac monitor reveals the rhythm above. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s dysrhythmia?
englishExplanation:
Long QT syndrome is a disorder characterized by prolongation of the QT interval on the ECG. QT prolongation can lead to ventricular dysrhythmias and subsequently, syncope or cardiac arrest. Long QT syndrome may be congenital or acquired and is associated with an increased risk of developing torsades de pointes, a characteristic, life-threatening cardiac dysrhythmia. Torsades de pointes (“twisting of the points”) is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the peaks of the QRS complexes appear to “twist” around the isoelectric line of the ECG. Certain classes of medications are a common cause of acquired long QT syndrome, including some antidysrhythmics, antimicrobials, and psychotropic medications. The clinical presentation of congenital long QT syndrome is variable. Some patients may be asymptomatic, while others may present with syncope or cardiac arrest. Dysrhythmias in patients with long QT syndrome may be triggered by multiple factors including exercise, stress, or medications. The medications known to cause QT prolongation may provoke dysrhythmias in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. The rhythm strip in the question above shows torsades de pointes in a patient with known congenital long QT syndrome. Ciprofloxacin is known to cause QT prolongation, should be avoided in patients with congenital long QT syndrome, and thus is the likely culprit.



Cephalexin (A), fosfomycin (C), and nitrofurantoin (D) are not known to cause QT prolongation.

One Step Further
Question:
Aside from fluoroquinolones, what are some other antibiotics with known risks for causing QT prolongation?

Reveal Answer:
Azithromycin, clarithromycin, and erythromycin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Torsades de Pointes

ECG: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation and QRS complex twisting around the isoelectric line
Most commonly caused by acquired or congenital long QT interval syndrome
Treatment
Unstable: immediate defibrillation
Stable: intravenous magnesium sulfate and discontinuation of the offending drug

question: Which of the following clinical manifestations carries the poorest prognosis for untreated aortic stenosis?
englishExplanation:
Multiple pathologic processes can lead to reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and resultant end organ dysfunction, but regardless of age, gender, or demographics, aortic stenosis is the most common cause of left ventricular outflow obstruction. The condition most commonly arises from degenerative calcification that occur over decades, with as many as 3% of patients over the age of 75 having some degree of stenosis. On physical exam, aortic stenosis is noted by a high-pitched systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border, which can radiate to the sternal notch and carotid arteries.

Insidious in its development, stenosis develops as calcification of the aortic valve over time without causing any discernible symptoms. As pressure increases in the left ventricle from progressive stenosis, concentric ventricular hypertrophy develops to compensate and preserve cardiac output. Gradually, this hypertrophy compromises myocardial oxygen supply due to decreased diastolic filling, ultimately decreasing coronary and systemic blood flow, which then manifests clinically. Early symptoms can range from exertional angina to decreased exercise tolerance and dyspnea on exertion. Afterload reduction with improved blood pressure control can be temporizing, but surgical intervention is vital once signs of severe stenosis develop. Of these clinical manifestations, the development of congestive heart failure carries the poorest prognosis and is indicative of an average life expectancy of 2 years without valve replacement.



When associated with aortic stenosis, angina pectoris (A) has a life expectancy of 5 years without valve replacement.

Atrial fibrillation (B)is a common dysrhythmia in patients with aortic stenosis, particularly once heart failure develops, but in and of itself does not carry prognostic value.

Syncope (D) indicates a slightly worse prognosis with an average life expectancy of 3 years without surgical intervention.

One Step Further

What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients under the age of 70?

Reveal Answer:
Congenital valve disease, such as a unicuspid or bicuspid aortic valve.

Murmur decreases with Valsalva
