In anterior leads (V2 and V3), ST segment elevation should be ≥ 1.5 mm in female patients, ≥ 2.0 mm in male patients ≥ 40 years, and ≥ 2.5 mm in male patients < 40 years
Treatment
Percutaneous coronary intervention: gold standard
Thrombolytic therapy
Aspirin
P2Y12 receptor blocker
Beta-blocker
Anticoagulation
Anterior wall ST elevation in leads V1 through V4
Inferior wall ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
Lateral wall ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6
Posterior wall ST depressions in leads V1 through V3 and elevations in leads V8 and V9

question: A 2-week-old boy presents with lethargy and a weak cry. At birth, there were no concerning signs or symptoms. He is tachycardic with poor central pulses, and his symptoms resolve after an infusion of alprostadil. Which of the following is the most likely cardiac defect in this patient?
englishExplanation:
The most common cause of shock in infants < 28 days old is sepsis. However, ductal-dependent congenital heart defects present similarly. These infants will be difficult to wake and will have decreased muscle tone, a prolonged capillary refill, and pallor, mottling, or cyanosis. The cyanosis in these cases can be from the patient’s cardiogenic shock or an underlying heart defect. Alprostadil is a prostaglandin that can reopen the ductus arteriosus and stabilize these patients, providing the key clue to the underlying diagnosis in this patient. Be ready to intubate such patients, as alprostadil can cause apnea.

Most congenital heart defects that depend on the ductus arteriosus to maintain systemic blood flow are obstructive. The left-sided congenital obstructive lesions that rely on the ductus are hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical aortic stenosis, and coarctation of the aorta. The right-sided congenital obstructive lesions are pulmonary atresia, pulmonary stenosis (including tetralogy of Fallot), and tricuspid atresia. Transposition of the great arteries is not a true obstructive process but also depends on the ductus to connect the pulmonary and systemic circulations.

Whether coarctation or other obstructive lesions are ductal dependent depends on the degree of obstruction. Patients with mild disease (e.g., mild pulmonary stenosis, mild coarctation of the aorta) will tolerate closure of the ductus, but those with critical and severe disease will not. Both coarctation of the aorta and a bicuspid aortic valve are more common in male patients and are associated with Turner syndrome. Coarctation is considered a lifelong disease even after surgical repair. Many of these patients will develop an aortic aneurysm or other aortic wall complications later in life.



An anomalous pulmonary venous return (A) is when the veins returning from the lungs attach to various locations. This is thought to be due to inappropriate involution of the collateral splanchnic venous plexus during development. One or more of these (e.g., partial or total anomalous pulmonary venous return) can attach to the vena cava, right atrium, innominate vein, or other venous structures. Depending on the degree of collaterals, these patients present with cyanosis and heart failure due to overcirculation when the pulmonary vascular resistance drops, but they do not rely on the ductus arteriosus for circulation.

An aortopulmonary window defect (B) occurs when there is a connection between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery. It is similar to a truncus arteriosus except that patients with this defect have an aortic and pulmonary valve. Depending on the size, these patients also present with heart failure due to overcirculation when the pulmonary vascular resistance drops, but they do not rely on the ductus for circulation.

An atrioventricular canal defect (C) involves an atrial septal defect, a ventricular septal defect, and abnormal mitral and tricuspid valves. This allows complete mixing of pulmonary and systemic blood and presents with cyanosis. These defects do not depend on the ductus for circulation.

Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) (E) is when the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left. This defect creates a separate circulation for the pulmonary and systemic systems. Unless there is mixing at the level of the atria, ventricles, or ductus, this defect cannot sustain life. TGA is a ductal-dependent lesion but universally presents with cyanosis at birth, which was not present in this patient.

One Step Further
Question:
What extracardiac defects are associated with coarctation of the aorta with a bicuspid aortic valve?

Reveal Answer:
Intracranial aneurysms.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Coarctation of the Aorta

Narrowing of descending aorta
Critical coarctation of the aorta: neonate, presents before 2 weeks when PDA closes with poor feeding, absent femoral pulses
Sx: headaches, dyspnea, leg claudication
PE: higher blood pressure in the arms than the legs, delayed femoral pulse
ECG: LVH
CXR: notching of ribs, three sign (indentation of aorta)
Dx: echocardiogram
Tx: prostaglandin E1 infusion to keep PDA open (neonate, critical coarctation), balloon angioplasty with stent placement or surgical correction
Associated with Turner syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, and intracranial aneurysms

question: A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department for fever and cough. His initial vital signs are a BP of 101/61 mm Hg, HR of 138 bpm, RR of 28/min, SpO2 of 86% on room air, and T of 38.1°C. His ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. He is started on an amiodarone infusion. His workup is also notable for a right lower lobe infiltrate on chest X-ray, for which he is started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. Several hours later, you are called to the bedside by the nurse due to an irregular rhythm on the monitor (shown above). He is obtunded and has a BP of 71/45 mm Hg. He has palpable pulses. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Increase the rate of the amiodarone infusion

englishExplanation:
This patient’s rhythm strip is consistent with torsades de pointes (TdP). TdP is a type of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PMVT) caused by prolonged QT. PMVT is characterized by a wide-complex tachycardia with variable QRS morphology from beat to beat. This patient was initiated on amiodarone and azithromycin, which are both QT-prolonging medications. His blood pressure and mental status are indicative of hemodynamic instability. Unstable PMVT is treated with defibrillation. Synchronized cardioversion is not performed for unstable TdP since it is difficult to synchronize with a polymorphic rhythm.



Epinephrine (B) would be indicated if this patient were pulseless, and furthermore, it would be indicated after defibrillation in pulseless ventricular tachycardia. This patient was started on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which was likely provoked by his current infection. Amiodarone is a QT-prolonging medication and likely contributed to the development of TdP, so increasing the rate of amiodarone infusion (C) may worsen his clinical status. Magnesium sulfate (D) is used to treat stable TdP. While it may be helpful for this patient, his current hemodynamic instability warrants defibrillation first. Potassium chloride (E) may be used for electrolyte repletion in the setting of hypokalemia. Hypokalemia may cause a prolonged QT interval. However, this patient’s QT prolongation is more likely due to his current medications.

One Step Further
Question:
Which antidysrhythmics are QT prolonging?

Reveal Answer:
Amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, procainamide, quinidine, and flecainide.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Torsades de Pointes

ECG: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation and QRS complex twisting around the isoelectric line
Most commonly caused by acquired or congenital long QT interval syndrome
Treatment
Unstable: immediate defibrillation
Stable: intravenous magnesium sulfate and discontinuation of the offending drug

question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the ED with palpitations. Vital signs are within normal limits. On cardiac auscultation, you note a regular rate and rhythm with a mid-systolic click. Her ECG shows normal sinus rhythm and laboratory tests are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Cardiothoracic surgery consult for operative repair

englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is suggestive of mitral valve prolapse, the most common valvular heart disease in the United States. In mitral valve prolapse, inherited defects in connective tissue proteins lead to myxomatous degeneration of one or both of the mitral valve leaflets, causing them to become floppy and billow backward into the left atrium. Most patients are asymptomatic, though associated symptoms can include atypical chest pain, palpitations, anxiety, and dyspnea. Most patients have a benign course, though in rare cases that progress to mitral regurgitation, mitral valve repair or replacement may be required. The classic finding on cardiac auscultation is the presence of a mid-systolic click. Maneuvers that decrease preload, such as the Valsalva maneuver or standing, cause the click to occur earlier, whereas maneuvers that increase preload, such as squatting, or increase afterload, such as handgrip, cause the click to occur later in systole. If mitral valve prolapse is suspected in the ED, referral for outpatient cardiology evaluation is indicated.



Cardiothoracic surgery consult for operative repair (A) is incorrect as most patients with mitral valve prolapse have a benign course and do not require surgery.

Hospital admission for cardiac monitoring (C) and emergent echocardiogram (B) are incorrect since outpatient workup is appropriate for suspected mitral valve prolapse.

One Step Further
Question:
What musculoskeletal findings can be associated with mitral valve prolapse?

Reveal Answer:
Scoliosis and pectus excavatum.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mitral Valve Prolapse

Presentation: palpitations, dyspnea, nonexertional chest pain, fatigue
Most cases are asymptomatic
PE will show midsystolic click and late systolic murmur, best heard at apex of heart
↑ preload → ↓ murmur
↓ preload → ↑ murmur
Association with Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos
Diagnosis is made on clinical exam and confirmed by echocardiography

question: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the emergency department with an acute onset of pressure-like, substernal chest pain that started 2 hours prior to arrival. His vital signs are T 98.6°F (37°C), HR 82 bpm, BP 150/85 mm Hg, RR 20/min, and SpO2 100% on room air. On exam, he is found to have diaphoresis. His ECG demonstrates new ST depressions in leads V5, V6, and II, compared to his previous ECG. His troponin I returns at 1.12 ng/mL. Serial ECGs demonstrate no change from the initial ED ECG. Despite multiple doses of sublingual nitroglycerin, aspirin administration, and a nitroglycerin infusion, the patient continues to have significant chest pain. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Admit the patient to the floor for serial troponins
Admit to the ICU and start a heparin infusion
Discharge the patient for outpatient stress testing

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and angina that is refractory to maximal medical therapy and should have an emergent cardiac catheterization performed. Medical therapy for the treatment of angina includes sublingual nitroglycerin and IV nitroglycerin for refractory cases. While emergent cardiac catheterization is generally reserved for patients with an ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) or STEMI equivalent, there are several indications for emergent cardiac catheterization for patients who do not meet STEMI criteria. These indications include, but are not limited to: NSTEMI with hemodynamic or electrical (ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation) instability, new onset heart failure, refractory angina, and select post-arrest patients. According to the AHA/ACC guidelines, immediate cardiac catheterization for the management of NSTEMI with refractory angina or hemodynamic or electrical instability is given class I level A evidence.



Discharging the patient (C) and admitting to the floor (A) are inappropriate dispositions in the setting of a patient with an NSTEMI with refractory angina. This patient likely will require admission to the ICU and a heparin infusion (B). However, the best next step in management is emergent cardiac catheterization.

One Step Further
Question:
In the setting of ST elevation myocardial infarction, what is the number needed to treat with aspirin to prevent one death?

Reveal Answer:
42.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Chest Pain

Stable angina: chest discomfort precipitated by activity but symptoms abate after rest
Unstable angina: ischemic symptoms suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome with or without ECG changes indicative of ischemia
NSTEMI: troponin elevation, ECG typically with ST depressions
STEMI: troponin elevation, ECG shows ST segment elevation
Atypical chest pain:
Female patients, older population, those with diabetes
Nausea or vomiting
Epigastric pain
Weakness
Chest pain absent in 12.5% of MI cases

question: Which of the following drugs may cause an exaggerated response to adenosine?
englishExplanation:
Adenosine is a naturally occurring purine nucleoside used primarily to terminate supraventricular tachycardia by slowing conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node. Adenosine exerts its electrophysiologic effects by binding to the A1 receptor on cardiac myocytes in the sinoatrial (SA) node, AV node, and atria. Activation of this G protein-coupled receptor leads to decreased cyclic adenosine monophosphate, increased potassium efflux, and decreased calcium influx. This causes decreased firing of pacemaker cells of the SA node and slowing of conduction through the AV node. Several drugs alter the effectiveness of adenosine. Dipyridamole is an antiplatelet agent that potentiates the effects of adenosine by inhibiting adenosine deaminase and blocking the reuptake of adenosine. The dose of adenosine should be reduced in patients who take dipyridamole. In contrast, methylxanthines, such as caffeine and theophylline, antagonize the adenosine receptor in a dose-dependent manner. Thus, patients taking these drugs may require higher doses of adenosine.



Caffeine (A) antagonizes the adenosine receptor and can inhibit the effectiveness of adenosine.

Metoprolol (C) is a beta-blocker commonly used to control heart rate in patients with rapid atrial fibrillation. While it does slow conduction through the AV node by inhibiting beta-1 adrenergic receptors, it does not interact with adenosine or the adenosine receptor. Patients taking beta-blockers do not require an adjusted dose of adenosine.

Theophylline (D) is a methylxanthine that antagonizes the adenosine receptor, thereby reducing the effectiveness of adenosine.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: adenosine is safe for the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia in pregnant patients.

Reveal Answer:
True.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) or Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT)

Common types include
Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT)
Atrial tachycardia
Most commonly caused by a reentrant pathway in the atrioventricular node
Clinical
Infants: poor feeding, fussiness, irritability
Older children: palpitations, chest pain, fatigue
Adults: palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath
PE: abrupt onset of tachycardia
Ventricular rate often 160–220 bpm in adults
HR > 180–220 bpm in children
HR up to 300 bpm in infants
Dx: ECG shows regular narrow complex tachycardia (P waves can be obscured at high HRs)
Stress testing or ambulatory monitoring may be needed
Tx: vagal maneuvers, drug therapy (adenosine), cardioversion
Can be associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

question: A 66-year-old woman presents with generalized weakness and dyspnea on exertion for 2 weeks. Vital signs are BP 80/45 mm Hg, HR 40 bpm, RR 16/min, and SpO2 97% on room air. Her rhythm strip is shown above. There are no other ST-segment abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Aspirin, heparin, and admission for acute coronary syndrome
Observation and arrangements for follow-up with cardiology

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with an unstable bradycardia and an ECG demonstrating second-degree type II heart block (Mobitz II). She should have a transcutaneous pacemaker placed and considered for a transvenous pacemaker. Second-degree atrioventricular (AV) blocks are characterized by the presence of one or more sinus impulses that do not conduct to the ventricles. There are two types of second-degree AV block. In type I (Wenckebach or Mobitz I) the ECG demonstrates a progressive lengthening of the PR interval and an eventual nonconducted P wave (dropped beat). In type II (Mobitz II) AV block, the ECG demonstrates dropped beats that are not preceded by lengthening of the PR interval. Whereas type I second-degree AV block typically requires no treatment, second-degree type II (Mobitz II) usually requires placement of a pacemaker even if the patient is asymptomatic.



New second-degree AV blocks may be caused by ischemia (A), but this patient is hypotensive and bradycardia, and the next intervention is to address her cardiac status by placing a transcutaneous pacemaker with conversion to a transvenous pacemaker.

Cardiac catheterization (B) is not required emergently as the patient does not demonstrate an ST elevation myocardial infarction.

The patient should be seen by a cardiologist while being monitored in the hospital, not as an outpatient (C), as this is a potentially lethal bradydysrhythmia.

One Step Further
Question:
What treatment is recommended for first-degree atrioventricular block?

Reveal Answer:
No specific treatment is needed for this entity.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Second-Degree Heart Block (Mobitz II)

PR interval will be fixed and consistent
Notable feature: dropped QRS beats
Immediate transcutaneous pacer pad placement with consideration for transvenous pacemaker
Can progress to complete heart block

question: A 36-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department with left leg swelling and pain. Duplex ultrasonography shows evidence of a 4 cm thrombus in one of the superficial tributary veins of the left leg with some vein wall thickening. What is the most appropriate next step in care?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis and requires nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for treatment. Thrombosis and phlebitis of the superficial veins are generally benign and can be treated with conservative care. Risk factors for superficial thrombophlebitis include intrinsic hypercoagulable states, varicose veins, intravenous catheter use, pregnancy, and history of vein excision or ablation. Uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis is considered low risk for progressive thromboembolic disease and can be characterized by venous segment involvement < 5 cm, being remote from the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions, and lack of medical risk factors for hypercoagulability. Initial treatment for uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis includes NSAIDs, extremity elevation, and compression therapy.

Complicated superficial thrombophlebitis carries a higher risk for progressive thromboembolic disease and refers to vein thrombosis > 5 cm, within 5 cm of a deep vein, recurrent or migratory thrombophlebitis, or suppurative thrombophlebitis. These patients require treatment with anticoagulation. Often, these situations may also require antibiotic administration or vein ligation.



Antibiotic therapy (A) is recommended for patients with suppurative thrombophlebitis, who often present with fevers, fluctuance, or purulent drainage.

Anticoagulation (B) is recommended for complicated superficial thrombophlebitis, given its risk of progressive thromboembolic disease, but is not indicated for uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis.

Vein ligation (D) of uncomplicated superficial thrombophlebitis leads to a higher risk of developing venous thromboembolism when compared to supportive care. However, in some cases of recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis, vein ligation may be required after the acute inflammation has subsided.

One Step Further
Question:
What type of cancer is associated with migratory thrombophlebitis?

Reveal Answer:
Pancreatic cancer.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Superficial Vein Thrombosis

Thrombosis of the axial veins (e.g., great saphenous, anterior accessory saphenous, small saphenous veins)
Risks: varicose veins, intravenous drug use, and hypercoagulability (e.g., pregnancy, malignancy)
PE: erythema and pain along the inner medial thigh
Dx: duplex ultrasound
Tx: depends on location, medical risk factors, and amount of vein involvement (> or < 5 cm)
Uncomplicated and low risk: NSAIDs and serial duplex ultrasound
Uncomplicated and intermediate or high risk: anticoagulation
Complicated or recurrent disease may require ligation or excision
Compression stockings may prevent reoccurrence

question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after having a syncopal episode while playing basketball. Vital signs are unremarkable. Physical examination is pertinent for a systolic murmur, best auscultated along the left sternal border. This murmur is worsened with standing and improves with hand grip. An ECG is performed. Which of the following ECG findings is most consistent with the patient’s likely diagnosis?

options.text: Deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V4–V6
Positive ECG deflection after the QRS segment in leads V1–V3
rsR’ with ST segment elevation followed by a downsloping inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2
Short PR interval followed by a slurred QR segment

correctAnswer: Deep Q waves in leads I, aVL, and V4–V6
englishExplanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy results in a dynamic and fixed subvalvular obstruction as a result of hypertrophy of the ventricular outflow tract. Exertional syncope is a common presentation, and this diagnosis must be considered in all cases of exertion-related syncope. The earlier the onset of symptoms, the greater the risk of mortality. A loud crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur may be heard at the left sternal border. The ECG is abnormal in the majority of cases, with left ventricular hypertrophy as the most common finding. Deep, dagger-like Q waves have also been described in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Diagnosis is excluded or confirmed with echocardiography. Patients should be advised against playing competitive sports to reduce the risk of sudden death. Beta-blockers are the mainstay of treatment with septal reduction surgery being used in severe cases.



Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, formerly known as arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, occurs when fibrous replacement of the myocardium results in a dilated right ventricle causing poor contraction. An epsilon wave, a positive ECG deflection after the QRS segment in leads V1–V3 (B), can be seen on ECG. Other ECG findings are T wave inversions and a prolonged S wave upstroke. Presenting symptoms can include congestive heart failure, cardiomegaly, and syncope or sudden cardiac death.

Brugada syndrome is an inherited disorder of myocardial depolarization that is caused by a sodium channelopathy. It is characterized on ECG by rsR’ with ST segment elevation followed by a downsloping inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2 (C).

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) is a ventricular preexcitation syndrome caused by an accessory conduction pathway. Patients with WPW are prone to a variety of supraventricular tachydysrhythmias. The ECG demonstrates a short PR interval followed by a slurred QR segment (D), which is classically called the delta wave.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: squatting will decrease the intensity of the murmur associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Reveal Answer:
True. Squatting will decrease the intensity, as will anything that increases preload or afterload.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy

Autosomal dominant, first-degree relatives
May present as sudden death in a young athlete
Sx: dyspnea on exertion (most common), syncope, orthopnea, chest pain, palpitations
PE: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that increases in intensity with Valsalva maneuver and decreases with squatting
Dx
ECG: repolarization changes, large-amplitude QRS, narrow deep Q waves inferior and lateral
Echocardiography: LVH with septal hypertrophy
Tx: refrain from vigorous physical activity, ICD for high-risk patients
Options for symptomatic patients: beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, myosin inhibitors (second-line)

question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the ED by EMS after she was found unresponsive. She was pulseless upon EMS arrival, and they immediately began high-quality CPR. Multiple rhythm checks showed ventricular fibrillation, and the patient received multiple rounds of defibrillation at 2 J/kg and 4 J/kg. She was also given a bolus of 5 mg/kg of IV amiodarone after a third defibrillation. CPR is continued upon arrival in the ED, and the subsequent rhythm check again shows ventricular fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
englishExplanation:
While ventricular fibrillation (Vfib) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT) are uncommon presenting rhythms for pediatric patients with cardiac arrest, children who present with these rhythms have more favorable prognoses than those with nonshockable rhythms. Patients who are in cardiac arrest should immediately be treated with high-quality CPR as soon as the arrest is identified. This consists of compressing the chest at least one-third of the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest and allowing for complete chest recoil between compressions to allow adequate filling of the cardiac chambers. Because cardiac arrest in children is most often a consequence of respiratory failure, there should be a particular focus on support of the airway, oxygenation, and ventilation.

Defibrillation for Vfib or pVT should be performed as soon as possible after identification of arrest, starting at a dose of 2 J/kg. If a second defibrillation is required, it should be performed at 4 J/kg and any further attempts should be at ≥ 4 J/kg and up to 10 J/kg. Beginning after the second defibrillation attempt, IV or IO epinephrine should be given every 3–5 minutes at a dose of 0.01 mg/kg, which equates to 0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000 concentration. If IV or IO access is not established, endotracheal epinephrine may be given at a dose of 0.1 mg/kg. If three defibrillation attempts are unsuccessful, antidysrhythmic agents should also be given with amiodarone 5 mg/kg or lidocaine 1 mg/kg.



12 J/kg (B) and 15 J/kg (C) are well above the recommended 10 J/kg for this scenario.

4 J/kg (D) is below the 10 J/kg that is recommended for further defibrillation attempts for pediatric patients in cardiac arrest due to Vfib, especially since the patient has already received multiple shocks at 2 J/kg and 4 J/kg.

Dual sequential defibrillation (E) is an emerging strategy for the treatment of patients with refractory Vfib, but data are lacking in the pediatric population, and it is not recommended at this point.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the recommended prehospital airway management strategy for pediatric cardiac arrest?

Reveal Answer:
Bag-mask ventilation, as observational studies have shown reduced survival with advanced airway techniques, presumably due to extended pauses in compressions.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pediatric Advanced Life Support: Pulseless Arrest

CPR + bag-mask ventilation
Chest compressions
15:2 (prepuberty) and 30:2 (postpuberty) if no advanced airway
100–120/min
At least one-third chest wall depth
Use thumb-encircling hands technique
Advanced airway: continuous chest compressions, breath every 2–3 seconds
Shockable rhythm: 2 J/kg, 4 J/kg, epinephrine every 3–5 minutes, amiodarone, lidocaine
Nonshockable rhythm: CPR and epinephrine ASAP, then every 3–5 minutes

question: Which of the following is the most common complication in patients with endocarditis?
englishExplanation:
Infective endocarditis is a spectrum of diseases causing infection of the various heart valves. These infections produce large, bulky, irregular vegetations resulting in destruction and perforations of the involved valve. Up to 70% of patients with endocarditis develop congestive heart failure. This is largely due to the spread of infection in cardiac tissue, causing distortion of valve leaflets, rupture of chordae tendineae, or perforation of the cardiac chamber. More than 50% of patients will present with a cardiac murmur. Dysrhythmia is another important cardiac manifestation of infective endocarditis. Risk factors for infective endocarditis include pre-existing valvular pathology, immunodeficiency states, and use of long-term IV infusions (IV drug misuse or long-term indwelling catheters). Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism affecting native heart valves, while viridans streptococci is the most common group of organisms affecting previously diseased valves. Prosthetic valves, on the other hand, are most commonly infected by coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species, such as S. epidermidis. Infective endocarditis most commonly involves the left-sided valves of the heart, except in patients with IV drug abuse in which right-sided valves are frequently infected as well.



Central nervous system (CNS) complications of endocarditis, such as meningitis (B) and seizure (D), are less common than cardiac complications. Up to 40% of patients experience CNS complications, the most common of which are cerebral ischemic events. Embolic stroke in the middle cerebral artery is the most common CNS manifestation.

Pulmonary infarction (C) is a potential complication of endocarditis, but it is not the most common. Endocarditis can cause arterial embolization and ischemia or abscess formation in virtually any organ system.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the blood culture-negative organisms that are associated with endocarditis?

Reveal Answer:
Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella (HACEK group).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bacterial Endocarditis

Risk factors: injection drug use, valvular heart disease
Sx & syndromes:
Mild and nonspecific febrile illness - fever, rash, cough, and myalgias
Acute heart failure
Focal neurological deficit from septic cerebral embolus
Altered mental status
Axial spine pain from osteomyelitis
Pneumonia from septic pulmonary emboli
PE: fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, murmur, Janeway lesions, anemia, nailbed hemorrhages, emboli (FROM JANE)
Dx: echocardiography and Duke criteria
Most commonly caused by:
IVDA: Staphylococcus aureus, tricuspid
Native valve: Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci (most common in previously diseased), mitral
GI malignancy: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis)
Tx: antibiotics
Dental prophylaxis indicated in some cases

question: A 32-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort that has worsened over the last 2 days. She had a mild upper respiratory infection last week but otherwise reports no significant medical history. She does not take any medications and reports no illicit drug use. On examination, vital signs show T 37.9°C, HR 132 bpm, BP 100/60 mm Hg, RR 16/min, and SpO2 98% on room air. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Chest radiograph demonstrates mild cardiomegaly without infiltrates. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST segment and T wave changes. Troponin I is 0.25 ng/mL. What is the likely cause of her symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient has findings concerning for myocarditis, an inflammatory disease of the myocardium. In resource-rich countries, viruses are most frequently implicated (e.g., H1N1 influenza virus, coronavirus [SARS-CoV-2], parvovirus B19, human herpes virus 6, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV), but it can also be caused by bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and helminths. Presentation is variable depending on the etiology and stage of the disease. Fatigue, fever, chest discomfort, dyspnea, and palpitations are common presenting symptoms in adults. Patients with advanced disease may present with dysrhythmias, heart failure, and cardiogenic shock. On physical exam, there may be tachycardia disproportionate to fever or discomfort, an S3 or S4 gallop, and signs of fluid overload. A friction rub may be heard because pericarditis often occurs concomitantly with myocarditis. The ECG is often abnormal, with changes including sinus tachycardia and widened QRS interval. There may be regional ST elevations that mimic acute myocardial infarction. Findings suggestive of pericarditis (e.g., diffuse ST elevation with PR segment depression) may also be present. Troponin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and white blood cell count may also be elevated but are not diagnostic. An echocardiogram will show decreased ventricular ejection fraction with hypokinesis and wall motion abnormalities. Endomyocardial biopsy has long been the gold standard for diagnosis but is being replaced with cardiovascular MRI.



Acute coronary artery thrombosis (A) can present with fatigue, chest pain, and dyspnea but is less likely in a young woman with no risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

Community-acquired pneumonia (B) typically presents with fever, cough, and dyspnea. Patients may be febrile and hypoxic, and chest X-ray will show an infiltrate.

Pulmonary embolism (D) may also present with dyspnea, chest pain, and tachycardia, but symptoms are typically more acute in presentation. This patient is also not tachypneic or hypoxic and has no noted risk factors for thromboembolic disease.

question: A 12-year-old boy presents to the ED after syncope. He is awake and alert on arrival. His heart rate is 180 bpm on the monitor. His 12-lead ECG is shown above. He has no significant medical history or prior surgeries. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his syncopal episode?
englishExplanation:
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is an elevated heart rate (often > 180 bpm in pediatric patients) originating in the atria somewhere other than the sinus node. Most of the time it is due to atrioventricular (AV) node reentry. On ECG, the QRS complex is usually regular, narrow, and rapid. P waves are often hidden within the QRS complexes. The occurrence of paroxysmal SVT peaks in late teens and young adults. The most common cause of syncope from SVT in pediatric patients is AV reentry tachycardia via an accessory pathway. SVT can lead to syncope if cardiac filling is impaired. Conditions such as Ebstein anomaly and surgically corrected transposition of the great arteries can cause episodic SVT. It can be difficult for clinicians to differentiate sinus tachycardia from SVT in children. SVT is more likely than sinus tachycardia if the rate is sustained > 220 bpm in an infant (> 180 bpm in a child) and is out of proportion to clinical status. Vagal maneuvers are often effective at terminating the dysrhythmia. If ineffective, adenosine is recommended to convert to sinus rhythm. Electrical cardioversion is indicated for patients who are hemodynamically unstable without IV access.



Dehydration (A), fever (B), pain, hemorrhage, sepsis, toxic ingestion, hyperthyroidism, or iatrogenic medication can cause high-rate sinus tachycardia.

It is the surgical correction of great vessel transposition (C), not the condition itself, that can cause episodic SVT.

One Step Further
Question:
How is the diving reflex performed on infants for supraventricular tachycardia?

Reveal Answer:
Place a bag of ice and water over the nose and face for 15–30 seconds.

question: A 72-year-old woman presents to the ED with syncope. She was walking across her home when she had mild chest pain and then passed out. She reports intermittent chest pain and shortness of breath, particularly when walking, that has worsened over the last month. Vital signs show a BP of 148/119 mm Hg, HR of 90 bpm, RR of 16 /min, and T of 37.3°C (99.1°F). On exam, she has a late-peaking systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Which of the following medications is the best choice to treat hypertension in a patient like this?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation of exertional chest pain, syncope, and a late-peaking systolic murmur radiating to the carotids indicates severe aortic stenosis. In this setting, careful blood pressure treatment is essential. Lisinopril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, is preferred for its afterload-reducing effect, which can improve cardiac output without significantly lowering preload or causing reflex tachycardia. It should be started at low doses and titrated cautiously.

Aortic stenosis is a prevalent valvular heart disease in adults > 65 years, characterized by progressive narrowing of the aortic valve orifice, which impedes left ventricular outflow during systole. This condition frequently coexists with cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, tobacco use, hypercholesterolemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Globally, rheumatic heart disease remains a significant etiologic contributor, particularly in regions with limited health care resources. In the early stages, patients are typically asymptomatic due to compensatory concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, which maintains cardiac output despite increased afterload. However, over time, this adaptive mechanism leads to impaired ventricular compliance, diastolic dysfunction, and increased myocardial oxygen demand.

As the valvular obstruction worsens, stroke volume declines, and both systemic perfusion and coronary blood flow are compromised. The classic symptom triad (dyspnea, angina, and exertional syncope) reflects progressive hemodynamic deterioration. Heart failure, particularly with preserved ejection fraction initially, signals advanced disease and portends a poor prognosis without valve replacement.

On physical examination, clinicians often identify a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur best heard at the right upper sternal border (second intercostal space), frequently radiating to the carotid arteries. Additional findings may include a soft or absent second heart sound and a parvus et tardus carotid pulse (diminished and delayed upstroke). Echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice, enabling direct assessment of valve anatomy, gradient severity, and ventricular function.

Treating comorbid conditions such as hypertension and heart failure in this population requires careful consideration. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, such as lisinopril, are considered safe and effective in patients with preserved hemodynamics, but should be initiated at low doses with cautious titration to avoid hypotension. Definitive treatment involves surgical aortic valve replacement or transcatheter aortic valve implantation in patients who are high-risk surgical candidates.



Furosemide (A) reduces preload and can precipitate hypotension and syncope in patients with aortic stenosis, where cardiac output is preload-dependent.

Hydralazine (B) is a direct vasodilator that lowers afterload abruptly and may worsen outflow obstruction or cause reflex tachycardia, increasing myocardial oxygen demand.

Metoprolol (D) slows the heart rate, which can be helpful in some cardiac conditions, but in severe aortic stenosis, it may lower cardiac output and exacerbate symptoms.

One Step Further
Question:
How long after the procedure does it take patients with aortic stenosis who have received percutaneous aortic balloon dilation to develop restenosis and clinical deterioration?

Reveal Answer:
6–12 months.

question: A 44-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain that occurs spontaneously with no clear provocation. He has a history of high blood pressure. His initial ECG and troponin are unremarkable. Upon further discussion with the patient regarding possible outpatient evaluation, he reports significant anxiety about having a heart attack and would like further testing more urgently. Which of the following further testing options would be most appropriate in this patient and rule out underlying coronary artery disease with a high negative predictive value?
englishExplanation:
The evaluation of chest pain can be challenging and costly in the emergency department. Given the high morbidity and mortality of missed acute coronary syndrome, many clinicians will use tools such as the history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponin (HEART) score to risk stratify patients and, in appropriate candidates, cardiac stress testing will be performed. However, cardiac stress testing can have low sensitivity, is time consuming, and often keeps patients in the hospital overnight, taking up hospital beds.

Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is a high-resolution and noninvasive method of assessing the coronary arteries. It has a high negative predictive value and can be used to risk stratify patients. Negative CCTA without concerning findings can support discharging a patient for further outpatient care. However, CCTA that is positive does not clearly delineate the clinical path forward. The significance of the anatomic lesions on CCTA does not always correlate to needing further intervention. Moreover, the study can be technically challenging to perform and interpret, and there is the risk of false positive results that result in increased unnecessary additional medical workup. While CCTA can be used to determine which patients may be safe to go home from the emergency department, has excellent visualization of the coronary anatomy, and can suggest the likelihood of ischemia based on the severity of coronary artery lesions, it does not directly measure myocardial perfusion or ischemia. Functional testing or clinical evaluation is required for this determination. Generally, the use parameters for CCTA are: do not use for a definite myocardial infarction, appropriate to use and further risk stratify for low-to-medium risk chest pain, and unclear to use in the case of high-probability coronary artery disease and chest pain caused by ischemia.

While CCTA has numerous advantages, it is not suitable for all patients. For people with known severe coronary artery disease (CAD), significant kidney impairment, or contraindications to iodinated contrast, alternative diagnostic approaches may be warranted. CCTA requires a heart rate within normal limits for optimal image acquisition. Patients with dysrhythmias may need pretest medication to control their heart rate and might not be ideal candidates for this test.



Cardiac catheterization (A) would be the gold standard test for assessing this patient’s coronary arteries but would be highly invasive and not clearly indicated in this patient. It is less suitable as an initial diagnostic test in patients with low to intermediate risk of CAD and unremarkable initial evaluations. It is typically reserved for patients for whom noninvasive testing has confirmed significant CAD or those with a high pretest probability of severe CAD, especially if revascularization is being considered based on clinical symptoms or other test results.

Exercise stress testing (C) is less likely to be useful in this patient without exertional symptoms. An exercise stress test assesses the heart’s response to physical activity and can indicate the presence of CAD by revealing symptoms or changes in the ECG during exercise. However, its sensitivity and specificity are lower compared to CCTA, meaning it might miss CAD in some patients or suggest CAD in those without it. It is particularly less informative in patients with a normal baseline ECG and troponin levels, like the scenario described. Moreover, exercise stress testing does not provide anatomical details of coronary arteries, which are crucial for definitive diagnosis and treatment planning.

Serial troponins (D) can be used to assess for acute myocardial ischemia causing troponin elevation but would not be useful in detecting underlying CAD not causing troponin elevation. Serial troponins do not provide information about the presence or severity of underlying CAD, which is the question’s focus. They are a diagnostic tool for acute conditions, not for assessing chronic CAD risk or the need for long-term management strategies.

One Step Further
Question:
How does a myocardial perfusion imaging scan work?

Reveal Answer:
Technetium-99m sestamibi travels into the myocardium in proportion to myocardial blood flow, delineating the more poorly perfused areas.

question: A 58-year-old man presents for evaluation of fatigue and shortness of breath for the last 2 months. Vital signs include a blood pressure of 135/85 mm Hg, heart rate of 40 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. His ECG is shown above. Which of the following best describes the rhythm seen?
englishExplanation:
Third-degree, or complete, heart block is characterized by absent conduction of all atrial impulses and complete electrical atrioventricular (AV) dissociation. The hallmark findings of third-degree AV heart block are regular P-P intervals unrelated to regular R-R intervals with P waves that appear to march through the QRST complexes. There are two independent pacemakers: one in the sinoatrial node and one either in the AV junction (narrow QRS complexes) or within the Purkinje fibers in the ventricles (wide QRS complexes).

Most patients will present with some degree of symptoms, though severity may vary. Typical symptoms include fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, syncope or presyncope, and sudden cardiac arrest. Patients who are hemodynamically unstable require immediate treatment with atropine and typically temporary pacing as well. A permanent pacemaker is indicated for most patients, though reversible causes (e.g., myocardial infarction, hypothyroidism) should be excluded first.



First-degree heart block (B) is defined by normal AV conduction with a prolonged PR interval (> 200 msec). There is a 1:1 relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.

In a junctional rhythm (C), the QRS complex is narrow (unless there is baseline QRS conduction aberrancy), and the rate is typically between 40 and 60 bpm. P waves may be negative or hidden within the QRS complex.

In Mobitz I (D), the PR interval progressively lengthens and the R-R interval progressively shortens until a beat is dropped. This cycle repeats itself, producing a pattern of grouped beating.

In Mobitz II (E), the PR interval is constant, but there are nonconducted P waves that lead to dropped beats. This block can deteriorate into third-degree heart block.

One Step Further
Question:
What effect will the administration of atropine have on third-degree heart block?

Reveal Answer:
It alters conduction ratios without changing the appearance of the ventricular escape rhythm.

question: A G10P9 woman at 39 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department in active labor. Within a minute of her arrival, she delivers a baby girl. The baby is covered in meconium, is blue and limp, and is not breathing. After warming, drying, and stimulating the baby, there is no change. The baby is placed on the monitor and has a heart rate of 77 bpm. Positive-pressure ventilation is initiated with room air and a peak inspiratory pressure of 20 cm H2O. After 15 seconds of positive pressure ventilation, there is no chest rise or change in the heart rate. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Continuing for a full 30 seconds, then reassessing
CPR with a compression to ventilation ratio of 3:1

englishExplanation:
The need for neonatal resuscitation can be difficult to predict, especially in a precipitous delivery in the emergency department. In the first 30–60 seconds after birth, it is essential for the clinician to warm, dry, and stimulate the baby. Neonates who are spontaneously breathing and who have good tone should receive routine newborn care and cord management. In non-breathing neonates, clinicians should provide additional stimulation by firmly rubbing their backs. If this is unsuccessful, performing a jaw thrust and placing a towel beneath the shoulders to open the airway is suggested. In the next 30 seconds, the heart rate and respiratory effort should be assessed. In neonates with a heart rate > 100 bpm but inadequate respiratory effort (e.g., cyanosis or labored breathing), clinicians should provide supplemental oxygen, as needed, and target an appropriate preductal oxygen saturation based on time after birth—remember that it takes > 10 minutes for a neonate to achieve an oxygen saturation of 100%.

For those with a heart rate < 100 bpm or apnea, positive pressure ventilation with room air oxygen can improve hemodynamic status. A T-piece or a flow-inflating bag can help to administer 30–60/min and will monitor peak inspiratory pressures. Peak inspiratory pressures of 20 cm H2O are a good starting point based on older guidelines, but at times, pressure as high as 40 cm H2O may be needed. The newest 2025 guidelines recommend a peak inspiratory pressure of 25 cm H2O. Adequate positive pressure ventilation should lead to an increase in heart rate and chest rise, improvement in cyanosis, and the baby may begin to breathe independently. If there is a considerable improvement, the baby may be taken off positive pressure ventilation and continue with routine newborn care.

Newborns who do not improve as fast will need continuous positive pressure ventilation. Most neonates will respond favorably to these initial steps, but if no improvement is seen, the next step is to optimize the positive pressure ventilation being provided. Adjust the mask to ensure it is sealed properly. Open the mouth with a jaw thrust and place the patient in the sniffing position. Suction the mouth and nose if an obstruction is seen. Increase the peak inspiratory pressure until chest rise is seen. In this patient, the initial peak inspiratory pressure of 20 cm H2O is reasonable, but no chest rise is seen, so the clinician should quickly titrate up until there is chest rise. If these steps are unsuccessful after 30 seconds of optimized positive pressure ventilation, proceed with endotracheal intubation. Also, if the heart rate remains < 60 bpm after 30 seconds of adequate positive pressure ventilation, CPR should be started.



Continuing current treatments (A) should only be done if there is a noticeable improvement. Neonatal care is often broken down into 30-second blocks, but the clinician should not wait for the time to elapse before making the necessary adjustments to unsuccessful treatments, especially in this setting of no chest rise.

While quickly proceeding to CPR with a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 3:1 (B) is important during neonatal resuscitation when the HR is < 60 bpm, the first step should be adequate positive pressure ventilation. Since this patient’s positive pressure ventilation was not adequate (i.e., no chest rise), adjustments should be made over the next 15 seconds, and if this remains unsuccessful, endotracheal intubation (C) and CPR should be considered.

Increasing supplemental oxygen to 100% (E), or any excessive oxygenation level in neonates, is associated with increased mortality. Neonatal resuscitation should start with room air oxygen. If more oxygen is needed, carefully titrate up the oxygen concentration to target the expected preductal oxygen saturation based on time after birth.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: naloxone should be given to neonates with respiratory depression who are born to mothers with recent opioid exposure.

Reveal Answer:
False. Naloxone can precipitate dangerous seizure activity in neonates and does not improve neonatal respiratory depression.

question: Which patient below is at greatest risk for developing a major adverse cardiac event per the HEART score?

options.text: 40-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, a 20-pack-year smoking history, and nonspecific repolarization on ECG
50-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and a normal ECG
60-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, family history of coronary artery disease, and nonspecific repolarization on ECG
70-year-old with a history of coronary artery disease and diabetes mellitus with a normal ECG

correctAnswer: 60-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, family history of coronary artery disease, and nonspecific repolarization on ECG
englishExplanation:
Chest pain is a common chief concern in the emergency department and accounts for over 6 million visits per year. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) accounts for only 12–15% of all cases. ACS is considered when there is evidence of myocardial ischemia or infarction and includes ST elevation myocardial infarction, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and unstable angina (UA). The first two are characterized by certain ECG findings or a rise in serum troponins. UA is typically a clinical diagnosis based on history, physical, dynamic ECG changes, or inducible ischemia on stress testing. Based on the patient’s history, physical examination, ECG, and laboratory evaluation, patients are assigned low, intermediate, or high risk for ACS. Risk tools have been created and validated in an attempt to help determine which patients are at low, intermediate, or high risk for major adverse cardiac events (MACE). The

HEART score is a commonly used tool in the United States that has been validated in the Netherlands as well as the United States when using two sets of troponins 3 hours apart. The HEART score consists of the history, ECG, age, risk factors, and troponins. History can be low, moderate, or highly suspicious, with each type of history respectively corresponding to 0, 1, or 2 points. The ECG can be normal, nonspecific repolarization, and ST depression, with each type of ECG finding respectively corresponding to 0, 1, or 2 points. The age ranges are < 45, 45–64, and ≥ 65 years of age, with each age range respectively corresponding to 0, 1, or 2 points. Risk factors can range from no known risk factors (0 points), one to two risk factors (1 point), and three or more risk factors (2 points). Risk factors include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, smoking, and a family history of cardiovascular disease. Lastly, troponins are either normal, one to two times normal, or greater than two times normal, with each category respectively corresponding to 0, 1, or 2 points.

Scores 0–3 are considered low risk with a MACE risk of 0.9–1.7%. Scores 4–6 are considered moderate risk with a MACE risk of 12–16%. Scores ≥ 7 are considered high risk with a MACE risk of 50–65%. Patients identified as low risk can be discharged home with primary care follow-up. Patients at moderate or high risk warrant observation or admission for further evaluation. The patient above is 60 years old (1 point) with three known risk factors (2 points) and nonspecific repolarization noted on ECG (1 point). This gives him a HEART score of 4, placing him at moderate risk of MACE at 12–16% even without knowing the present illness history or the troponins.



A 40-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, a 20-pack-year smoking history, and nonspecific repolarization on ECG (A); 50-year-old with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and a normal ECG (B); and 70-year-old with a history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and diabetes mellitus with a normal ECG (D) all have scores of 3 (CAD by itself is not one of the risk factors in the original study). These scores are based on age, risk factors, and ECG findings from the HEART scoring tool. A history of CAD alone does not count as a risk factor per the HEART score. With these findings alone, these patients would be considered low risk for MACE at 0.9–1.7%. This does not take into account the history or a set of troponins, and thus these patients may still be at intermediate or high risk.

question: A 70-year-old man presents to the emergency department with black stools for 3 days. He has conjunctival pallor and dry mucous membranes. His vital signs are T 98.9°F (37.2°C), RR 18/min, HR 130 bpm, BP 96/50 mm Hg. After the nurse obtains two large-bore intravenous lines, the patient becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse. The monitor shows sinus rhythm with a rate of 80 bpm. Chest compressions are initiated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
This patient is in cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA). Management includes high-quality chest compressions at a rate of 100 compressions/minute and epinephrine every 3–5 minutes as needed while searching for and treating reversible causes (GI bleeding in this case). These causes include hypothermia, hypoxemia, hypovolemia, hyperkalemia, coronary or pulmonary thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, toxic ingestion, cardiac tamponade, and severe acidosis. Epinephrine 1 mg IV is given every 3–5 minutes until a perfusing organized cardiac rhythm and return of spontaneous circulation is achieved, or the patient converts to a rhythm requiring defibrillation. PEA is considered a nonshockable rhythm, meaning that defibrillation is not indicated.



Amiodarone (A) is not recommended in the setting of PEA.

Defibrillation with 200 J (B) is incorrect, as this is only indicated in the setting of ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

Orotracheal intubation (D) should be attempted as soon as feasible to establish a secure airway in the setting of cardiac arrest. However, oxygen may be delivered by other means (e.g., bag-valve mask ventilation) while CPR is being performed and medications are being delivered.

What coronary artery anomaly is most associated with sudden cardiac death?

question: You attend to the vaginal delivery of a newborn girl who is born at 40 weeks gestation. Upon delivery, you note meconium-stained amniotic fluid. On physical examination, the respiratory rate is 77/min, the heart rate is 110 bpm, and there is nasal flaring and intercostal retractions along with peeling skin and decreased vernix. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This postmature newborn is exhibiting signs consistent with meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). It is defined as respiratory distress in newborn infants born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) whose symptoms cannot be otherwise explained. MAS involves intrauterine passage of meconium, aspiration, and pulmonary disease that results in hypoxemia and acidosis. Clinical features include a history of MSAF or evidence of meconium staining on physical examination. Depending upon how long the infant has been exposed in utero, the vernix, umbilical cord, and nails may be meconium-stained. Affected infants are usually postmature or small for gestational age. Infants with MAS typically have respiratory distress with marked tachypnea and cyanosis. Reduced pulmonary compliance and use of accessory muscles of respiration are evidenced by intercostal and subxiphoid retractions and abdominal breathing. The initial chest film may show streaky, linear densities similar in appearance to transient tachypnea of the newborn. As the disease progresses, the lungs typically appear hyperinflated with flattening of the diaphragms. Diffuse patchy densities may alternate with areas of expansion. A variety of techniques have been recommended to reduce the incidence of MAS. Suctioning of the oropharynx before delivery of the shoulders was considered routine, but a randomized controlled trial demonstrated this to be of no benefit. Elective and routine endotracheal intubation and direct suctioning of the trachea were initially recommended for all meconium-stained newborns. However, a randomized controlled trial demonstrated that there was no value in performing this procedure in babies who were vigorous at birth. In the presence of meconium-stained amniotic fluid, a newborn born at term, who is breathing or crying, and has good tone, should undergo routine care. This is not the case for depressed infants born to mothers with meconium-stained amniotic fluid since they are at increased risk of developing MAS. While tracheal suctioning has not been associated with a reduction in the incidence of MAS or mortality in these infants, the evidence is lacking to support any change in this intervention. Performing endotracheal suctioning of nonvigorous babies with meconium-stained amniotic fluid is still a recommended action. However, if attempted intubation is prolonged and unsuccessful, bag-mask ventilation should be considered, particularly if there is persistent bradycardia.



Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (A) is seen in infants who require supplemental oxygen for at least 28 postnatal days. Respiratory distress syndrome (C) presents with respiratory distress in preterm infants due to surfactant deficiency. Transient tachypnea of the newborn (D) is seen in term and late preterm infants with milder respiratory distress.
