Rapid Review
Inguinal Hernias

Bimodal: < 1 and > 40 years old
Direct
Protrudes directly through the Hesselbach triangle and medial to the inferior epigastric artery (IEA)
Bulge decreases upon reclining
Indirect
​​Most common type
Protrudes through internal ring, lateral to IEA
Mnemonic: MDs don’t lie
​Medial to IEA: direct
Lateral to IEA: indirect
Strangulation risk: indirect > direct
Strangulated or incarcerated hernias: emergent surgery consultation

question: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department for evaluation of chest pain and difficulty swallowing. The symptoms have been occurring intermittently for 1 week. He has no shortness of breath or fevers. He has noticed that his symptoms worsen when he eats certain foods. The patient states that he had an endoscopy for similar symptoms in the past and was told that he had abnormal cells in his esophagus. He does not remember what medications he was prescribed after he had the endoscopy and is not currently taking any medications. Physical exam reveals no abnormalities. His BP is 125/70 mm Hg, HR is 70 bpm, RR is 16/min, SpO2 is 99%, and T is 97.9°F (36.6°C). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical therapy?

options.text: Dietary modification and swallowed fluticasone propionate
Proton pump inhibitor and aerosolized fluticasone propionate
Proton pump inhibitor and oral prednisone

correctAnswer: Dietary modification and swallowed fluticasone propionate
englishExplanation:
The patient is describing symptoms of eosinophilic esophagitis, most appropriately treated with dietary modification and swallowed topical glucocorticoids, such as fluticasone propionate or budesonide. Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic immunologic condition in which eosinophils infiltrate the esophagus and induce an inflammatory response. Food allergens are the most common triggers, but aeroallergens and GERD can also contribute. A history of dysphagia and esophageal food impactions in an adult or child should raise suspicion for eosinophilic esophagitis. Other symptoms may include atypical chest pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn. Diagnosis is made by endoscopy, typically demonstrating edema, multiple esophageal rings, whitish exudate, and sometimes strictures. The histologic analysis will demonstrate eosinophilia within the esophageal mucosa. Peripheral blood eosinophilia is not specific but may be seen in 25–50% of patients with the condition.

Dietary modification is a mainstay of treatment since patients with eosinophilic esophagitis have high rates of food allergies. Swallowed topical glucocorticoids are effective in over half of patients, but the disease often recurs when therapy is discontinued. Proton pump inhibitors are used in conjunction with the avoidance of triggers and topical glucocorticoids. There is emerging evidence that biological therapies that target cytokines may be beneficial but are currently reserved for patients who do not improve with first-line therapies. Esophageal dilation is indicated in patients who develop esophageal stricture and can be beneficial in treating dysphagia but does not address the underlying inflammatory condition.



Systemic glucocorticoids, such as prednisone (A, D), are not shown to have any benefit beyond what is achieved with topical glucocorticoids. Furthermore, they are not recommended due to high rates of associated side effects. Inhaled fluticasone propionate or budesonide (C) may be used in treatment but are generally not recommended over the swallowed route of administration. Additionally, dietary modification is an essential element of treating eosinophilic esophagitis due to its significant association with food allergies.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of esophageal chest pain?

Reveal Answer:
GERD.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EoE)

Clinical: dysphagia with solid foods, food impaction, chest pain not responsive to antacids, GER-like symptoms, epigastric pain, vomiting (children)
Associated with asthma, eczema, food allergies
Dx: endoscopy, esophageal biopsies (≥ 15 eosinophils/hpf)
Treatment: diet modifications (eliminate food allergies), PPI, topical (swallowed) steroids (e.g., budesonide), immunomodulators

question: A 4-week-old baby boy is brought to the emergency department for vomiting for 5 days. Initially, the parent thought the baby was just regurgitating milk, but now the vomiting is more forceful, and the baby does not seem to be able to keep milk down. The vomiting is nonbilious and nonbloody. There is no associated diarrhea. On exam, vital signs show HR 182 bpm, RR 30/min, and T 37.6℃. The baby is ill appearing but nontoxic and you feel a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely laboratory abnormality that will be found in this patient?
englishExplanation:
This baby is presenting with a history and examination that is consistent with pyloric stenosis. It results from pyloric muscle hypertrophy that obstructs gastric outflow. Most cases occur in male patients and most cases are diagnosed before 10 weeks of life. The presentation usually includes nonbilious projectile vomiting associated with dehydration and weight loss. Palpation of the hypertrophied pylorus or findings of an “olive” in the right upper quadrant is pathognomonic for the disease. Initially, the vomiting can be mild, but it will progress over a few days. Emergency department treatment includes correction of dehydration and electrolyte disorders. At the onset of symptoms, electrolytes are usually normal, but once the illness has been present for a few days, the most common electrolyte abnormality is hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Patients will have low chloride, low potassium, and elevated bicarbonate.



Hyperchloremic alkalosis (A) is a nonentity and is unlikely to be found in any patient. Hyperchloremia can be associated with acidosis but not usually alkalosis. Any entity that causes bicarbonate losses, such as severe diarrhea or a pancreatic fistula, can lead to hyperchloremic acidosis.

Hyperkalemic acidosis (B) is unlikely to be found in an infant with pyloric stenosis. If this electrolyte abnormality is found, then a search for other entities such as adrenal crisis from congenital adrenal hyperplasia should be sought after.

Hypokalemic acidosis (D) would be found in patients with excessive diarrhea and laxative use. Renal tubular acidosis can also lead to hypokalemic acidosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the diagnostic procedure of choice to diagnose pyloric stenosis?

Reveal Answer:
Abdominal ultrasound.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pyloric Stenosis

2–8 weeks of age, boys > girls
Sx: nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeding, early satiety
PE: dehydration, RUQ olive-like mass
Lab results: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
Dx: ultrasound or UGI series (string sign)
Tx: fluid and electrolyte replacement, pyloromyotomy

question: A 54-year-old man presents to the ED with severe, sudden-onset lower chest pain. He appears in distress and refuses to change positions in the bed. His vital signs are BP 94/72 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm, RR 20/min, T 100.1°F (37.8°C), and SpO2 100% on room air. An upright chest X-ray is obtained and shown above. An ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia but no other acute findings. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with findings of pneumoperitoneum on chest X-ray concerning for perforated peptic ulcer disease. The most common cause of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is a bacterial infection with Helicobacter pylori and medications such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or corticosteroids. H. pylori are spiral- or corkscrew-shaped, flagellated, urease-producing, gram-negative bacteria. Risk factors for PUD unrelated to H. pylori infection include chronic NSAID use, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, Behçet disease, older age, Crohn disease, stress, and cytomegalovirus infection.

PUD is a chronic ulcerative disease of the stomach and duodenum, the latter being affected more commonly. Many people infected with H. pylori are asymptomatic, and only 1–10% of infected patients develop PUD. In patients whose symptoms are not NSAID-related, cure rates exceed 80% with the eradication of H. pylori. Diet and alcohol use do not predispose to PUD. The most classic symptom of PUD is burning epigastric pain that often awakens the patient at night when gastric emptying occurs. Food, milk, or antacids may reduce symptoms. Patients > 65 years may present with atypical features, such as no pain, nausea, vomiting, pain not relieved with food, weight loss, anorexia, or gastrointestinal bleeding.

Epigastric tenderness may be the only examination finding and is neither sensitive nor specific for PUD. An abrupt onset of symptoms with peritoneal abdominal findings suggests a perforated ulcer. Diagnosis of PUD is ideally with endoscopy, but only patients with red flag signs and symptoms should be referred for this. These include new symptoms in patients aged ≥ 50 years, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, dysphagia or odynophagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, abdominal mass or adenopathy, or a family history of upper gastrointestinal malignancy. NSAID-related PUD should be managed with H2 receptor blockers (e.g., ranitidine), proton pump inhibitors (e.g., pantoprazole), antacids, and sucralfate. H. pylori-related PUD should be managed with triple therapy with a proton pump inhibitor, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin (or metronidazole in penicillin-allergic patients).



Chronic alcohol ingestion (B) does not predispose to PUD. While chronic tobacco use (C) is a risk factor for PUD, it is not the most common cause.

Violent emesis (D) may lead to transmucosal tearing of the esophagus, known as Boerhaave syndrome. These patients are ill-appearing with hypotension, tachycardia, chest pain, and hematemesis and may have crepitus on palpation of the chest wall indicating free mediastinal air from esophageal rupture. This patient has a perforated viscus.

One Step Further
Question:
Helicobacter pylori is a known carcinogen for which two malignancies?

Reveal Answer:
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma and gastric adenocarcinoma.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Peptic Ulcer Disease

Most commonly caused by H. pylori infection or NSAID use
Most common cause of upper GI bleed in adults
May be asymptomatic or present with upper abdominal pain/discomfort
Duodenal ulcer: pain may be alleviated by ingesting food (mnemonic: DUDe, give me food)
Gastric ulcer: pain may be exacerbated by ingesting food
Diagnosis is confirmed by upper endoscopy
Tx options may include lifestyle modifications, discontinuing offending agents, PPI, histamine H2 blocker
Complications include bleeding, perforation, gastric outlet obstruction

question: Which of the following is the most common liver disorder in the United States?
englishExplanation:
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as non-alcohol-related fatty liver disease, is a more or less benign condition that has become increasingly common in the United States and Western Europe as weight gain and obesity have become more common. It is now the most common liver disorder in the United States and other industrialized countries. In this type of liver disease, the liver functions normally and looks normal under the microscope, except for accumulations of fat within cells. Cardiometabolic risk factors that are required for a formal diagnosis include one of the following: hypertension, elevated BMI, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance or diabetes. MASLD is often detected when imaging tests of the abdomen are obtained for other reasons (e.g., an ultrasound to look for gallstones). Liver function blood tests are either normal or slightly increased.

The diagnosis may be confirmed with a right upper quadrant ultrasound examination. If the liver function tests are significantly elevated or if there are other signs of liver disease and inflammation (e.g., jaundice), then a liver biopsy may be recommended to look for other conditions such as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), formerly known as non-alcohol-related steatohepatitis. Weight loss is the mainstay of treatment, and people with liver disease should be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B if they are not already immune. Certain medications and supplements (e.g., glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists, vitamin E) may be indicated depending on the clinical scenario. MASLD can progress to MASH, which is the third leading (and most rapidly increasing) indication for liver transplantation in the United States.



Alcohol-related liver disease (A) encompasses a spectrum of liver injuries, including steatosis, alcohol-related hepatitis, and cirrhosis. The disease progression is influenced by the quantity and duration of alcohol intake, with genetic, environmental, and nutritional factors also playing a role. Clinical findings can vary from asymptomatic in early stages to jaundice, abdominal pain, and liver dysfunction in more severe cases.

Hepatitis A (B) is spread by the fecal-oral route directly via person-to-person contact or indirectly through the ingestion of contaminated water or food (raw or undercooked shellfish). There is no carrier state, and it does not cause chronic liver disease.

Hepatitis B (C) is spread primarily by the percutaneous route but also may be transmitted by intimate contact via bodily fluids. Fulminant liver failure develops in 1% of cases. The carrier state is associated with an increased risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatitis C (D) is the most common form of viral hepatitis in the United States. Prior to 1992, most cases of hepatitis C occurred in association with the transfusion of blood and blood products. During this time, hepatitis C was referred to as posttransfusion hepatitis. In resource-rich settings, the risk of hepatitis C from blood transfusion has essentially been eliminated. Percutaneous exposure (e.g., injection drug use, health care-associated exposures) is the most efficient means of transmission.

One Step Further
Question:
Which is more elevated in alcohol-related hepatitis, aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase?

Reveal Answer:
Aspartate aminotransferase is greater than alanine aminotransferase in alcohol-related liver disease, compared to the opposite in viral hepatitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (Non-Alcohol-Related Fatty Liver Disease)

Common cause of chronic liver disease
Associated with elevated BMI, insulin resistance, DM type 2, high triglycerides or cholesterol, hypertension
Dx: ALT > AST (liver transaminase levels may be within normal limits), fatty infiltration on imaging (e.g., U/S)
Exclude other causes of hepatitis (e.g., alcohol, medications, viral)
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (non-alcohol-related steatohepatitis)
Biopsy required for Dx
Steatosis with inflammation (fibrosis and cirrhosis may be seen, although not required for diagnosis)
Tx options may include weight loss, abstinence from alcohol, vaccination for hepatitis A and B, statins

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction?
englishExplanation:
Patients with small bowel obstruction present with nausea, vomiting, cramping, intermittent poorly localized abdominal pain, and obstipation. Physical exam findings include signs of dehydration, abdominal distention, mild, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and tympany to percussion. The most common cause of small bowel obstruction is postoperative adhesions. Other causes include tumors, hernias, intussusception, bezoars, Crohn disease, and foreign bodies.



Diverticulitis (B) is one of the more common causes of large bowel obstruction but is not a significant cause of small bowel obstruction. Neoplasm (C) is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction. Neoplasm is also a cause of small bowel obstruction but is not the most common cause. Volvulus (D) is an uncommon cause of small bowel obstruction.

One Step Further
Question:
What abdominal radiography findings indicate small bowel obstruction?

Reveal Answer:
Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Small Bowel Obstruction

Risks: prior abdominal or pelvic surgery, neoplasm, hernia, abscess
Sx: bilious vomiting, abdominal pain
PE: possibly high-pitched bowel sounds
Dx: X-ray with dilated bowel, air-fluid levels, a stack of coins or string of pearls sign
Diagnosis is made by imaging, most often with CT
Tx: NPO, IVF, possible NG tube, surgery

question: Which of the following is the most common surgical emergency in patients 65 years of age and older?
englishExplanation:
Acute cholecystitis is the most common surgical emergency in patients ≥ 65 years of age. Vascular disasters such as aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, mesenteric ischemia, and myocardial infarction, always need to be considered in patients with abdominal pain. However, the prevalence of biliary tract disease is more common. Typically, upper abdominal pain, especially right upper quadrant pain is present along with nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Older patients are less likely to present with fever, leukocytosis, or significant tenderness. Ultrasound is the initial imaging choice, looking for gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid. HIDA scans are used if ultrasound is nondiagnostic for admitted patients with high suspicion of acute cholecystitis. Fluid resuscitation, early antibiotic administration, and cholecystectomy reduce mortality and morbidity in older patients.



Appendicitis (A) in older patients is less common and patients tend to present later than young patients, with higher rates of perforation and other complications.

Diverticulitis (C) has a wide range of severity often treated medically with antibiotics initially. Surgery is needed for persistent abscess formation, phlegmon, or perforation.

Pancreatitis (D) is the most common cause of nonsurgical abdominal pain in older patients. Gallstones and idiopathic causes are the most frequent etiologies of pancreatitis in older patients compared to gallstones and alcohol in younger patients.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the term for acute cholecystitis when gas-forming organisms create air in the gallbladder wall?

Reveal Answer:
Emphysematous cholecystitis caused by Clostridial species. This has a five times greater operative mortality.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cholecystitis

Sx: steadily increasing RUQ or epigastric pain after eating fatty foods, fever
PE: Murphy sign, Boas sign (hyperaesthesia, increased or altered sensitivity, below the right scapula)
Diagnosis
Initial: U/S
Gold standard: HIDA
Most commonly caused by obstruction by a gallstone
Acalculous disease can occur when critically ill
Treatment is cholecystectomy, antibiotics, and percutaneous cholecystostomy tube when critically ill or if have comorbidities and do not improve on antibiotics

question: A 32-year-old man presents with chest pain and shortness of breath, worsening over the last 24 hours. For the last 3 days, he has had a “stomach virus” with multiple episodes of vomiting and then retching dry heaves. On physical examination, he is ill-appearing. Vital signs are BP of 120/84 mm Hg, HR of 112 bpm, RR of 14/minute, and T of 101.8°F (38.8ºC). Which of the following do you expect to find on radiographic imaging?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with chest pain and shortness of breath following several days of vomiting and retching, accompanied by a fever and an ill appearance. These symptoms raise suspicion for Boerhaave syndrome (spontaneous esophageal rupture), which can occur after forceful vomiting or retching.

Boerhaave syndrome is typically caused by a rapid rise in intraluminal pressure within the esophagus during retching or vomiting, but perforation can also occur following a procedure or ingestion of a foreign body. Patients often present with severe chest pain, neck pain, odynophagia, shortness of breath, and fever. If the lower esophagus is involved, there may be abdominal pain radiating to the back or shoulders.

A chest X-ray is often the first imaging modality obtained and reveals an abnormality in up to 90% of cases, such as pneumomediastinum, mediastinal widening, subcutaneous emphysema, infiltrates, or pleural effusion (more commonly left-sided due to distal esophageal perforation, but effusions can occur on either side). A water-soluble contrast esophagram is useful for identifying the site of perforation, but a CT scan with oral contrast may be preferred for its higher sensitivity.

Medical management of esophageal perforation is appropriate for patients with contained leaks within the neck or mediastinum, minimal symptoms, and no signs of sepsis and when the injury is not in neoplastic tissue, the abdomen, or proximal to an obstruction. The patient must have access to contrast studies at any time, and an experienced thoracic surgeon should be available. Treatment includes avoiding oral intake for at least 7 days, providing parenteral nutrition, administering intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as piperacillin-tazobactam) for 7 to 14 days, and careful placement of a nasogastric tube. If there is clinical deterioration, such as the development of free extravasation, extension of the perforation, persistent fever, sepsis, progression of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax, or empyema, surgical intervention is required.



Air under the diaphragm (A) is seen in cases of perforation within the intra-abdominal cavity.

A distended gastric bubble (B) implies problems with either motility, gastric emptying, or mechanical obstruction at some point in the intestinal tract distal to the stomach.

A lower lobe pneumonia (C) may ultimately develop if the patient continues to have leakage of fluid into the mediastinum or thoracic cavity, although this does take time to develop. The patients will more likely have a pneumonitis pattern on imaging rather than lobar infiltrate.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name of a crunching sound heard on auscultation from mediastinal air?

Reveal Answer:
Hamman sign.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Boerhaave Syndrome

Sx: severe chest pain
PE: Hamman crunch (mediastinal crackling with each heartbeat)
Chest X-ray: pneumomediastinum
Diagnosis is made by esophagram with water-soluble oral contrast
Caused by a full-thickness esophageal rupture, with iatrogenic > forceful vomiting
Most common location is left posterolateral distal esophagus
Treatment is emergent surgical consult and broad-spectrum antibiotics

question: A 93-year-old woman presents to the ED with abdominal pain and constipation. On physical exam, her abdomen is diffusely tender and firmly distended with some guarding in the mid-abdomen. She is treated with sigmoidoscopy and rectal tube decompression and improves. Which of the following would have been the most appropriate initial imaging modality for this patient's condition?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
MRI of the pelvis with contrast

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with sigmoid volvulus. Sigmoid volvulus is the most common site of volvulus. Diagnosis of sigmoid volvulus is primarily with abdominal X-ray, which is diagnostic in 80% of patients. Abdominal X-ray reveals an inverted U-shaped, dilated sigmoid with the limbs of the sigmoid colon directed toward the pelvis. It is often referred to as the “coffee-bean sign.” Risk factors for sigmoid volvulus include nursing home residence, older age, being bedbound or immobile, and chronic constipation. Management of sigmoid volvulus is with sigmoidoscopy and rectal tube decompression the volvulus.



While sigmoid volvulus would often be seen on CT abdomen and pelvis (B), MRI pelvis with contrast (C), and an upper GI series (D), an abdominal X-ray is the quickest and easiest test to confirm this diagnosis and is often sufficient for gastroenterology to initiate the appropriate therapy in a timely manner.

One Step Further
Question:
For what disease process is an upper GI series the best initial test?

Reveal Answer:
Malrotation and midgut volvulus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Sigmoid Volvulus

Loop of bowel that twists around itself and its associated mesentery
Risk factors: advanced age, residence in long-term care facility, neurologic or psychiatric disease due to alterations in colonic motility, chronic constipation
Sx: gradual-onset diffuse abdominal pain, distention, constipation
Abdominal X-ray: U-shaped dilated loop of colon (coffee bean sign)
CT: whirl sign with a bird’s beak
Tx: endoscopic decompression to reduce volvulus, surgery for gangrene or inability to reduce volvulus
Elective surgery to prevent recurrence recommended
Complications: ischemia, gangrene, perforation

question: A 32-year-old man presents to the ED with chest pain and shortness of breath. He was sick with gastroenteritis for several days before his current symptoms began. Vital signs are a T of 102°F (38.9°C), HR of 118 bpm, BP of 108/70 mm Hg, RR of 22/min, and SpO2 of 93% on room air. A chest radiograph is shown above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The patient’s symptoms of chest pain, shortness of breath, and recent history of gastroenteritis coupled with the finding of pneumomediastinum (air in the mediastinum) on the chest radiograph strongly suggests an esophageal rupture, also known as Boerhaave syndrome. This is a life-threatening condition due to the risk of mediastinitis, an infection resulting from leakage of esophageal contents into the mediastinum. This condition often arises following forceful vomiting or other events causing sudden spikes in esophageal pressure, such as childbirth, severe coughing, or weightlifting. In Boerhaave syndrome, the most common site of spontaneous rupture is the distal esophagus, but rupture can occur in the proximal portion in some cases. Clinical manifestations vary depending on the location of the tear and the time elapsed since the rupture, with rapid development of fever, chest pain, and shortness of breath as inflammation progresses. Lower esophageal perforations may also cause abdominal pain and pain radiating to the shoulder.

The Mackler triad (vomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema) is characteristic of esophageal rupture but is only seen in < 50% of cases. Radiographic findings (particularly pneumomediastinum on chest X-ray) are strongly suggestive of esophageal rupture, but some cases may present with effusions, especially if the rupture occurs at the distal esophagus, leading to a left-sided pleural effusion due to the weaker posterolateral wall on the left. A proximal esophageal rupture is more likely to cause a right-sided effusion. Given the low sensitivity of chest X-ray alone, contrast esophagography with a water-soluble contrast agent is recommended to confirm diagnosis and locate the tear.

Treatment of esophageal rupture requires urgent surgical consultation, as untreated rupture carries a high risk of mortality. Initial management involves IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent or manage mediastinitis. Additionally, gastrointestinal decompression using a nasogastric tube may help relieve esophageal pressure, but it carries a risk of worsening contamination in the mediastinum if not carefully placed. Surgical options range from direct repair of the tear to esophageal diversion or resection in severe cases, with the choice of intervention depending on factors like the patient’s stability and the duration since rupture.



Myocarditis (B) is most commonly caused by a viral infection of the myocardium. Patients develop symptoms of chest discomfort with shortness of breath. Echocardiography demonstrates an impaired ejection fraction. A chest X-ray may show an enlarged cardiac silhouette if cardiomyopathy has already developed but should not have mediastinal air. The ECG may show ST segment and T wave changes, and the troponin level is elevated in this condition.

Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (C) develops as a result of some toxic ingestions (e.g., salicylate, opiates). On X-ray, vascular congestion is present with a normal heart size.

Pneumonia (D) is identified on chest X-ray either as a lobar infiltrate, frequently with air bronchograms, or a diffuse interstitial pattern in some of the atypical or viral etiologies.

One Step Further
Question:
When is endoscopy used in the diagnosis of Boerhaave syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
When the location of the perforation is unclear from imaging alone.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Boerhaave Syndrome

Sx: severe chest pain
PE: Hamman crunch (mediastinal crackling with each heartbeat)
Chest X-ray: pneumomediastinum
Diagnosis is made by esophagram with water-soluble oral contrast
Caused by a full-thickness esophageal rupture, with iatrogenic > forceful vomiting
Most common location is left posterolateral distal esophagus

question: A 20-year-old man presents to the ED after a suicide attempt. The patient states he ingested household drain cleaner 1 hour ago. He has mild throat and epigastric abdominal pain. Vital signs, physical exam, chest X-ray, abdominal X-ray, and lab tests are all unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Discharge home if he becomes asymptomatic after 6 hours of observation

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with symptoms suggestive of injury from an alkali ingestion and he should be admitted to the ICU for further care and urgent endoscopy. Strong alkalotic solutions contain sodium and potassium hydroxide and are commonly found in household cleaning products and drain cleaners. Alkali-containing solutions produce injury through liquefactive necrosis, which can lead to perforation, mediastinitis, peritonitis, respiratory distress, and shock. The initial ED care of patients suspected of significant alkali ingestion is mainly supportive. The airway should be secured early in those with respiratory distress, stridor, and voice alterations. Patients should be fluid resuscitated with IV crystalloids. Proton pump inhibitors may also be considered. Patients with alkali ingestion should undergo early endoscopy to assess the extent of esophageal injury. Patients with a history to suggest significant ingestion or signs of significant injury such as vomiting, difficulty handling secretions, oropharyngeal changes, or aversion to food intake should undergo endoscopy within 12–24 hours.



Activated charcoal (A) is contraindicated in patients with caustic ingestions except in special circumstances of zinc chloride or mercuric chloride ingestion. Charcoal is largely ineffective and will impede visualization during endoscopy.

Discharging home if asymptomatic after 6 hours of observation (B) is incorrect. Symptomatic patients with a history of ingestion should be admitted for supportive care and upper endoscopy to assess the degree of injury. Patients who are truly asymptomatic and have a low-risk ingestion can be observed for 4–6 hours before discharge as long as they have close GI follow-up.

Patients with clinical or radiographic evidence of perforation require an emergent surgery consult (C). Indications for emergency surgery include peritonitis, pneumomediastinum, or pneumoperitoneum.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common delayed complication associated with esophageal injury from alkali ingestion?

Reveal Answer:
Esophageal stricture.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Caustic Ingestions

Presentation: chest pain, dysphagia, drooling
Alkali: corrosive damage with liquefactive necrosis
Acid: coagulation necrosis
Management: NPO, endoscopy, monitor airway
Monitor children with history of possible ingestion

question: A 71-year-old man presents with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and nausea, which have become progressively worse over the past 48 hours. He has no significant medical history and does not have drug allergies. His vital signs are within normal limits. The physical exam is significant for left lower quadrant abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Abdominal CT reveals uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Diverticula are saclike protrusions of the colonic wall. Diverticulosis, which refers to the presence of diverticula, is associated with a diet low in fiber. The frequency of diverticular disease increases with age. The mean age at admission for acute diverticulitis is 63 years. Fecal material present in the diverticulum may harden, forming a fecalith. This leads to increased susceptibility to bacterial infection or inflammation. Patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis classically present with left lower quadrant pain with associated tenderness on examination. Associated symptoms include anorexia, nausea, and vomiting. CT of the abdomen should be performed to establish the diagnosis as well as to exclude complications. Patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis are generally appropriate for outpatient therapy that includes the selective use of oral antibiotics for 7–10 days. While there is evidence from 2021 that patients may not benefit from the routine use of antibiotics, the emergency medical treatment recommendations align with the American College of Physicians and the American Gastroenterological Association in the use of antibiotics on a selective basis. This means that antibiotics should be considered in older patients (> 70 years), those with significant comorbidities like diabetes or immunosuppression, or those with unreliable follow-up care. Appropriate regimens include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and metronidazole, ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate.



Emergency surgery (A) is not indicated for uncomplicated diverticulitis. However, surgical consultation is necessary for patients with complications such as peritoneal signs or evidence of free air on imaging. Treatment with imipenem (C) or piperacillin-tazobactam (D) are appropriate antibiotic regimens for patients with complicated diverticulitis but are not warranted for this patient with uncomplicated diverticulitis.

One Step Further
Question:
Why is colonoscopy usually avoided in acute diverticulitis?

Reveal Answer:
Increased risk of perforation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Diverticulitis

Sx: abdominal pain localized to the left lower quadrant, fever, nausea, vomiting, and a change in bowel habits
PE: localized guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness
Diagnosis is confirmed by CT with IV contrast: thickened bowel wall, fat stranding
May show complications (bowel perforation, abscess, fistula, obstruction)
Consider treatment with supportive care or antibiotics based on risk factors and presentation
Antibiotics to cover gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria, bowel rest, and surgery (in severe cases)
High-fiber diet can help in prevention

question: A 13-month-old girl presents to the emergency department with constipation. She has been passing hard stools for the last 2 weeks and seems to grunt, strain, and stiffen her legs with stooling. The stools have intermittent isolated streaks of bright red blood, and physical exam shows an anal fissure. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s constipation?
englishExplanation:
Anal fissures are the most common cause of rectal bleeding in infants and toddlers. They are typically posterior midline and present with painful defecation, fussiness, and streaks of bright red blood on the stool or diaper. Risk factors include low-fiber diets, inadequate fluid intake, and stool withholding behavior. On examination, a small linear tear near the anal verge is often visible.

The most appropriate first-line treatment for pediatric constipation complicated by a benign anal fissure is oral polyethylene glycol (PEG), an osmotic laxative. PEG is effective, well tolerated, and widely used for both disimpaction and maintenance therapy in children. In this scenario, the fissure is caused by hard stools, and addressing the underlying constipation is critical to allow healing and prevent recurrence.

Rectal therapies may worsen fissure pain and fear of defecation, increasing withholding. Education about hydration, diet, and stooling habits is also essential.



Observation alone (A) is insufficient, as untreated constipation will perpetuate the fissure and may lead to chronic withholding, stool retention, and worsening symptoms. Early, effective laxative therapy is key to breaking the cycle of painful defecation and constipation.

While mineral oil (B) can be used for constipation, it is not recommended in young children due to the risk of aspiration and lipoid pneumonia, especially in children under 2 years old. PEG is a safer and equally effective alternative for this age group.

Rectal interventions (D) are painful and distressing in children with anal fissures and may exacerbate stool withholding. They should be avoided unless oral options are ineffective or not tolerated. This patient has a visible fissure and painful defecation, so a nontraumatic, oral regimen is preferred.

Surgery (E) is not indicated for a simple anal fissure in a child, especially one with a clear history of constipation and no systemic symptoms. Surgical consultation is reserved for refractory cases or when fissures are off-midline and raise suspicion for alternative causes (e.g., Crohn disease, trauma).

One Step Further
Question:
What reported side effect of sodium phosphate enemas limits its use to twice every 24 hours in children?

Reveal Answer:
Hypocalcemic tetany and life-threatening hyperphosphatemia.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Constipation in Pediatrics

Newborns should pass meconium stool within 48 hours
By age 3, children should have one bowel movement per day
Hirschsprung disease: absent stool in vault, delayed meconium
Functional constipation: toilet-training, stool-withholding behaviors, painful bowel movements, large bulky stools
Tx
Osmotic laxatives: polyethylene glycol, lactulose
Stimulants: senna, bisacodyl
Stool softeners: docusate
Fleet enema contraindicated in infants (due to hypocalcemia)

question: Which of the following patients most likely has developed a sigmoid volvulus?

options.text: A 35-year-old woman with a history of constipation from opioid misuse who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting
A 45-year-old woman who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting whose only history is a large uterine tumor that was removed 2 years ago
A 65-year-old woman who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting after an appendectomy 3 weeks ago
An 80-year-old woman with a history of Parkinson disease who lives in a care facility and was sent to the emergency room with a report of abdominal pain and vomiting

correctAnswer: An 80-year-old woman with a history of Parkinson disease who lives in a care facility and was sent to the emergency room with a report of abdominal pain and vomiting
englishExplanation:
A colonic volvulus occurs when a part of the colon twists on its mesentery resulting in acute obstruction. The most common type of colonic volvulus is sigmoid volvulus. Chronic constipation and high-fiber diets lead to an overloaded sigmoid colonic loop which makes it susceptible to torsion along the mesentery. The presence of a gravid uterus or a large pelvic mass can also alter the position of the intra-abdominal organs, predisposing them to the formation of volvulus. A complete volvulus leads to the development of a closed-loop obstruction of the affected colonic segment. Increased dilation of the bowel loop compromises the vascular supply, eventually leading to ischemic gangrene and bowel wall perforation. Patients at greatest risk for sigmoid volvulus include institutionalized patients with neuropsychiatric disorders and nursing home patients. Psychotropic drugs interfere with colonic motility and prolonged recumbency in nursing homes leads to chronic constipation. Additionally, chronic use of laxatives and enemas increases the risk even more. Other patients at risk for sigmoid volvulus include those with pelvic masses or pregnancy. Although less commonly seen, patients with adhesions, internal herniations, intussusceptions, intestinal malrotations, and malignancies are also at risk. Of the options given above, the older patient with Parkinson disease who lives in a care facility is at the highest risk and most likely to develop sigmoid volvulus.



A 35-year-old woman with a history of constipation from opioid misuse who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting (A) is at slight risk for sigmoid volvulus, but due to her young age, she is less likely at this point to develop the disease. This young woman is more likely to have other disease processes causing her symptoms. A 45-year-old woman who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting, whose only history is a large uterine tumor that was removed 2 years ago (B), is also at slight risk for volvulus due to her history of a pelvic mass. However, the mass has already been removed, so it no longer affects the lie of the intra-abdominal organs. Finally, a 65-year-old woman who presents with abdominal pain and vomiting after an appendectomy 3 weeks ago (C) is also at slight risk for volvulus due to adhesions, but again there would more likely be other causes for her abdominal pain and vomiting.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most likely reason that patients are at risk for developing cecal volvulus?

Reveal Answer:
Whereas sigmoid volvulus is usually an acquired condition, cecal volvulus is usually due to congenital incomplete dorsal mesenteric fixation of the cecum.

Sx: gradual-onset diffuse abdominal pain, distention, constipation
