Tx options include surgical excision for lesions with a low recurrence risk, Mohs micrographic surgery for lesions with a high recurrence risk
Prevention includes sunscreen, UV light protection

question: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a fever and irritability for 1 day. Her parent reports decreased oral intake today. The girl has some congestion and says her mouth hurts. Vital signs include a T of 38.7℃ (101.7℉), HR of 140 bpm, and RR of 20/min. You notice one small ulcer on her left inner cheek and another on the left side of her tongue. What is the most likely cause of this syndrome?
englishExplanation:
This patient is likely presenting with either herpangina or hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Clinical syndromes are characterized by an oral enanthem and a maculopapular or vesicular rash to hands and feet. Most cases occur in children under 5 years of age. The most common cause of HFMD is coxsackievirus. The virus is usually transmitted person to person through either the fecal-oral route or through contact with oral or respiratory secretions.

Enterovirus A71 is more common in the Asian-Pacific regions, but coxsackievirus is more common overall. Diagnosis is made clinically. Laboratory studies are not required. Complications of herpangina and HFMD are rare. Treatment is supportive with ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and oral hydration. No specific antiviral exists for treatment.



Echovirus (B) is another cause of herpangina and HFMD, but it is not as common as coxsackievirus, particularly in the United States.

Primary herpes simplex virus (C) gingivostomatitis consists of erythema and edema of the gingiva with clusters of vesicles. The gums are friable and usually bleed easily. The rash in this question is not characteristic of herpes gingivostomatitis.

Varicella-zoster virus (D) is responsible for chickenpox, which presents as a diffuse vesicular rash in children, but it is not responsible for oral lesions.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the typical viral agent that causes severe cases of herpangina and hand, foot, and mouth disease, which can lead to severe complications from the illness?

Reveal Answer:
Enterovirus A71.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease

Most often in children < 5 years old
Most commonly caused by coxsackie A virus
Sx: rash, decreased appetite, fever
PE: oral enanthem plus a macular, maculopapular, or vesicular rash on the hands and feet
Tx: supportive care

question: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a leg rash. He notes worsening redness of his left leg over the past 3 days. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin, and a recent diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia, for which he completed a course of antibiotics while in the hospital. Vital signs show T of 101.1°F (38.4°C), HR of 109 bpm, RR of 18/min, and BP of 104/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 10 cm × 6 cm area of erythema extending from the dorsum of the foot to the mid-shin with associated swelling. There is no fluctuance, induration, or purulent drainage. Initial laboratory evaluation shows a white blood cell count of 15.2/µL. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Warm compresses and oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

englishExplanation:
Cellulitis is defined as a bacterial infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat that results from bacterial penetration through the superficial skin barrier. It is most commonly seen in middle-aged and older adults and has a seasonal predilection for warmer months in nontropical areas. Risk factors for developing cellulitis include skin barrier disruption due to trauma, edema, obesity, and immunosuppressive states (e.g., diabetes, HIV). The most common bacterial species implicated in cellulitis are group A Streptococcus (e.g., S. pyogenes), with Staphylococcus aureus infection occurring less commonly. Risk factors for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection, specifically, include antibiotic use in the last 6 months and recent hospitalization, both of which are present in this case, as well as injection drug use, history of MRSA infection, and recent surgery.

The clinical presentation of cellulitis generally involves a combination of cutaneous erythema with associated edema and warmth on palpation, most commonly involving the lower extremities. Symptoms are nearly always unilateral and may also include petechiae, hemorrhage, or superficial bullae. Purulence and systemic symptoms may or may not be present. Diagnosis of cellulitis is generally based on clinical assessment, and treatment hinges on the need to cover for MRSA when prescribing antibiotics. Because this patient has signs of systemic infection (e.g., fever, leukocytosis) and diabetes, he warrants MRSA coverage. His systemic toxicity, in particular, warrants parenteral antibiotic therapy in the form of intravenous vancomycin. Other indications for parenteral antibiotics include extensive erythema or rapid progression of symptoms, immune compromise, and inability to tolerate or absorb oral therapy.



Incision and drainage (B) is indicated in the treatment of cutaneous abscesses but is not routinely used in the emergency department for cellulitis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (C) provides MRSA coverage and can be used when oral antibiotics are appropriate, but this patient’s systemic infectious signs and risk factors warrant parenteral antibiotic therapy. Needle aspiration (D) typically is not recommended for the treatment of cutaneous abscesses and certainly does not have a role in the management of cellulitis. Warm compresses and NSAIDs (E) may provide the patient some symptomatic relief but would not treat the underlying cause of his symptoms and would likely lead to worsening of his infection.

One Step Further
Question:
What complication is associated with cellulitis of the medial third of the face?

Reveal Answer:
Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cellulitis

Commonly caused by group A Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus
Sx: pain, redness, swelling
More indolent onset than erysipelas
PE: tenderness, erythema with poorly demarcated borders, lymphedema, ± purulence
Abx selection depends on uncomplicated vs complicated cellulitis, PCN intolerance, MRSA risk factors, and purulence

question: A 22-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus presents to the emergency department with the above dermatologic finding. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s presentation?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings suggestive of molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by human poxvirus. Molluscum contagiosum is typically seen in pediatric patients, athletes, and immunosuppressed patients. It presents with a localized infection with a firm and dome-shaped papule on the skin that has a shiny surface with central umbilication. The diagnosis is typically made clinically. However, in uncertain cases, biopsy and histology can confirm the diagnosis. Treatment includes measures, such as cryotherapy or curettage, that can be performed on an outpatient basis.



Herpes simplex virus (A) presents with painful vesicular lesions that can be treated with acyclovir.

Human herpesvirus 8 (B) is the viral etiology of Kaposi sarcoma, which presents with red and violaceous skin lesions that are seen in patients with human immunodeficiency virus. Antiretroviral therapy is used to treat Kaposi sarcoma by raising the CD4 count.

Human papillomavirus (C) can cause condyloma acuminata or warts, which present with a cauliflower-appearing lesion and can be removed for cosmetic purposes.

One Step Further
Question:
Where is oral Kaposi sarcoma most commonly found?

Reveal Answer:
On the palate.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Molluscum Contagiosum

Common in childhood, can also occur in healthy adults
Spread through direct skin-to-skin contact or fomites
Sx: Small, skin-colored papules, sometimes associated with pruritus or inflammation
PE: multiple waxy, dome-shaped papules with an umbilicated appearance
Etiology: poxvirus
Self-limiting: typically resolves without treatment within 6–12 months, but removal can be considered if lesions are symptomatic

question: A 68-year-old man presents to the ED with a large skin lesion on his nose as shown above. Exposure to which of the following is associated with the development of this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient's lesion is a squamous cell carcinoma. Arsenic exposure is a known risk factor. Squamous cell cancer is a malignancy of epidermal keratinocytes and commonly affects the head, face, or neck areas. On physical exam, it presents as a well-defined red or brown thickened patch that may have associated crusting or oozing. The main risk factors include sun exposure, human papillomavirus infection, chronic arsenic exposure, and ionizing radiation. Chronic arsenic exposure typically results from contaminated drinking water. Treatment from the ED includes referral to a dermatologist for biopsy and surgical excision.



Lead (B) poisoning most commonly occurs in children who ingest paint chips or dust containing lead. It is associated with irreversible neurocognitive deficits.

Nickel (C) is a metal commonly used in jewelry and a frequent cause of contact dermatitis.

Zinc (D) exposure is not associated with squamous cell cancer.

One Step Further
Question:
What is actinic keratosis?

Reveal Answer:
A precancerous lesion that can become squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Second most common skin cancer
Risk factors include exposure to UV light (e.g., sunlight, tanning bed), arsenic, radiation, HPV infection
Actinic keratosis is a precursor
Sx: nonhealing lesion that sometimes bleeds
PE (varies by subtype): red, scaly, hyperkeratotic papule or plaque, ulceration
Most common on sun-exposed areas (e.g., head, neck, hands, lip)
Dx: clinical exam, dermoscopy, skin biopsy to confirm
Tx options (depending on risk of recurrence) include curettage and electrodessication, cryotherapy, surgical excision, and radiation therapy
Prevention includes sunscreen and UV light protection

question: A 27-year-old man presents to the ED with a growing lump on his lower back. The exam demonstrates a firm subcutaneous mass with a central punctum and no associated erythema or pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with clinical exam findings consistent with an epidermoid cyst (often incorrectly referred to as a sebaceous cyst). Epidermoid cysts are benign subcutaneous lesions that arise from the accumulation of keratin within a dilated follicular infundibulum. These cysts often present as slow-growing, skin-colored nodules with a central punctum. Patients report a long-standing cutaneous mass that may become intermittently tender or inflamed. Spontaneous rupture can occur, leading to drainage of thick, waxy material composed of keratin. In contrast, the presence of dull, viscous purulent drainage suggests secondary infection.

Although mild inflammation does not preclude primary excision, the procedure can be technically more difficult during an active inflammatory episode due to tissue friability. In such cases, initial treatment with NSAIDs and a short course of antibiotics may be used to reduce inflammation, with definitive excision deferred until the area is quiescent.



Cutaneous abscesses (A) are painful on palpation, often with associated superficial cellulitis or surrounding erythema.

Lipomas (C) are benign, well-circumscribed subcutaneous tumors that do not extrude contents or have a central punctum.

Verruca vulgaris (D), or common warts, are benign epidermal neoplasms caused by human papillomavirus, commonly found on the hands, soles, face, or genital tract, and usually regress spontaneously within 2 years.

One Step Further
Question:
Is malignant transformation possible in an epidermoid cyst?

Reveal Answer:
Malignant transformation of an epidermoid cyst is extremely rare. When it does occur, the most commonly associated malignancy is squamous cell carcinoma.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epidermoid Cyst (Epidermal Inclusion Cyst)

“Sebaceous cyst” misnomer
Clinical diagnosis
Treat with steroids, I&D, excision
Refer to dermatology for follow-up

question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a rash. She has a medical history of heroin use and works as a migrant farmer. Physical exam is notable for salmon-colored skin lesions over the extensor surfaces, which appear as scales over a red base. When one of the scales is removed, punctate bleeding is noted. Which of the following is associated with the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: High risk of progression to malignancy

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings suggestive of psoriasis. Psoriasis is an autoimmune condition with a complex pathophysiology that involves Th17 cells among many other cell types and chemical mediators. The presenting finding is typically a salmon-colored rash with silver scales on the extensor surfaces. Removal of the silver scales can lead to punctate bleeding, also referred to as Auspitz sign. The treatment of psoriasis involves emollients, topical therapies (including steroids, vitamin D, and tar), and in severe cases, immunomodulators and ultraviolet (UV) therapy. UV therapy is typically indicated in severe and extensive disease that does not respond to other medical interventions, given the risk of damage and malignancy that can occur with its use. Patients will typically report a remission or improvement in their symptoms in the summer months, which is a result of increased outdoor activities and sun exposure that leads to increased UV light exposure.



Antibiotic use (A) is associated with a fixed drug eruption that presents with a hyperpigmented lesion that can demonstrate central necrosis, typically in the same location of the body when a particular drug is given to a patient. High risk of progression to malignancy (B) describes actinic keratosis, which is a premalignant scaly lesion that occurs in sun-exposed areas that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. Underlying infection (D) describes the characteristic rash of secondary syphilis that is often confused with pityriasis rosea, which presents with a salmon-colored herald patch that is highly pruritic. It could also describe pustular skin lesions seen in gonococcal arthritis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the term for the warty lesions found in syphilis?

Reveal Answer:
Condyloma lata.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Psoriasis

Sx: rash on extensor surfaces of arms and legs
PE: bilateral sharply marginated papules or plaques with silvery scales, Auspitz sign (scale removal produces blood droplets), nail pitting
Treatment: topical corticosteroids, emollients, phototherapy, biologic agents

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with painful, erythematous nodules on her lower extremities. She reports no history of trauma. She also has malaise and a low-grade fever that started a few days prior to the appearance of the rash. Which of the following features in her medical history would be most likely?

options.text: Recent urinary tract infection treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

englishExplanation:
Erythema nodosum is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that results in inflammation of the dermis and adipose tissue. Women are three times as likely to be affected than men, with most cases occurring during the second to fourth decades of life. Prodromal symptoms of malaise, arthralgias, and low-grade fever are often present, followed but the appearance of tender, erythematous nodules. Although classically taught to be found on the anterior tibial surface, the nodules can also appear on the trunk and upper extremities.

While often idiopathic, infection is the most commonly identified cause, with most cases secondary to recent streptococcal infection, such as streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection. Other causes include medications, systemic diseases such as lupus, ulcerative colitis, and sarcoidosis, and pregnancy. Diagnosis is clinical. Management consists of symptomatic treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, rest, and elevation, as well as evaluation for a possible underlying etiology. Potassium iodide and corticosteroids are other potential treatment options in patients with significant symptoms. The nodules typically resolve in 3–8 weeks.



Sulfonamides (e.g.,trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (B)) have been implicated in the development of erythema nodosum, but medications, in general, are a less frequent cause of erythema nodosum than infection.

A less aggressive form of sarcoidosis (C) has been associated with erythema nodosum and often occurs with hilar adenopathy and arthralgias (Lorgren syndrome).

Ulcerative colitis (D) has also been associated with erythema nodosum, although both ulcerative colitis and sarcoidosis are less likely than infection to be the cause.

One Step Further
Question:
Other than sulfonamides, what are two other medications associated with erythema nodosum?

Reveal Answer:
Penicillins and oral contraceptives.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Nodosum

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a tender and swollen area on her lateral thigh. She has had swelling there for several years, but over the last 3 days, the swelling has increased and the area has become red and painful. On examination, she appears well with normal vital signs. On her lateral right thigh, there is a round, tender area of swelling and redness with central fluctuance. What is the best way to minimize the recurrence of this entity?

options.text: Create a large incision and recommend repeated incision and drainage with frequent packing changes for several days
Give intravenous antibiotics until complete resolution
Inject triamcinolone acetonide after incision and drainage

englishExplanation:
Epidermoid cysts, improperly called sebaceous cysts, are the most common cutaneous cysts. They can occur anywhere on the body and usually present as nodules with a central punctum. The cyst wall contains stratified squamous epithelium, and the cavity is filled with keratinous material. The cysts can remain dormant for several years, and there is not a good way to know which cysts are at risk for inflammation and abscess formation. Cysts are infected with bacteria when they become larger, painful, and erythematous. Fluctuant cysts require incision and drainage. To treat the abscess, anesthesia should be injected around the lesion rather than into it to avoid rupturing the cyst wall. Then a small incision with a number 11 blade or a 4 mm punch should be performed. The cyst contents can be expressed with lateral pressure, and hopefully, the cyst wall will be released from the surrounding tissues and can be extracted through the incision. The best way to prevent recurrence is to completely remove the cyst wall. Unfortunately, this can be difficult for severely inflamed and infected cysts. If needed, the patient should be referred for follow-up care and removal of the cyst wall when the inflammation has improved.



Creating a large incision and recommending repeated incision and drainage with frequent packing changes for several days (B) would not necessarily prevent the recurrence of this cyst. A larger incision is likely to rupture the cyst wall, making it much more difficult to remove.

Giving intravenous antibiotics until complete resolution (C) is not necessary. When inflamed, many of these cysts do not require any antibiotic therapy for resolution. Antibiotics are only recommended for severe surrounding cellulitis or those that do not respond to drainage alone.

Injection of triamcinolone acetonide after incision and drainage (D) would not be appropriate. Mildly inflamed, uninfected epidermoid cysts may resolve on their own. Injection of triamcinolone acetonide may hasten the resolution of the inflammation and prevent infection, but the patient in this question has a fluctuant lesion, which suggests abscess formation requiring more than triamcinolone acetonide injection, and triamcinolone will not prevent recurrence.

One Step Further
Question:
What underlying diagnosis is suggested by epidermoid cysts, unusual in number and location?

Reveal Answer:
Gardner syndrome, a rare inherited condition characterized by familial adenomatous polyposis of the colon.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epidermoid Cyst (Epidermal Inclusion Cyst)

“Sebaceous cyst” misnomer
Clinical diagnosis
Treat with steroids, I&D, excision
Refer to dermatology for follow-up

question: An 18-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash that began 1 month ago when she noticed a large patch on her neck. After about a week, it developed into the more diffuse papulosquamous rash that she presents with now. You inform the patient that the rash will last 8–12 weeks and then prescribe cetirizine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pityriasis rosea is a common acute eruption that usually affects children and young adults. The cause is unknown. It is characterized by the formation of an initial herald patch, followed by the development of a diffuse papulosquamous rash. This condition is difficult to identify until the appearance of characteristic, smaller, secondary lesions that follow the Langer lines. The rash of pityriasis rosea typically lasts 8–12 weeks, with complete resolution in most patients.

An important goal of treatment is to control pruritus, which may be severe. Zinc oxide, calamine lotion, topical steroids, and oral antihistamines are usually helpful. Systemic steroids are generally not recommended. Patients should be reassured about the self-limited nature of pityriasis rosea. Persistence of the rash or pruritus beyond 12 weeks should prompt reevaluation of the original diagnosis, consideration of biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, and questioning the patient again about the use of medications that may cause a rash similar to that of pityriasis rosea.



Findings of contact dermatitis (A) can include erythema, vesicles, bullae, exudates, and crusting from the breaking of blisters, swelling, and scaling. Taking a careful history and patch testing are often the key to diagnosis.

In scabies (C), patients present with a pruritic rash that is often worse at night. Skin findings include papules, nodules, burrows, and vesiculopustules. The distribution includes the interdigital spaces, wrists, ankles, waist, groin, and axillae. Pruritic nodules around the axillae or umbilicus or on the penis and scrotum are highly suggestive of scabies.

Tinea corporis (D) is a fungal skin infection characterized by red, itchy, and often ring-shaped lesions on the body. More lesions can develop, but they are typically similar in morphology.

Tinea versicolor (E) presents with hypopigmented, pink to brown macules and patches on the trunk with fine scale. Versicolor means varied colors, and this tinea tends to be white, pink, and brown. Tinea versicolor is found on the back, chest, abdomen, and upper arms, often in a cape-like distribution.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the characteristic pattern seen when lesions follow the Langer lines in pityriasis rosea?

Reveal Answer:
Fir-tree pattern.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pityriasis Rosea

History of a larger lesion 1 week prior (herald patch)
Sx: rash on the trunk or proximal extremities
PE: diffuse papulosquamous rash, pine tree-like distribution
Condition often self-limited
Tx may include topical corticosteroids/oral antihistamines as needed for associated pruritus

question: A 24-year-old man presents for evaluation of a rash. He has a history of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and takes methylphenidate twice daily. The patient reports a mildly pruritic rash on his back and trunk that progressively spread over the last week. You examine and note the rash seen above. There are no lesions on the soles or palms. Which of the following historical elements is most likely to be obtained upon further questioning?

options.text: A larger 2 to 5 cm erythematous patch preceded the diffuse rash
Fever that resolved after 3 days followed by onset of the rash
Oral mucosal lesions preceded the onset of rash
Painless ulcer on the penis 6 weeks before rash began
Travel to the Southeast US occurred a week before the rash

correctAnswer: A larger 2 to 5 cm erythematous patch preceded the diffuse rash
englishExplanation:
This patient has pityriasis rosea. This is a mild skin eruption that is self-limited, usually lasting 4 to 7 weeks. There is no clear etiology of the rash, but infection with herpesvirus 7 or a fungus is suspected. Patients are most commonly asymptomatic but occasionally have a prodrome of malaise, headache, and pharyngitis.

Prior to the onset of the diffuse rash, patients may recall a herald patch described as a 2 to 5 cm erythematous oval plaque similar to the smaller more diffuse lesions. The rash is described as following a fir-tree pattern on the trunk, classically following the skin cleavage lines. Pityriasis rosea typically resolves spontaneously and no specific treatment is required other than symptomatic care, which can include topical corticosteroids for pruritus.



Fever that resolves followed by onset of rash (B) is the most common clinical presentation of roseola infantum, or sixth disease. It is typically caused by human herpesvirus 6 and most often affects children between the ages of 7 and 13 months. While fever can be part of a prodrome before the onset of pityriasis rosea, a fever that resolved before onset of rash is not associated with pityriasis.

Oral mucosal lesions (C) are rare with pityriasis. Oral lesions called Koplik spots, which are white or grey lesions with an erythematous base, may occur on the buccal mucosa with measles virus infection prior to the onset of a rash. The erythematous, maculopapular rash that occurs with measles classically begins on the face and then spreads to the trunk and extremities.

A painless ulcer on the penis weeks to months before a rash (D) is suggestive of syphilis. The painless ulcer, referred to as a chancre, occurs during primary syphilis. The rash that occurs during secondary syphilis may resemble that of pityriasis rosea, except that typically the palms and soles are also involved with syphilis infection.

A history of travel to the Southeast US (E) before the onset of rash should raise an index of suspicion for an infectious etiology to the rash like Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a tickborne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. This illness occurs most commonly in late spring and early summer and is characterized by a rash that starts distally and spreads to the core.

One Step Further
Question:
Is the rash of pityriasis rosea contagious?

Reveal Answer:
No, the rash cannot be spread by direct contact.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pityriasis Rosea

History of a larger lesion 1 week prior (herald patch)
Sx: rash on the trunk or proximal extremities
PE: diffuse papulosquamous rash, pine tree-like distribution
Condition often self-limited
Tx may include topical corticosteroids/oral antihistamines as needed for associated pruritus

question: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 weeks of intense pruritus. He reports no sick contacts, fever, new detergent or soaps, or outdoor activity. He currently lives in a local shelter and reports having been treated for “skin problems” as a child. An example of his skin findings is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Eczema is a chronic, often relapsing pruritic skin disorder characterized by intense pruritus, early age at onset (90% before age 5 years), generalized dry skin, and a personal or family history of atopic disorders (e.g., allergic rhinitis, asthma). It is often referred to as the “itch that rashes,” owing to the intensity of pruritus that may lead to excoriations and superimposed secondary bacterial infection. The infant form primarily affects the face, diaper area, and extensor surfaces, whereas older children and adults usually have skin findings on the flexor surfaces, face, neck, and chest. The cornerstone of care is proper skin hygiene and topical corticosteroid ointments such as betamethasone or fluticasone.



Psoriasis (B) is characterized by well-demarcated, raised erythematous papules with white or silver plaques or scales. It more often affects extensor surfaces (e.g., elbows, knees) but can also affect the scalp, trunk, and nails. Psoriatic arthritis is common in up to 25% of patients. Scabies (C) is a mite infestation characterized by intense nocturnal itching, often in the web spaces of digits, axillae, buttocks, and genitals. A linear thin, thread-like burrow caused by tunneling of the mite is pathognomonic. Seborrheic dermatitis (D) is a chronic papulosquamous skin condition characteristically affecting areas with increased sebaceous follicles or glands, such as the face, scalp, ears, and intertriginous areas. Lesions are typically pink to erythematous and may cause excessive flaking.

One Step Further
Question:
What two medical conditions are associated with seborrheic dermatitis?

Reveal Answer:
HIV and Parkinson disease.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)

Risk factors: history of asthma, hay fever, food allergies
Sx: itchy, scaly rash on arms, often worse in the winter
PE: thick, leathery, hyperpigmented areas on flexor surfaces
infants: extensor surfaces, spares diaper area
Tx: emollients and moisturizers, topical corticosteroids, tepid bathing, topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus
Complications: eczema herpeticum, S. aureus infection

question: An 8-year-old girl presents with a 4-day history of progressive rash accompanied by fever. The rash (shown above) started on the face with subsequent spread to the torso, followed by involvement of the extremities. The highest temperature over the past 24 hours is 102.3°F (39.1°C). No other symptoms are noted. She was diagnosed with partial seizures 3 weeks ago and was started on oxcarbazepine. Which of the following is associated with this rash?
englishExplanation:
These clinical features are consistent with drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS), also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). This is considered a T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction and is associated with specific human leukocyte antigen polymorphisms. Reactivation of herpes viral infection (human herpesvirus 6, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus) is also believed to play a role in many cases of DIHS. Skin findings begin as a maculopapular eruption progressing to coalescing plaques that are symmetrically distributed on the torso and extremities. The pattern of spread is from head to toe. Facial edema is common. Mucosal involvement can occur in half of cases but is generally mild. Generalized lymphadenopathy is common. Eosinophilia occurs in 82–95% of cases. Solid organ involvement is seen in up to 90% of cases, and liver involvement is seen most commonly. Elevations of liver transaminases up to 10 times the upper limit of normal are seen in half of those with liver involvement, although progression to liver failure is rare. Kidney involvement as acute interstitial nephritis occurs in up to one-third of patients. Pulmonary and cardiac involvement occur less commonly.



Anemia (A) is generally not seen in DIHS. Neutrophilia, contrasted with neutropenia (C), is seen in most patients. Thrombocytosis (D) is not commonly described in DIHS, although thrombocytopenia is occasionally seen.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the most common medications associated with drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Anticonvulsant medications, with aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) being most often implicated.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Drug-induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DIHS) (Formerly Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms, DRESS)

Severe T cell-mediated drug reaction (anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, vancomycin)
Begins 2–6 weeks after initiation of drug
Clinical
Fever, lymphadenopathy
Cutaneous: facial edema, polymorphic coalescing rash (mild mucous membrane involvement)
GI: hepatitis or cholestasis (most common), pancreatitis
Kidney: proteinuria, acute interstitial nephritis
Pulmonary: pneumonitis, interstitial pneumonia
Cardiac: myocarditis
Lab results: leukocytosis, eosinophilia, transaminitis, pancytopenia (severe)
Diagnosis: clinical symptoms, exposure to common drugs
Treatment: corticosteroids, cyclosporine, immunomodulators

question: An 82-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair and has a history of dementia presents from a skilled nursing facility with low back pain. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On physical examination, there is an erythematous area overlying the sacrum with full-thickness skin loss and visible subcutaneous fat. Which of the following is the correct staging of this patient’s pressure-induced skin injury?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with a history and physical examination consistent with a stage 3 pressure-induced skin ulcer. Pathogenesis involves external forces to the skin in combination with host-specific factors. Risk factors include immobility, malnutrition, decreased skin perfusion, and neurological disorders that lead to sensory loss such as delirium, dementia, spinal cord injury, and neuropathy. Thus, pressure-induced skin injuries are common in patients who reside in long-term care facilities and hospitals. Injuries are classified in stages based on erythema, thickness, and visualized subcutaneous fat, tendon, joint, bone, or eschar. Stage 3 pressure-induced skin ulcers are full-thickness injuries with subcutaneous fat visible. Treatment involves continued wound care, pain control, and monitoring for infection and progression of disease.



Stage 1 (A) pressure-induced injury is classified as an intact area of nonblanching erythema that lasts for > 1 hour after relief of external pressure.

Stage 2 (B) pressure-induced injury is a partial-thickness disruption of the dermis.

Stage 4 (D) pressure-induced injury is a full-thickness loss of tissue with visible muscle, tendon, joint, or bone.

One Step Further
Question:
What are two commonly used risk assessment tools for patients with pressure ulcers?

Reveal Answer:
Norton score and Braden scale.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pressure-Induced Skin and Soft Tissue Injuries

Stage 1–4
Stage 1: nonblanchable erythema of intact skin
Stage 2: partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis
Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss (subcutaneous fat may be visible)
Stage 4: full-thickness skin and tissue loss (exposed bone, tendon, or muscle)
Risk factors: immobility, malnutrition
Most common location is by bony prominences
Tx: prevention, frequent repositioning, skin assessment at hospital admission
Treat associated infection if present

question: A 78-year-old man presents to the ED with a worsening rash. He underwent a liver transplant 11 years ago and has taken tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone consistently since the surgery. He reports a good quality of life after his transplant. He avoids alcohol and manages stress by taking frequent fishing trips. The lesions as shown above are scattered and crusty and located primarily on his head. He reports that they have been present for several months but have recently changed in appearance. Which of the following is this patient at risk of developing?
englishExplanation:
This patient has actinic keratoses, which are a precursor for squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma is a malignancy of epidermal keratinocytes. It is usually caused by ultraviolet light exposure, and those with fair skin are at highest risk. Other causes of squamous cell carcinoma include human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, arsenic exposure, and immunocompromised status (such as patients with histories of taking immunosuppressive medications for solid organ transplants).

These lesions most commonly arise on sun-exposed areas, particularly the lip, ear, head, and neck. They appear as a well-defined red or brown thickened patch. Diagnosis is by biopsy, which will show malignant transformation of keratinocytes. Lesions > 2 cm in diameter and > 4 mm deep have a high risk of metastases. Treatment is with 5-fluorouracil ointment, cryosurgery, or full surgical excision.



Basal cell carcinoma (A) is a malignancy arising from the basal layer of the epidermis or follicular structures. It usually appears as a nonhealing, ulcerated wound with raised borders. It does not arise from actinic keratoses.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (B) is a rare type of cancer that affects the skin and originates from T lymphocytes. Immunosuppression (as in the case above) is a risk factor for the development of this condition. However, actinic keratoses, as depicted above, are not precursors for this condition.

Kaposi sarcoma (C) is a tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is classically seen in patients with HIV as an AIDS-defining illness when the CD4 count decreases to a low enough level.

Malignant melanoma (D) classically presents as a darkly pigmented lesion in sun-exposed areas with irregular borders. It does not arise from actinic keratoses.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: generally, dermatologists and experts recommend using a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 50 or higher.

Reveal Answer:
False. The recommendation is an SPF of 30 or higher.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Actinic Keratosis (AK)

Risk factors: extensive sun exposure, male sex, advancing age
PE: rough, scaly, erythematous papule, macule, or plaque on sun-exposed areas
Dx: clinical, may need biopsy
Tx: cryotherapy, fluorouracil for multiple lesions
Potential to progress to squamous cell carcinoma

question: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents for a new rash that has developed on her legs and buttocks over the last 24 hours. According to one parent, the child was ill with a sore throat and fever last week, but those symptoms improved. She spent the weekend at a friend’s house, and the parent is unsure whether the patient is allergic to something at that house because this morning she came home with a rash. She reports no respiratory symptoms. She reported right ankle pain earlier in the day but now says her left wrist and her right knee are hurting instead. On exam, her vital signs are normal. She is nontoxic appearing and does not have any joint swelling. You notice a purpuric and petechial rash on her bilateral legs and buttocks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
The patient in this question is presenting with signs and symptoms characteristic of immunoglobulin A vasculitis (formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura), a systemic vasculitis involving the small blood vessels of the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and joints. It typically occurs in children, generally around ages 4–8 years. A large number of patients will have a preceding upper respiratory infection, and many will have group A beta-hemolytic streptococci cultured from the oropharynx. The hallmark of the illness is a purpuric or petechial rash that is most prominent on the lower extremities and buttocks. Arthralgias are common, and many patients experience abdominal pain. A self-limited glomerulonephritis can develop and is manifested as hematuria. Most cases resolve on their own and do not require any therapy. Corticosteroids do not reduce the risk of abdominal or renal complications from the illness.



Meningococcal disease (B) that causes a petechial rash is generally associated with Neisseria meningitidis, which can lead to meningitis, bacteremia, and ultimately sepsis. Symptoms usually begin with an upper respiratory infection, and later, patients develop fever, myalgias, headaches, and vomiting. Petechiae develop on the wrists and ankles and are the first sign of septicemia. Patients quickly decompensate as the rash spreads to the rest of the body and becomes more purpuric and confluent. The patient in this question is not presenting with signs of meningitis and is not toxic appearing.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever (C) is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. It is transmitted by the bite of a tick. The petechial rash usually starts on the wrists and ankles and spreads centrally to the trunk and proximal extremities. Patients generally have a fever, headaches, myalgias, and malaise. There was no mention of a tick bite in this patient, and her rash is not typical of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

Rubella (D)is an infection caused by the rubella virus. The illness is generally mild, and the rash of rubella usually starts on the face and spreads downward. A fever, sore throat, and fatigue may occur. The rash fades after about three days. The patient in this question does not have a rash consistent with a rubella infection.

One Step Further
Question:
Which bacterial gastrointestinal organism is associated with development of immunoglobulin A vasculitis?

Reveal Answer:
Campylobacter jejuni enteritis

Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 50-year-old man presents to the ED with a rash and mouth pain. He developed oral ulcers several weeks prior to the onset of the rash, and they have persisted despite antiviral and antifungal therapy. His vital signs are unremarkable. On physical exam, flaccid blisters and erythematous erosions are noted across his trunk and extremities that spare the palms and soles. There are erosions on the buccal mucosa and hard palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pemphigus vulgaris is a life-threatening, autoimmune blistering disease characterized by flaccid blisters and erosions of the skin and mucous membranes due to intraepidermal deposition of autoantibodies. Autoantibodies target desmogleins, which are transmembrane glycoproteins involved in maintaining tissue integrity, leading to acantholysis, or loss of cell-cell adhesion between keratinocytes. It most commonly presents in adults ages 40–60 and affects male and female patients equally. Almost all patients with pemphigus vulgaris have mucosal involvement, which may precede the development of cutaneous blisters. Mucosal lesions are typically painful erosions, and intact blisters are rarely seen. The oral cavity is the most common site of mucosal lesions, but the esophagus, conjunctiva, nasal mucosa, anus, labia, and vagina can be involved. Pain from severe oral erosions can lead to decreased oral intake, dehydration, and malnutrition. Over half of patients will also develop cutaneous manifestations. The classic skin lesions are flaccid blisters that easily rupture, leading to painful erosions that may ooze or bleed. Cutaneous blisters can affect any part of the body and are often widespread, but the palms and soles are typically spared. Without treatment, loss of the epithelial barrier can result in mortality from fluid losses and secondary bacterial infection.

The diagnosis is made through the combination of clinical findings, lesional biopsy for histopathology, perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence, and detection of serum autoantibodies. The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids. Steroid-sparing agents are often added, including azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin. Prior to the use of systemic corticosteroids, pemphigus vulgaris was usually a fatal disease. With current treatment, mortality ranges from 5–15%.



Bullous pemphigoid (A) is an autoimmune blistering disease of older patients, characterized by tense, pruritic blisters, as opposed to the painful, flaccid blisters of pemphigus vulgaris. A minority of patients with bullous pemphigoid have mucosal involvement.

Erythema multiforme (B) presents with a characteristic targetoid rash and variable mucosal involvement. The classic target lesions have a dusky central area of necrosis surrounded by a lighter area of edema and an outermost area of erythema.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) (D) is an important diagnosis to consider in any patient presenting with a painful rash and mucosal lesions, as it is life-threatening. However, SJS has a rapidly evolving course. The fact that this patient had oral ulcers for several weeks prior to the onset of the rash makes this diagnosis unlikely. Additionally, a patient with SJS who has progressed to widespread cutaneous involvement will appear ill, often with abnormal vital signs.

One Step Further
Question:
What percentage of patients with erythema multiforme have oral involvement?

Reveal Answer:
70%.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pemphigus Vulgaris

Autoimmune blistering disorder due to anti-desmosome antibodies
Most common in age 40–60
Sx: painful flaccid bullae on mucosal surfaces
PE: flaccid blisters that extend with lateral pressure (Nikolsky sign positive) involving mucous membranes
Dx: confirmed by biopsy
Tx: high-dose steroids, supportive care
Other options may include immunosuppressives, IV immunoglobulins, immunoadsorption, rituximab
Complications: dehydration, secondary infection, thromboembolism (can have high mortality without treatment)

question: Which of the following is most commonly associated with erythema nodosum?
englishExplanation:
Erythema nodosum, thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a systemic disease or medication, is a vasculitis involving the venules and veins of the skin. It affects young adults primarily in their second to fourth decades, with women affected almost four times as often as men. A prodrome of nonspecific symptoms, including fever, malaise, and myalgias, is followed by the development of subcutaneous nodules, primarily on the anterior tibial surfaces. Lesions may also be seen on the forearms, trunk, and thigh. The nodules are often erythematous, well-circumscribed, and very tender. While many cases are found to be idiopathic, the most commonly implicated disease is a preceding streptococcal infection. Patients may give a history consistent with preceding streptococcal infection (e.g., fever and sore throat), and an antistreptolysin O titer should be checked. Treatment includes symptomatic care with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Inflammatory bowel disease (A), particularly Crohn disease, has been implicated in cases of erythema nodosum but not as commonly as streptococcal infection.

Patients with sarcoidosis (B) are at increased risk for developing erythema nodosum, but this is not as common of a preceding illness as a streptococcal infection.

Tuberculosis (D) has also been associated with the development of erythema nodosum, but preceding streptococcal infection is more common.

One Step Further
Question:
What care is indicated in patients with erythema nodosum who do not improve with NSAIDs or who have severe, debilitating disease?

Reveal Answer:
Corticosteroids.

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: Which of the following conditions is the rash seen above associated with?
englishExplanation:
The image represents impetigo, a pustular eruption most commonly seen in preschool children. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis results from an antecedent infection of the skin or throat caused by nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis usually occurs 1–2 weeks after pharyngitis and 3–6 weeks after skin infection. The incidence is decreasing in the United States but is still common in some rural areas. It appears to result from the deposition of circulating immune complexes in the kidney. This leads to decreased glomerular filtration, allowing proteins to flow freely into the urine. Urinalysis shows significant blood and protein with RBC casts in 60% of cases. Pyuria with granular or hyaline casts also may be found.



Impetigo is not associated with arthritis (B). Other skin conditions, such as psoriatic arthropathy, occur in up to 20% of patients with psoriasis.

Clostridioides difficile (C) bacteria proliferate when the normal bowel flora is substantially reduced by antibiotic therapy. If the bacteria produce sufficient quantities of toxin, colitis develops.

There are a number of cutaneous manifestations of secondary syphilis (D). Lesions may be erythematous or pink macules or papules, usually with a generalized symmetrical distribution.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of impetigo?

Reveal Answer:
Staphylococcus aureus followed by group A Streptococcus.

Contagious epidermal infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS)
Most common in children < 6 years (can affect any age, including adults)
Risk factors: skin trauma, insect bites, eczema, scabies
Sx: nonpainful, pruritic lesions on the face
PE: papules and weeping vesicles with honey-colored crust, most common on the face
Bullous impetigo: vesicles form bullae that rupture and leave brown crust, more common on trunk
Tx
Limited number of lesions: topical mupirocin
Numerous lesions or involvement of more than one area: oral antibiotics (cephalexin or dicloxacillin)
Complications: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with a distinctive nonblanching rash on his buttocks and lower extremities and mild bilateral knee pain. He has no other concerns at this time. He appears nontoxic and his abdominal exam is benign. What test should be performed at this time?
englishExplanation:
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) is an IgA-mediated vasculitis of unknown etiology that commonly causes nephritis, and a screening urinalysis should be performed in the emergency department when the diagnosis is suspected. Patients with HSP are typically 3–10 years of age and present typically with palpable purpura on the buttock and extensor surfaces of the lower extremities. They also may have arthralgias or arthritis. These children appear nontoxic and have no mucous membrane involvement. The main predictor of long-term outcomes is the development of kidney involvement. Children should be screened by urinalysis on diagnosis and followed for 6 months.



An abdominal radiograph (A) would be an appropriate test if the patient presented with abdominal pain. Children with HSP can develop abdominal sequelae including intussusception and bowel perforation. Should sepsis with bowel perforation be a consideration, blood culture, abdominal radiographs, and empiric antibiotics would be appropriate. Generally, the standard test for intussusception is an abdominal ultrasound with radiological-assisted reduction in cases in which bowel perforation is not suspected. Children with free air on the abdominal radiograph should be immediately referred to surgery.

Blood cultures (B) are not useful in uncomplicated HSP as the disease is immune-mediated.

Platelet counts (C) in HSP are expected to be normal. If the diagnosis is in question, a platelet count may be of value.

What is the classic finding on kidney biopsy in a patient with IgA vasculitis?

Crescentic changes of the glomeruli.

question: A 7-day-old boy presents to the emergency department with a fever, irritability, and a peeling skin rash. The parents report some nasal congestion and redness in the eyes but no oral lesions. The physical exam reveals the findings above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by infection with Staphylococcus aureus. It is most common in young children and newborns in the first week of life. Patients present with a fever and diffuse erythroderma and blisters with scaling of the skin. Patients will also experience conjunctivitis. Areas of high mechanical stress, such as the flexural areas, will blister and slough off. Patients often appear ill. Management is centered on resuscitation with crystalloid fluids, blood cultures, and antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus. It is appropriate to cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and narrow the coverage spectrum later. Patients require admission to a burn unit for care.



Cellulitis (A) presents with warmth, erythema, and tenderness at a focal site of infection. The diagnosis can be made clinically, though ultrasound may demonstrate edema and cobblestoning. It is not associated with diffuse erythroderma and skin peeling.

Necrotizing fasciitis (B) is a lethal diagnosis with a rapidly progressive skin infection, fever, tenderness, and possibly crepitus (if a gas-producing organism is present). Often, areas of dark necrosis can be seen on exam, which is not present in this patient. Patients may demonstrate hemodynamic instability that rapidly worsens.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) is associated with medication exposure, though infections and other antigens may lead to this condition. Patients present with erythema and blistering of their skin that is similar in appearance to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. A differentiating factor is mucosal surface involvement, which is not found in this patient.

Question:
What hypersensitivity reaction presents with target-shaped lesions on the skin?

Reveal Answer:

question: A 16-year-old boy presents to the ED with a rash. It began 1 week ago with a single patch that was about 5 cm on his stomach, and has now worsened and spread along his back. It is mildly pruritic and only involves the torso. He has no fevers, cough, or other symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Pityriasis rosea is a common benign rash that occurs in children and young adults. It is recognized by the appearance of a herald patch 5–10 days before a widespread systemic eruption that is most prominent on the trunk and proximal limbs. The lesions are usually round, about 1 cm, and slightly raised. The widespread rash follows cleavage lines, giving it the appearance of a Christmas tree or a fir tree pattern on the back.

It is thought to be caused by a virus, debatably attributed to a reactivation of human herpesvirus 6, 7, or 8. It can often be mistaken for tinea corporis. Secondary syphilis can have a similar appearance, especially when considering that pityriasis rosea occasionally appears on the palms or soles. Treatment for asymptomatic patients is simply reassurance. Some patients have itching that is worse at night, which can be treated with a bland emollient or lubricating lotion with menthol or camphor, with or without an oral antihistamine.



There is limited evidence that acyclovir (A) or ultraviolet light causes more rapid resolution, but the data is weak and these therapies are only recommended in severe cases.

Fluconazole (B) is appropriate for tinea corporis but not pityriasis rosea. If the presentation is not clear, tinea corporis can be differentiated from pityriasis by a positive potassium hydroxide preparation on skin scrapings, best taken from the border of a plaque.

The rash from syphilis is usually diffuse, symmetric, and macular or papular and includes the palms or soles. It can have a similar appearance but often includes additional systemic symptoms and is treated with penicillin (C).

One Step Further
Question:
What clinical presentation is infection with human herpesvirus 7 associated with in young children?

Reveal Answer:
Febrile seizures.

History of a larger lesion 1 week prior (herald patch)

PE: diffuse papulosquamous rash, pine tree-like distribution

question: A 27-year-old man with AIDS has the rash shown in the picture above. What type of isolation is required if he is admitted?
englishExplanation:
Varicella-zoster virus (human herpesvirus 3) is the causative agent in both chickenpox and shingles. Herpes zoster, shown in this patient, occurs from reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus that has been dormant in a dorsal root nerve ganglion since an episode of chickenpox. Most reoccurrences occur in older (> 55 years) and immunocompromised patients. Prior to the onset of rash, patients experience tingling or hyperesthesia in the dermatome. Painful, vesicular lesions then appear on the skin along the distribution of the dermatome. Patients are considered infectious from 5 days before the appearance of the rash until 5 days after the appearance of the vesicles. If the patient is immunocompromised with localized herpes zoster, standard precautions plus airborne (negative pressure room) and contact precautions should be followed until disseminated infection is ruled out.



Droplet precautions (B) are indicated for viruses with larger respiratory particles. These precautions include a mask worn when entering a patient’s room. One of the most common indications for droplet precautions is influenza.

Positive pressure (C) precautions involve positive air pressure such that the air inside the patient’s room is forced out of the room into the surrounding environment. This type of isolation is sometimes used in patients with neutropenia.

Standard precautions (D) are universal for every patient in the hospital setting and are not unique to any particular disease entity.

One Step Further
Question:
Does the use of corticosteroids decrease the incidence of post-herpetic neuralgia?

Reveal Answer:
A recent Cochrane review does not support this practice.

PE: rash with unilateral, dermatomal distribution that does not cross midline
Dx: based on clinical presentation, PCR if confirmation needed
Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (not typically done)
Tx: antiviral therapy (best if started within 72 hours)
Postherpetic neuralgia: when pain persists beyond 3 months in the same distribution as a preceding documented episode of acute herpes zoster

question: A 62-year-old man presents with right-sided chest pain for 4 days. The pain is unilateral and of a deep burning and stabbing quality. He uses tobacco daily and reports a long-term history of COPD, which is managed with tiotropium 18 mcg dry powder per capsule inhaled once daily and albuterol 90 mcg/actuation inhaled once or twice every 2–4 hours as needed. Vital signs today are a BP of 121/91 mm Hg, HR of 98 bpm, RR of 15/min, and T of 98.5°F (36.9ºC). Cardiac exam reveals a regular rate and rhythm. On pulmonary exam, there is a slightly prolonged expiratory time. Physical exam of the chest reveals a normal anteroposterior diameter with a light pink vesicular dermatitis on the right side. An ECG is performed and shown above. What management should be initiated?

options.text: Cephalexin 500 mg PO four times daily
Nitroglycerin 0.6 mg SL as a single dose
Prednisone 60 mg PO once daily for 2 weeks

englishExplanation:
This patient presents with herpes zoster (shingles) and should have appropriate pain control started, such as acetaminophen. Herpes zoster results from the reactivation of dormant varicella-zoster virus developing in patients with a history of chickenpox. Risk factors for the development of herpes zoster include advanced age, immunocompromised status, and chronic lung or kidney disease.

Typically, pain in a dermatomal distribution precedes the eruption of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the same dermatome. The vesicles are cloudy at first and progress to crust formation later in the course. The pain associated with the disease is often severe and debilitating. Patients may not initially see a dermatitis and may report unilateral deep burning or stabbing chest pain. If no obvious rash is initially present, a chest X-ray or ECG may be performed to rule out cardiovascular concerns, both of which are typically unremarkable in patients with herpes zoster.

The mainstay of treatment is pain control and oral antiviral medications, depending on the timing of symptom onset and comorbidities. Orally administered corticosteroids were commonly recommended in the treatment of herpes zoster, but given recent clinical trials showing variable results, they are not typically recommended.



Antibiotics such as cephalexin (B) are only indicated if there is a superinfection of the lesions.

Antihistamines such as fexofenadine (C) have not been shown to hasten the rate of healing or aid in symptom relief in patients with varicella-zoster.

Nitroglycerin (D) is used for patients with anginal chest pain or pain associated with acute coronary syndrome.

Corticosteroids such as prednisone (E) have not been proven to be beneficial, although when combined with antivirals, such as valacyclovir, they may help with pain reduction.

One Step Further

What complication should herpes zoster lesions at the tip of the nose alert the clinician to?

Reveal Answer:
Ocular herpes zoster is correlated with lesions at the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign).

question: A 15-month-old girl presents due to a progressive rash and fever. She has had thick white nasal discharge and some left eye crusting with discharge for the preceding week. Fever as high as 103.3°F (39.6°C) has been present for the past 3 days. Areas of the skin are red with superficial peeling and crusting present on the face and upper chest, as shown above. She has been fussy, and the parents note that she is uncomfortable when held. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her findings?
englishExplanation:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) occurs following the release of exotoxins (epidermolytic toxin A and B) associated with a focal infection due to Staphylococcus aureus that results in a generalized indurative or sunburn-like erythema (erythroderma) of the skin accompanied by marked skin tenderness. The exotoxins produce a split high within the superficial layers of epithelium, resulting in superficial skin peeling, blistering, and crusting.

These skin findings are especially pronounced around the mouth and nose or within the axillary and inguinal regions where skin friction plays a role in skin breakdown and peeling (positive Nikolsky sign). Mucous membranes are typically spared in SSSS. The outer two-thirds of the lip (dry surface) is keratinized and may manifest with superficial peeling, while the inner one-third of the lip is not keratinized and thus is not involved. Other mucous membranes (e.g., intraoral) are not keratinized and remain unaffected, which is an important clinical differentiator between SSSS and other mucocutaneous syndromes.

Treatment includes the use of a first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin), penicillinase-resistant penicillins (nafcillin or oxacillin), and vancomycin in areas with a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus.



Impetigo (A) is a localized infection due to S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is not accompanied by fever or other signs of systemic illness.

The mucous membrane findings in Kawasaki syndrome (B) include coarse vascular injection of the eyes with deep hemorrhagic crusts of the lips and mouth.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (D) is marked by deeper skin erosions, blistering, and desquamation due to inflammatory cleavage at the epidermal-dermal junction. Significant involvement of mucous membranes is characteristic of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, not SSSS.

One Step Further
Question:
How do staphylococcal epidermolytic toxins lead to associated skin findings in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
These toxins produce cellular changes resulting in disruption of the stratum granulosa layer of the epidermis manifesting clinically as superficial skin peeling and tender, flaccid bullae.

question: A 65-year-old man presents to the ED with a painful rash on his right upper arm that he first noticed 2 days ago. It has since rapidly progressed to involve his lateral upper arm and anteromedial axilla and has spread inferiorly near the elbow and antecubital fossa. His vital signs include a BP of 90/45 mm Hg, HR of 115 bpm, and T of 38.3°C. There is erythema, warmth, and exquisite tenderness to palpation over the site. Which of the following additional findings would support a diagnosis of a necrotizing soft tissue infection?
englishExplanation:
Necrotizing soft tissue infections are caused by microbial invasion of the skin, fascia, and muscle. Two types of infection have been described. Type 1 infections comprise up to 75% of cases and are polymicrobial, including aerobes and anaerobes. Type 2 infections comprise 20–30% of cases and are monomicrobial, with the most common isolates including group A Streptococcus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Less common etiologies, such as Vibrio vulnificus or fungi, more commonly affect immunocompromised patients. As sanitation efforts have improved, Clostridioides species have become uncommon. Older age or a history of diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney or liver disease, heart disease, active malignancy, immunocompromised state, intravenous drug use, alcohol use, frequent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory use, or chronic skin infection or decubitus ulcers is a risk factor for the disease. In the early stages, infections may present with pain out of proportion to physical examination findings, followed by rapid tissue destruction and toxin release. The diagnosis of necrotizing soft tissue infections is clinical, and a high index of suspicion should be maintained in patients with bullae formation, crepitus (though only seen in up to 50% of patients), and necrotic skin. Evidence of systemic illness (e.g., tachycardia, hypotension, mental status changes) may represent an evolving bacteremia, which is seen in 25–30% of cases. Imaging may demonstrate soft tissue gas, though this is not required for the diagnosis. The presence of inflammatory laboratory results (e.g., C-reactive protein elevation, leukocytosis, anemia, hyponatremia, creatinine elevation, and hyperglycemia) embodied by the well-known laboratory risk indicator for necrotizing fasciitis score support the diagnosis. Prompt surgical exploration (i.e., incision and debridement) is the mainstay of diagnosis and treatment. Early empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy should include a carbapenem (e.g., imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) or piperacillin-tazobactam, an agent with anti-MRSA activity (e.g., vancomycin or linezolid), and clindamycin due to its antitoxin effects. Despite early antibiotic therapy and surgical intervention, the mortality rate remains up to 10% in the United States.



Erythema with a dusky center (B) is a common finding in erythema multiforme, which is a circumscribed erythematous area with central dusky or purplish skin, depending on the patient’s baseline skin tone. A positive Nikolsky sign (C) is present when there is a separation between layers of keratinocytes, which is nonspecific and can be seen in a variety of mostly immune-mediated skin disorders (e.g., Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris). Raised tender nodularities (D) describe the lesions of erythema nodosum. Silver patches and plaques (E) are the characteristic examination findings of plaque psoriasis.

One Step Further
Question:
What microbe typically causes cellulitis with well-demarcated, raised erythema?

Reveal Answer:
Group A Streptococcus.

Type 1: polymicrobial
Type 2: a single organism (most commonly group A Streptococcus)
Myonecrosis
Traumatic (Clostridium perfringens)
Spontaneous (Clostridium septicum)
Pain out of proportion to exam
Systemic signs of infection
Cellulitis progresses to dusky blue with bullae or vesicles

Emergent surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics

question: A 19-year-old man presents with concerns of a progressive rash developing over the past 3 days. He reports no fever, headache, or arthralgia. His vital signs include blood pressure of 124/78 mm Hg, heart rate of 96 bpm, respiratory rate of 14 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation of 99%, and temperature of 99.0°F (37.2°C). His dermatologic evaluation is shown in the image above. The same lesions are also found on his palms and soles. What is the most likely cause of the lesions?
englishExplanation:
This patient has erythema multiforme, an acute immune-mediated self-limited rash characterized by target-shaped skin lesions. The most common known causes include reactivated herpes simplex, Mycoplasma pneumonia, and upper respiratory tract infections. Rarely, it can be associated with allergens, drugs, connective tissue diseases, and internal malignancies.

While it can present with multiple forms, such as red macules and papules, urticarial-like lesions, vesicles, and bullae, most of these will evolve over 24–48 hours to form 1–3 cm target lesions. Diagnosis is based on this classic clinical appearance, with a central lesion surrounded by a pale area of edematous skin and a surrounding sharp discrete ring of erythema. Lesions appear in crops, resolve in 2–4 weeks, and often involve the palms and soles. Involvement of oral mucosa differentiates erythema multiforme major from erythema multiforme minor. Treatment involves symptomatic treatment and topical steroids, systemic steroids with taper for severe disease or mucosal involvement, and antiviral suppressive therapy for recurrent lesions associated with herpes.



Erythema marginatum is the cutaneous manifestation of acute rheumatic fever (A). It involves migratory pink annular lesions with sharp margins that affect the trunk and sometimes the limbs. They usually do not include the face, palms, or soles. They appear and disappear within hours, similar to urticaria. This evanescent feature differentiates them from the fixed lesions of erythema multiforme.

Drug reaction (B) is a less common cause of erythema multiforme than herpes simplex.

Lyme disease (D)can often be diagnosed by erythema migrans, an expanding large red annular lesion with central clearing at the site of a tick bite that can grow to 10 cm. There can be multiple concentric rings due to hematogenous spread.

Secondary syphilis (E) usually involves the palms but does not appear as target lesions. Secondary syphilis characteristically appears as pink scaly 1–2 cm patches.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name given to wart-like genital lesions associated with secondary syphilis?

Reveal Answer:
Condyloma lata.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Multiforme (EM)

Most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Drugs: sulfa, oral hypoglycemics, anticonvulsants, penicillin, NSAIDs (SOAPS)
Patient presents with acute onset of symmetric target lesions on palms and soles, face and trunk may also be involved
Erythema multiforme minor: localized eruption of the skin with minimal or no mucosal involvement
Erythema multiforme major: one or more mucous membranes are involved
PE: target-like rash with a central dark papule surrounded by a pale area and a halo of erythema
Tx: usually self-limiting, supportive care

question: A 55-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents to the emergency department with diffuse sloughing of his skin with blisters that extend easily when lateral pressure is applied to them. The lesions cover his entire torso and back and are also found within his mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings covering roughly 36% of his body (using the rule of nines) suggestive of a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is a life-threatening autoimmune condition of the skin that presents with diffuse sloughing of the skin covering at least 30% of the body with associated mucosal lesions. Potential causes of toxic epidermal necrolysis include drugs (such as allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs), and infections (such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae). The disorder can also occur spontaneously without a known trigger. Minor pressure can be applied to blisters resulting in sloughing (Nikolsky sign). The treatment of toxic epidermal necrolysis is typically admission to a burn center, supportive therapy, and possibly immunomodulators (though there is not sufficient evidence to suggest this is standard of care). Patients will require pain control, nutritional support, and meticulous wound care. Currently, there is no clear evidence suggesting a benefit of steroids in toxic epidermal necrolysis, and treatment requires an emergency dermatology consult. The mortality of this condition is high (> 30%).



Erythema multiforme (A) presents with annular target-shaped lesions with central pallor or necrosis that occurs secondary to infection or medications and can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (B) presents with macular erythema and widespread exfoliation typically in the setting of fever and tachycardia with tender skin and mucosal sparing.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (C) is essentially a less severe form of toxic epidermal necrolysis and presents with dermatologic lesions or skin detachment on < 10% of the body. Using the rule of nines, this patient’s lesions cover his chest and back, meaning that 36% of his body is covered, suggesting a diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the best initial antibiotic for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Nafcillin, oxacillin, or vancomycin if there is a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

Severe mucocutaneous reaction with epidermal necrosis and detachment
Etiology: medications (e.g., sulfonamides, anticonvulsants), infection (e.g., Mycoplasma)
PE: vesicles, bullae, and skin detachment, often including mucous membranes
Extent of involvement
Stevens-Johnson syndrome: < 10% of the body surface area detached
Toxic epidermal necrolysis: > 30% of the body surface area detached
Tx: stop the offending agent, supportive care and crystalloid administration, transfer to specialized center
SCORTEN scale is used to determine prognosis and clinical setting for Tx in adults

question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a rash that started as pruritic lesions that progressed to tense blisters. Physical exam is notable for the skin lesions shown above that do not slough when lateral pressure is applied to them. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings suggestive of bullous pemphigoid, an autoimmune blistering disorder that is more often found in those > 60 years. Bullous pemphigoid presents initially with pruritic eczematous, papular, or urticarial-like skin lesions. These skin lesions can subsequently progress to the classical tense bulla with a thick covering that does not slough when pressure is applied to them (a negative Nikolsky sign). This is in contrast to pemphigus vulgaris, which presents with flaccid blisters that slough or extend easily when pressure is applied to them. The lesions are typically highly pruritic and can ultimately rupture leaving erosions and crusts that eventually heal. The diagnosis is made clinically. However, a biopsy can confirm the diagnosis. The treatment of bullous pemphigoid is initially topical steroids. Systemic steroids or doxycycline might be required for widespread disease.



Dermatitis herpetiformis (B) presents with highly pruritic grouped papules and vesicles that appear similar to a herpes infection. This condition is commonly seen in celiac disease, which presents with diarrhea and weight loss secondary to exposure to gluten-containing foods.

Pemphigus foliaceus (C) presents similarly to pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid blisters that rupture easily when pressure is applied to them. It can be differentiated from pemphigus vulgaris by its typical absence of mucosal lesions.

Pemphigus vulgaris (D) presents with flaccid bullae that rupture easily when pressure is applied to them with lesions that can be found in the oral mucosa. The treatment of pemphigus vulgaris is systemic steroids.

One Step Further
Question:
What immune deficiency can be seen in celiac disease?

Reveal Answer:
IgA deficiency (leading to repeat infections of the mucosal surfaces).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bullous Pemphigoid

Autoimmune blistering condition
Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with an itchy rash to the groin. The rash is scaly and has a reddish-brown color. It does not fluoresce under a wood lamp. What is the pathogen responsible for this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient has tinea cruris, otherwise known as jock itch. It is caused by a dermatophyte, most commonly Trichophyton rubrum. Infection occurs at the epidermal layer and results in inflammation and hyperplasia of the skin that produces areas of scaly skin with dermatitis. Tinea cruris does not fluoresce under a wood lamp. Microscopic examination of a potassium hydroxide wet mount will reveal segmented hyphae consistent with Trichophyton rubrum. Treatment involves topical antifungal agents for 2 weeks.



Candida (A) produces a superficial irritation rash that will fluoresce under a wood lamp and may produce satellite lesions.

Corynebacterium minutissimum (B) is a bacterium that causes a dermal infection, most often in the genitocrural areas, that fluoresces a deep red under a wood lamp.

Sporothrix schenckii (C) causes a granulomatous infection from direct inoculation of the skin by spores. The most often source is soil and plants.

One Step Further
Question:
What should be a consideration in recurrent fungal infections?

Reveal Answer:
Diabetes alters the urogenital flora making fungal infections more common and can be screened with historical information of polyuria or point of care testing with a finger-stick blood test for glucose.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tinea

Capitis (scalp): children, kerion
Corporis (body): red, annular, raised, central clearing
Cruris (inguinal area): excessive perspiration, occlusive clothing
Pedis (feet): sweaty feet
Unguium (nails): raised and discolored nail, nail plate white, thick, crumbly
Capitis or unguium Tx: PO antifungals
