question: A 48-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the ED, brought in by family, with altered mental status, fever, and a “female problem” that has rapidly evolved over 12 hours. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and alcohol use disorder. Current medications are lisinopril and metformin, but the patient is chronically noncompliant. On exam, the patient’s vital signs include an oral T of 102.5°F (39.2°C), BP of 84/66 mm Hg, HR of 120 bpm, and RR of 24/min. Her peripheral capillary blood sugar is 350 mg/dL. She appears to be seriously ill, is pale, and has delayed capillary refill. The labia and perineum are significantly swollen bilaterally and deeply erythematous with a very indurated texture. There is a 2 cm blackened area on the inferior aspect of the left labia majora. Swelling does not permit visual inspection of the vagina or cervix. Of the options below, which best describes your clinical diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Fournier gangrene is a type of necrotizing fasciitis that is commonly thought to be specific to male genitalia. However, the term includes female labial and perineal necrotizing fasciitis as well. The most common predisposing factors are diabetes and excessive alcohol use, but other factors include extremes of age, malignancy, chronic steroid use, cytotoxic drugs, malnutrition, drug use, human immunodeficiency virus, and other causes of immunocompromise. This patient has two of these factors (diabetes and alcohol use disorder). Common findings of Fournier gangrene include abnormal vital signs, severe site pain or pain out of proportion to physical findings (at least early in the course), severe swelling, site warmth and woody induration, altered mental status, hemorrhage, rapidly advancing infection, crepitus, hemorrhage, sloughing, and blistering. The disease may begin gradually and often originates from local skin infections or trauma. Colorectal causes include local infections of the perineum, anal fissures, colon rupture, rectal carcinoma, and perianal surgery. Urologic causes include chronic urinary tract infections, neurogenic bladder, and epididymitis. Additional sites of origin for women include Bartholin gland abscess, episiotomy, hysterectomy, and septic abortion. Pediatric sites of origin include insect bites, burns, trauma, and circumcision. About 25% of all cases are judged idiopathic. Resulting inflammation and edema lead to the destruction of affected tissue via endarteritis. Infection tends to dissect along perifascial planes, permitting rapid extension and progression to gangrene. Fascial necrosis in Fournier gangrene can advance at 2–3 cm per hour. Mortality rates, even with aggressive treatment and early identification, are generally 20–40%. The most common microorganisms include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant varieties), and Bacteroides fragilis. Most cases are polymicrobial, with group A Streptococcus being the most common organism in monomicrobial cases.



Bartholin gland abscess (A)and cellulitis (B)are incorrect. Both entities can be the site of origin of Fournier gangrene, but the pathognomonic findings of tissue necrosis, widespread tissue involvement and rapid spread, and severe, woody induration plus risk factors are concerning for progression to necrotizing fasciitis.

Phlegmasia cerulea dolens(D) is incorrect. Findings may be similar, but this disorder is caused by ileofemoral vein thrombosis, which may be extensive enough to result in arterial insufficiency and gangrene. Workup should identify the presence of thrombosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Brodie sign?

Reveal Answer:
Brodie sign is the appearance of a black spot on external affected tissue; it signals the beginning of very rapid propagation of necrosis and is accompanied by clinical deterioration.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Fournier Gangrene

Necrotizing fasciitis of the genital region
Risk factors: diabetes, immunocompromised status, PVD, obesity
Sx: genital swelling and pain out of proportion to visual inspection
Systemic symptoms (fever, lethargy) may be present
Advanced-stage Dx: crepitus, purpura, bulla, patchy black discoloration
Tx: broad-spectrum antibiotics, emergent surgical debridement

question: A 67-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 days of myalgias, headache, and low-grade fever. Today, he noticed the lesion on his nose, as shown above. What is the next step in management?
englishExplanation:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus, a potentially sight-threatening infection, is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion. Patients often present with a prodrome of fever, headache, malaise, and hypesthesia in the affected eye and forehead, followed by a vesicular rash along the trigeminal dermatome. Vesicular lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) are associated with a high risk of herpes zoster ophthalmicus as this area is innervated by the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which also innervates the globe. Ophthalmologic examination is a crucial step in this patient’s evaluation as early diagnosis of ocular involvement is critical in preventing the progression of infection and loss of vision. Findings can include hyperemic conjunctivitis, episcleritis, and punctate keratitis. Emergent ophthalmologic consultation is indicated when the diagnosis is suspected. Treatment includes oral antiviral agents.



Discharging with acyclovir (A) is the appropriate treatment for uncomplicated herpes zoster involving a trunk or extremity dermatome.

Treatment with prednisone (B) is controversial. Studies have not shown a clear benefit with the addition of prednisone to antiviral medications when treating herpes zoster. Systemic steroids are also associated with potential complications, such as hyperglycemia and secondary bacterial infection.

A lumbar puncture (D) is indicated in those cases in which patients with evidence of herpes zoster have symptoms concerning for meningeal involvement.

One Step Further
Question:
What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
Triad of ipsilateral facial paralysis, ear pain, and vesicles in the auditory canal and auricle due to reactivation of varicella zoster virus within the geniculate ganglion.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus

Reactivation of latent VZV in CN V1 distribution
Sx: eye pain, redness, tearing,
PE: vesicular rash in CN V1 distribution
Hutchinson sign
Punctate epithelial keratitis, pseudodendrites
Tx: ophthalmology consultation and oral or IV acyclovir (or similar agent)
Complication is acute angle-closure glaucoma

question: A 40-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension presents with a large mass on her back. She states that it has been there for roughly 1 year, and the appearance is bothersome to her. She reports no fevers, pain, or restricted motion. On examination, the patient has a 3 cm skin-colored, soft, mobile mass on her back overlying the right scapula. There is no tenderness, induration, or punctum. What is an ultrasound of this mass most likely to show?

options.text: Anechoic poorly defined structure with collections of internal echogenic fluid
Hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement
Hypoechoic free fluid separating subcutaneous tissue and fat
Hypoechoic well-circumscribed mass with pulsation on color Doppler
Well-circumscribed circular hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic rim

correctAnswer: Hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement
englishExplanation:
This patient has a lipoma. A lipoma is a mass consisting of mature fat cells enclosed in a thin fibrous capsule. Lipomas are typically diagnosed clinically by their appearance as soft, skin-colored, painless nodules ranging from 1 cm to > 10 cm. Occasionally, an ultrasound may be needed to differentiate a lipoma from other skin lesions such as epidermoid cysts or ganglion cysts. Ultrasound commonly shows a hyperechoic or isoechoic mass without posterior acoustic enhancement. It is important to note that while the majority are hyperechoic or isoechoic, they can occasionally be hypoechoic. Lipomas are benign and do not need to be removed unless bothersome to the patient. Generally, the removal of lipomas requires a surgical referral.



Anechoic poorly defined structure with collections of internal echogenic debris (A) best describes an abscess. Anechoic coloring is due to fluid that does not reflect ultrasound waves, and echogenic debris may represent purulence. In this patient without overlying erythema, pain, or fluctuance, abscess is unlikely.

Hypoechoic free fluid separating subcutaneous tissue and fat (C) describes cobblestoning. Cobblestoning on ultrasound represents edema in the subcutaneous tissue, which may represent cellulitis or simple edema.

Hypoechoic masses with pulsation on color Doppler (D) may represent pseudoaneurysms. In this patient with a mass, one should always evaluate the mass under color Doppler before any incision to ensure the mass does not have pulsatile, arterial blood flow. These most commonly are associated with femoral or radial artery procedures, so this mass over the scapula is most likely not a pseudoaneurysm.

Well-circumscribed circular hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic rim (E) describes an epidermoid cyst. These cysts can be difficult to differentiate from lipomas, as they are also skin-colored and mobile, so ultrasound is the first-line tool used to differentiate the two.

One Step Further
Question:
What lesion clinically resembles a lipoma except it is painful and found primarily in children, adolescents, and individuals with HIV after starting antiretroviral therapy?

Reveal Answer:
Angiolipoma.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Lipoma

Benign soft tissue tumor composed of fat cells enclosed within a thin fibrous capsule
More common in adults
Type depends on histology
Can be associated with syndromes (e.g., Gardner syndrome, multiple symmetric lipomatosis)
Tx: excision if needed

question: A 74-year-old man presents to the ED with blistering on his extremities. On physical exam, tense bullae are noted on the arms and legs. Nikolsky sign is negative. There is no oral involvement. Which of the following is part of the appropriate treatment for this disease process?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms and physical exam findings consistent with bullous pemphigoid. Bullous pemphigoid is a chronic bullous disease that involves IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane (subepidermal). It is the most common bullous disease and is classically seen in adults > 60 years. It may be caused by repeated skin trauma and the presence of other inflammatory skin conditions such as psoriasis. However, it is often idiopathic.

Signs and symptoms include a pruritic rash that evolves into tender, tense bullae occurring most often over the legs, forearms, and axillae. Mucosal involvement is uncommon. Nikolsky sign is negative. Diagnosis is made by needle biopsy to discriminate from pemphigus vulgaris. However, it may be differentiated clinically based on the differences between the two, as pemphigus vulgaris includes oral involvement, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, while bullous pemphigoid does not.

Initial management includes general wound care, steroids (topical or systemic), and doxycycline. This disease process often improves and relapses spontaneously. Dapsone and immunomodulators such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, and methotrexate may be needed for refractory cases. Mortality, though rare, is most commonly caused by sepsis. Overall, bullous pemphigoid has a relatively good prognosis when compared to pemphigus vulgaris.



Burn center admission (A) would be appropriate if this patient had Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). However, there is no evidence of recent infection or medication use and no description of sloughing skin. Additionally, Nikolsky sign is positive in SJS and TEN. Patients with bullous pemphigoid more often follow a prolonged, relapsing and remitting course, and general wound care is recommended instead of burn center care.

Clindamycin (B) would be appropriate for necrotizing fasciitis, which may exhibit blistering but is also characterized by pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, and gas in the tissues. These patients also tend to be febrile and have abnormal vital signs.

Vancomycin (D) would be appropriate for inpatient treatment of severe cellulitis. This would be warranted if he had vital sign abnormalities or had not improved with outpatient treatment for cellulitis. Vancomycin should be reserved for instances of concern regarding methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

One Step Further
Question:
Why is clindamycin used in patients with necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome?

Reveal Answer:
It not only treats the bacteria but also aids in neutralizing the exotoxin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bullous Pemphigoid

Autoimmune blistering condition
Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

question: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parent for 1 week of pruritic rash, as seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pityriasis rosea is an exanthematous skin condition that involves the trunk and proximal extremities. In most cases, pityriasis rosea begins with a characteristic herald patch, which is pink or salmon colored with scaling along the margins and central clearing. This is followed by the development of smaller oval lesions that follow the lines of skin cleavage, most noticeable on the back as the classic Christmas tree appearance. The cause of pityriasis rosea is unknown but thought to be viral in etiology. Pityriasis rosea is self-limited and typically resolves without intervention in 8–12 weeks. Antihistamines can be used to help with pruritus.



Nummular eczema (A) presents with pruritic plaques that most commonly involve the extremities.

Sporotrichosis (C), also known as rose gardener disease, is a fungal infection that classically presents with lesions in a lymphatic distribution in the upper extremities. Pulmonary involvement may also occur.

Tinea versicolor (D) is a skin condition caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur and presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented lesions.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment of choice for tinea versicolor?

Reveal Answer:
Topical antifungals (e.g., terbinafine, azole antifungals).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pityriasis Rosea

History of a larger lesion 1 week prior (herald patch)
Sx: rash on the trunk or proximal extremities
PE: diffuse papulosquamous rash, pine tree-like distribution
Condition often self-limited
Tx may include topical corticosteroids/oral antihistamines as needed for associated pruritus

question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ED due to abdominal pain. For the past week, he has had intermittent abdominal pain without a clear pattern in onset or remission and intermittent roving joint pains. Prior to the onset of these symptoms, he had a bilateral lower extremity macular and erythematous rash that developed into several small palpable areas of purpura with surrounding patchy nonblanching erythema and purplish color. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal upon further evaluation?
englishExplanation:
IgA vasculitis is most common between the ages of 3 and 15 years with a male predominance. It results from IgA deposition of unknown etiology in tissues with resulting cytotoxic immune system activity. The most common set of guidelines used to direct further investigation was published in 2005 by the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR). The presence of purpura is mandatory for diagnosis, and one of the following must be present: abdominal pain, acute arthralgias, or signs of kidney involvement on urinalysis. These criteria are sensitive but not specific.

Further testing and expert consultation are required for patients meeting these guidelines. IgA vasculitis does not cause significant alterations in platelet counts, platelet function, coagulation factor levels, or coagulation factor activity. The most common laboratory abnormalities are microscopic hematuria and proteinuria due to IgA deposition within the nephrons and resulting kidney injury. In pediatric patients, the diagnosis is clinical. A skin or kidney biopsy is required in adult patients to rule out other more common causes of small vessel vasculitis. Treatment of IgA vasculitis is typically supportive. Most episodes self-resolve and do not recur. Monitoring for recovery of kidney function is important in patients with significant kidney involvement.



Coagulation studies (A) and a complete blood count (B) will be unremarkable in a patient with isolated IgA vasculitis. These are far more likely to be abnormal in adult patients, whose purpura is commonly the result of diseases that affect platelet or clotting factor function.

Abnormalities in the ophthalmologic examination (C) are extremely rare in IgA vasculitis. The presence of uveitis, iritis, or conjunctivitis is suggestive of another underlying condition.

One Step Further
Question:
How is testicular pain due to IgA vasculitis differentiated from testicular torsion in a symptomatic patient?

Reveal Answer:
Scrotal ultrasound will show normal or increased blood flow in IgA vasculitis, whereas blood flow will be decreased in testicular torsion.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 7-year-old girl presents to the ED with a fever, mouth and eye pain, and a rash. Past medical history is unremarkable outside of a recent prolonged cough. On physical exam, you note the above. Nikolsky sign is positive. Which of the following are the most common infectious etiologies of this disease process?

options.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae and herpes simplex virus

correctAnswer: Mycoplasma pneumoniae and herpes simplex virus
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting symptoms and physical exam findings consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). SJS and TEN are variants of a disease spectrum with life-threatening mucocutaneous manifestations. SJS is the formal diagnosis when the lesions involve < 10% of the total body surface area (TBSA), while TEN involves > 30%. It is more common in male individuals and older adults and is caused by the autoimmune detachment of the epidermis and mucous membranes that results in widespread erythema and bullous lesions.

Most cases are medication related. Infectious causes are more likely in children and younger adults. The most common infectious causes of SJS and TEN are Mycoplasma pneumoniae and herpes simplex virus. Signs and symptoms of SJS and TEN include fever, recent upper respiratory tract infection, purulent sputum, and the classic rash. The rash begins as atypical target-like lesions and progresses to painful bullae on an erythematous base. There is a positive Nikolsky sign as the epidermis separates with slight lateral pressure. There is universal mucous membrane involvement and frequent eye erythema, pain, and discharge.

Diagnosis is classically clinical. However, if there is diagnostic uncertainty, a skin biopsy may be required. Management is supportive with hydration as if these lesions were a large burn. Patients should be admitted to a burn center for management of this disease process. Ophthalmology should be consulted if there is any indication of ocular involvement. Mortality depends upon the degree of TBSA involvement because larger areas lead to an increased risk of infection.



Chlamydia pneumoniae and adenovirus (A), Staphylococcus aureus and coxsackievirus A (C), and Streptococcus pneumoniae and varicella-zoster virus (D) are not commonly implicated infectious etiologies of SJS or TEN.

One Step Further
Question:
What medication classes are most commonly implicated in causing erythema multiforme?

Reveal Answer:
Sulfonamides, oral hypoglycemics, anticonvulsants, penicillin, and NSAIDs.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

Severe mucocutaneous reaction with epidermal necrosis and detachment
Etiology: medications (e.g., sulfonamides, anticonvulsants), infection (e.g., Mycoplasma)
PE: vesicles, bullae, and skin detachment, often including mucous membranes
Extent of involvement
Stevens-Johnson syndrome: < 10% of the body surface area detached
Toxic epidermal necrolysis: > 30% of the body surface area detached
Tx: stop the offending agent, supportive care and crystalloid administration, transfer to specialized center
SCORTEN scale is used to determine prognosis and clinical setting for Tx in adults

question: A 73-year-old man presents with a painful wound on his lower leg. An image of the wound is provided above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Venous stasis ulcers are a condition caused by chronic venous insufficiency. Damaged venous valves in conditions such as phlebitis and varicose veins are the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. This can then lead to stasis of venous blood flow, which causes edema and stasis dermatitis. Early stasis dermatitis is characterized by an orange-like skin hyperpigmentation and dependent edema. The skin may also become dry, tight, and hairless. Locations commonly involved in stasis dermatitis are the medial distal and pretibial areas of the legs. Chronic stasis dermatitis leads to worsening edema and, eventually, ulceration. The most common sites of venous stasis ulcers are the bilateral malleoli and the medial aspect of the calf. Symptoms include pain, cramping, leg heaviness, and fatigue. Diagnosis is made clinically. Treatment is limb elevation, compression stockings, and local wound care. Cases complicated by a secondary bacterial infection should be treated with antibiotics.



Arterial ulcers (A) are most often caused by chronic changes due to peripheral artery disease. Ulceration is typically very painful and often occurs at pressure points such as the base of the heel and the toe joints.

Diabetes-related ulcers (B) usually result from minor trauma that goes unnoticed due to underlying neuropathy. Over time, ulcerations form in pressure points such as the plantar metatarsal heads and heel.

Pressure ulcers (C) are caused by prolonged periods of external force on the skin. They are most common among patients who are hospitalized or reside in a long-term facility with underlying risk factors such as immobility, dementia, and diabetes mellitus. Ulceration may occur anywhere on the body, predominantly in pressure points such as the sacrum, coccyx, heels, or hips.

One Step Further
Question:
Which condition is diagnosed with an ankle brachial index?

Reveal Answer:
Peripheral artery disease.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Venous Insufficiency

Most commonly caused by venous valvular abnormalities
Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, advancing age, prolonged standing, family history of venous insufficiency
Sx: leg swelling
PE: skin changes, ulceration, edema, varicose veins
Dx: often made by history, physical exam
Tx: leg elevation, compression therapy, ulcer care, ablation

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parents with arthralgias, abdominal pain, and a new-onset rash, as shown in the image above. His urinalysis is positive for blood. The most likely diagnosis is associated with which one of the following?
englishExplanation:
IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting children between 2 and 11 years of age, caused by deposition of IgA immune complexes. Etiology of the immune complex deposition is unclear. However, there appears to be an association with preceding upper respiratory infection. The classic triad of symptoms includes abdominal pain, arthritis, and a palpable purpuric rash, most commonly involving extensor surfaces of the lower extremities and buttocks. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding occur in 50–75% of cases. IgA vasculitis is associated with IgA nephropathy, also known as Berger disease (not to be confused with Buerger disease, or thromboangiitis obliterans), a glomerulonephritis caused by immune complex deposition in the renal mesangium. IgA nephropathy is a nephritic syndrome that may present with hypertension, azotemia, hematuria, proteinuria, and edema. Treatment for IgA vasculitis is supportive. Consultation with a pediatric nephrologist is recommended in patients with kidney involvement.



Coronary artery aneurysm (A) formation in children is a feared complication of Kawasaki disease.

Polyarteritis nodosa, a medium-vessel vasculitis typically affecting visceral and renal vessels, is associated with hepatitis B seropositivity (C).

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (D) is a progressive disease that causes bile duct scarring. It is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, most often ulcerative colitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What pediatric surgical pathology is associated with IgA vasculitis?

Reveal Answer:
Intussusception, which occurs in about 3% of cases.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 34-year-old man presents with a rash on his chest for 3 months. It is not itchy. He states the rash worsened in the summer. He has a history of migraine headaches, for which he uses sumatriptan as needed. He is sexually active with one partner and uses condoms. His vital signs include a blood pressure of 112/78 mm Hg, heart rate of 76 bpm, respiratory rate of 12/min, oxygen saturation of 99%, and temperature of 98.5°F. The patient’s chest is seen above. There is no lymphadenopathy and no palm or sole involvement. Which of the following treatments is most likely indicated?

options.text: Cephalexin 500 mg PO three times daily for 7 days
Penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM once
Topical permethrin 1% cream rinse applied once and repeated in 7 days
Topical selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion applied once daily for 7 days
Topical triamcinolone 0.1% ointment applied twice daily for 2 weeks

correctAnswer: Topical selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion applied once daily for 7 days
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with tinea versicolor requiring treatment with topical selenium sulfide. Tinea versicolor is a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia furfur (formerly Pityrosporum ovale).

Typically, patients will present with scaly patches on the chest and trunk, but occasionally, the rash will spread to the limbs. There may be mild pruritus associated with the rash. Patients often seek care after sun exposure because the affected areas do not tan and will appear hypopigmented. The diagnosis is made based on clinical presentation but can be confirmed by a potassium hydroxide preparation from scraping of the patches. The treatment for tinea versicolor is with 2.5% selenium sulfide lotion, imidazole cream, or oral fluconazole. Recurrence is common (15–50%).



Cephalexin (A) is a first-generation cephalosporin with activity against many Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species but no antifungal activity. It is used in bacterial skin conditions, such as cellulitis and impetigo.

Penicillin G benzathine (B) is the preferred treatment for secondary syphilis. Secondary syphilis presents with enlarged lymph nodes and a macular rash on the trunk, palms, and soles that develops weeks to months after the initial chancre.

Topical permethrin (C) is not effective in treating tinea versicolor but is effective in the treatment of scabies and lice.

Topical triamcinolone (E) is a corticosteroid that may reduce itching but will not treat the underlying disease.

One Step Further
Question:
What treatment can be given for prophylaxis against repeat episodes of tinea versicolor?

Reveal Answer:
Monthly application of selenium sulfide lotion or ketoconazole lotion.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tinea Versicolor

Most commonly caused by Malassezia species (e.g., M. furfur)
PE: hypopigmented areas that do not tan, scaly patches on the chest and trunk
Diagnosis is made by KOH preparation of skin scraping
Treatment is topical selenium sulfide 2.5% or topical ketoconazole

question: A 16-year-old girl develops tender, slightly raised nodules on the pretibial surfaces, as pictured above. Which of the following is the most common bacterial organism associated with these findings?
englishExplanation:
These tender erythematous to violaceous pretibial nodules are characteristic of erythema nodosum (EN). The most common bacterial organism associated with EN is Streptococcus pyogenes. EN is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction. It occurs most often among female patients between the ages of 20 and 50. It is three to six times more common among female individuals than male individuals. In most clinical series, it is unexplained (idiopathic) or primary in 30–55% of patients. Secondary causes include infection (bacterial, fungal, atypical, viral), inflammatory bowel disease, medications (oral contraceptives, penicillins, sulfonamides), malignancy (Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myelogenous leukemia), and pregnancy. Streptococcus pyogenes has been identified as a trigger in almost half of secondary EN cases. Primary EN will undergo spontaneous remission within 1–2 weeks in most cases. Secondary EN will typically remit following identification and treatment of the inciting cause. Recommendations for treatment of EN include rest and the use of NSAIDs.



Bartonella henselae (A), the agent of cat scratch disease, produces a papular rash and regional lymphadenopathy. Tularemia, caused by Francisella tularensis (B), includes symptoms of skin ulcers, swollen and painful lymph glands, and inflamed eyes (Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome). Mycobacterium tuberculosis (C) is associated with 2–22% of secondary EN cases, with the highest numbers seen in regions of the world where tuberculosis is endemic.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the dose of potassium iodide that is recommended to treat dermatoses like erythema nodosum?

Reveal Answer:
300 mg three times daily in patients with erythema nodosum not associated with tuberculosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Nodosum

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the ED with his parent for evaluation of a rash. The patient has been afebrile but has multiple pearly, skin-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this finding?
englishExplanation:
Molluscum contagiosum is a self-limited epidermal skin condition caused by a double-stranded DNA poxvirus. Populations most commonly affected are children ages 2 to 6 years old or immunocompromised individuals. Molluscum contagiosum is spread through direct contact with infected persons or contact with fomites. The characteristic lesions are 1–5 mm discrete, flesh-colored, pearly, dome-shaped papules with umbilicated centers. They may occur anywhere on the body and may coalesce in clusters in the groin or genitalia of sexually active individuals. Patients with AIDS may have particularly large lesions on the face. Autoinoculation causes further spread of lesions. A typical course lasts 6 to 9 months, and lesions may spread to distant sites. Patients should be advised against sharing clothing, bedding, personal hygiene products or instruments, and showers with others. Liquid nitrogen cryotherapy may be used for isolated lesions that are few in number, depending on the individual. Other options include immunotherapy with Candida or Trichophyton antigen.



Bunyavirus (A), or Bunyaviridae, is a large group of single-stranded RNA viruses that are transmitted through arthropods and cause hemorrhagic fever. Coxsackievirus (B) is responsible for herpangina and hand, foot, and mouth disease, which are both characterized by grouped clear fluid-filled vesicles. Human metapneumovirus (C) is a single-stranded RNA virus that is responsible for many pediatric lower respiratory infections.

One Step Further
Question:
Children with what skin condition may develop hundreds of molluscum contagiosum lesions if infected?

Reveal Answer:
Atopic dermatitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Molluscum Contagiosum

Common in childhood, can also occur in healthy adults
Spread through direct skin-to-skin contact or fomites
Sx: Small, skin-colored papules, sometimes associated with pruritus or inflammation
PE: multiple waxy, dome-shaped papules with an umbilicated appearance
Etiology: poxvirus
Self-limiting: typically resolves without treatment within 6–12 months, but removal can be considered if lesions are symptomatic

question: A 82-year-old patient with history of advanced dementia presents with altered mental status. As part of a full physical evaluation, you note a 4 x 6 cm area of ulceration over the sacrum with exposed adipose tissue and areas of granulation tissue but no visible bone or muscle. A small area of eschar is noted at the superior aspect of the wound. There is no purulent drainage or fluctuance. What is the best next step in management of this pressure injury?

options.text: Debridement of eschar in the emergency department followed by application of an occlusive, dry dressing
Hydrogel dressing and surgical consultation for debridement
Wet to dry dressing and intravenous antibiotics

correctAnswer: Hydrogel dressing and surgical consultation for debridement
englishExplanation:
Pressure ulcers are graded on a scale of 1 to 4 based on the involvement of various tissues. Stage 3 pressure ulcers are characterized by full thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat may be exposed but bone, muscle, and tendons are not. Granulation tissue is often visible and there may be areas of eschar or slough present. Treatment of pressure ulcers of all stages includes proper positioning of the patient to avoid prolonged pressure in any area, pain management, and optimization of nutrition. Although all ulcers are colonized with bacteria, only those wounds with evidence of active infection should be cultured and treated with antibiotics. Specific wound management varies based on the stage of the ulcer. Stage 3 ulcers should be covered with a dressing that keeps the wound moist while the surrounding skin is kept dry. This can be accomplished with saline-moistened gauze or hydrogel dressing. As necrotic tissue impedes wound healing, surgical consultation for debridement should be requested for patients with ulcers that have overlying necrotic tissue and eschar.



A stage I ulcer consists of intact skin with nonblanching erythema. These ulcers can be covered with a transparent film (A) and special attention should be paid to proper positioning and nutrition to prevent continued injury. Debridement of eschar in the emergency department followed by application of an occlusive, dry dressing (B) is incorrect because wounds should be kept moist to facilitate reepithelialization. Intravenous antibiotics (D) are not indicated in this patient because there is no evidence of superimposed infection, such as surrounding erythema, warmth, foul odor, or purulent drainage.

One Step Further
Question:
What are risk factors for pressure ulcer development?

Reveal Answer:
Immobility, malnutrition, decreased perfusion, and sensory loss.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pressure-Induced Skin and Soft Tissue Injuries

Stage 1–4
Stage 1: nonblanchable erythema of intact skin
Stage 2: partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis
Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss (subcutaneous fat may be visible)
Stage 4: full-thickness skin and tissue loss (exposed bone, tendon, or muscle)
Risk factors: immobility, malnutrition
Most common location is by bony prominences
Tx: prevention, frequent repositioning, skin assessment at hospital admission
Treat associated infection if present

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a skin lesion. He states he has had this before, but this time it is more severe. He otherwise feels well and has no other concerns today. He does not have any pain or pruritus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Psoriasis is a dermatologic condition that is associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B27. It is an autoimmune condition related to CD4 and CD8 T cells. Patients present with a silvery scale with a salmon undertone. However, on darker skin, the rash can appear dark brown or purplish. The skin lesion has a sharp margin and is described as a plaque on an erythematous base. It is a relapsing and remitting condition with triggers, including physiologic stressors such as infection or trauma. When the scale is removed, pinpoint bleeding may be noted (termed the Auspitz sign). Other manifestations of psoriasis may include psoriatic arthritis, nail pitting, and an increased risk of acute coronary syndrome. The diagnosis is made clinically and can be supported by biopsy. Treatment depends on the severity of the condition and may include topical emollients, topical steroids, vitamin A and D ointment, coal tar, and immunomodulators. UV therapy may be used in severe cases with significant total body surface area involvement.



Atopic dermatitis (A) or eczema is more common in patients with an atopic history (asthma and seasonal allergies). It presents with pruritic, scaly lesions that are more common on the flexor surfaces. The diagnosis is made clinically, and treatment includes topical corticosteroid therapy with emollients. Erythema multiforme (B) is a hypersensitivity reaction that may occur secondary to herpes infection, Mycoplasma infection, and after exposure to certain medications. It presents with a target-like lesion on the skin. Treatment is aimed at addressing the underlying cause. Impetigo (C) is a bacterial infection commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. It presents with pruritic, honey-crusted lesions that are more common in patients who engage in contact sports. Management for limited disease includes topical antibiotics such as mupirocin. Extensive disease involves treatment with oral antibiotics such as cephalexin. All linens must be thoroughly washed during this condition to avoid reexposure and reinfection.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the classic rash seen in Lyme disease?

Reveal Answer:
Erythema migrans.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Psoriasis

Sx: rash on extensor surfaces of arms and legs
PE: bilateral sharply marginated papules or plaques with silvery scales, Auspitz sign (scale removal produces blood droplets), nail pitting
Treatment: topical corticosteroids, emollients, phototherapy, biologic agents

question: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a rash on his anterior chest. He states the lesions are painful, and he describes a burning sensation in the affected areas. The physical exam is notable for bullae and flaccid blisters, which extend easily when lateral pressure is applied to them. The exam is also notable for similar lesions on the mucosal surfaces. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Pemphigus vulgaris occurs secondary to antibodies against desmoglein 3 or both desmoglein 1 and 3. It presents with mucosal involvement (which is a unique feature and often noted first) and cutaneous involvement. Patients will demonstrate bullae and flaccid blisters that extend easily or slough when lateral pressure is applied (termed a positive Nikolsky sign). The dermatologic findings are painful rather than pruritic. Potential exacerbating factors include infections, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and medications. The diagnosis can be confirmed with a biopsy, and treatment involves steroids and immunomodulators in conjunction with a dermatology consult.



Bullous pemphigoid (A) presents with thick bullae that are widespread, tense, and pruritic. In contrast to the dermatologic lesions that rupture easily in pemphigus vulgaris, the skin lesions in bullous pemphigoid are thick and do not slough or extend easily (a negative Nikolsky sign).

Pemphigus foliaceus (B) presents with scaly and crusted erosions on an erythematous base, which can be painful and described as burning. Unique features of this pathology include superficial skin blistering without mucous membrane involvement and without involvement of the deeper epithelium.

Pemphigus herpetiformis (C) presents with the clinical findings of dermatitis herpetiformis including excoriations, erythematous and urticarial plaques, and papules with vesicles. The underlying pathophysiology is similar to pemphigus vulgaris with IgG against epidermis desmoglein components.

One Step Further
Question:
What disease is dermatitis herpetiformis classically associated with?

Reveal Answer:
Celiac disease.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pemphigus Vulgaris

Autoimmune blistering disorder due to anti-desmosome antibodies
Most common in age 40–60
Sx: painful flaccid bullae on mucosal surfaces
PE: flaccid blisters that extend with lateral pressure (Nikolsky sign positive) involving mucous membranes
Dx: confirmed by biopsy
Tx: high-dose steroids, supportive care
Other options may include immunosuppressives, IV immunoglobulins, immunoadsorption, rituximab
Complications: dehydration, secondary infection, thromboembolism (can have high mortality without treatment)

question: A 5-year-old boy presents with the above rash, which has worsened over the last 3 days. It is extremely itchy, keeping him from being able to sleep. He has no systemic symptoms, vital signs are within normal limits for age, and the exam is unremarkable other than the above rash. The rash is mostly between the fingers but is also located over the wrists and axilla. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Clotrimazole 1% cream two times per day for 14 days
Hydrocortisone 1% cream two times per day for 14 days
Mupirocin 2% cream three times per day for 5 days
Permethrin 5% cream one time each week for 2 weeks

correctAnswer: Permethrin 5% cream one time each week for 2 weeks
englishExplanation:
The infestation of the skin by a female Sarcoptes scabiei mite can cause scabies, an infectious and intensely pruritic illness. The mites mate on the skin surface, and the female then burrows into the skin, creating a shallow well, which she then extends by a few millimeters every 24 hours while laying eggs. The eggs hatch within a few days, and the mite dies in the burrow within a few weeks. Mites not on the skin die within a few days, so transmission is usually through close contact, not through fomites. The mite, mite feces, and eggs cause a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is extremely itchy.

The classic illness is first recognized about a month after primary inoculation by 1–2 mm red papules. The burrows of the female mite are sometimes visible but other times difficult to see due to excoriation. Extreme itching is universal and worse at night. The rash is most prominent in the webs of the fingers, flexor aspects of the wrists, extensor aspects of the elbows, anterior axillary folds, waist, umbilicus, and the lower buttocks and adjacent thighs.

Unusual manifestations are crusted scabies, which occur in immunocompromised patients. It is more severe and diffuse and presents with a prominent scale that becomes almost wart-like with crusts and fissures, but it does not itch. Small infants also often lack the interdigital manifestations with lesions mostly on the trunk.

The treatment for scabies is a permethrin 5% cream, which should be applied to the scalp and entire body from the neck down. This should be left in place for 8–14 hours (depending on the reference text) before rinsing. This should be reapplied in 1 week in a similar fashion. Alternative therapies include sulfur ointment, crotamiton lotion, or lindane lotion. Lindane lotion can cause neurotoxicity (especially in children), should be avoided whenever possible, and is contraindicated in children with poorly controlled seizures. Immunocompromised children are sometimes also treated with oral ivermectin.



Clotrimazole (A) is the appropriate treatment for tinea corporis or a diaper candidal infection, which is recognized by an annular skin lesion or discrete erythematous papules and plaques with satellite lesions in the diaper area. Candidal diaper dermatitis is usually easily differentiated from scabies even in young infants, as it is isolated to the diaper area.

Hydrocortisone (B) is a commonly used topical treatment of eczema, which is also intensely pruritic but presents with dry, scaly, or excoriated patches not seen in this patient.

Mupirocin (C) is typically recommended for superficial bacterial infections such as impetigo, which usually presents as superficial papules with surrounding erythema. These papules break and develop characteristic golden crusts and usually involve the area around the face not seen in the patient above.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for canine scabies caused by cuddling a puppy with mange?

Reveal Answer:
Nothing. It is self-limited in humans since humans are not a suitable host for the parasite.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Scabies

Most commonly caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis
Sx: severe pruritus that is worse at night
PE: small papules, vesicles, and burrows in the webbed spaces of the fingers and toes
Dx: made by microscopic visualization
Tx: permethrin 5% (infants > 2 months old) or oral ivermectin (ivermectin not first line in pregnancy or in children < 15 kg)

question: A 20-year-old woman is started on lamotrigine after she was diagnosed with epilepsy. She presents to the emergency department with a new-onset rash 10 days after initiating the antiepileptic therapy. She notes that preceding the onset of the rash, she had fevers, malaise, and anorexia. The patient’s temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), blood pressure is 136/73 mm Hg, heart rate is 101 bpm, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Physical examination reveals multiple exfoliative skin lesions, tender erythema, bullae formation, and mucositis involving approximately 40% of her total body surface area. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Supportive treatment and transfer to a burn center

correctAnswer: Supportive treatment and transfer to a burn center
englishExplanation:
This patient has toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), a potentially life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction that is characterized by exfoliative skin lesions, tender erythema, and bullae formation involving > 30% of total body surface area (TBSA). It is more severe but less common than Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), which typically involves < 10% of TBSA. The most frequent triggers for TEN/SJS are medications, including allopurinol, lamotrigine, antibacterial sulfonamides, nevirapine, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). After medications, the next most common trigger is Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Patients often exhibit a prodromal phase of fever, malaise, and anorexia for 1–2 weeks. The onset of the characteristic rash can occur anywhere from 4 days to 4 weeks after continuous use of the medication. The majority of cases of TEN/SJS have mucosal lesions. Treatment includes cessation of the suspected offending medication and supportive treatment, including intravenous fluid resuscitation, electrolyte replacement, wound care, infection prevention, and pain control. Patients with signs of infection should be promptly covered with antibiotics. However, prophylactic antibiotics are not generally recommended. After supportive treatment is initiated, definitive care should be continued at a burn unit, if available.



Dermatology consultation (A) and surgical debridement (D) are not routinely indicated in the initial, acute treatment of TEN/SJS. The use of corticosteroids (B) in the management of TEN is controversial as there is conflicting evidence regarding improvement in mortality and complication rates associated with their use.

One Step Further
Question:
What is necrotizing fasciitis?

Reveal Answer:
A rapidly progressive, emergent, polymicrobial infection of fascia with subcutaneous tissue necrosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

Severe mucocutaneous reaction with epidermal necrosis and detachment
Etiology: medications (e.g., sulfonamides, anticonvulsants), infection (e.g., Mycoplasma)
PE: vesicles, bullae, and skin detachment, often including mucous membranes
Extent of involvement
Stevens-Johnson syndrome: < 10% of the body surface area detached
Toxic epidermal necrolysis: > 30% of the body surface area detached
Tx: stop the offending agent, supportive care and crystalloid administration, transfer to specialized center
SCORTEN scale is used to determine prognosis and clinical setting for Tx in adults

question: A 5-month-old male infant presents to the ED, brought by his parent, for a severe rash. She states the baby has been teething recently and has been having several loose stools per day. The baby is in daycare, and the childcare workers are not able to change his diapers as frequently as he is stooling. On examination, he has an erythematous perianal rash with denuded skin but no satellite lesions. Which of the following is the recommended first-line therapy?
englishExplanation:
Diaper dermatitis is a common pediatric problem and is caused and exacerbated by overhydration of the skin from prolonged skin contact with feces and urine. Peak incidence is 9–12 months of age. Simple measures can be taken to improve and prevent diaper dermatitis. Infant skin benefits from diaper-free periods, allowing the skin to air dry. Cleaning is best done by patting the skin (as opposed to vigorously scrubbing) with a soft cloth and using lukewarm water. Commercial wipes impregnated with fragrance, alcohol, or other chemicals may further irritate the skin. Superabsorbent disposable diapers help maintain a dry environment. Additionally, a protective barrier ointment or paste containing either zinc oxide or petroleum should be used at every diaper change. Other options for complex cases include low-potency topical corticosteroids and sucralfate, which has antibacterial properties. Some rashes may become secondarily infected with Candida species and require topical antifungal therapy. Candida lesions are typically well-demarcated, erythematous lesions with smaller satellite lesions that are separate from the larger areas of dermatitis. Parents should be educated about these measures to prevent further instances of diaper rash. An acronym to remember these is ABCDE: air, barrier, cleansing, diaper, education.



Betamethasone cream (A) is a higher-potency topical corticosteroid that is not safe for infants’ thin skin.

Mupirocin ointment (B) is used to treat impetigo due to gram-positive skin flora.

Topical clotrimazole (C) is an azole antifungal that may be required for secondary fungal infection from Candida species. However, this is not typically the first-line treatment for a rash that does not appear to have fungal elements.

One Step Further
Question:
Why are breastfed infants less likely to get diaper dermatitis?

Reveal Answer:
The pH of their feces is lower.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Contact Dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis
Most commonly caused by nickel, poison ivy, soaps, and topical meds (neomycin)
Dx: patch test
Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction
Id reaction: generalized cutaneous reaction in areas not exposed to allergen
Irritant contact dermatitis
Caused by prolonged contact with water, detergents, solvents, acids, alkali
PE: scaly plaques, vesicles, bullae
Sx: pruritus, burning
Tx: avoid causative agents, emollients, topical corticosteroids

question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for oral lesions for 3 weeks. She has multiple oral lesions that are painful to the touch and with oral intake of food and fluids. She has not had similar symptoms in the past. She had negative serum HIV viral load, oral herpes simplex virus, chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis tests 1 week ago. She reports no other associated symptoms. Physical examination shows over 50 ulcers that are 0.5–1 cm in diameter and well-defined with a thin ring of erythema and a white base. There is no significant oral edema, intolerance of secretions, or stridor. A full surface skin examination reveals no other lesions. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
Aphthous ulcers (commonly called canker sores) are defined as discrete, painful, 3–5 mm oval ulcers with a rim of erythema and a white or yellow adherent central exudate located in the oral cavity. Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) is the regular recurrence of multiple ulcers that last up to 14 days. Some patients present with complex RAS, when the lesions last 4–6 weeks, occur more frequently, may be associated with similar genital lesions, and are larger in diameter. RAS can be treated with topical agents. Clobetasol 0.05% gel three times daily and sucralfate rinse four times daily are the most commonly available, effective, and tolerated treatments. Patients with complex RAS rarely achieve control of symptoms with topical therapies. Patients with a large number of ulcers (like this patient), a history of recurrence, or symptoms lasting longer than 14 days (also this patient) are likely to require a 4–7 day course of oral prednisone 20–40 mg once daily. Furthermore, for patients with refractory disease not controlled by topical therapies, oral corticosteroids are best.



Oral lidocaine suspension (B) would likely provide relief of this patient’s symptoms in the short term but is not a sustainable treatment. Oral lidocaine suspensions require frequent redosing, are less effective than corticosteroids, and may be associated with methemoglobinemia in the setting of overuse. Intravenous corticosteroids (C) are unnecessary for the treatment of aphthous stomatitis. Oral treatment is sufficient. Topical corticosteroids (D) are the best initial treatment for patients with RAS who do not have features of complex disease. This patient’s numerous ulcers and duration of symptoms suggest that systemic treatment would be beneficial.

One Step Further
Question:
What autoimmune condition typically presents with recurrent aphthous ulcers and genital lesions?

Reveal Answer:
Behçet disease.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aphthous Ulcers

Recurrent
Clinical: yellow centers surrounded by red halo, 3–5 mm, round or oval
Location
Buccal or lip mucosa
Rarely labia minora (aka Lipschütz ulcer)
Dx: clinical, do not biopsy
Treatment: supportive, viscous lidocaine, diphenhydramine liquid, topical corticosteroids

question: A 17-year-old boy with a history of asthma presents with an itchy, scaly rash on his arms and legs. He states he has had the rash on and off for years but has never been on treatment for it. The itching is severe and keeps him up at night. Vital signs include a BP of 112/74 mm Hg, HR of 68 bpm, RR of 16/minute, and a T of 98.8°F. Physical examination reveals erythematous areas to the bilateral antecubital and popliteal fossae, which are thick and leathery with excoriations. What management is indicated?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with an exacerbation of atopic dermatitis requiring topical corticosteroid treatment. It is a common dermatologic condition. It is often referred to as eczema or chronic dermatitis. Patients with atopic dermatitis have abnormal humoral and cell-mediated immunity, but the exact mechanism of the disease is unknown. There is an increased risk of atopic dermatitis in individuals with a personal or family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or atopic dermatitis.

Atopic dermatitis may be acute or chronic. Acute disease usually presents as intensely pruritic erythematous skin lesions with papules, vesicles, exudation, and crusting. The lesions of chronic atopic dermatitis are still erythematous and pruritic but with associated scaling, excoriations, and lichenification (skin thickening). In infants ages 0 to 2 years of age, the lesions are most commonly on the face, trunk, or extensor surfaces. In adolescents and adults, the flexor surfaces (i.e., antecubital and popliteal fossae), wrists, ankles, face, and hands are most likely to be involved. It is a chronic disease that waxes and wanes and is often worse in the winter, when the weather is cold and dry, and when the skin is exposed to irritants such as certain soaps, lotions, detergents, or cleaning products.

In general, treatment is directed at controlling inflammation, dryness, and itching. The mainstay of treatment for patients’ atopic dermatitis is topical corticosteroids, including hydrocortisone, desonide, fluocinolone, and triamcinolone. Antihistamines may also be necessary for symptomatic relief. In addition, patients should be advised to avoid scented products, wear lightweight clothing, avoid hot baths, and wash clothing in dye-free, unscented detergent.



Oral cephalexin (A), a first-generation cephalosporin, may be used for cellulitis or other bacterial infections. However, atopic dermatitis is not caused by bacteria, and thus cephalexin is not indicated for its treatment. Cellulitis is associated with acute erythema, warmth, and edema of the skin but does not appear in a symmetrical pattern or chronically over many years.

Oral steroids, such as prednisone (B), are rarely used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis, as topical agents are adequate, and systemic corticosteroids are associated with more adverse effects and risk of rebound of symptoms after discontinuation. Oral prednisone may be used if symptoms are severe and require rapid relief during acute exacerbation. This patient does not have symptoms that are severe enough to warrant systemic corticosteroids.

Topical clindamycin (C) is an antibacterial agent that may be used for the treatment of acne vulgaris or rosacea but is not useful for atopic dermatitis. Acne vulgaris presents with comedones, pustules, or papules, most commonly on the face, upper torso, or proximal arms. Rosacea is associated with facial erythema and papules, pustules, telangiectasia, or rhinophyma.

Topical silver sulfadiazine (E) is a topical antibiotic that is most often used for burn wounds but is not useful for the treatment of atopic dermatitis. This patient has no history of a burn.

One Step Further
Question:
Why should fluorinated corticosteroids not be applied to the face?

Reveal Answer:
Repeated use can produce permanent cutaneous atrophy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)

Risk factors: history of asthma, hay fever, food allergies
Sx: itchy, scaly rash on arms, often worse in the winter
PE: thick, leathery, hyperpigmented areas on flexor surfaces
infants: extensor surfaces, spares diaper area
Tx: emollients and moisturizers, topical corticosteroids, tepid bathing, topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus
Complications: eczema herpeticum, S. aureus infection

question: A 12-year-old boy presents with intermittent abdominal pain and a rash as seen in the image above. There is no fever. Which of the following is a complication of this disease?
englishExplanation:
Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a small vessel vasculitis caused by the deposition of immune complexes in blood vessels. In approximately half of cases, it is preceded by an upper respiratory infection. It is also induced by vancomycin, cefuroxime, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. HSP is characterized by palpable purpura as well as gastrointestinal and kidney symptoms. The disease almost always occurs under the age of 20, and children < 5 years are more frequently affected. Classically, symptoms appear 1–2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. The triad of signs and symptoms is purpura, arthralgias, and abdominal pain. The purpura typically affect dependent regions of the body and thus are seen on the legs and buttocks. Patients develop colicky abdominal pain and may even have hematochezia due to gastrointestinal vasculitis. Rarely, intussusception occurs. Kidney manifestations include glomerulonephritis presenting with hematuria, red cell casts, and azotemia. Treatment is supportive.



Aseptic meningitis (A) is not associated with HSP.

Coronary artery abnormalities (B) are a complication of Kawasaki disease in children. Signs of Kawasaki disease include fever for > 5 days, strawberry tongue, cervical adenopathy, conjunctivitis, and desquamation.

Diarrhea (C) is not a classic complication of HSP. Approximately 30% of children develop bloody stool from gastrointestinal vasculitis and may even show obstructive symptoms if they develop intussusception.

One Step Further
Question:
Is thrombocytopenia present in IgA vasculitis?

Reveal Answer:
No.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the ED with tender erythematous nodules on the anterior surface of the lower extremities, as shown above. She was ill 3 weeks ago with a headache, fever, and sore throat that lasted 4 days. She had been doing well until the nodules appeared yesterday. What is the most appropriate treatment for her symptoms?
englishExplanation:
Ibuprofen is the most appropriate treatment because the patient presents with erythema nodosum, which is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. NSAIDs help reduce pain, swelling, and inflammation in the subcutaneous fat, which is the hallmark of erythema nodosum.

Erythema nodosum is an inflammatory condition that affects the dermis and subcutaneous fat, characterized by tender, erythematous or violaceous nodules, most often located on the anterior shins. These nodules may also appear on the arms or trunk and are frequently preceded by fever or joint pain, especially in the ankles or knees. As the nodules evolve, they often take on a yellow-purple hue and may resemble bruises. The condition is more common in women aged 30–50 years.

Erythema nodosum is associated with various underlying conditions, including infections (streptococcal pharyngitis, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis), inflammatory diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease), pregnancy, malignancy, and medications (oral contraceptives, sulfonamides such as sulfasalazine and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, penicillins, cephalosporins, minocycline, phenytoin, NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen, bromides, and methotrexate). Despite these associations, about half of all cases have no identifiable cause.

Treatment focuses on identifying and treating the underlying etiology. Supportive care includes leg elevation, rest, and use of elastic stockings to relieve discomfort and swelling. NSAIDs can help alleviate pain, and in more severe cases, potassium iodide may be prescribed. The condition is self-limited, resolving within 3 to 8 weeks.



Amoxicillin (A) would be appropriate if she had an ongoing streptococcal infection, but her prior illness resolved 3 weeks ago, so antibiotics are not indicated now.

Azithromycin (B) is used for atypical bacterial infections like Mycoplasma, which is not the cause here, especially with a classic history of recent Streptococcus-like illness.

Prednisone (D) may be considered in severe or refractory erythema nodosum, but it is not first line and should be avoided unless necessary due to potential immunosuppressive effects.

One Step Further
Question:
Why are NSAIDs used as part of the treatment for erythema nodosum if they can cause it?

Reveal Answer:
In most cases, the cause is not a medication but an infection, systemic illness, or idiopathic condition. So while NSAIDs can rarely trigger erythema nodosum, they are more often part of the treatment.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Nodosum

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: A 72-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, diabetes, and coronary artery bypass graft presents with a rash. This morning, she awoke with a fever of 101.2°F (38.4ºC) accompanied by right leg myalgias. An erythematous rash subsequently appeared on her right calf and has begun to rapidly spread up her leg. She states that the rash is intensely painful. Physical exam reveals an erythematous rash with overlying bullae. What additional finding would best support the diagnosis of erysipelas rather than necrotizing fasciitis?

options.text: Pain out of proportion to exam

englishExplanation:
Erysipelas is an infection of the superficial lymphatics and upper dermis. It is characterized by profound erythema and marked dermal edema resulting in well-demarcated borders. It may also present with a peau d’orange appearance, as well as with vesicles, bullae, and lymphangitis. The rate of spread is often rapid, and accordingly, early necrotizing fasciitis must be ruled out. Risk factors for erysipelas include lymphatic dysfunction, venous insufficiency, edema, and immunocompromise. While erysipelas is classically thought of as occurring on the face, 80% of cases will present in the lower extremities. Group A streptococci are responsible for most cases of facial erysipelas, and a history of pharyngitis preceding the infection is not uncommon. Alternatively, lower extremity infections are more likely to include group B, C, F, and G Streptococcus. Penicillin is the antibiotic of choice for mild cases of erysipelas. However, more severe cases require cefazolin or vancomycin.



Crepitus (A) occurs with necrotizing fasciitis, not erysipelas. The sound of crepitus is crackling under the skin due to gas-forming organisms like Clostridium perfringens.

Pain out of proportion to the exam (B) is always a concerning finding for soft tissue infections and is suggestive of a severe infection. It can be present in necrotizing fasciitis. However, anesthesia to touch can also be present depending on the stage of infection.

Skin sloughing (C) occurs more often with necrotizing fasciitis. However, erysipelas can have areas of necrosis, and in the resolving phase, desquamation can occur.

One Step Further
Question:
What physical finding on the face can differentiate erysipelas from cellulitis?

Reveal Answer:
Ear involvement (Milian ear sign).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erysipelas

Most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes infection (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes)
Sx: malaise, fever, chills, nausea
PE: intense and deeply erythematous, sharply demarcated elevated shiny patch
Tx
Mild infections: oral amoxicillin or cephalexin
Infections with systemic compromise: parenteral cefazolin, ceftriaxone, or flucloxacillin

question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a painful rash in her axilla. Physical examination reveals the finding above. She notes she has had episodes of this same rash for the past 2 years. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Hidradenitis suppurativa is a relapsing and remitting inflammatory condition in the areas where there are apocrine glands (most commonly the axillary region). It presents with painful, recurrent nodules and abscess formation, often with cellulitis. It is more common in individuals who have an overweight BMI. The diagnosis is made based on the clinical picture of relapsing and remitting symptoms. Treatment is focused on prevention with good hygiene, including antibacterial soaps and topical antibiotics such as clindamycin. Oral antibiotics are indicated when cellulitis is present. Incision and drainage should be performed if a large abscess is present. However, given the chronic nature of this condition, incision and drainage should be used judiciously, as scarring can occur if performed regularly.



Cellulitis (A) presents with redness, warmth, and tenderness to palpation of the skin with cobblestoning seen on ultrasound. While cellulitis may be present in this patient, the underlying cause of their relapsing symptoms is better explained by hidradenitis suppurativa.

Necrotizing fasciitis (C) presents with erythema, warmth, tenderness, crepitus (if a gas-producing organism is present), fever, hemodynamic instability, and rapidly progressive symptoms. Remarkable tenderness to palpation is noted on exam, and patients are often ill appearing.

Pyoderma gangrenosum (D) is associated with autoimmune conditions (such as inflammatory bowel disease) and malignancy. It may present with a seemingly pyogenic wound (though no infection is present) with ulceration and a violaceous border. Treatment is focused on addressing the underlying cause.

One Step Further
Question:
What infectious agent causes vesicles, ulcers, and pustules that are often clustered and associated with burning neuropathic pain?

Reveal Answer:
Herpes simplex virus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hidradenitis Suppurativa

Chronic skin disorder that involves follicular occlusion and inflammation
Sx: inflammatory nodules in intertriginous areas (e.g., axilla, inguinal area) that may recur
PE: tender nodules, purulent malodorous drainage, draining skin tunnels
Tx options (depending on severity): intralesional steroids, topical clindamycin, oral antibiotics, biologics (refractory disease)
Hurley staging system describes the severity of disease

question: A 69-year-old woman presents with a rash on her arm that began with several “very itchy spots” about 2 weeks ago. She is concerned since it appears to be getting worse and more widespread. Her skin examination is shown above. Her oropharynx is clear. She reports no fevers, travel, or sick contacts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Bullous pemphigoid is a type of blistering disease of the skin. The typical patient is between 60 and 80 years old, and there is an equal incidence in men and women. It is an inflammatory autoimmune disease due to immunoglobulin G autoantibodies against proteins in the basement membrane zone between the dermis and epidermis. Thus, the cleavage point is relatively deep, yielding thick, tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign (lateral pressure on normal skin adjacent to a lesion does not dislodge the epidermis). Bullae develop from significantly pruritic urticarial plaques and papules on normal or erythematous skin over a period of weeks to months. This disease can persist for years, and the bullae eventually rupture, resulting in crusts and erosions. The trunk and extremities are the sites most often involved, while mucous membrane involvement is uncommon. Autoantibodies can be detected in most patients and about half will show blood eosinophilia. Diagnosis requires histopathology and immunofluorescence studies in consultation with a dermatologist.

Treatment includes high-potency topical steroids if the disease is localized or oral prednisone or doxycycline for extensive disease. Immunosuppressant medications such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, and methotrexate are also used. Many patients require treatment for years to achieve long-term remission. The course of the disease is usually benign, although fatalities are possible, usually due to sepsis from infection or treatment complications.



Pemphigus vulgaris (B)is a life-threatening autoimmune blistering disease with an intraepidermal cleavage plane producing large, fragile bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign. Most patients have mucous membrane involvement.

Pustular psoriasis (C) usually presents with large amounts of small vesicles filled with whitish fluid on erythematous, tender skin. Patients are often febrile and acutely ill, particularly if the lesions are generalized.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (D)is a poorly understood life-threatening condition, most likely representing the same process as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and erythema multiforme, but involving > 30% of the body surface area. Large, flaccid bullae may develop within hours on erythematous, tender skin, which leads to shedding of the epidermis in large sheets. The Nikolsky sign is positive and mucous membrane involvement is common and extensive.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common misdiagnosis for bullous pemphigoid?

Reveal Answer:
Urticaria.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Bullous Pemphigoid

Autoimmune blistering condition
Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

question: An otherwise healthy 38-year-old man reports 6 days of a painful boil on his upper back. Vital signs are BP of 128/82 mm Hg, HR of 70 bpm, RR of 16/min, and T of 98.6°F. He has been applying warm compresses to the area, but it is increasing in size and the pain is worsening. On exam, you palpate a 1 x 1 cm erythematous, tender, fluctuant abscess without induration or surrounding cellulitis. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Continue warm compresses and discharge home
Perform incision and drainage and prescribe IV antibiotics
Perform incision and drainage and prescribe oral antibiotics

englishExplanation:
Incision and drainage only are the recommended treatments for simple abscesses in otherwise healthy patients. Abscesses are formed by collections of pus in the dermis and deeper layers of the skin most often as a result of infection, usually Staphylococcus aureus. They present as painful, erythematous, fluctuant, and tender nodules with or without surrounding erythema that may spontaneously drain purulent material. Systemic symptoms are uncommon.

Furuncles and carbuncles are two forms of abscesses caused by infected hair follicles that occur most commonly in areas of friction and perspiration, such as the axillae, buttocks, back of the neck, and face. A furuncle is a single small abscess in the subcutaneous tissue that develops as a result of an infected hair follicle, while a carbuncle consists of a collection of several infected hair follicles that produce a single abscess. Larger furuncles, carbuncles, and abscesses require incision and drainage.

Untreated abscesses may lead to cellulitis and systemic infections. Recurrent infections in the same location are usually the result of a local defect such as a cyst, hidradenitis suppurativa, or a retained foreign body, but immunodeficiency should be considered in a patient with recurrent infections arising in multiple sites.

Incision and drainage

Warm compresses (A) are recommended and usually sufficient for small skin abscesses. Most small abscesses will drain spontaneously and resolve without further intervention. Treatment with warm compresses failed in this case.

IV antibiotics (B) are indicated only in the most severe cases in immunocompromised individuals or when there are signs of serious systemic infection. In these cases, IV antibiotics are started prior to incision and drainage. Appropriate IV antibiotics include vancomycin and daptomycin.

Oral antibiotics (C) are indicated when there is surrounding cellulitis, in immunocompromised individuals, or when there are signs of systemic infection. Appropriate oral antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and minocycline.

Only prescribing antibiotics (E) is not an effective therapy for a simple abscess since incision and drainage optimizes the likelihood of cure.

One Step Further
Question:
What are some risk factors for developing skin abscesses?

Reveal Answer:
Diabetes mellitus, immunodeficiency, and breaches to the skin barrier.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Incision and Drainage of Cutaneous Abscesses

MRSA is a frequent cause
Simple cutaneous abscesses: antibiotics not indicated
Small abscesses: packing not indicated
Complications: bleeding, extension, neurovascular injury

question: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pruritus of his skin. He went camping yesterday evening and noticed symptoms this morning. He reports wearing sunblock appropriately. His T is 98°F (36.7°C), BP is 120/81 mm Hg, HR is 72 bpm, RR is 14/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. The physical exam is shown above. This skin finding is primarily on his extremities but is also found on the face and torso. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Topical emollients and topical triamcinolone with oral prednisone

correctAnswer: Topical emollients and topical triamcinolone with oral prednisone
englishExplanation:
Allergic contact dermatitis is a hypersensitivity reaction (type IV) that occurs when exposed to certain antigens. Allergic contact dermatitis presents with erythema and vesicles and is often confined to the site of exposure, with some minor spreading beyond this area. This patient is likely experiencing allergic contact dermatitis based on his exposure to plants while camping. Irritant contact dermatitis presents similarly but is more directly confined to the site of exposure, and dry skin and scaling may be additional features. It is more commonly associated with chemical exposures.
