question: An 8-day-old former 38-week gestation infant girl presents to the emergency department with a foul-smelling umbilical stump and umbilical stump drainage. She had routine prenatal care and went home from the hospital with her parents after birth. She has not yet established care with her pediatrician. She has lost 5% of her birth weight but is waking to feed and making the expected number of wet and dirty diapers. She has had no fevers, vomiting, diarrhea, or coughing. She is vigorous, and her exam is remarkable for the above finding. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral cephalexin and close outpatient follow-up

englishExplanation:
Omphalitis describes cellulitis of the umbilical stump and the surrounding tissue. The umbilical stump becomes a necrotic nidus of infection that is colonized by the maternal genital tract or the environment. Infection is uncommon in infants with proper newborn care, but when it occurs, it is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and species of group A Streptococcus. It is rarely caused by gram-negative enteric bacteria or group B Streptococcus.

Omphalitis usually presents before 14 days of life with circumferential erythema of the umbilical stump. Foul drainage and odor are common findings but not exclusive to omphalitis, as many umbilical stumps smell foul without infection and have a small amount of drainage. Antiseptic care at delivery alone is sufficiently protective against omphalitis, so additional treatment is usually not indicated. When this is not available, a single treatment of topical chlorhexidine or alcohol at birth is protective. Risk factors for omphalitis include prematurity and a complicated delivery. When infection occurs, it spreads to the abdominal wall or deeper into the peritoneum, umbilical and portal vessels, and the liver. It can develop into necrotizing fasciitis or sepsis, and these infants have high morbidity and mortality rates. Cultures of the stump drainage should be taken prior to starting antibiotics. Infants with signs of systemic illness (e.g., fever, irritability) should have a full septic workup. Omphalitis is treated with intravenous antibiotics such as nafcillin and gentamicin. Vancomycin is added if there is a high community prevalence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.



Dry cord care (A) describes proper umbilical cord care to reduce the risk of omphalitis after an antiseptic delivery where no additional medication is needed. This patient has developed an infection requiring antibiotics instead of only cord care.

Oral cephalexin and close outpatient follow-up (C) is inappropriate treatment despite this infant’s well appearance and lack of systemic symptoms. Sepsis is a common complication of omphalitis, necessitating a more vigorous approach to care. Cephalexin alone also does not provide appropriate coverage for this polymicrobial infection.

Topical silver nitrate application (D) treats an umbilical cord granuloma, not omphalitis. An umbilical cord granuloma presents as a soft, pink, friable mound of granulation tissue at the base of the umbilicus that is typically only identified after cord separation. There may be mild serosanguinous drainage, but there should not be purulent drainage or surrounding erythema and induration, as noted in this patient.

One Step Further
Question:
At what age should a patient with an uncomplicated umbilical hernia be referred to surgery for repair?

Reveal Answer:
At 2 years of age, especially if the hernia has not reduced in size.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Omphalitis

Polymicrobial infection of the umbilicus
PE: purulent discharge from stump with surrounding erythema or induration
Dx: clinical
Tx: treat for gram-positive and gram-negative organisms (e.g., nafcillin and gentamicin)
Culture before starting antibiotics
Monitor for sepsis, necrotizing fasciitis

question: A 54-year-old man with diabetes presents with severe leg pain. The pain has worsened over the last two days with increased swelling of the calf. He has no chest pain or shortness of breath. Vital signs are: T 101.8°F, BP 98/62, HR 118, RR 18. Physical examination is notable for erythema of the calf, severe tenderness, and crepitus. You initiate IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT scan with intravenous contrast of the lower extremity
Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity
Measurement of serum lactate and CPK

englishExplanation:
Necrotizing fasciitis is an infection of the subcutaneous tissue that spreads rapidly across the fascial planes and is often fatal even with aggressive treatment. Risk factors for necrotizing infections include diabetes, vascular insufficiency, and immunosuppression. Classically, patients have pain out of proportion to examination. Later findings include diffuse swelling, erythema, induration, and crepitus. The gold standard for diagnosis is direct visualization in the operating room by a surgeon. Surgeons may elect to perform a bedside biopsy prior to full exploration. Management includes aggressive IV hydration, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgical debridement.



CT scan with intravenous contrast of the lower extremity (A) may demonstrate findings suggestive of a necrotizing infection including subcutaneous gas, stranding along the fascial planes, or fluid collection. However, the negative predictive value of CT scan has not been quantified and is not yet considered the gold standard. Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity (B) may be helpful in identifying venous thrombosis as a cause of edema and fullness of the leg. Additionally, sonography may visualize an area of deep fluid collection and may demonstrate artifact from a significant amount of subcutaneous air, if present. Measurement of serum lactate and CPK (C) is helpful when positive but not sensitive enough to rule out the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) incorporates other laboratory markers (CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) into a decision-rule, however, it lacks sufficient sensitivity in larger studies.

One Step Further

What is the name of necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum?

Reveal Answer:
Fournier gangrene.

question: A 78-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a chief concern about a new rash. The patient has a medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. He states the rash started 3 days ago with a red lesion that was pruritic. Yesterday, he noticed this lesion had transformed into a 5 mm blister. Today, he states the lesion has increased in size to approximately 1.5 cm, and there are now several other new lesions. There is associated pruritus which he states is quite severe. He’s otherwise feeling well and has no other symptoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. His physical examination reveals several tense fluid-filled bullae and blisters on bilateral upper extremities. Traction on the skin does not produce any extension of the bullae or blisters. There are no other lesions or concerning findings on physical examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune disorder that causes blistering and formation of bullae. This disorder is caused by immunoglobulins and complement deposition within the epidermal basement membrane. This deposition is ultimately what leads to the presentation of blister and bullae formation. Classically this occurs in older patients, usually over the age of 60. This is a chronic disorder and is known for fluctuating exacerbations and remissions. Clinical features may include a prodromal phase that precedes the formation of blisters. This prodromal phase is characterized by pruritic eczematous, papular, or urticarial-like skin lesions. This may be the only clinical feature a patient develops, whereas others develop 1–3 cm bulla. The bullae are tense with an erythematous, urticarial, or noninflammatory base. Pruritus is commonly associated with the bullae and can be quite severe. Extension of the blister with skin traction (Nikolsky sign) is not present. This, along with how tense the blister is, helps differentiate bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris.

Diagnosis is made by both clinical and laboratory findings. Although clinical findings may suggest the diagnosis, other disease processes can present similarly. Thus, laboratory confirmation is needed. Skin biopsy from the edge of an intact blister or serum testing evaluating for basement membrane antibodies helps confirm the diagnosis. Treatment consists of both topical and systemic glucocorticoids, with topical being first-line. When the disease process is extensive or if topical treatment is not practical, feasible, or fails, systemic treatments should be administered.



Pemphigus vulgaris (B)is a life-threatening blistering disease that is characterized by acantholysis secondary to the binding of circulating IgG to epithelial cells. It is the most common form of pemphigus but still remains a rare disorder. Flaccid bullae that extend with skin traction are classic characteristics that help differentiate the disease process from other blistering diseases. The average age of onset is between 40 and 60 years and both men and women are equally affected. Clinical features include flaccid bullae or blisters that will almost always have mucosal involvement. In fact, the oral cavity represents the most common initial site of disease. The blisters rupture easily resulting in painful erosions. The diagnosis is made by clinical, histologic, and serological findings.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (C)is caused by certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus that release an exfoliating toxin that results in impaired cell adhesion, blistering, and superficial denuding of the skin. It most commonly occurs in infants and young children. Patients classically present in the first week of life and are febrile and irritable with diffuse blanching erythema that is often around the mouth. Flaccid blisters occur 1–2 days after initial presentation. The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation which includes a positive Nikolsky sign and skin biopsy. Treatment consists of intravenous penicillinase-resistant penicillin (nafcillin or oxacillin) or vancomycin in areas with a high prevalence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (D) is a severe mucocutaneous reaction that is most commonly triggered by medications and is characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis. Toxic epidermal necrolysis is on a continuum with Stevens-Johnson syndrome with the latter being diagnosed when < 10% of the total body surface area is involved. When > 30% of the body surface area is involved, toxic epidermal necrolysis is diagnosed. Medications such as allopurinol, anticonvulsants, lamotrigine, sulfonamide antimicrobials, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are the medications that most commonly trigger the reaction. Clinical features include a prodromal phase which includes a fever and influenza-like symptoms that occur 1–3 days before the onset of cutaneous lesions. These lesions are classically erythematous macules with purpuric centers that are ill-defined and often coalesce. Mucosal involvement occurs in the majority of patients. Nikolsky sign is often present on examination. Diagnosis is made by clinical features noted above with a suggestive history of drug exposure. A skin biopsy should be obtained to confirm the diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What infectious organism is responsible for cases of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis?

Reveal Answer:
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the second most common cause behind medications, particularly in children.

Most common in patients aged > 60 years
Sx and findings: intensely pruritic lesions → large, tense blisters or bullae → rupture w/ formation of erosion/crust
PE: tense and firm blisters that do not extend with lateral pressure
Nikolsky sign negative: absence of slippage of the epidermis from the dermis when slight rubbing pressure is applied to the skin
Tx options: wound care, corticosteroids, doxycycline, immunosuppressants

question: A 1-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parent for a rash. He recently started going to daycare and some children there have also been diagnosed with a rash. Today she noted the lesions on his back. What is the appropriate treatment for these lesions?

options.text: Reassurance of spontaneous resolution over the next few days to weeks
Reassurance of spontaneous resolution over the next few months to years

correctAnswer: Reassurance of spontaneous resolution over the next few months to years
englishExplanation:
Reassurance of spontaneous resolution over the next few months to years is the most appropriate treatment for uncomplicated molluscum contagiosum in children. Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus of the same name. As shown in the photo above, they appear as painless and nonpruritic pearly, dome-shaped, umbilicated lesions across the face, trunk, and extremities. Diagnosis is clinical but can be confirmed with a Giemsa stain of the core showing intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies—aptly named molluscum bodies. The virus is spread via skin-to-skin contact. The virus is seen in three primary populations: children, sexually active adults, and patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Children present most commonly as the patient above, with a risk for exposure (e.g., school, daycare) and anywhere from a few to > 100 lesions. Sexually active adults present with < 20 lesions across their genitalia, buttocks, and lower abdomen. These patients should be offered additional sexually transmitted infection testing. Diffuse and refractory disease is seen in the immunocompromised population and most commonly in patients with HIV. As noted above, reassurance of spontaneous resolution is the mainstay of treatment. However, in immunosuppressed patients, curettage or cryotherapy may be offered alongside continued HIV treatment.



Reassurance of spontaneous resolution over the next few days to weeks (B) is incorrect, as molluscum lesions can take as long as 18 months to resolve.

Oral acyclovir suspension (A) is an appropriate treatment for varicella or chickenpox, which is a viral infection that is easily spread from child to child, especially when in close proximity (e.g., the patient’s daycare). However, varicella starts on the trunk and appears as teardrop vesicles on an erythematous base. Diagnosis is largely clinical, though a Tzanck smear of the vesicles will show giant cells with inclusion bodies. Treatment is primarily supportive with acetaminophen and antihistamines. Acyclovir is not commonly used except for small children, infants, and immunocompromised patients.

Topical mupirocin 2% ointment (D) is the treatment for impetigo, a superficial infection caused most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. Impetigo presents as erythematous vesicles across the face, neck, and extremities that rupture and create erosions surrounded by golden crusts. Systemic antibiotics, such as clindamycin, can be given when lesions are widespread and topical coverage is difficult to accomplish.

One Step Further
Question:
What acquired immunodeficiency syndrome-defining illness resembles molluscum contagiosum with widespread centrally umbilicated skin lesions?

Reveal Answer:
Disseminated cryptococcosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Molluscum Contagiosum

Common in childhood, can also occur in healthy adults
Spread through direct skin-to-skin contact or fomites
Sx: Small, skin-colored papules, sometimes associated with pruritus or inflammation
PE: multiple waxy, dome-shaped papules with an umbilicated appearance
Etiology: poxvirus
Self-limiting: typically resolves without treatment within 6–12 months, but removal can be considered if lesions are symptomatic

question: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with pain in his left ankle and leg. He indicates that today he was cleaning his house when he suddenly noticed redness, swelling, and pain in his left ankle. He reports no injury or known insect bite. Since the onset of symptoms 2 hours ago, his pain has worsened significantly, and the redness has now spread up to his knee. Vital signs show HR 118 bpm, BP 127/89 mm Hg, RR 12/min, and T 37.9℃. On examination, his left ankle is erythematous, swollen, and exquisitely tender to the touch. The redness extends up to his left knee but is less painful there. No induration, fluctuance, or crepitus is found. He continues to report severe pain in the leg despite intravenous hydromorphone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Skin and soft tissue infections can be mild conditions such as cellulitis, abscess, and fungal infections to more severe infections such as necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome. The source of a skin infection may not always be evident, but many infections arise from a break in the skin such as a cut, injection, or abrasion. Hematogenous seeding from another infected site is another possible source. Most skin infections present with erythema, warmth, and some induration. Important clinical features that are present in this patient with a skin infection include rapidly advancing erythema, systemic toxicity detected in an elevated heart rate, and severe pain that is out of proportion to physical exam findings. These aspects all suggest that this patient most likely has necrotizing fasciitis.

Necrotizing fasciitis is an aggressive infection of the subcutaneous tissue that spreads rapidly along the fascial planes. Typical bacterial isolates include group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides and Clostridium. Most cases are polymicrobial. Necrotizing fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis and should be suspected in patients such as the one in this question. Other signs of necrotizing fasciitis include altered mental status, hemorrhage, blistering, and crepitus. Crepitance describes skin that feels crackly, and it suggests underlying subcutaneous emphysema from gas-forming organisms. Crepitus is diagnostic but not required for a diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis.



An abscess (A) occurs when bacteria accumulate below the epidermis and draw neutrophils and cytokines to the site, which promotes the development of purulence. The overlying epidermis prevents drainage and eventually, a painful, red mass is seen. It is often tender and warm. The fluid collection under the epidermis is described as fluctuant. The patient in this question does not have a painful, red, fluctuant mass.

Cellulitis (B)is an inflammatory condition of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that is the result of a bacterial infection. It may be purulent or nonpurulent. The cardinal and typical feature of cellulitis is confluent inflammation due to increased blood flow. Induration can be found and simply means a hardening of the skin as it becomes engorged with interstitial fluid and takes on the appearance of an orange peel. The patient in this question, at the very least, has cellulitis, but his physical exam findings, pain out of proportion to exam, and the rapidity of his worsening redness should lead the clinician toward a diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis.

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (D) is a severe, toxin-mediated syndrome that rapidly progresses to shock, with multiorgan failure and, eventually, death. The syndrome is caused by group A streptococci, often in the setting of a severe soft tissue infection. Patients may have viral symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, myalgias, and chills. High fever with tachycardia and hypotension are typical and altered mental status is common. A diffuse rash can be present in a minority of patients. Although this patient has a more serious infection than typical cellulitis, he is not presenting with shock at this time and his rash is localized rather than confluent.

Reveal Answer:

question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the ED with red bumps on the front of her legs for 2 days and joint pain for 1 week. On exam, the patient has multiple erythematous, tender, immobile nodules on her shins bilaterally. Her medical history includes ulcerative colitis. What initial pharmacotherapy should be given to this patient?
englishExplanation:
The patient is presenting with erythema nodosum, a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction that most often presents as erythematous, tender, nonulcerated, immobile nodules on the shins. Common triggers for erythema nodosum include infection, drugs, pregnancy, malignancy, and inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and sarcoidosis. Oftentimes, nodules may follow a prodrome of fatigue, fever, malaise, arthralgias, or upper respiratory infections. Erythema nodosum is usually a self-limiting condition that typically resolves within several weeks.

Treatment is largely supportive, and first-line initial medical interventions for symptom relief include NSAIDs and potassium iodide. Although sometimes difficult to obtain, potassium iodide can lead to a quick improvement and is a favored choice when rapid resolution is desired. NSAIDs are also efficacious and, due to widespread clinical use and limited adverse effects, are most often used to treat erythema nodosum.



Antibiotics (A) would be inappropriate at this time. Although infectious causes should be ruled out, there is no indication for antibiotics in the treatment of erythema nodosum.

Antihistamines (B) do not play a significant role in the treatment of erythema nodosum.

For refractory cases and severe presentations, systemic steroids (C) may be a useful medication. However, potassium iodide and NSAIDs are first-line treatment options.

One Step Further
Question:
What progressive disease of the hepatobiliary system is associated with ulcerative colitis?

Reveal Answer:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis.

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department with the rash seen above. He was recently diagnosed with an infection that is being appropriately treated, but he is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction that presents with a targetoid rash with central necrosis and bullae. It is commonly associated with herpes simplex virus but can occur secondary to many infectious etiologies or as a reaction to medications. There is no direct treatment for erythema multiforme. However, any underlying infection should be treated, and any potential exacerbating medications should be held. Mild cases can be treated with antihistamines and topical steroids. Extensive disease, including mucous membrane involvement, may require hospitalization and supportive therapy. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is thought to be a progression of erythema multiforme and presents with more extensive skin and oral mucosa involvement and can occur in the setting of fever. As Stevens-Johnson syndrome progresses, it can become toxic epidermal necrolysis, which presents with diffuse sloughing of the skin and is associated with high mortality.



Erythema marginatum (A) presents as a serpiginous, macular lesion with a pale center, is not pruritic, and is seen in rheumatic fever.

Erythema migrans (B) presents with a target-shaped lesion and is seen in Lyme disease, which can present with facial nerve palsy, arthritis, and heart block.

Erythema nodosum (D) is a panniculitis, which presents with painful, tender, and raised nodules, often on the anterior lower extremities. It can be seen in certain infections and as a reaction to certain medications.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment of erythema migrans?

Reveal Answer:
Doxycycline.

Most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Drugs: sulfa, oral hypoglycemics, anticonvulsants, penicillin, NSAIDs (SOAPS)
Patient presents with acute onset of symmetric target lesions on palms and soles, face and trunk may also be involved
Erythema multiforme minor: localized eruption of the skin with minimal or no mucosal involvement
Erythema multiforme major: one or more mucous membranes are involved
PE: target-like rash with a central dark papule surrounded by a pale area and a halo of erythema

question: A 33-year-old woman presents to the ED with the lesions seen above. She began taking an antibiotic for her urinary tract infection 2 days prior to noting the lesions. Which of the following signs and symptoms would also be expected in this patient?
englishExplanation:
The lesions are due to erythema nodosum, an inflammatory reaction between the dermis and adjacent adipose tissue. It is thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to various infections, drugs, or a systemic disease. Sulfonamides, oral contraceptives, penicillins, and phenytoin are often implicated. The patient is likely taking sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim for her UTI. A variety of infections and systemic disorders such as streptococcal infections (most common infection), sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, lymphoma, and leukemia are associated with erythema nodosum.

The hallmark lesions of erythema nodosum are tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules that have a blue hue as they resolve. Symmetrical pretibial involvement is most common, although the extensor surfaces of the forearm, thigh, and trunk may also be affected. Patients may have just the nodules or may have systemic symptoms, including fever and malaise. Arthralgias are seen in 90% of patients at some time during the disease course and have been known to persist for up to 2 years after resolution. The skin eruption can last up to 8 weeks.

Treatment is mainly supportive with the identification of the underlying disorder. NSAIDs may be useful in controlling the arthralgias.



Extensor, not flexor (B), surfaces are usually involved in patients with erythema nodosum.

Mucous membranes (C) are not involved as in other disorders such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis.

The skin lesions of erythema nodosum are tender, not nontender (D).

One Step Further
Question:
What are the five Ps of lichen planus?

Reveal Answer:
Purple, planar, polygonal, pruritic, and papules.

question: A 67-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a chief concern about a rash on her legs. Physical exam is shown above. Which of the following is the underlying pathophysiology of the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with findings suggestive of venous stasis, which occurs secondary to venous valvular incompetence. Patients with venous stasis typically have risk factors such as connective tissue diseases, obesity, a sedentary lifestyle, smoking, and previous deep vein thrombosis. Common presenting symptoms include pain, heaviness in the leg, swelling, dry and tight skin, muscle cramps, and pruritus. The pathophysiology is related to a backup of blood in the venous system. Typically, blood is pushed forward through the venous system by a combination of pressure from cardiac activity as well as skeletal muscle contraction (thus why being sedentary is a risk factor), which pushes blood through the venous system back toward the heart. Venous valves prevent blood from flowing back. However, when chronic stasis, pressure, or stress is applied to the valves, they can become incompetent, leading to tortuous veins and the stasis of venous blood. The treatment of venous stasis involves activity, as tolerated, compression stockings, and, in refractory cases, vascular surgery.



Arterial insufficiency (A) is the pathophysiology of vascular claudication, which presents with burning pain in the lower extremities that worsens with exertion and is relieved with rest.

Endothelial dysfunction (B) is the pathophysiology thought to cause digital ischemia or necrosis in sepsis (rather than the effect of vasopressors). A “sticky” endothelium during this inflammatory process can lead to impaired blood delivery in smaller blood vessels, promoting digital ischemia.

Vasospasm (C) is the underlying pathophysiology of Raynaud phenomenon, which presents with severe pain and discoloration of the hands secondary to emotional or physical stressors. This is a transient condition, and when the vasospasm resolves, perfusion returns to the hands.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most effective intervention for vascular claudication?

Reveal Answer:
Lifestyle interventions, including graded exercise, smoking cessation, and proper diet.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Venous Insufficiency

Most commonly caused by venous valvular abnormalities
Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, advancing age, prolonged standing, family history of venous insufficiency
Sx: leg swelling
PE: skin changes, ulceration, edema, varicose veins
Dx: often made by history, physical exam
Tx: leg elevation, compression therapy, ulcer care, ablation

question: A 27-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use presents to the ED with the skin rash shown above. He also has these dermatologic findings in his antecubital fossa bilaterally, which he states are pruritic. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with pruritic, scaly, erythematous plaques on the palms and antecubital fossae, which are classic for eczema (atopic dermatitis), particularly in areas of chronic irritation, like where intravenous drug use might introduce allergens or irritants. The pruritus, bilateral distribution, and chronicity support an inflammatory rather than infectious or fungal etiology. Topical corticosteroids like hydrocortisone reduce inflammation and are first-line therapy for mild eczema.

Eczema and atopic dermatitis are often used interchangeably and present with a range of clinical patterns, including truncal involvement. A key feature of chronic eczema is intense pruritus that leads to scratching and perpetuates the rash, particularly at night and in response to heat or sweating. Individuals with atopy often have a personal or family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or sensitive skin. Acute lesions appear as erythematous, swollen plaques with small vesicles, while subacute lesions are more scaly. Chronic eczema presents with thickened, lichenified skin and enhanced skin markings due to persistent rubbing and scratching, sometimes with excoriations.

Treatment focuses on minimizing triggers and maintaining skin hydration. Harsh soaps and known irritants should be avoided. After bathing, moisturizers like plain petroleum jelly should be applied promptly. Topical steroids are selected based on severity and location, ranging from low-potency hydrocortisone to high-potency clobetasol. Ointments are generally more effective, but creams are acceptable alternatives. Severe contact dermatitis may require oral corticosteroids, with dosing tailored by age. Oral antihistamines can help treat nighttime itching, and signs of bacterial superinfection (such as crusting and drainage) should prompt treatment with antibiotics like cephalexin or dicloxacillin.



Azithromycin and ceftriaxone (A) are appropriate treatments for urethritis that has progressed to disseminated gonococcal disease, which can manifest initially with pustular skin lesions and a hot and inflamed joint.

Penicillin (B) is the appropriate treatment for syphilis, which can present with an eruption of skin lesions that appear similar to pityriasis rosea, with lesions that affect the palms and soles. Pityriasis rosea initially manifests as a hyperpigmented herald patch that is highly pruritic. Patients who present with pityriasis rosea should also be worked up for a new syphilis infection if appropriate risk factors, such as intravenous drug use or risky sexual behavior, are present.

Topical clotrimazole (C) is the appropriate treatment for tinea corporis (ringworm), which presents with a ring-shaped lesion that is highly pruritic.

One Step Further
Question:
What pathology presents with the Auspitz sign (punctate bleeding with removal of a scale)?

Reveal Answer:
Psoriasis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)

Risk factors: history of asthma, hay fever, food allergies
Sx: itchy, scaly rash on arms, often worse in the winter
PE: thick, leathery, hyperpigmented areas on flexor surfaces
infants: extensor surfaces, spares diaper area
Tx: emollients and moisturizers, topical corticosteroids, tepid bathing, topical tacrolimus or pimecrolimus
Complications: eczema herpeticum, S. aureus infection

question: A 6-year-old boy presents for evaluation of a rash beginning 3 days ago that has progressed to cover his bilateral lower extremities and buttocks. His parent says the boy has no medical conditions and is fully immunized. A review of systems is positive for a recent sore throat, abdominal pain, and joint pain that resolved last week. Vital signs are within normal limits. On physical exam, the patient has a nonblanching, palpable rash on both legs. What abdominal complication is most commonly associated with the suspected diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV), formerly called Henoch-Schönlein purpura, is the most common systemic vasculitis in children. It is primarily a childhood disease and typically affects children 3–15 years old. The pathogenesis of IgAV is an immune-mediated vasculitis that is associated with IgA deposition thought to occur after a recent upper respiratory infection. Clinical manifestations include palpable purpura without thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, arthralgias or arthritis, abdominal pain, and kidney involvement.

Features develop over a course of days to weeks and vary in the order of their presentation, with purpura and joint pain commonly presenting first. Intussusception is the most common gastrointestinal complication and occurs secondary to a lead point that is caused by edema and hemorrhage. The diagnosis is typically made clinically and is straightforward when purpura without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is present along with two of the other three features (arthritis or arthralgias, abdominal pain, and kidney disease). However, the classic rash may be absent in up to 25% of patients, making the diagnosis harder to determine.

The treatment for IgAV is primarily supportive, as the majority of patients will recover spontaneously. Pain should be treated with acetaminophen or NSAIDs, with corticosteroids being reserved for cases that are severe and refractory to the treatments above. Close consultation with a nephrologist should occur if kidney involvement is present. Hospitalization is warranted for patients with the inability to maintain adequate hydration with oral intake, severe abdominal pain, significant gastrointestinal bleeding, changes in mental status, severe joint involvement limiting ambulation or self-care, or kidney insufficiency (elevated creatinine), hypertension, or nephrotic syndrome.



Appendicitis (A)presents with right lower quadrant pain that classically follows nonspecific periumbilical pain. Patients have severe tenderness with associated rebound tenderness and guarding. Although appendicitis should be considered in patients of all ages presenting with abdominal pain, it is not the most common complication for IgAV.

Malrotation (C)occurs secondary to the failure of the superior mesenteric artery to rotate completely during embryology. This results in bilious vomiting with associated abdominal distention, tenderness, and, at times, peritonitis. Patients may also demonstrate hemodynamic compromise in severe cases. Presentation most commonly occurs in patients < 1 year old, with a vast majority occurring in patients < 5 years old. Malrotation is not a complication of IgAV.

Pancreatitis (D) is an uncommon complication of IgAV.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name of the exam finding with appendicitis when palpation in the left lower quadrant reproduces pain in the right lower quadrant?

Reveal Answer:
Rovsing sign.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of tobacco use presents to the ED with the finding shown above. He is retired from working as a professional winemaker. He reports no fevers, chills, or rapid weight loss. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common cancer in humans and is caused by exposure to ultraviolet light, particularly the ultraviolet B spectrum. It is more common in older patients, but its incidence in patients < 50 is increasing. Light-skinned individuals are more at risk, as darker skin is inherently protected from photodamage by melanin. BCC occurs on sun-exposed areas, most commonly on the head and neck, but may appear anywhere. Characteristic lesions may appear translucent or ulcerated with telangiectasias and a rolled or pearly border. Diagnosis is by interpretation of punch biopsy or shave biopsy. Treatment options include surgical excision, Mohs microsurgery, electrodesiccation and curettage, and irradiation.



Endocarditis (B) may present with skin or nail findings related to disseminated bacterial infection such as petechiae from septic emboli, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, microabscesses, and purpura.

A Lisch nodule (C) is a pigmented iris hamartoma seen in patients with type I neurofibromatosis. They are usually yellow-brown, oval, or round papules that do not affect vision.

Melanoma (D) lesions are characteristically asymmetric with irregular borders and irregular pigmentation, and they frequently change color, size, or shape over time.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most prevalent carcinogen in humans?

Reveal Answer:
Ultraviolet light from the sun.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Basal Cell Carcinoma

Most common type of skin cancer
Sx: painless, slow-growing lesion
Subtypes include nodular (most common), superficial, morpheaform
Nodular: pearly papule with rolled borders or telangiectasia on face, ears, neck
Superficial: slightly scaly plaque on trunk
Dx: clinical exam, dermoscopy, shave, punch, or excisional biopsy
Tx options include surgical excision for lesions with a low recurrence risk, Mohs micrographic surgery for lesions with a high recurrence risk
Prevention includes sunscreen, UV light protection

question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for evaluation of a skin lesion. She first noticed the lesion 1 month ago. She has a history of asthma, and her daily medications include montelukast and beclomethasone. Vital signs include a BP of 116/74 mm Hg, HR of 76 bpm, RR of 16/minute, and a T of 98.7°F. Which of the following would be most concerning for melanoma?
englishExplanation:
Melanoma is a highly aggressive malignancy of melanocytes in the skin. Although it is the least common skin malignancy, it has the highest mortality. The peak incidence occurs between 20 and 45 years old, which is much younger than the other two forms of skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma). Any new mole after age 35 needs a dermatologic evaluation since people rarely form new moles at this age.

The mnemonic ABCDE helps to remember the characteristics of melanoma: asymmetry, border (irregular), color (different shades, not uniform), diameter (> 6 mm), and evolution. Areas of pigment variation describe changes in color and a lack of uniformity of the lesion.



Central ulceration (B) most commonly occurs with basal cell carcinoma but can also occur with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. It is less common for central ulceration to occur with melanoma in adults, though ulcerated lesions may be seen more often in children.

Other similar lesions (C) are more likely to be a benign process. Patients may have nevi or skin moles that appear similar, but as a lesion progresses to become melanoma, it looks different from other moles on the body.

A pearly border (D) is more consistent with basal cell carcinoma. These lesions often begin as a pearly papule with telangiectasias.

Regular borders (E) are uncommon, as the malignancy does not grow in a uniform pattern.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the prognostic indicator of a melanoma lesion?

Reveal Answer:
Depth of invasion.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Melanoma

Risk factors: UV light exposure (e.g., Hx severe sunburns), personal or family Hx melanoma or dysplastic nevus syndrome, fair skin, immunosuppression
Sx and findings: new or changing mole, nonhealing skin lesion, associated pruritus or bleeding
PE: look for ABCDE
Asymmetry
Border irregularity
Color variation
Diameter
Evolution
Dx: biopsy (excisional or punch)
Tx options (depending on risk of recurrence) include excision with adequate margins, adjuvant therapies (e.g., immunotherapy)
Tumor depth is an important prognostic factor

question: A patient presents to the ED for evaluation of a skin lesion. Just beneath the midline of the left clavicle, there is a symmetric 1 cm skin-colored nodule, mobile when palpated, and with a central punctum. The lesion has been present for several years. Over the course of a week, the lesion has become increasingly painful, with scant surrounding erythema and fluctuance in the lesion itself. Which of the following is the best initial step in management for this lesion?
englishExplanation:
Epidermoid cysts (commonly called sebaceous cysts) result from the accumulation of keratin-rich material within a dermis-like cyst wall. A diagnosis of epidermoid cysts is typically made in the presence of a discrete nodule with a central punctum that is mobile on palpation. The diagnosis can be complicated by localized infection or inflammation, which can occur spontaneously and involve a substantial amount of surrounding tissue.

Fluctuance of an epidermoid cyst should prompt incision and drainage. Antibiotics are not necessary if the patient has good access to follow-up, as cyst contents are often sterile. In the absence of fluctuance, drainage is not required, and injection of steroids into the lesion is sufficient. Injections consist of triamcinolone and are typically performed in the outpatient setting.



Excision (A) of an epidermoid cyst is typically performed in the outpatient setting by a dermatologist. Lesions should not be excised when inflamed, as there is a greater risk of secondary infection and poor wound healing.

Local steroid injection (C) is not appropriate in the setting of fluctuance.

Oral antibiotics (D) are unlikely to be helpful, as most cysts are sterile, even in the presence of inflammation.

Oral NSAIDs (E) may speed the resolution of inflammation but are not a replacement for a local steroid injection or incision and drainage.

One Step Further
Question:
What genetic syndrome is associated with epidermoid cysts?

Reveal Answer:
Gardner syndrome.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epidermoid Cyst (Epidermal Inclusion Cyst)

“Sebaceous cyst” misnomer
Clinical diagnosis
Treat with steroids, I&D, excision
Refer to dermatology for follow-up

question: A 72-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 15 x 10 cm area of erythema on the left shin that has been progressing for the past 12 hours. He states he scraped his leg on the frame of his car while he was changing the oil 2 days ago. The patient’s history is significant for peripheral vascular disease and diabetes that is poorly controlled due to the patient not following treatment recommendations. He reports fever, chills, and rigors for the past 2 hours. Results of a bedside ultrasound show cobblestoning with a fine netlike area of hypoechoic stranding. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Carbuncle; oral clindamycin and topical bacitracin

englishExplanation:
Cellulitis presents with localized erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain involving the soft tissues. It is a bacterial infection that affects the deeper layers of the skin and underlying tissue. It is most commonly caused by Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species that enter the skin through a cut, scrape, or other skin integrity breakdown. Prompt medical attention is essential for the diagnosis and treatment of cellulitis. Mild cases are treated with oral antibiotics (cephalosporin, dicloxacillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin). Moderate cases requiring intravenous antibiotics are best treated with a penicillin, ceftriaxone, cefazolin, or clindamycin, while severe cases should be treated with intravenous vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam. Risk factors that may influence the management of cellulitis include a patient’s age, overall health status, immunosuppression, the likelihood of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, peripheral vascular disease, prior episodes of cellulitis, and chronic conditions like diabetes. These factors may influence the choice and duration of antibiotics and the need for hospitalization.



Abscesses (A) are collections of pus within body tissues. They often present as localized soft tissue swelling, erythema, and fluctuance and should be treated with incision and drainage. Ultrasound findings of an abscess include a localized fluid-filled or hypoechoic area in the soft tissue, which is inconsistent with this patient’s exam and ultrasound findings.

Carbuncles (B) are large abscesses that develop from multiple infected hair follicles. They typically develop in the thick skin along the back, back of the neck, or thighs. Carbuncles require incision and drainage. More severe infections may require oral antibiotics, such as clindamycin, and topical bacitracin. The current patient's exam and ultrasound findings are inconsistent with a carbuncle.

Impetigo (D) begins as a single pustule on the face, progressing to multiple lesions with golden yellow crusts. Treatment may involve oral antibiotics or topical medications like mupirocin. The location and description of the skin findings described for this patient do not suggest impetigo.

One Step Further
Question:
What condition affects the apocrine sweat glands and can present with recurrent abscess formations in the axillae and groin that resemble furunculosis?

Reveal Answer:
Hidradenitis suppurativa.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cellulitis

Commonly caused by group A Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus
Sx: pain, redness, swelling
More indolent onset than erysipelas
PE: tenderness, erythema with poorly demarcated borders, lymphedema, ± purulence
Abx selection depends on uncomplicated vs complicated cellulitis, PCN intolerance, MRSA risk factors, and purulence

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the ED with frank hematuria. On physical exam, you see the above. Which of the following is the classic triad of findings associated with this disease process?

options.text: Altered mental status, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia
Fever, altered mental status, petechial rash
Palpable purpura, diffuse arthritis, abdominal pain
Vomiting, paroxysmal abdominal pain, currant jelly stool

correctAnswer: Palpable purpura, diffuse arthritis, abdominal pain
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms of immunoglobulin A vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP). IgA vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis that occurs primarily in children. It presents with the classic triad of purpura, arthritis, and abdominal pain. It is preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection in approximately half of patients. It is also known to be caused by exposure to specific medications including vancomycin, cefuroxime, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. Signs and symptoms of the disease include palpable purpura of the lower extremities and buttocks (dependent areas), colicky abdominal pain, bloody stool, arthritis of the wrists, elbows, and knees, scrotal edema, gross hematuria (rare), and hypertension secondary to kidney involvement. Diagnosis is clinical. However, there are laboratory tests that should be performed. Kidney impairment is the most serious complication of IgA vasculitis and occurs in ~ 40% of patients. Thus, a serum creatinine level should be checked. Colicky abdominal pain may represent the associated phenomenon of ileoileal intussusception and requires an abdominal ultrasound to identify it. Management of IgA vasculitis is supportive. Most patients have spontaneous resolution of symptoms in 4–5 weeks.



Altered mental status, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia (A), in addition to kidney failure and fever, make up the classic pentad associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Patients with IgA vasculitis generally have normal to elevated platelets and no evidence of hemolytic anemia.

Fever, altered mental status, petechial rash (B) is often seen with Neisseria meningitidis infections, bacteremia, or Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Patients with Neisseria meningitidis may develop diffuse intravascular coagulation, which results in hemolysis.

Vomiting, paroxysmal abdominal pain, currant jelly stool (D) is the classic triad associated with intussusception. While patients with IgA vasculitis may have ileoileal intussusception, it is rare and not part of the classic triad associated with this disease process.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most appropriate therapy for Rocky Mountain spotted fever?

Reveal Answer:
Doxycycline.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 34-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis develops a tender rash as pictured above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient has erythema nodosum, an inflammatory and immunologic reaction of the subcutaneous fat that most commonly affects women ages 15–30 years. The rash presents with numerous tender subcutaneous nodules that are most commonly seen in the pretibial areas of bilateral lower legs but may also be seen in the arms. Lesions are initially bright red and slightly elevated but become less raised and yellow or violet, resembling bruises, as they resolve over 1–2 weeks. The disease is self-limited, but complete resolution of the rash may take 3–6 months due to recurrent new lesions. Other common symptoms include fever and arthralgias. The most common cause, especially in children, is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction after a strep infection. In adults, it may also be seen as a result of inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, malignancy, or a reaction to drugs, such as oral contraceptives, sulfonamides, penicillins, or immunizations. Treatment is symptomatic and aimed at the underlying cause.



Erythema marginatum (A) involves migratory pink annular lesions with sharp margins that affect the trunk and sometimes the limbs. They often appear and disappear within hours, similar to urticaria. It is one of the major Jones criteria for diagnosing acute rheumatic fever. Similar to erythema nodosum, it occurs after an acute streptococcal infection.

Erythema migrans (B) is an expanding red annular lesion with central clearing at the site of a tick bite that can grow up to 10 cm in size. It is seen in Lyme disease. There can be multiple lesions due to hematogenous spread of infection.

Erythema multiforme (C) involves many fixed lesions that evolve into target lesions over 1–2 days. Areas affected may include oral mucosa, palms, and soles. Similar to erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme has many possible causes. However, inflammatory bowel disease is more commonly known to cause erythema nodosum.

One Step Further
Question:
Within how many days of symptom onset must antibiotics be started to prevent acute rheumatic fever after streptococcal pharyngitis?

Reveal Answer:
Within 9 days.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Nodosum

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide

question: A 2-week-old female patient is brought to the emergency department for a red lesion that has been increasing in size over the last week. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the lesion pictured above?
englishExplanation:
The picture above shows an infantile hemangioma, a type of vascular tumor and the most common tumor of infancy. Most hemangiomas are not present at birth but become evident in the first days to weeks of life. Hemangiomas are characterized by a phase of proliferation in the first year of life with growth in the size of the lesion followed by a phase of involution, marked by gradual regression of the lesion. Diagnosis is typically clinical, though in more ambiguous cases biopsy may be done for confirmation. While the majority of hemangiomas are uncomplicated and self-limited, ulceration, bleeding, or infection may occur. Hemangiomas that involve the airway may result in airway compromise and should be considered in children with cervicofacial mandibular distribution of hemangiomas that develop hoarseness or stridor.



The majority of infantile hemangiomas are self-limited and resolve by 9 years of age. As such, incision and drainage (A), surgical consultation (C), and topical silver nitrate (D) would not be indicated.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment of bleeding from an infantile hemangioma?

Reveal Answer:
Direct pressure (the vast majority are small and self-limited).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Infantile Hemangioma

Majority are not present at birth, become apparent in the first days to months of life
Rapid growth in first 5 months → involution at 12 months → regresses by 9 years old
Dx: clinical
Dermatology referral: segmental (clusters), ulcerated, obstructs vision or feeding, bleeding, infection, causing deformity, more than five, sacral area, cervicofacial
Tx: observation, topical beta-blocker (low risk), oral propranolol (high risk or complicated) ideally by 4 weeks old

question: A 7-day-old boy presents with umbilical cord discharge and redness. The infant was born at home via an uncomplicated delivery, has been eating well, and is afebrile. Examination is significant for normal vital signs for age and an erythematous cord stump with 1 centimeter of surrounding erythema and purulent discharge. Which of the following is the appropriate management of this infant's condition?

options.text: Admission for empiric treatment with vancomycin
Discharge with topical mupirocin to the umbilicus
Wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin

correctAnswer: Wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin
englishExplanation:
This infant’s clinical presentation is most consistent with a diagnosis of omphalitis. Omphalitis is an infection of the umbilicus, umbilical stump, and surrounding tissues seen in neonates. It is a rare condition but has a high mortality rate. Additionally, it must be differentiated from normal cord separation that may have cord discharge but will not have surrounding erythema. Patients commonly present with purulent discharge and local erythema and induration of the surrounding skin. More severe cases may present with fever, diffuse abdominal erythema, and poor feeding, which should be concerning for sepsis or more advanced spread. Localized omphalitis can easily spread through the umbilical vein, leading to portal vein thrombosis as well as intra-abdominal spread causing peritonitis or necrotizing fasciitis.

Risk factors include male sex, home birth (or other nonsterile birth), prolonged labor, and prolonged rupture of membranes. Most cases are polymicrobial in nature, including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, as well as gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli. Given this, initial treatment should include wound culture and inpatient treatment with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin. Wound culture can be helpful due to the wide variety of potential pathogens, including anaerobes. Additionally, patients with systemic signs such as fever or poor feeding should have blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid cultures obtained to rule out sepsis.



Admission for empiric treatment with vancomycin (A) is incorrect as it does not include gram-negative coverage and also does not include a wound culture to help direct care. Discharging with oral amoxicillin (B) is incorrect as these patients should be admitted for parenteral antibiotics given the severity of the infection and their young age. Discharging with topical mupirocin (C) is also not correct, as neither discharge planning nor topical treatment would be adequate care.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the expected age at which cord separation should occur?

Reveal Answer:
4–7 days.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Omphalitis

Polymicrobial infection of the umbilicus
PE: purulent discharge from stump with surrounding erythema or induration
Dx: clinical
Tx: treat for gram-positive and gram-negative organisms (e.g., nafcillin and gentamicin)
Culture before starting antibiotics
Monitor for sepsis, necrotizing fasciitis

question:
A 59-year-old man presents with a new, diffuse skin rash and facial swelling. He was discharged 3 weeks ago after a myocardial infarction. His hospitalization was complicated by an episode of gout. The patient's home medications include aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, allopurinol, and esomeprazole. On exam, he has significant facial edema without throat swelling or difficulty breathing. He also has a morbilliform rash with scattered bullae. His laboratory results are as follows:

White blood cells: 11,900/µL

Neutrophils: 63%

Lymphocytes: 17%

Eosinophils: 14%

Blood urea nitrogen: 48 mg/dL

Creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL

Aspartate aminotransferase: 28 U/L

Alanine aminotransferase: 102 U/L

Alkaline phosphatase: 98 U/L

Which medication is the likely etiology of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient with recent initiation of multiple new drugs found with facial edema, skin rash, eosinophilia, and elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) most likely has drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome (DIHS, also known as drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)) precipitated by allopurinol. DIHS is one of the severe cutaneous adverse reactions that also include Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. DIHS is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction that leads to T cell-mediated attack on native tissues. It is a life-threatening disease, with mortality > 10%. Allopurinol is known to trigger DIHS in patients of Asian ancestry (most notably Han Chinese, Thai, and Korean patients) due to higher expression of HLA-B58 in these populations. The American College of Rheumatology recommends screening for HLA-B58 before initiating treatment with allopurinol. The hallmark features of DIHS include rash, liver enzyme elevation (> 90%), eosinophilia (> 60%), and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (> 60%). DIHS is treated by removing the offending agent and initiating systemic corticosteroids. Intravenous immune globulin has also been suggested as a potential treatment for severe cases, but this is based on case reports.



Atorvastatin (B) and other statins can cause initial ALT elevations in patients but do not cause skin rash, eosinophilia, or edema. The ALT elevations associated with statins are transient and do not reflect liver injury or necessitate medication withdrawal.

Lisinopril (C) and other angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can trigger angioedema through bradykinin-mediated vasodilation but have no associated rash, ALT elevations, or eosinophilia.

Metoprolol (D) has been associated with drug-induced liver injury, but this side effect is rare and would not be accompanied by edema or skin rash.

One Step Further
Question:
How long after medication induction does drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome develop?

Reveal Answer:
Generally 2–4 weeks, but it can present as late as 16 weeks.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Drug-induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome (DIHS) (Formerly Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms, DRESS)

Severe T cell-mediated drug reaction (anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, vancomycin)
Begins 2–6 weeks after initiation of drug
Clinical
Fever, lymphadenopathy
Cutaneous: facial edema, polymorphic coalescing rash (mild mucous membrane involvement)
GI: hepatitis or cholestasis (most common), pancreatitis
Kidney: proteinuria, acute interstitial nephritis
Pulmonary: pneumonitis, interstitial pneumonia
Cardiac: myocarditis
Lab results: leukocytosis, eosinophilia, transaminitis, pancytopenia (severe)
Diagnosis: clinical symptoms, exposure to common drugs
Treatment: corticosteroids, cyclosporine, immunomodulators

question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the ED with a rash that began 2 days ago. She is also having a nonproductive cough and shortness of breath. On physical exam, she has oral erosions and a diffuse rash. The skin lesions have a dusky center with a surrounding erythematous halo. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Erythema multiforme (EM) is an immune-mediated cutaneous disorder characterized by target lesions. These lesions have a dusky center with surrounding erythema, giving the classic target appearance. Skin lesions are often accompanied by erosions or bullae involving mucosal areas such as the oropharynx or genitals. Infections, medications, malignancy, autoimmune disease, and immunizations have been implicated as potential causes of erythema multiforme. Erythema multiforme can also be seen in patients with Mycoplasma pneumoniae and serologic testing may be helpful in patients with respiratory symptoms.



Stevens-Johnson syndrome (B)may present with mucosal skin findings but target skin lesions are more characteristic of erythema multiforme. Unlike erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome is more commonly caused by medications.

Urticaria (C) typically presents as erythematous and edematous plaques with associated pruritus. Urticaria is often triggered by exposure to a known allergen.

Vasculitis (D) can present with target lesions, and a biopsy may be needed to differentiate erythema multiforme from vasculitis. In a patient with respiratory symptoms consistent with pneumonia and a rash, erythema multiforme is more likely.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of erythema multiforme?

Reveal Answer:
Herpes simplex virus (HSV).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Multiforme (EM)

Most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Drugs: sulfa, oral hypoglycemics, anticonvulsants, penicillin, NSAIDs (SOAPS)
Patient presents with acute onset of symmetric target lesions on palms and soles, face and trunk may also be involved
Erythema multiforme minor: localized eruption of the skin with minimal or no mucosal involvement
Erythema multiforme major: one or more mucous membranes are involved
PE: target-like rash with a central dark papule surrounded by a pale area and a halo of erythema
Tx: usually self-limiting, supportive care

question: A 9-year-old boy presents to the ED with bilateral knee pain, low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for the past 4 days. His vital signs are blood pressure of 116/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 98 bpm, respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute, and a temperature of 38.1°C (100.6℉). On examination, you note the rash seen above. Urinalysis is positive for hematuria. What patient education should be provided to this boy and his family?

options.text: Despite plasma exchange, most patients progress to chronic kidney impairment
Kidney biopsy is necessary to make the diagnosis
Long-term prednisone therapy improves 5-year survival to > 50%
The disease is self-limited, and most cases resolve within 6–8 weeks
Without treatment, the disease carries a mortality rate of 80% at 1 year

correctAnswer: The disease is self-limited, and most cases resolve within 6–8 weeks
englishExplanation:
The patient has immunoglobulin A vasculitis, formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP). This small-vessel vasculitis predominantly occurs in small children. Most cases follow an upper respiratory tract infection.

Immunoglobulin A vasculitis classically presents with fever, abdominal pain, arthritis, hematuria, and a pathognomonic round, palpable, symmetrical rash that appears on the dependent areas of the legs and buttocks. NSAIDs, dapsone, and prednisone have all been shown to relieve symptoms. The course of disease is typically self-limited. Most cases resolve within 6–8 weeks, with a recurrence rate of up to 33%.



Plasma exchange (A) has been found to be successful in the treatment of microscopic polyangiitis. In immunoglobulin A vasculitis, most patients do not progress to chronic kidney impairment.

Kidney biopsy (B) is typically only indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain or if there are clinical findings of severe kidney involvement. Confirming the diagnosis through biopsy (of kidney or skin) is more important in adult patients as adults have a lower incidence of immunoglobulin A vasculitis and a higher incidence of other forms of vasculitis that may mimic immunoglobulin A vasculitis.

Prednisone (C) therapy has increased the 5-year survival rate to > 50% in eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome), which is typically associated with fever, weight loss, malaise, and pulmonary symptoms, but it does not affect survival in immunoglobulin A vasculitis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis), not immunoglobulin A vasculitis, once carried a 1-year mortality rate of 80% (E), but the combination of cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids has been successful in inducing remission in > 90% of patients.

One Step Further
Question:
What specific gastrointestinal disorder is associated with immunoglobulin A vasculitis?

Reveal Answer:
Intussusception.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care
Complications: nephropathy (ESKD more common in adults), intussusception (more common in children)

question: A 4-year-old boy with no significant medical history presents to the ED with his parent for generalized abdominal pain. His parent also notes that the patient has been nauseated and was seen by his pediatrician last week for knee pain and constipation. His vital signs are within normal limits. His abdomen is soft without significant tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is the most common systemic vasculitis in children, with peak incidence at 5–7 years of age. The disease shows seasonal variation with increased incidence in autumn and winter and a strong association with a preceding upper respiratory infection. The pathogenesis involves IgA-dominant immune complex deposition in small blood vessels, particularly leading to leukocytoclastic vasculitis. This immune-mediated process affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys.

The classic tetrad includes palpable purpura, arthralgia or arthritis, abdominal pain, and kidney involvement (e.g., hematuria, proteinuria). Diagnosis requires purpura or petechiae with lower limb predominance plus at least one of four additional features: abdominal pain, histopathology showing IgA deposition, arthritis or arthralgia, or kidney involvement. The purpura is nonthrombocytopenic and typically appears as round or oval palpable lesions predominantly on the lower extremities and buttocks. Gastrointestinal manifestations range from mild abdominal pain to severe complications, including gastrointestinal bleeding, intussusception, and bowel perforation. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, including a detailed skin exam to identify cutaneous lesions, with laboratory testing used to exclude other causes of purpura and identify kidney involvement when necessary. Imaging may be considered when severe abdominal symptoms suggest a complication.

IgA vasculitis spontaneously resolves in nearly all children, making supportive care the primary management strategy in the ED. Treatment focuses on symptom management with NSAIDs or acetaminophen for arthralgia and adequate hydration. Corticosteroids should not be used prophylactically, as systematic reviews demonstrate they do not prevent complications such as kidney disease or intussusception. However, corticosteroids may be beneficial for severe abdominal pain or established nephritis. The most significant long-term complication is kidney involvement, which occurs in up to one-half of patients and can persist or relapse over the course of years. End-stage kidney disease develops in a small minority of patients, while other acute complications include testicular involvement or orchitis and rarely pulmonary or CNS involvement.



Imaging studies such as abdominal X-ray (A) and ultrasound (B) are not routinely indicated in the initial evaluation of suspected IgA vasculitis. They should be reserved for cases in which severe abdominal symptoms suggest a potential complication such as intussusception.

There is no evidence presented in this case to suggest an ongoing GI bleed, so a digital rectal exam (C) would not be indicated.

A urinalysis (E) is often included in the standard workup of IgA vasculitis but should not be performed prior to a comprehensive skin exam to identify cutaneous lesions, the presence of which is mandatory to make the diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What finding can help distinguish between septic arthritis and IgA vasculitis in a child who refuses to bear weight?

Reveal Answer:
IgA vasculitis often affects both lower extremities symmetrically, while septic arthritis is typically unilateral.

Rapid Review

Immunoglobulin A Vasculitis (Formerly Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)

IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis most common in children 3–15 years old
10% of cases occur in adults
Risk factors: history of recent URI
Sx: rash that begins on buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthralgia, hematuria, proteinuria
PE: pink papules → raised purpura → ecchymosis that is not painful
Tx: supportive care

question: A 47-year-old man with diabetes presents to the emergency department with a dusky right leg with foul-smelling hemorrhagic bullae and palpable crepitus. In addition to immediate surgical consultation, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
englishExplanation:
This patient has signs and symptoms concerning for a severe, necrotizing soft tissue infection which requires broad-spectrum antibiotics. These infections are most commonly polymicrobial, including gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic species. Therefore, the combination of intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate antimicrobial coverage. Clindamycin should also be administered for its antitoxin effects. Risk factors for necrotizing soft tissue infections include diabetes mellitus, advanced age, heart disease, alcohol use disorder, peripheral vascular disease, human immunodeficiency virus, intravenous drug use, and chronic skin infections. Either direct invasion from direct skin trauma (e.g., surgical incision, insect bite) or hematogenous spread are common mechanisms of infection. Patients are usually systemically ill and require aggressive fluid resuscitation, antimicrobial coverage, and early surgical consultation.



Neither combination of ceftriaxone and doxycycline (A) nor levofloxacin and tobramycin (B) would provide sufficient anaerobic coverage to treat necrotizing soft tissue infections. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cephalexin (C) would not provide sufficient gram-negative or anaerobic coverage.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: antibiotics alone are effective for some types of necrotizing soft tissue infections?

Reveal Answer:
False. Surgical intervention is the cornerstone of management.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Necrotizing Fasciitis and Myonecrosis

Necrotizing fasciitis
Type 1: polymicrobial
Type 2: a single organism (most commonly group A Streptococcus)
Myonecrosis
Traumatic (Clostridium perfringens)
Spontaneous (Clostridium septicum)
Pain out of proportion to exam
Systemic signs of infection
Cellulitis progresses to dusky blue with bullae or vesicles
Radiograph: subcutaneous emphysema
Emergent surgical debridement, broad-spectrum antibiotics

question: A 3-week-old term girl presents with a rash that has been present since birth. She is eating well, has regained her birth weight, and is making normal wet and dirty diapers. She has had no fevers. There is no family history of asthma or eczema. Her parents are concerned because her rash has worsened over the last week. Your exam shows a well appearing, alert infant with vital signs within normal limits for age and the above rash. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Salmon-colored greasy patches with yellow scale characterize seborrheic dermatitis (i.e., cradle cap) that occurs most commonly on the scalp but can also be found in the diaper area and axillae. The rash seems more upsetting to the parents than the infants, as they otherwise are asymptomatic and healthy. The rash can appear severe, especially when it develops into dark red patches in the diaper area and trunk. It usually clears without treatment within 2–3 months but can last 8–9 months. For seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, removing dry, flaky skin with a soft brush after using oil or petrolatum can improve the appearance and help with the anxiety of the parents. While conservative treatment is recommended, the rash can be improved with topical corticosteroids or ketoconazole cream in severe cases.



Acropustulosis of infancy (A) is an uncommon, benign, chronic, and recurrent pustular rash on the palms and soles of infants, although it can involve the scalp. However, unlike the flaky lesions found in this patient, the lesions appear pustular.

Atopic dermatitis (B) can appear much like seborrheic dermatitis initially but usually has a waxing and waning course and a family history of atopy.

Erythema toxicum (C) is an extremely common benign rash with blotchy macules and papules usually clustered over the face, trunk, and proximal extremities that fade over 5–7 days but can recur for several weeks. It is flea-bitten, not flaky, in appearance.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a known, transient complication of seborrheic dermatitis in dark-pigmented infants?

Reveal Answer:
Postinflammatory hypopigmentation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Seborrheic Dermatitis

Chronic relapsing dermatitis caused by oversecretion of sebaceous material and hypersensitivity to the yeast Malassezia furfur (formerly Pityrosporum ovale)
Worse in winter, improves in summer
Children: 3 weeks to 12 months old, peaks at 3 months
PE: dandruff, erythematous plaques covered with yellow, greasy scales located on scalp, ears, face (eyebrows, nasolabial folds), chest, groin
Tx: emollients, OTC selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole shampoo for scalp, corticosteroid creams, ketoconazole cream for skin
Severe and acute onset may be associated with HIV infection

question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and asthma presents with tender nodules on the lower extremities. Before the appearance of the rash, she describes 3 days of low-grade fever and myalgias. Her exam is shown above. Which of the following is the best next step in treating this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient presents with erythema nodosum, an inflammatory reaction of the dermis and adipose tissue. It is thought to be a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a medication or systemic disease. While most cases are idiopathic, the most commonly implicated disease is a preceding streptococcal infection. Other diseases associated with erythema nodosum include systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, lymphoma, and inflammatory bowel disease. Commonly implicated medications include sulfonamides, phenytoin, penicillins, and oral contraceptives. Erythema nodosum is more common in women, particularly in the second to fourth decades of life. Following a prodrome of nonspecific symptoms, such as low-grade fever and myalgias, patients develop tender, erythematous nodules, most commonly on the anterior tibial surfaces. They can also be seen on the upper extremities or trunk. Management is twofold: symptomatic treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, rest, and elevation of the legs, as well as evaluation for a possible underlying etiology. The nodules often resolve in 3–8 weeks.



Cetirizine (A) is a nonsedating antihistamine that is used in treating seasonal allergies and urticaria. Urticaria is characterized by raised erythematous wheals with pale centers. Individual hives are usually transient, although additional lesions may continuously develop.

Potassium iodide (C) can be used to manage severe pain associated with erythema nodosum. However, a trial of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be pursued first.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) treats purulent cellulitis associated with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Antibiotics are not indicated in the management of erythema nodosum.

One Step Further
Question:
What sexually transmitted infection has been associated with erythema nodosum?

Reveal Answer:
Chlamydia trachomatis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Erythema Nodosum

In adults, F > M
Causes: idiopathic, streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, fungal infections, IBD, tuberculosis, leukemia, lymphoma, OCPs, sulfa drugs, pregnancy
Symptoms: violaceous tender nodules (most often on shins), arthralgias
Treatment: NSAIDs, potassium iodide
