Most commonly caused by S. aureus, streptococci
Risks: sinusitis, orbital trauma or surgery, odontogenic infection
Sx: eyelid swelling, pain with eye movement
PE: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, decreased vision
Dx: clinically and confirmed with CT scan
Tx: ophthalmology evaluation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, hospital admission
Complications: orbital abscess, vision loss, intracranial infection

question: A 30-year-old man with no previous eye history presents to the emergency department with pain and photophobia in his right eye after working on a wood carving project. He thinks wood got into his eye when he was carving. On examination, the patient is having difficulty opening his right eye due to pain and he has excessive tearing. He reports blurry vision. After the installation of tetracaine, the pain begins to subside, and he is able to open his eye for examination. A small foreign body is visualized over the lateral cornea and is removed with a cotton swab. Fluorescein staining shows a small epithelial defect at the site of the previously noted foreign body. The remainder of the ophthalmic exam is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.text: Polymyxin plus neomycin plus hydrocortisone drops

englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with symptoms of a corneal abrasion and he was found to have a small corneal foreign body. Any patient who has severe eye pain with photophobia or foreign body sensation preventing the opening of the eye generally can be presumed to have a corneal epithelial defect. Corneal abrasions can be classified as traumatic, contact lens-related, or spontaneous. Spontaneous defects in the corneal epithelium may occur without any obvious injury. Eyes that have had a previous injury are prone to spontaneous abrasions. On examination of a patient with symptoms of corneal abrasion or foreign body, the clinician should first ensure there is no penetrating trauma or ruptured globe. The diagnosis of corneal abrasion should be confirmed with fluorescein staining. All foreign bodies should be removed with irrigation, a cotton swab, or with a foreign body spud within 24 hours of injury. Patients should be treated with topical antibiotics to prevent superinfection. An ointment is theoretically better because it provides lubrication, but many patients prefer drops instead. Since there is not any mention of contact lens use in this patient, appropriate treatment for this patient’s corneal abrasion and foreign body would include polymyxin plus trimethoprim drops. The pain can be treated with topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.



Cyclopentolate drops (A) are parasympathetic medications that inhibit the miotic, or pupil-constricting, response to light. These drops can help with any photophobia symptoms, but they will not relieve the foreign body sensation. The effect of the drops can last for 24–36 hours and, generally, small abrasions heal within that period of time. Therefore, these drops are not recommended unless patients have very large corneal abrasions with significant photophobia. Additionally, this option did not include antibiotic treatment, which is the only recommended therapy for corneal abrasion and foreign bodies.

Gentamicin drops (B) would be indicated for patients who wear contact lenses. Such patients are at risk for infection from Pseudomonas species, so fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides are indicated. This patient does not wear contact lenses and aminoglycosides should be avoided because they can be toxic to the epithelium.

Polymyxin plus neomycin plus hydrocortisone drops (C) should be avoided because the use of steroids slows epithelial healing and reduces host resistance to superinfection.

One Step Further
Question:
What physical examination finding would suggest an open globe injury?

Reveal Answer:
A teardrop or misshapen pupil.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Foreign Bodies

Apply topical anesthesia
Use cotton-tipped applicator, needle with the slit lamp, or Alger brush to dislodge
If metallic object, remove rust rings in 24–48 hours
Consult ophthalmology for large or deep foreign bodies
Postprocedure topical antibiotics

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with nasal congestion and facial pain. Her symptoms started 12 days ago and have not improved. Her vital signs are a T of 101°F (38.3°C), BP of 120/80 mm Hg, HR of 90 bpm, RR of 16/min, and SpO2 of 98%. On physical exam, she has tenderness to percussion of the bilateral maxillary sinuses and purulent green nasal discharge. Which of the following is an indication to treat this patient with antibiotics?
englishExplanation:
Acute rhinosinusitis refers to inflammation of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses. It can be caused by allergens, irritants, and infections from viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Common symptoms include nasal congestion and discharge, facial pain, headache, fever, and anosmia. Up to 98% of cases of acute rhinosinusitis are viral in etiology, most of which will resolve with time and should be treated with supportive measures. Yet, surveys show that antibiotics are prescribed for 81% of adults presenting to the outpatient setting with symptoms of acute rhinosinusitis. To avoid unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions, it is important to identify which patients are most likely to have a bacterial cause of their symptoms. According to the Infectious Diseases Society of America, three clinical scenarios are indicative of likely bacterial rhinosinusitis for which antibiotics should be prescribed. The first is a patient presenting with persistent symptoms lasting ≥ 10 days without clinical improvement, as most uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infections (URIs) last 5–10 days. The second is a patient presenting with severe symptoms or high fever (> 102°F, or 39°C) as well as purulent nasal discharge or facial pain for at least 3–4 days at the beginning of the illness. Fever or purulent discharge alone is not indicative of bacterial infection. However, fever from an uncomplicated viral URI typically presents early and resolves after the first 24–48 hours, and the nasal discharge from a virus starts clear and turns purulent after the first 4 days. Thus, the combination of both fever and purulent discharge early on in the illness is what distinguishes a likely bacterial infection. Finally, a patient presenting with worsening symptoms of fever, headache, and nasal discharge after a typical viral URI that lasted 5–6 days and was initially improving is likely to have a secondary bacterial process.



Facial tenderness (B) is not an indication to treat with antibiotics, as it can be seen in both bacterial and viral rhinosinusitis. Fever (C) alone does not indicate a bacterial cause, as patients with viruses often present with a fever early on in the illness. Rather, a high fever along with purulent discharge or facial pain that presents at the beginning of the illness and lasts for 3–4 days suggests a likely bacterial cause. Purulent nasal discharge (D) can be present in both viral and bacterial rhinosinusitis. Nasal discharge from a viral URI tends to start clear and turn purulent after about 4 days, whereas nasal discharge from a bacterial infection often starts as purulent.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the antibiotic of choice for the treatment of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis?

Reveal Answer:
Amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Sinusitis

Sx: nasal congestion, pain or pressure over sinuses, ear pain or pressure, headache, fever
PE: purulent rhinorrhea
Most commonly caused by viral URI
If viral, Tx is supportive care
Bacterial sinusitis: persistent and not improving (≥ 10 days), worsening or double sickening (≥ 5–6 days)
Onset of severe symptoms: fever ≥ 39.0°C (102.2°F) and purulent nasal discharge (≥ 3–4 days at the beginning of illness)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Complications: frontal bone osteomyelitis (Pott puffy tumor), orbital cellulitis, sinus venous thrombosis, extension into meninges or brain

question: A 12-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset right-sided facial swelling associated with a foul taste in her mouth. Physical exam reveals an underweight teenage girl. She has difficulty opening her mouth. The oropharynx is clear without swelling or exudates. There is swelling and tenderness to the right preauricular space, extending beyond the angle of the mandible. Temperature is 39.7°C, blood pressure is 114/64 mm Hg, and heart rate is 134 bpm. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with acute bacterial parotitis. Risk factors for parotitis include old age, sialoliths, neoplasms, Sjögren syndrome, and HIV. Bacterial parotitis is rare in older children and adolescents but can occur more often in those with anorexia and bulimia. This patient’s fever is an indicator of severe infection that is unlikely to respond to oral antibiotics. Other indicators include leukocytosis and significant comorbidity (e.g., immunosuppressed). Additionally, the patient’s degree of swelling is concerning for possible extension into the deeper structures of the neck. Notable complications of parotitis include airway compromise, Lemierre syndrome, and facial nerve palsy.

Bacterial causes are often polymicrobial, with Staphylococcus aureus, viridans group streptococci, and Eikenella corrodens comprising commonly cultured pathogens. The antibiotic choice must cover Staphylococcus with consideration for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage if the patient has any risk factors (e.g., prior MRSA infection or nursing home resident). Ampicillin-sulbactam is available in IV formulation, has broad spectrum coverage, and is the first-line therapy for bacterial parotitis.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate (A) and cephalexin (C) are appropriate first-line oral antibiotics for patients without signs of severe infection (e.g., fever, leukocytosis, and significant comorbidity).

Moxifloxacin (D) is available in IV formulation and has anti-staphylococcal and broad-spectrum coverage. However, it is not the first line for parotitis and is contraindicated in pediatric patients due to tendinopathy.

One Step Further
Question:
What antibiotic is appropriate for a pediatric patient with bacterial parotitis and a severe penicillin allergy?

Reveal Answer:
Clindamycin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Parotitis

Bacterial (suppurative) and viral (nonsuppurative) causes
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, but anaerobes common too
Viral causes can include mumps, influenza, and coxsackievirus
Noninfectious causes: sialolithiasis, alcohol use disorder, diabetes, uremia, certain drugs (anticholinergics, antihistamines), malignancy
Risk factors: age < 1 year, older age, recent surgery or intubation, dehydration, poor oral hygiene, eating disorders
Sx: pain and tenderness with trismus and dysphagia
PE: unilateral, firm, erythematous swelling of the pre- and postauricular areas that extends to the angle of the mandible
DDx: bacterial causes are more often unilateral, whereas viral parotitis is often bilateral
Suppurative parotitis is also associated with purulent discharge, whereas viral or noninfectious parotitis is not
Dx: clinical, but CT can detect abscess
Tx: hydration, often broad-spectrum antibiotics
Complications: respiratory obstruction, septic thrombophlebitis (Lemierre syndrome), bacteremia, osteomyelitis

question: A young adult presents to the ED with acute tooth pain. He has a history of multiple dental caries, but this pain has gradually worsened over the past 2 days. On exam, tooth 31 is exquisitely tender to percussion and has a large eroded area of enamel. Swelling is seen in the surrounding gingiva but not in the buccal or submandibular soft tissues. The patient is afebrile with no other concerns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Acute pain, swelling, and mild tooth elevation are characteristic of a periapical abscess. Exquisite sensitivity to percussion or chewing on the involved tooth is a common finding. Periapical abscesses occur when there is significant erosion of the pulp with bacterial overgrowth and are usually associated with dental caries or nonviable teeth.

Treatment is with antibiotics (penicillin or amoxicillin with or without metronidazole), appropriate analgesia, incision and drainage, and urgent dental follow-up for definitive care.



An acute tooth fracture (A) is usually suggested by a history of the patient feeling their tooth break. It usually occurs in the setting of local trauma or biting on a hard object. A chronically fractured tooth may be a nidus for the development of a periapical abscess.

Alveolar osteitis (dry socket) (B) is suggested by a history of a recently pulled tooth that has become exquisitely painful.

Ludwig angina (C) is an infection that spreads into the submandibular soft tissues and can be an airway emergency.

Pulpitis (E) is inflammation of the dental pulp and can cause tooth pain, but the presence of swelling in the surrounding gingiva and exquisite tenderness to percussion suggests the infection has progressed to a periapical abscess.

One Step Further
Question:
What organisms account for most cultivable flora in a healthy oral cavity?

Reveal Answer:
Streptococcus species, Peptostreptococcus, Veillonella, and diphtheroids.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Periapical Abscess

Risk: dental caries
PE: pain on tooth percussion, erythematous and fluctuant swelling of the gingiva
Tx: consider I&D, antibiotics, urgent dental referral

question: A 39-year-old woman presents to the ED with pain and swelling around the eye as shown above. Vital signs include a T of 98.9°F (37.2°C), BP of 116/76 mm Hg, HR of 82 bpm, RR of 17/min, and SpO2 of 99% on room air. Extraocular movements and vision are intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: Obtain CT scan of the face
Perform incision and drainage in ED
Recommend warm compresses and ophthalmology follow-up

englishExplanation:
Dacryocystitis is an acute infection of the lacrimal sac that typically results from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, leading to stasis of tears and subsequent bacterial overgrowth. The condition is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, although other organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and gram-negative bacteria may also be implicated. It often presents unilaterally with localized swelling, erythema, and marked tenderness over the area between the medial canthus and the nasal bridge. Patients may also exhibit epiphora (excessive tearing), purulent discharge from the puncta, and in some cases, fever or malaise.

Initial treatment includes systemic oral antibiotics to target likely pathogens and supportive care. Oral antibiotics can be used, and the choice should depend on allergy status and local resistance patterns for methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Adjunctive measures include warm compresses to promote drainage and gentle massage of the lacrimal sac to facilitate decompression. Avoid forceful manipulation in severe cases, especially when abscess formation is suspected, as this can lead to rupture or spread of infection.

If left untreated or inadequately treated, dacryocystitis can lead to serious complications, including preseptal or orbital cellulitis, abscess formation, and rarely, cavernous sinus thrombosis. Chronic or recurrent cases may require surgical intervention such as dacryocystorhinostomy to establish a new drainage pathway and prevent recurrence. Prompt recognition and appropriate treatment are essential to avoid complications and preserve ocular health.



Topical antibiotics (B) are insufficient, as this is a deeper skin infection rather than a superficial eye condition like conjunctivitis or blepharitis.

CT scan of the face (C) is unnecessary unless there are signs suggesting orbital cellulitis such as ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, decreased vision, or systemic toxicity.

Incision and drainage in the ED (D) is not appropriate for patients with dacryocystitis. Referral to ophthalmology for surgical drainage of the lacrimal gland should be considered when infection does not resolve with oral antibiotics or if an abscess forms.

Warm compresses (E) can aid in treatment but alone are inadequate for resolution without systemic antibiotics. Delaying antibiotic treatment can lead to worsening of the infection or the development of complications.

One Step Further
Question:
What bacterial pathogen is most commonly implicated in hordeolum?

Reveal Answer:
Staphylococcus species.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Dacryocystitis

Enlargement and inflammation of the nasolacrimal sac
Sx: rapid-onset unilateral severe pain, redness, and epiphora (tearing eye)
PE: swelling, redness, and tenderness at the medial canthus
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Treatment is systemic antibiotics

question: A 76-year-old woman presents to the ED with the sudden onset of a nosebleed 1 hour prior to arrival. Her medical history includes atrial fibrillation and hypertension, and she is anticoagulated on warfarin. Her temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg, heart rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate is 20/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. There is brisk bleeding from the right naris noted on physical exam. Bleeding persists despite anterior nasal packing, and posterior epistaxis is suspected. Which of the following is the best next step in treatment?

options.text: Placement of a balloon or Foley catheter

correctAnswer: Placement of a balloon or Foley catheter
englishExplanation:
Epistaxis is classified as anterior or posterior based on the source of bleeding. Anterior epistaxis is far more common and occurs in the nasal septum, at Kiesselbach plexus. Often, this condition can be managed conservatively with pressure or nasal clamping. Silver nitrate cautery can be attempted if an area of bleeding can be identified. If these attempts are unsuccessful, nasal packing with a nasal tampon or a nasal balloon should be performed. The use of thrombogenic foams has also been shown to be effective, and some new evidence suggests that tranexamic acid may also be useful.

Brisk bleeding despite appropriate treatment of suspected anterior epistaxis suggests a posterior source. Posterior epistaxis occurs less frequently and arises from the sphenopalatine artery. Bleeding can be significant and difficult to control, and packing is required with either a balloon catheter or a Foley catheter. Timely otorhinolaryngology consultation should be initiated in these patients, and patients with posterior epistaxis require hospitalization out of concern for hypoxic complications. Although the benefit of antibiotics is unclear, current recommendations are to prescribe prophylactic antibiotics for any patient who will have nasal packing in place for more than 48 hours. Typically, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is prescribed to prevent Staphylococcus aureus infections and potential toxic shock syndrome.



Placement of a nasal clamp (B) and nasal tampon (C) and the use of silver nitrate cautery (D) are all methods used to control anterior epistaxis and would not be expected to be successful in treating suspected posterior epistaxis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common site of venous posterior epistaxis?

Reveal Answer:
Woodruff plexus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epistaxis

Most common source
Anterior bleeds: Kiesselbach plexus
Posterior bleeds: sphenopalatine artery
Treatment
Anterior bleeding: direct pressure, topical vasoconstriction (oxymetazoline), chemicalcautery with silver nitrate (if vessel visualized), packing
Posterior bleeding: packing (nasal balloon or Foley catheter)
Admit patients with posterior packing to a monitored bed
Possible complications: septal necrosis (if both sides of septum cauterized), toxic shock syndrome (prolonged packing), infection

question: What is the most common infectious etiology of conjunctivitis in adults?
englishExplanation:
Viral conjunctivitis is the most common type of conjunctivitis in adults and is most often caused by adenovirus. Patients present with symptoms of redness, watery or mucoserous discharge, and irritation. It is typically bilateral (but may initially affect only one eye), and there is often a preceding or concomitant upper respiratory illness. Physical examination findings include preauricular lymphadenopathy, diffuse conjunctival injection, and enlarged follicles on the inferior palpebral conjunctiva. Visual acuity, examination of the cornea and anterior chamber, and intraocular pressures are normal.

Treatment consists of supportive care with cool compresses. Some patients may get relief from an over-the-counter topical antihistamine or ocular decongestant, but this treats only the symptoms and not the cause. Topical antibiotics are reserved for those patients in whom the etiology is unclear or if there is concern for a superimposed bacterial infection.



Enterovirus (B) may also cause viral conjunctivitis but is less frequently implicated than adenovirus.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (C) is a concerning cause of bacterial conjunctivitis in patients who wear contact lenses.

Staphylococcus aureus (D) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (E) are common causes of bacterial conjunctivitis, but neither are responsible for the majority of cases overall.

One Step Further
Question:
What pathogen is the most likely cause in a neonate presenting with conjunctivitis 5–14 days after delivery?

Reveal Answer:
Chlamydia trachomatis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Viral Conjunctivitis

Most commonly caused by adenovirus
Presents with bilateral red or pink eyes, gritty feeling in eye
PE: preauricular lymphadenopathy, watery or scant mucoid discharge
Tx: compresses, artificial tears, topical antihistamines or decongestants for itching and redness

question: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dizziness. The patient has a medical history significant for hyperlipidemia and hypertension. He states the symptoms started yesterday. They have been intermittent, lasting anywhere between 20 and 40 minutes at a time before resolving on their own. He describes his dizziness as a “room-spinning sensation.” The patient is also reporting an annoying ringing sound that is associated with the dizziness. The spinning sensation is made worse with head movement as well as positional changes. What would the clinician expect to find on physical examination?
englishExplanation:
Ménière disease is a vestibular disorder that is a result of excessive endolymphatic fluid pressure. This is characterized as peripheral vertigo (originating in the peripheral nervous system) as opposed to the more serious central vertigo (originating in the central nervous system). It can occur at any age but is more common to present between the ages of 20 and 40 years. Clinical features include episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus. Horizontal or rotational nystagmus may be noted on exam. The vertigo is said to be a true spinning sensation that has an onset and offset. Patients typically tend to cycle between active symptoms and prolonged periods of remission. The vertigo has been reported to last between 20 minutes and up to 24 hours with associated nausea and vomiting being common.

The diagnosis is based on clinical features. The American Academy of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck surgery requires two spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting at least 20 minutes, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus to be present. Treatment consists of lifestyle adjustments, medical treatments, and interventional treatments. Lifestyle adjustments include avoidance of alcohol, caffeine, stress, high salt intake, monosodium glutamate, nicotine, and allergies as these are commonly known triggers. Medical management includes treating acute episodes with vestibular suppressants and antiemetics such as meclizine, dimenhydrinate, scopolamine, promethazine, prochlorperazine, or lorazepam. Diuretics and betahistine are used to prevent attacks by reducing the degree of endolymphatic hydrops. Vestibular rehabilitation is another potential medical therapy that can be used for patients with Ménière disease. If patients continue to have intractable and severe symptoms despite the above treatments, more invasive treatments may be warranted. Some of these treatments consist of surgical labyrinthectomy, vestibular nerve injection, or intratympanic gentamicin. Surgical decompression and sacculotomy are other procedures available.



Sensorineural hearing loss, not conductive hearing loss (A), is associated with Ménière disease. Conductive hearing loss can be seen with middle ear effusions, tympanic membrane ruptures, or cerumen impaction. Evaluation of the ear is typically unremarkable in Ménière disease. Middle ear effusion (B) and tympanic membrane abnormalities are not commonly seen. Horizontal or rotational nystagmus, not vertical nystagmus (D), is commonly seen with vertigo associated with Ménière disease. Vertical nystagmus is associated with a more ominous, central lesion.

One Step Further
Question:
What is thought to cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)?

Reveal Answer:
BPPV is most commonly attributed to calcium debris within the posterior semicircular canal but may also occur in the lateral and anterior semicircular canals.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: During your evening shift, you receive a telehealth call from staff at a local referral hospital regarding a 3-year-old child who presented with a 12-hour history of progressive noisy, labored breathing. You are told that the child appears ill, has a fever, and prefers to sit upright in a tripod position. Other symptoms include pain with swallowing and drooling. The staff is planning to draw lab tests and place an intravenous line. They obtained a soft tissue lateral neck radiograph, as shown above. After reviewing the lateral neck radiographic image with them, which of the following is your priority recommendation?

options.text: Administer a dose of oral dexamethasone
Hold on attempts at vascular access and contact your critical care transport team
Obtain lab tests, establish vascular access, and have them call back with an update
Trial a dose of racemic epinephrine via nebulizer

correctAnswer: Hold on attempts at vascular access and contact your critical care transport team
englishExplanation:
The presenting symptoms are suggestive of infection involving the supraglottic airway. The lateral neck radiograph reveals enlargement and thickening of the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, referred to together as the thumb sign, consistent with epiglottitis. In addition, there is obliteration of the vallecular airspace. The soft tissue landmarks of a normal lateral neck radiograph are shown below. The normal epiglottis is relatively large in appearance in the pediatric population. It has a broad omega-shaped profile. The aryepiglottic folds have a thin, concave appearance. The caliber of the prevertebral soft tissues should be less than half of the width of the adjacent vertebral body. The immediate goal in this situation would be a monitored transport of the child to a setting where controlled airway and vascular access may be undertaken. Therefore, you should have the consulting hospital hold on attempts at vascular access and contact the critical care support team.



Administering anything by mouth (A) would be contraindicated in a child with a critical airway.

Interventions like laboratory draws or attempts at vascular access (C) should be deferred to a controlled setting, as they may upset the child, precipitating airway obstruction and the need for emergent airway control. The initial goal is to keep the child as comfortable as possible, usually seated upright, to optimize the upper airway.

Nebulized treatments like racemic epinephrine (D) are not proven to be beneficial for this form of infectious acute upper airway obstruction (some sources suggest it as a possible adjunct treatment while others recommend against its use). This patient’s X-ray is not consistent with croup, which would benefit from treatment with racemic epinephrine. X-ray findings in croup include tapering or narrowing of the airway below the vocal cords.

One Step Further
Question:
What proportion of patients with epiglottitis will show evidence of subglottic edema on lateral neck radiographs?

Reveal Answer:
25%.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epiglottitis

Most commonly caused by H. influenzae (decrease since Hib vaccine), Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species
Sx: rapid onset of fever, muffled voice, dysphagia, respiratory distress
PE: sore throat, stridor, leaning forward, drooling, red swollen epiglottis on direct visualization
Imaging: enlarged epiglottis (thumbprint sign) on lateral neck X-ray
Tx: airway management and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin AND antistaphylococcal)

question: An 11-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with nasal congestion, sneezing, and watery, itchy eyes for 2 weeks. His parent reports a family history of seasonal allergies, but they have not tested the child yet. He seems to have these symptoms every year at this time. He appears nontoxic, and his vital signs are within normal limits. Both of his eyes have mild conjunctival injection, but his exam is otherwise unremarkable. What treatment has been shown to provide the most effective nasal congestion relief for this syndrome?
englishExplanation:
Allergic rhinitis affects millions in the United States and is strongly associated with comorbid conditions, including asthma, eczema, chronic sinusitis, and headaches. The condition occurs when disruption of the epithelial barrier allows allergens to penetrate the nasal mucosal epithelium, triggering an inflammatory response and production of allergen-specific IgE. This patient is presenting with classic symptoms, including nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, postnasal drainage, and sneezing, as well as symptoms of concomitant allergic conjunctivitis (e.g., eye watering, itching). Symptoms often follow a seasonal pattern as exposure to pollen and other environmental allergens waxes and wanes. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination, with confirmation through aeroallergen skin prick testing or specific IgE testing.

Treatment selection depends on symptom severity and frequency. For mild intermittent allergic rhinitis, first-line options include oral second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, loratadine) and intranasal antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine). However, for persistent moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis, which is most likely in this case, intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) are the preferred first-line monotherapy. Patients can be safely discharged with intranasal corticosteroids, which are available over the counter and have clinical effects within a day, though the peak effect may take several weeks. The most common adverse effect of intranasal corticosteroids is epistaxis, and proper technique involves directing the spray away from the nasal septum toward the middle of the eye. Pharmacotherapy for children aged 6 years or older does not differ from adults except for medication dosing.



While azelastine (A) is an effective intranasal antihistamine and represents a reasonable first-line option for mild allergic rhinitis, it has modest effects on nasal congestion compared to intranasal corticosteroids and is not the most effective treatment for this symptom.

Intranasal cromolyn (B) is suggested only as an option for episodic allergen exposures taken just prior to exposure and is considered a fourth-line treatment for persistent allergic rhinitis. It is far less effective than intranasal corticosteroids for nasal congestion.

Oral antihistamines like cetirizine (D) have only modest effects on nasal congestion, with a small effect size (standardized mean difference −0.33), and are less effective than intranasal corticosteroids for this specific symptom.

While intranasal saline (E) has a strong recommendation for use in allergic rhinitis and can provide symptomatic relief, it is not the most effective treatment for nasal congestion compared to intranasal corticosteroids.

One Step Further
Question:
What organism is associated, though rarely, with fatal complications when tap water is used for nasal irrigation?

Reveal Answer:
Naegleria fowleri.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Allergic Rhinitis

History of asthma, atopic dermatitis, and sinusitis
Sx: sneezing, rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion
PE: infraorbital edema and darkening, transverse nasal crease, pale edematous nasal turbinates, cobblestoning of the posterior pharynx
Dx: based on clinical history, may be confirmed with skin testing or allergen-specific IgE
Tx: glucocorticoid nasal spray, removal of the allergen source (if known)
Associated with nasal polyps, asthma, and aspirin sensitivity (Samter triad)

question: A healthy 21-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for right ear pain and swelling. She had her helix pierced 1 week ago and, for the past several days, noted increasing swelling and pain in that area. Examination is significant for normal vital signs, erythema, and swelling of the upper helix and triangular fossa with loss of anatomic markings. She has pain with movement of the upper ear lobe, no fluctuance or palpable abscess, and a normal auditory canal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient’s condition?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin for 1 week and otolaryngology follow-up in 24 hours

correctAnswer: Oral ciprofloxacin for 1 week and otolaryngology follow-up in 24 hours
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is most consistent with auricular perichondritis, a bacterial infection of the skin and perichondrium of the ear, most often following penetrating trauma such as ear piercing. Patients will present with a tender, swollen, and warm auricle with a normal internal ear and tympanic membrane exam. Some patients may also have an abscess or systemic symptoms requiring more aggressive treatment. Healthy patients without immunocompromising conditions and no systemic symptoms should receive oral ciprofloxacin for 1 week and otolaryngology follow-up in 24 hours. Quinolones are preferred first-line agents in perichondritis, as many cases are caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Other bacteria involved include skin flora such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Patients with abscess formation or systemic symptoms should receive IV antibiotics and a surgical consult, as these patients are at higher risk of auricular necrosis and poor cosmetic outcomes.



Admission for surgical management (A) would be appropriate in patients with perichondritis complicated by abscess formation.

Oral cephalexin (B) or topical mupirocin (D) would not provide coverage for P. aeruginosa, which is the most common bacteria implicated in perichondritis. Some references advocate adding topical mupirocin to cover for Staphylococcus aureus, but this treatment would not be appropriate without a fluoroquinolone.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the appropriate management for auricular hematomas?

Reveal Answer:
Incision and drainage with application of compressive dressing to prevent reaccumulation.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Perichondritis

Infection of connective tissue and cartilage of the ear
Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common organism
Risks: trauma, burns, skin breakdown, piercing
Sx: redness, pain, erythema to pinna and cartilaginous portion of ear, spares lobule
Sometimes associated with abscess
Tx: consider I&D, obtain wound culture
Antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., levofloxacin)
Otolaryngology follow-up

question: A 29-year-old man with a history of sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with a painful eye. He reports the pain started without incident and has been worsening. He decided to seek medical care when his coworkers noticed that his eye looked different, as seen above. On exam, his intraocular pressure is 22 mm Hg in the affected eye and 17 mm Hg in the unaffected eye. Ophthalmology has been called to evaluate. What management is contraindicated in this patient’s care?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s exam is consistent with a hyphema likely caused by his underlying sickle cell disease. A hyphema is a spontaneous or post-traumatic collection of blood in the anterior chamber. Diagnosis is clinical. Notably, the layering of blood may not be apparent on exam until the patient sits upright, as the blood commonly layers posteriorly while supine or reclined. Unless associated with other sequelae of direct ocular trauma, most hyphemas have a good prognosis. Risk factors for permanent vision loss include sickle cell disease, coagulopathies, and large-volume hyphemas. Patients commonly present after direct ocular trauma or with medical comorbidities that are at risk for spontaneous hyphemas. They may describe eye pressure or pain (due to increased intraocular pressure) or change in vision, especially with accommodation. The mainstay of treatment is the management of the underlying cause and control of intraocular pressure. Common medications used to manage elevations in intraocular pressure include topical timolol and acetazolamide. Notably, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, are contraindicated in patients with sickle cell disease and hyphemas, as they may worsen sickling and further inhibit outflow via the trabecular meshwork. All patients with hyphemas should be evaluated by an ophthalmologist to assess the risk of rebleeding, which can lead to permanent vision loss.



Treatment of hyphemas centers around intraocular pressure control. This may be obtained by head of bed elevation (A) to prevent the settling of blood clots and subsequent occlusion of the trabecular meshwork, and topical timolol (D), which decreases the secretion of aqueous humor.

Topical prednisolone (C) may be associated with a lower risk of rebleeding but does not directly alter intraocular pressure. None of these treatments are contraindicated if the patient has sickle cell disease.

One Step Further
Question:
What anterior chamber finding indicates a globe perforation in the setting of a foreign body injury?

Reveal Answer:
Hyphema or microhyphema.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hyphema

Often history of blunt or penetrating trauma
Sx: blurry vision
PE: decreased visual acuity and blood in anterior chamber
Tx: gentle ambulation, head elevation of 30–45° for large hyphemas
> 50% hyphema, those with sickle cell disease, and those taking anticoagulants should be admitted
Topical or oral agents to lower IOP
Urgent ophthalmology follow-up or consult in the hospital

question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department for mild upper respiratory symptoms. However, during your exam, you find he has significant bilateral cerumen impaction. His parent reports he has had no ear concerns, ear drainage, or signs of hearing loss. Which of the following is the best method for cerumen removal in this patient?
englishExplanation:
Most patients with ear canal cerumen are asymptomatic. When it causes symptoms, cerumen impaction can cause hearing loss, ear pain, ear fullness, dizziness, and occasionally a reflex cough. Cerumen can vary from a soft liquid consistency to firm chunks. Removal attempts typically involve irrigation, manual removal, and cerumenolytics. Irrigation can result in water retention or incompletely removed cerumen. Manual removal can cause ear canal abrasions or bleeding. Cerumenolytics can lead to allergic reactions and otitis externa. Both ear irrigation and manual removal can result in tympanic membrane perforation, hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. As such, routine cerumen removal is not recommended in patients without symptoms such as hearing loss, ear pain, or ear fullness. Cerumenolytics are safe in patients with an intact tympanic membrane. They are shown to be more effective than no treatment, but a large percentage of patients with cerumen impaction will clear the impaction spontaneously. Patients with a history of frequent otitis media or tympanic membrane perforation (e.g., tympanostomy tubes, ruptured otitis media) should not be given cerumenolytics. No single cerumenolytic has been shown superior to others. None should be used for more than 4 days to prevent accumulation behind cerumen and possible skin irritation. Common cerumenolytics include hydrogen peroxide, mineral oil, docusate sodium, and carbamide peroxide. Peroxide-containing cerumenolytics should be avoided in patients with dry skin.



Bilateral ear irrigation (A) or manual removal with a curette (D) are indicated in the emergency department if the patient has symptoms of ear pain, ear fullness, or hearing loss.

Home remedies such as a cotton swab (C), bobby pin, or ear vacuum kit are not studied or recommended.

One Step Further
Question:
Which patients may benefit from routine cerumen removal?

Reveal Answer:
Those who cannot express symptoms (e.g., infants, toddlers, developmentally delayed).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cerumen Removal

Inspect TM
Cerumenolytics (carbamide peroxide)
Irrigation
Manual maneuvers
Advise patients not to use cotton swabs
ENT referral

question: An 82-year-old man with a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease and stroke presents to the ED with epistaxis. Current medications include metoprolol and aspirin. On examination, after asking the patient to gently blow his nose, there is brisk bleeding coming from the left naris. There is also blood seen coming from the right naris as well as down the posterior pharynx. Which of the following is most likely going to control his epistaxis?

options.text: Application of silver nitrate to the left anterior septum
Instillation of oxymetazoline and nasal pressure
Placement of a double-balloon epistaxis catheter
Placement of a nasal tampon in the left naris

correctAnswer: Placement of a double-balloon epistaxis catheter
englishExplanation:
The vast majority of epistaxis is the result of an anterior source of bleeding from Kiesselbach plexus. Posterior epistaxis is less common overall but more likely to be seen in older patients with comorbidities such as hypertension. Features on physical examination that make a posterior source more likely include brisk hemorrhage from bilateral nares with significant blood seen in the posterior pharynx and bleeding that cannot be controlled with vasoconstrictors and anterior packing. Based on this patient’s age, medical history, and exam findings, a posterior source is most likely. Bilateral anterior packing may be helpful in controlling posterior epistaxis by increasing the tamponade of the nasal septum. If that fails, the placement of a double-balloon epistaxis catheter is likely to control the bleeding.

The catheter is placed in the nose, the posterior balloon is inflated, and the catheter is pulled anteriorly. The anterior balloon is then inflated. Alternatively, a Foley catheter can be placed in the nasopharynx. The Foley balloon is inflated and pulled anteriorly until firmly seated. The anterior naris is then packed with petroleum jelly gauze. In addition to hemorrhage control, resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood products may be necessary. Coagulopathy, if present, should be corrected. Persistent hypertension should be lowered as this can reduce hydrostatic pressures and may help with clot formation. If these measures are unsuccessful, patients may require either embolization by interventional radiology or arterial ligation by an otolaryngologist.



Anterior epistaxis is more likely to be less brisk than posterior epistaxis, and blood is typically seen coming from one naris. If the source of bleeding is visualized on the anterior septum, the application of silver nitrate (A) may control the bleeding.

A first step in attempting to control epistaxis, whether anterior or posterior, is the instillation of oxymetazoline and nasal pressure (B). While this may be effective in cases of mild anterior epistaxis, it is unlikely to control epistaxis from a posterior source.

Likewise, the placement of a unilateral nasal tampon (D) is a good option for the management of an anterior hemorrhage. Nasal tampons that control anterior epistaxis should be left in place for 48–72 hours before removal. Although commonly prescribed after a nasal pack is placed, antibiotics have not been shown to reduce the risk of the development of toxic shock syndrome or sinusitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most likely source of posterior epistaxis?

Reveal Answer:
The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal division of the internal maxillary artery.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epistaxis

Most common source
Anterior bleeds: Kiesselbach plexus
Posterior bleeds: sphenopalatine artery
Treatment
Anterior bleeding: direct pressure, topical vasoconstriction (oxymetazoline), chemicalcautery with silver nitrate (if vessel visualized), packing
Posterior bleeding: packing (nasal balloon or Foley catheter)
Admit patients with posterior packing to a monitored bed
Possible complications: septal necrosis (if both sides of septum cauterized), toxic shock syndrome (prolonged packing), infection

question: A 55-year-old man presents with ear pain. He has a history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. He states his symptoms started 3 days ago after scratching his ear on a tree branch and have progressively worsened. His exam is remarkable for a tender, swollen, and erythematous auricle. His pain worsens with deflection of the auricle. The tympanic membrane is well visualized and clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Perichondritis is an infection of the overlying skin and perichondrium of the external ear. Predisposing risk factors for the development of perichondritis include surgery, ear-piercing burns, frostbite, insect bites, and contact sports. The most common organism that leads to the disorder is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but Staphylococcus aureus is also an important organism to consider. Clinical features include a swollen, warm, tender, and erythematous auricle, which may include the ear lobule. Pain with deflection of the auricle is also commonly noted. This is often associated with a fever, and the tympanic membrane is typically unaffected. Outpatient management with oral antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin) and close follow-up in 48 hours is appropriate for healthy patients. There should also be consideration given to the use of topical antibiotics to cover Staphyococcus aureus. In patients who are immunocompromised or have diabetes, hospitalization with parenteral antibiotics is advised.



An auricular hematoma (A)can develop from almost any type of trauma and results from tearing of blood vessels between the perichondrium and the cartilage. This results in auricular deformation that obscures the normal contour of the ear. For small hematomas < 2 cm, needle aspiration may be used as a treatment option. However, incision and drainage is often required (when hematomas are > 2 cm or for those that have failed needle aspiration), followed by pressure dressing application and close follow-up with an otolaryngologist. This patient does not have a history of significant trauma, nor does he have features consistent with an auricular hematoma on physical exam.

Malignant otitis externa (B) is a potentially life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal involving the pinna and soft tissues with variable extension to the skull base. This begins as a simple otitis externa that spreads to the deeper tissues. Patients with malignant otitis externa have significant auditory canal involvement, obscuring the tympanic membrane when severe, which helps differentiate this from perichondritis.

Mastoiditis (C)results from the spread of infection from the middle ear to the mastoid air cells. Patients will typically have otalgia, fever, and otorrhea, as well as postauricular erythema, swelling, and tenderness. This can progress to protrusion of the auricle and obliteration of the postauricular crease. This patient does not demonstrate physical exam features consistent with malignant otitis externa.

One Step Further
Question:
True or false: antibiotic coverage for malignant otitis externa requires Pseudomonas aeruginosa coverage.

Reveal Answer:
True.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Perichondritis

Infection of connective tissue and cartilage of the ear
Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common organism
Risks: trauma, burns, skin breakdown, piercing
Sx: redness, pain, erythema to pinna and cartilaginous portion of ear, spares lobule
Sometimes associated with abscess
Tx: consider I&D, obtain wound culture
Antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., levofloxacin)
Otolaryngology follow-up

question: A 42-year-old plumber presents after splashing drain cleaner into his eye. He irrigated his eye with water for 30 minutes at the job site and then came directly to the emergency department. What is the next step in management?

options.text: Check ocular pH and continue irrigating the eye until the pH remains neutral
Discharge home with erythromycin ointment if visual acuity is normal
Use phenylephrine drops for cycloplegia to help alleviate patient discomfort

correctAnswer: Check ocular pH and continue irrigating the eye until the pH remains neutral
englishExplanation:
Chemical burns to the eye are an ocular emergency and require swift treatment to limit the extent of injury. Exposure to alkaline substances, such as drain cleaners, ammonia, lye, and bleach, causes liquefactive necrosis that can penetrate and dissolve tissues until removed. These burns tend to be deeper and more catastrophic than acid burns, which cause coagulation necrosis that limits the depth of penetration. Immediate treatment includes copious irrigation for at least 30 minutes, ideally at the scene prior to transfer to the hospital. The pH should be checked and irrigation should continue until the pH remains neutral 30 minutes after the last irrigation. Ophthalmology consultation is indicated for all chemical burns.



Alkali burns can result in increased intraocular pressure (A). However, the first line of treatment is continued irrigation until a neutral pH is obtained, not checking the intraocular pressure.

Discharging home (C) is not recommended until the eye has been adequately irrigated and a full eye examination is completed.

Cycloplegic drops are indicated once irrigation is complete, but phenylephrine (D) should not be used as it can result in worsening ischemia of the limbus due to constriction of the blood vessels.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the best way to check the pH of the eye?

Reveal Answer:
Using pH paper dipped into the inferior conjunctival fornix.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Chemical Burns

Acidic burns
Coagulative necrosis
Corneal ulceration with limited depth of injury
Tend to be self-limited
Alkali burns
Liquefactive necrosis that leads to deeper damage (cornea, iris, lens)
Penetrates faster and deeper than acidic burns
Irreversible blindness within minutes if untreated
Glaucoma complication
Irrigate until pH 7.0–7.4
Do not delay to perform a comprehensive eye exam

question: Which of the following commonly causes artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space on lateral neck X-rays?
englishExplanation:
The retropharyngeal space is a potential space located posterior to the pharynx and anterior to the cervical spine. It is best evaluated on lateral neck X-rays. Widening of this space can indicate serious pathology such as retropharyngeal abscess, hematoma, or malignancy. However, several technical and physiologic factors can lead to false, or artifactual, widening. Emergency clinicians should recognize these factors to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary interventions.

Neck flexion during imaging is the most common cause of artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space. When the neck is flexed, the soft tissues posterior to the pharynx are compressed and appear thicker on X-rays. This positioning alters the normal anatomic relationships and exaggerates the prevertebral soft tissue shadow, mimicking pathology. Proper technique requires the neck to be in a neutral or slightly extended position to accurately assess the retropharyngeal space.

Other factors that may influence the appearance of the retropharyngeal space include the phase of respiration and patient cooperation. Imaging during expiration, crying in pediatric patients, or poor inspiratory effort can also falsely increase the apparent thickness of the prevertebral soft tissues. Therefore, X-rays should ideally be obtained during quiet inspiration with the patient calm and properly positioned.

In the ED, accurate interpretation of lateral neck X-rays is critical, particularly when evaluating for deep neck space infections. Misinterpretation due to positioning artifacts can lead to unnecessary CT, antibiotic use, or surgical consultation. Conversely, failure to recognize true widening may delay the diagnosis of life-threatening conditions, such as retropharyngeal abscess or expanding hematoma, which can compromise the airway.



A cervical spine fracture (A) may be associated with prevertebral soft tissue swelling due to hematoma, which represents true, not artifactual, widening. This is a concerning and clinically significant finding rather than a benign imaging artifact. Therefore, this option does not represent a common cause of false widening and should prompt further evaluation.

Deep inspiration (B) actually helps reduce the apparent thickness of the retropharyngeal space by expanding the airway and surrounding soft tissues. X-rays are ideally obtained during inspiration for this reason. Therefore, deep inspiration does not cause artifactual widening and instead improves diagnostic accuracy.

Esophageal dilation (C) is not a typical cause of retropharyngeal space widening on plain X-rays. The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea and does not significantly alter the prevertebral soft tissue contour in a way that mimics retropharyngeal pathology. This finding would be better evaluated with other imaging modalities if clinically suspected.

While supine positioning (E) can slightly affect soft tissue appearance, it is not a primary or common cause of significant artifactual widening of the retropharyngeal space. Positioning of the neck, specifically flexion versus extension, plays a much larger role. Supine films may be less ideal than upright films, but they do not typically produce the marked widening seen with neck flexion.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the upper limit of normal of the retropharyngeal space at C6 of a typical pediatric patient?

Reveal Answer:
14 mm (about the width of the C6 vertebral body on lateral neck X-ray).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retropharyngeal Abscess

Risks: trauma or URI
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, respiratory anaerobes, foreign body
Sx: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, neck pain
PE: trismus, stridor, nuchal rigidity, muffled voice, cri du canard (duck quack)
Toxic-appearing child, 3–5 years old
X-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space twice the size of the vertebral body
Dx: CT imaging, if patient is stable
Tx: airway control as needed, intravenous antibiotics, surgery for I&D

question: A 21-year-old man presents for evaluation of a sore throat with a fever for 2 days. On examination, his oropharynx is erythematous with enlarged tonsils and bilateral exudates. In addition to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which of the following has been shown to produce the greatest reduction in pain?
englishExplanation:
Dexamethasone administered in a single dose of 0.6 mg/kg up to a maximum of 10 mg is associated with a reduction of pain and duration of pain in patients with moderate to severe pharyngitis. The medication is available orally or parenterally and has the same effectiveness in either form. The mainstay of therapy for patients with pharyngitis is treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents.



Acetaminophen (A) is an appropriate analgesic to use in the treatment of pharyngitis. However, this medication has no underlying anti-inflammatory properties and will not address the underlying cause of pain.

Intravenous hydration (C) is sometimes administered to patients who report decreased intake due to their throat pain but will likely not impact their degree of pain directly.

Penicillin (D) is often prescribed for patients with exudative pharyngitis. However, data do not suggest any significant impact on pain or duration of pain as a result of the administration of antibiotics. Additionally, many antibiotics carry the risk of allergic reaction or side effects like diarrhea which should be considered before their administration. In children, antibiotics are usually administered as a preventive measure against the development of rheumatic heart disease from streptococcal infections.

One Step Further
Question:
What causative organism of pharyngitis also is the most common cause of septic arthritis in young patients?

Reveal Answer:
Neisseria gonorrhea.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pharyngitis

Most commonly caused by viral > bacteria (GAS, S. pyogenes)
Centor criteria: estimates probability pharyngitis is streptococcal based on PE and Sx
Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate or swelling, fever, absence of cough, age 3–14 years
Modified Centor criteria: +1 for age < 15 years, −1 for age > 45 years
Treatment
Viral: supportive
Bacterial
Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line
Patients with penicillin allergy: cephalexin, cefadroxil (avoid in individuals with immediate-type hypersensitivity to penicillin), clindamycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin (resistance of GAS to these agents is known well and varies geographically and temporally)

question: A 5-month-old girl with no significant medical history and no allergies presents with fever and nasal congestion for 1 day. Examination reveals an uncomfortable but well-appearing infant with a fever to 102.7°F. Otoscopic evaluation reveals bilateral nonmobile, bulging tympanic membranes. Which of the following treatment regimens is appropriate?

options.text: Observation and close follow-up without initial antibiotics
Oral high-dose amoxicillin with clavulanic acid

englishExplanation:
This patient has bilateral acute otitis media (AOM), evidenced by the nonmobile, bulging tympanic membranes and fever. AOM is common in pediatric patients and a common indication for antibiotics.

AOM is commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Oftentimes, the infection can resolve without further intervention. Patients who are ≥ 6 months old with unilateral AOM and severe symptoms, as well as patients who are < 24 months with bilateral AOM, should receive antibiotic therapy. High-dose amoxicillin is the initial treatment of choice in patients without penicillin allergy.



Intramuscular ceftriaxone (A) is indicated for the treatment of AOM if first-line therapy is ineffective or if the patient has a history of a mild penicillin reaction (e.g., rash).

Observation and close follow-up without initial antibiotics (B) has recently become a treatment option endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in select groups. The AAP recommends observation and repeat evaluation in 48–72 hours for patients 6 months to 2 years old with unilateral AOM without otorrhea and in children > 2 years of age with unilateral or bilateral AOM without otorrhea.

Oral azithromycin (C) can be used as an alternative to amoxicillin in patients with a severe penicillin allergy (e.g., anaphylaxis).

High-dose amoxicillin with clavulanic acid (E) can be used in patients who have received a beta-lactam antibiotic in the past 30 days.

One Step Further
Question:
What defines severe acute otitis media?

Reveal Answer:
Moderate to severe otalgia, otalgia for at least 48 hours, otorrhea, or temperature > 39°C (102.2°F).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Otitis Media in Pediatrics

Most often infant or young child
Most common bacteria isolated include H. influenzae (nontypable), S. pneumoniae, and M. catarrhalis (there is decreased incidence of S. pneumoniae due to PCV13 vaccination)
Sx: ear pain, middle ear effusion + signs of infection or inflammation (fever, otorrhea, pus)
PE: erythema, bulge and decreased mobility of TM, purulent fluid
Tx: amoxicillin, consider amoxicillin-clavulanate in otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome
Consider period of observation if patient ≥ 2 years old and immunocompetent with mild symptoms

question: A 42-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and diabetes presents to the emergency department with redness, swelling, and mild pain around her left eye for 2 days. She reports no vision changes or fever. She remembers rubbing and scratching around her eye a few days ago but does not recall any trauma. On exam, she has erythema with edema of the upper eyelid as well as under her left eye. Her conjunctivae are clear, and no foreign bodies are found. Extraocular movements are intact, and her vision is 20/30 in both eyes. What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment for this illness?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs of preseptal cellulitis, an infection of the anterior portion of the eyelid that does not involve the orbit or other orbital structures. It is generally a mild condition that has few complications when treated appropriately. Symptoms can be similar to orbital cellulitis, a more severe infection involving the orbit. However, in contrast to orbital cellulitis, preseptal cellulitis does not present with ophthalmoplegia, pain with eye movements, and proptosis. Preseptal cellulitis generally arises from external bacterial sources with the most common etiologies being Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and other streptococcal species. Blood cultures are rarely positive and site cultures are difficult to obtain. Treatment is done empirically and should cover sinus and skin flora. However, the choice of treatment has been made more difficult with the emergence of community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Empiric antibiotic therapy that has good coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and coverage for streptococcal species is clindamycin with amoxicillin-clavulanate. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can substitute for clindamycin. Most patients can be treated with oral antibiotics on an outpatient basis.



Oral cefdinir (A) was previously a good treatment option for preseptal cellulitis. However, it does not have activity against community-acquired MRSA. It is no longer recommended as initial therapy unless also treating with an antibiotic that provides coverage for MRSA.

Topical ciprofloxacin drops (C) would be recommended therapy for a patient with bacterial conjunctivitis or corneal abrasion with risk factors for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. This patient has signs and symptoms of preseptal cellulitis, not conjunctivitis.

Topical erythromycin ointment (D) is therapy for mild bacterial conjunctivitis. As already mentioned, this patient has signs and symptoms of preseptal cellulitis, not conjunctivitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What imaging study can help a clinician differentiate orbital cellulitis from preseptal cellulitis?

Reveal Answer:
Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the orbits.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Preseptal Cellulitis (Periorbital Cellulitis)

Anterior to the orbital septum, does NOT involve the globe or orbital septum
More common in children
Risks: trauma, bites, other facial infection (e.g., dacryocystitis)
Sx: periorbital pain, swelling, erythema
Dx: clinical diagnosis, consider CT if unsure of orbital involvement
Tx: usually oral antibiotics are sufficient

question: A 72-year-old man presents with a painful red eye and visual loss worsening over the last 24 hours. He recently had cataract surgery. Examination of the eye reveals the image above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation of pain, progressive vision loss, eye redness, and hypopyon (yellow layering in the anterior chamber) is highly suggestive of postoperative endophthalmitis, a serious intraocular infection that occurs after intraocular surgery, most commonly cataract surgery. The rapid progression within 24 hours is characteristic of acute post-surgical bacterial endophthalmitis, which is most often caused by coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, or Streptococcus species.

Endophthalmitis is caused by microbial invasion of the intraocular spaces, leading to a severe inflammatory response with purulent accumulation. Risk factors include recent intraocular surgery, wound leaks, immunosuppression, and contaminated surgical instruments or intraocular lenses. Patients classically present with eye pain, photophobia, conjunctival injection, corneal edema, hypopyon, and decreased visual acuity. The hallmark feature, hypopyon, represents inflammatory exudate pooling in the anterior chamber and is a key diagnostic clue.

Diagnosis is clinical but confirmed with aqueous or vitreous tap cultures. Emergency department management includes urgent ophthalmology consultation, intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin plus ceftazidime), and possible vitrectomy in severe cases. Prompt treatment is crucial to prevent complications such as retinal detachment, phthisis bulbi, and permanent blindness.



Acute angle-closure glaucoma (A) can present with eye pain and vision loss, but it is distinguished by a fixed, mid-dilated pupil, a cloudy cornea, and elevated intraocular pressure. Hypopyon is not a feature of glaucoma.

Bacterial keratitis (B) involves corneal ulceration, fluorescein uptake, and stromal infiltrates, often following contact lens use or trauma. Unlike endophthalmitis, bacterial keratitis does not typically present with hypopyon unless it is severe.

A hyphema (D) is blood in the anterior chamber, usually caused by trauma. When the patient is in an upright position, blood will layer along the inferior aspect of the anterior chamber. As the hyphema increases in size, it elevates intraocular pressure. In some cases, admission is warranted for patients with large hyphemas (> 50%), sickle cell disease, and those taking anticoagulants. Treatment is aimed at decreasing pressure with topical (beta-blocker, alpha-agonist, or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) and systemic therapy (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, mannitol).

Traumatic iritis (E) occurs after blunt trauma in which the iris and ciliary body are inflamed, causing ciliary spasm. Patients report significant photophobia and eye pain. Examination of the eye reveals perilimbal conjunctival injection (also called ciliary flush) and a small, poorly dilating pupil. Photophobia occurs when light is shone on both the affected and unaffected eye. On slit lamp exam, cells (white and red) and flare (protein) are noted in the anterior chamber. Treatment is with a topical cycloplegic agent to minimize spasm.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for herpes zoster keratoconjunctivitis?

Reveal Answer:
Systemic antiviral therapy (acyclovir).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Endophthalmitis

Bacterial or fungal infection of the vitreous or aqueous humor
Most commonly caused by exogenous sources (e.g., from eye surgery, intravitreal injections, ocular trauma)
Tx depends on various factors such as underlying cause and may include intravitreal antibiotics, surgery

question: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sore throat. He reports no cough or runny nose but does report subjective fevers. His T is 101°F (38.3°C), BP is 122/80 mm Hg, HR is 91 bpm, RR is 14/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals significant oropharyngeal erythema but no exudates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in care?

options.text: CT scan of the neck with contrast
Reassurance and oral hydration at home

englishExplanation:
Pharyngitis is most commonly caused by viral etiologies. For this reason, empiric antibiotic treatment is not indicated. The most common presenting symptoms are a sore throat, pain with swallowing, fever, tonsillar exudates, and palatal petechiae. Testing for streptococcal pharyngitis can be performed but should be limited to patients meeting certain criteria. A rapid antigen test should not be done empirically, as false positive results are common and unnecessary antibiotics will subsequently be prescribed, resulting in harm. If there is an obvious viral constellation of symptoms, rapid antigen testing is not recommended. If the patient’s Centor score is ≥ 2, rapid streptococcal antigen testing is recommended. This patient has a Centor score of 2 since he lacks a cough and has a fever with a sore throat. The differential should always be considered when deciding to treat, including other possible causes of bacterial pharyngitis, such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Treatment for this patient, if his rapid streptococcal antigen test is positive, would be amoxicillin.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate administration (A) would be an option for appropriate treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis once supported by a positive rapid streptococcal antigen test and exam findings suggesting a bacterial cause. Amoxicillin without clavulanate is still recommended first before the use of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

A CT scan of the neck with contrast (B) is appropriate when there is concern for an underlying mass or abscess. Voice changes, trismus, respiratory distress, or an inability to swallow or tolerate secretions could warrant CT imaging.

Reassurance and oral hydration at home (D) are appropriate for managing viral pharyngitis, which will self-resolve. Since this patient has a Centor score of 2, rapid streptococcal antigen testing should be performed.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis presents with stridor, high fever, purulent secretions, and tracheal tenderness in a toxic-appearing patient?

Reveal Answer:
Bacterial tracheitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pharyngitis

Most commonly caused by viral > bacteria (GAS, S. pyogenes)
Centor criteria: estimates probability pharyngitis is streptococcal based on PE and Sx
Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate or swelling, fever, absence of cough, age 3–14 years
Modified Centor criteria: +1 for age < 15 years, −1 for age > 45 years
Treatment
Viral: supportive
Bacterial
Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line
Patients with penicillin allergy: cephalexin, cefadroxil (avoid in individuals with immediate-type hypersensitivity to penicillin), clindamycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin (resistance of GAS to these agents is known well and varies geographically and temporally)

question: A 78-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of painless vision loss in her right eye. She has a past medical history significant for hypertension, cerebral vascular accident, and atrial fibrillation. She is no longer on anticoagulation secondary to frequent falls. The patient states the symptoms started 40 minutes prior to arrival. Other than a right-sided mild headache she has no other complaints today. Vital signs are all unremarkable. Physical examination is remarkable for a heart exam that reveals an irregular rhythm with a regular rate and afferent pupillary defect on the right. She denies any temporal tenderness to palpation. Visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye and light perception only for the right eye. What additional historical or physical finding would you expect with this patient?

options.text: Cherry red macula on fundoscopic examination

correctAnswer: Cherry red macula on fundoscopic examination
englishExplanation:
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) classically presents with a sudden onset of painless severe monocular vision loss. This is often associated with amaurosis fugax. If the occlusion occurs in the central artery, a patient will experience complete visual loss, whereas if the occlusion occurs in one of the arterial branches, then there will be sudden partial vision loss. Classically this presents with abrupt vision loss, with a large majority only being able to count fingers or have some light perception. An afferent pupillary defect and a cherry red spot (red macula) with surrounding opacification of the surrounding retina on fundoscopic evaluation may also be present. A thorough evaluation of an embolic source should be obtained, with the carotid arteries or heart being the most common sources of embolism. Temporal arteritis must be excluded as a diagnosis. The American Heart Association recommends that institutions develop protocols for the rapid evaluation of CRAO in a stroke center. There is a paucity of evidence regarding the best treatment for CRAO, but thrombolytics are reasonable within an appropriate time frame (< 4.5 hours). Other traditional treatments, digital orbital massage, acetazolamide, and timolol, have not proved beneficial.



Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (B) is a gaze abnormality that is characterized by impaired or weak adduction with horizontal eye movement of the affected eye as well as an abduction nystagmus of the opposite eye. This results from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, most commonly due to stroke or demyelination (multiple sclerosis). If the cause was due to multiple sclerosis, the patient would have painful, not painless, vision loss.

Jaw claudication (C) in a patient experiencing acute or subacute monocular vision loss is concerning for temporal arteritis, also known as giant cell arteritis. Temporal arteritis is a systemic vasculitis that can cause ischemic optic neuropathy. Patients classically are women older than 50 years of age. Associated symptoms are headache, jaw claudication, scalp or temporal tenderness, fatigue, sore throat, or anorexia. An afferent pupillary defect is often present, and fundoscopic examination may reveal flame hemorrhages. When suspected, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein (CRP) should be obtained, as both are typically elevated, with the CRP being the most sensitive of the two. Without a correct diagnosis or treatment, bilateral blindness can occur.

Central vein occlusion (D) causes acute, painless monocular vision loss similar to central retinal artery occlusion. Optic disc edema, retinal hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots, also known as “blood and thunder,” will be present on optic examination. Vision loss is generally not as severe, with more blurring than complete vision loss compared to the arterial counterpart, and no immediate treatment is required other than discontinuing predisposing drugs (oral contraceptives or diuretics). Consultation with an ophthalmologist should be obtained.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the gold standard for diagnosing giant cell arteritis?

Reveal Answer:
Temporal artery biopsy.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion

Sx: sudden, painless monocular vision loss
Funduscopy: retinal whitening, cherry-red spot, boxcar appearance (from segmental blood flow)
Tx: ocular emergency, evidence unclear regarding optimal therapy

question: Which of the following is most strongly associated with oral cancer?

options.text: Fixed white plaque on the tongue
Fluctuant mass adjacent to the tonsil
Scrapable white film on the tongue
White buccal mucosal lesions on an erythematous base

correctAnswer: Fixed white plaque on the tongue
englishExplanation:
Oral leukoplakia is defined as a persistent, fixed white plaque or patch in the oral cavity. It may present on the oral mucous membranes, side of the tongue, or palate. It is considered a precancerous lesion and has a strong association with the development of oral squamous cell carcinoma. There are many different subtypes of leukoplakia, including proliferative leukoplakia, which has a > 70% chance of developing into squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors for leukoplakia include male sex, age > 40, alcohol use disorder, tobacco use, areca nut use, history of previous similar lesions, and infection with certain subtypes of human papillomavirus. Oral hairy leukoplakia is another subtype of leukoplakia triggered by Epstein-Barr virus. Unlike other leukoplakias, oral hairy leukoplakia is unique in that it is not a precancerous lesion. Patients with lesions consistent with leukoplakia should nonetheless receive close follow-up and be monitored for progression to cancer.



A fluctuant mass adjacent to the tonsil (B) is seen in patients with peritonsillar abscesses. It is not a precancerous condition.

A scrapable white film on the tongue (C) is seen in patients with oral candidiasis, most often caused by the fungus Candida albicans. It is not a precancerous condition.

White buccal mucosal lesions on an erythematous base (D) are characteristic of Koplik spots, a pathognomonic lesion for measles.

One Step Further
Question:
What is another name for Epstein-Barr virus?

Reveal Answer:
Human herpesvirus 4.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Oral Leukoplakia

Dysplasia of the squamous epithelium of oral mucosa
Associated with an increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma
Risk factors: tobacco and alcohol use, HPV infection
PE: white patches or plaques in the oral cavity that cannot be wiped off
Dx: biopsy
Tx: may include observation or surgical excision
CAUTION: NOT the same as oral hairy leukoplakia

question: A 17-year-old vaccinated and otherwise healthy boy presents to your ED with right-sided anterior neck stiffness and pain. He had a sore throat 1 week ago and tested negative for Streptococcus. He does not report a headache or posterior neck pain. Vital signs show a temperature of 39.8°C, heart rate of 140 bpm, respiratory rate of 26/min, and blood pressure of 124/82 mm Hg. He is toxic appearing but alert and answering questions appropriately. He refuses to move his head to the right or flex his neck. He has moderate soft and mobile anterior cervical lymphadenopathy greater on the right and exquisite tenderness over his right anterior neck. His oropharynx shows mild erythema without uvular deviation or tonsillar hypertrophy. The Kernig sign is negative. Of the following, which is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Septic thrombophlebitis (i.e., Lemierre syndrome) is an infected clot of the jugular vein caused by local invasion from bacterial pharyngitis. Septic thrombophlebitis is most commonly caused by the particularly virulent gram-negative anaerobic bacteria Fusobacterium necrophorum, although some literature reports an increase in cases caused by Staphylococcus aureus. It most commonly affects patients ages 16–25 years, usually within a week of pharyngitis. These patients classically present with fever, pharyngitis, or peritonsillar abscess. These patients are described as toxic in appearance with fever, anterior neck pain, and stiffness, as well as possible respiratory distress from septic pulmonary emboli.
