Patients will require analgesia and may benefit from a nerve block.



Dilute hydrogen peroxide rinses (A) will not provide benefit in this situation. One goal is to maintain the seal of the socket through packing or dental sealing. Rinsing with hydrogen peroxide will interfere with this. Rinsing with dilute hydrogen peroxide is part of the treatment for acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis.

Incision and drainage (B) is not indicated for the treatment of dry socket. There is no abscess collection and nothing to drain. The pain is caused by the dislodgement of the blood clot with subsequent inflammation.

A root canal (D) includes opening the pulp chamber of a tooth, removing the pulp, and irrigating and sterilizing the canal in which the pulp sits. This is performed to remove diseased pulp tissue and requires the presence of a tooth. Since the entire tooth has been removed prior to the development of dry socket, this technique does not apply.

One Step Further
Question:
What is expected on physical examination of dry socket?

Reveal Answer:
Exposed bone and no clot in the extraction site.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Alveolar Osteitis (Dry Socket)

Typically presents 3–5 days after extraction
Most commonly caused by loss of healing clot exposing the underlying bone
Symptoms: radiating pain, halitosis
PE: inflammation and local osteitis with a clean extraction site
Treatment is via packing socket with iodoform gauze and eugenol oil

question: A 45-year-old man with a medical history of HIV and thyroid cancer treated with surgery and radiation presents with a nonhealing oral ulcer. He has a 25 pack-year history of cigarette smoking. On physical exam, he has multiple dental caries, and there is an irregularly shaped ulcer on the lateral tongue. Which of the following is this patient’s greatest risk factor for oropharyngeal cancer?

options.text: Radiation to the head and neck

englishExplanation:
Worldwide, over 400,000 people die of head and neck cancer each year. Cancer of the oral cavity accounts for about half of head and neck cancers, and the majority of these are squamous cell carcinomas. Mortality rates from oral cancer remain high, so early detection and prevention are key. A new or nonhealing lesion of the oropharynx should be evaluated in the context of the patient’s risk factors for oral cancer, and those at high risk should be referred for further evaluation. Tobacco use (e.g., cigarettes, pipes, cigars, chewing tobacco) and alcohol consumption are the two greatest risk factors for developing oral cancer. There is an estimated 5- to 25-fold increased risk of oral cancer among people who smoke cigarettes regularly. This risk is dose dependent and decreases with smoking cessation. Alcohol consumption is an independent risk factor for oral cancer and functions synergistically with tobacco to increase risk. Several viral infections are also associated with oral cancer, including human papillomavirus (HPV), Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV. HPV 16 is considered a major etiologic factor in those who do not use tobacco or alcohol and is most commonly associated with cancer of the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV-associated oral cancers have a more favorable prognosis compared to those associated with tobacco and alcohol use. Other risk factors include chronic inflammation, possibly from oral Candida infection or poor oral hygiene, immunodeficiency due to HIV or solid organ transplant, genetic predisposition, alcohol-based mouthwash, radiation, and a diet high in preserved meats and low in fruits and vegetables.



Immunodeficiency (A), particularly due to HIV, is associated with an increased risk of oral cancer, and patients with HIV have around a two- to threefold increased risk of head and neck cancer. However, tobacco use confers a greater risk.

Poor oral hygiene (B) has been linked to the development of oral cancer, possibly due to chronic inflammation. However, the causal relationship between cancer and oral hygiene has not been established, and tobacco use is a more definitive risk factor.

While prior radiation to the head and neck (C) is associated with an increased risk of oral cancer, the overall risk is low.

One Step Further
Question:
Which type of head and neck cancer is most strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus?

Reveal Answer:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Head and Neck Cancers

Risk factors include alcohol or tobacco use, HPV infection, EBV infection (nasopharyngeal carcinoma)
Most common type: squamous cell carcinoma
Locations
Sinuses
Oral cavity
Nasopharynx
Oropharynx
Hypopharynx
Larynx

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with visual changes. She notes progressive worsening vision in her right eye over the last 2 days and reports pain with movement of her eye. On examination, she has an afferent pupillary defect in that eye and a swollen optic disc on funduscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Optic neuritis results in monocular vision loss from demyelination of the optic nerve. Most commonly, patients are between the ages of 15 and 45 years, and there is a 30–40% association with multiple sclerosis. Examination reveals decreased visual acuity and an afferent pupillary defect. Funduscopic examination demonstrates a normal or swollen optic disc. Without treatment, patients progress to their poorest vision in approximately 1 week, with slow improvement over the next several weeks. Steroid therapy may be started. However, its long-term benefit remains unclear.



Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) (A) presents with sudden, painless vision loss. While an afferent pupillary defect may be observed in CRAO, funduscopic examination will typically reveal a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea.

Macular degeneration (B) characteristically causes progressive loss of central vision. The most common form is age-related macular degeneration, although it may result from trauma, radiation exposure, inflammatory or infectious disease, vascular disease, or hereditary disease. Visual loss continues, and it is the leading cause of legal blindness in the US.

Papilledema (D) may appear similar to optic neuritis on funduscopic examination, although it is more commonly bilateral. In papilledema, swelling of the optic disc results from increased intracranial pressure. The pupil examination and visual acuity should remain within normal limits, and ocular pain is typically absent.

Retinal detachment (E) may cause visual loss, classically beginning with flashes of light or floaters, followed by a falling curtain over the visual field. Bedside ultrasound can demonstrate the separation of retinal layers from the accumulation of fluid, aiding in the diagnosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is an afferent pupillary defect?

Reveal Answer:
The patient’s pupil appears to paradoxically dilate when the swinging light is moved from the unaffected to the affected eye. Common causes include central retinal artery or vein occlusion, optic neuritis, and retrobulbar neuritis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Optic Neuritis

Most commonly caused by multiple sclerosis
Sx: acute monocular vision loss, pain worse with eye movements, loss of color (red) vision, and transient worsening of vision with increased body temperature (Uhthoff phenomenon)
Dx: made clinically
Bedside US might be helpful, MRI will confirm demyelination
Tx: IV methylprednisolone

question: A 49-year-old man with diabetes is transferred from an outside hospital for facial swelling. He has had a fever and odynophagia after a recent tooth extraction. On physical examination, he has swelling and erythema in the submental space. A CT of the neck demonstrates soft tissue stranding of the submental and submylohyoid space with a developing phlegmon. When he returns from CT, his voice is muffled, and he is having difficulty tolerating his secretions. Which of the following is the best next intervention at this time?
englishExplanation:
Ludwig angina is a potentially life-threatening, rapidly progressive, infection of the three mandibular spaces: the submental, sublingual, and submandibular spaces. These spaces track down into the mediastinum and communicate directly with the parapharyngeal space, which makes airway compromise a concerning complication. All three spaces must be involved bilaterally for the infection to be considered Ludwig angina. The most common cause of Ludwig angina is odontogenic from an infected mandibular molar.

Patients often present with elevation of the tongue, tense induration of the submandibular tissue, trismus, drooling, stridor, dysphagia, and dyspnea. The diagnosis can be made clinically, but if able to be obtained, a CT scan of the soft tissues of the neck with IV contrast may show an abscess, phlegmon, or subcutaneous air from gas-producing organisms. Broad-spectrum antibiotics covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms should be given. Early orotracheal intubation is essential for securing the airway, as airway compromise may progress rapidly. Emergent surgical or ENT consultation is indicated while preparing for airway management.



Bedside incision and drainage (A) is not appropriate for managing Ludwig angina due to concerns about airway compromise. Antibiotics alone are often sufficient, but if surgical intervention is required, it should be done in the operating room with otolaryngology or oromaxillofacial surgery.

Because Ludwig angina is primarily odontogenic, patients may need to have their infected teeth extracted. Although a dentistry consultation (B) may eventually be needed, securing the airway and administering IV antibiotics should not be delayed.

Soft tissue ultrasound (D) may demonstrate cellulitis changes or focal abscess, but performing it may delay appropriate management such as airway intervention. Clinicians should not rely on ultrasound findings to make management decisions.

One Step Further
Question:
What antibiotics should be added if Eikenella species are suspected?

Reveal Answer:
Fluoroquinolones, specifically moxifloxacin.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ludwig Angina

Aggressive, rapidly spreading cellulitis of bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces
Risks: dental infections (molars), immunodeficiency, diabetes
PE: tongue elevation, brawny edema under the chin, dysphagia, dysphonia, drooling
Dx: clinical, CT
Tx: fiberoptic or awake intubation, IV antibiotics, ENT consultation

question: A 52-year-old man with a history of diabetes presents to the emergency department with congestion and sinus pressure. He initially thought his symptoms were improving, but they are worse on day 6. Today, he also developed a fever of 39.1°C and noticed purulent nasal drainage. He has no other concerns. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation:
Sinusitis is most commonly caused by viral organisms. Patients may present with congestion, facial pain and pressure, and tenderness to percussion over the sinuses. This diagnosis is often made clinically, and treatment is with supportive care as there is generally little benefit to antibiotic therapy. However, there are some indications for treating possible bacterial sinusitis, and these include persistent symptoms lasting ≥ 10 days without clinical improvement, severe symptoms or signs of high fever (≥ 102°F [39°C]) with purulent nasal discharge or facial pain for ≥ 3 days at the beginning of the illness, and as with this patient, worsening symptoms or signs (e.g., fever, headache, or increase in nasal discharge) 5–6 days after an initial period of improvement (double-sickening). Symptomatic treatment includes analgesics, saline irrigation of the nares, and decongestants. The first-line antibiotic therapy for patients with bacterial sinusitis is amoxicillin-clavulanate.



A CT scan of the head (B) may be indicated for toxic-appearing patients or when there is concern for an intracranial infection, which can present with fever, confusion, neurologic deficits, and seizures.

Levofloxacin (C), doxycycline, and cefdinir are considered second-line treatments for bacterial sinusitis in patients who are allergic to amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Saline irrigation and reassurance (D) is the appropriate management for sinusitis in patients with < 10 days of symptoms and no alarming features for bacterial infection, such as purulent discharge, fever, and prolonged or rapidly worsening symptoms.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the three most common bacterial causes of sinusitis?

Reveal Answer:
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Sinusitis

Sx: nasal congestion, pain or pressure over sinuses, ear pain or pressure, headache, fever
PE: purulent rhinorrhea
Most commonly caused by viral URI
If viral, Tx is supportive care
Bacterial sinusitis: persistent and not improving (≥ 10 days), worsening or double sickening (≥ 5–6 days)
Onset of severe symptoms: fever ≥ 39.0°C (102.2°F) and purulent nasal discharge (≥ 3–4 days at the beginning of illness)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Complications: frontal bone osteomyelitis (Pott puffy tumor), orbital cellulitis, sinus venous thrombosis, extension into meninges or brain

question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with dental pain. He does not have a fever, chills, neck pain, or trouble swallowing. Physical examination is notable for the finding in the image above. The gum is tender but nonfluctuant. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
englishExplanation:
Pericoronitis is a general term to describe swelling of the soft tissues surrounding the teeth. It is associated with trauma, an erupting tooth (in particular, wisdom teeth, as is likely the case in this patient), and infection. Symptoms may include pain, swelling, difficulty biting or chewing, and sometimes, a bad taste in the mouth due to pus from the infected area. The diagnosis can be supported when a flap of tissue or gum is seen that is tender with manipulation. A thorough examination that includes looking for signs of infection should take place. Irrigation should take place, as bacteria or food may be lodged in place. Treatment typically involves improving oral hygiene to clear the infection, using medications to manage pain and inflammation, and, in some cases, surgically removing the gum flap or the affected tooth to prevent recurrence. If there are no signs of infection, pain medications such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen may be given. Patients should be given dental follow-up instructions as well.



Amoxicillin-clavulanate (A) is appropriate management of gingivitis and infection-causing pericoronitis. This patient does not have clear signs of infection, and his symptoms seem to be due to an erupting wisdom tooth.

A dental splint (B) stabilizes teeth in the case of injury or certain dental conditions, such as temporomandibular joint disorders, or to prevent bruxism (teeth grinding). It is not a direct treatment for general dental pain without a specific diagnosis that indicates its use, and it addresses none of the underlying issues directly causing dental pain, such as infection or inflammation. It is a supportive measure rather than a primary treatment strategy.

Performing incision and drainage (D) is appropriate management of a dental abscess that presents with a tender, fluctuant mass. The exam in this patient shows swelling over a portion of the gum without abscess.

One Step Further
Question:
Why should a febrile patient without a sore throat or concerning exam findings avoid having a rapid streptococcal test performed?

Reveal Answer:
Because false positive results may lead to unnecessary treatment.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pericoronitis

Localized inflammation or infection caused by the trapping of food and organisms under a flap of gum
Sx: pain in the jaw, trismus
Tx: supportive care, NSAIDs; antibiotics if infection present

question: A 21-year-old woman presents to the ED with left ear pain. The ear exam is normal, but on palpation of the jaw, there is tenderness over the coronoid process. A clicking can be felt with jaw opening. What is the appropriate management for this patient's condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient has temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction. The TMJ joins the temporal bone to the mandible. Facial muscles that control chewing attach at this joint, including the temporalis at the coronoid process. Dysfunction of the joint can be due to arthritis, trauma, and oral habits, such as teeth grinding. TMJ dysfunction is isolated to the joint itself but can refer pain to the ear, head, neck, and eye. The physical exam will reveal tenderness by palpating the mandible, especially at the coronoid process. Opening and closing the mouth will also produce a palpable click due to malocclusion of the joint. Treatment involves recommending cessation of contributory processes and beginning nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Referral to the patient’s dentist can be recommended for follow-up.



Occlusal splints (B) are not typically recommended as first-line therapy in patients with TMJ disorders unless there is severe bruxism or nighttime clenching. Instead, recommending a soft diet or avoidance of jaw grinding should be encouraged along with NSAID treatment.

Otolaryngology consultation (C) is incorrect and would be recommended if the patient had an emergency such as Ludwig angina.

Penicillin V (D) is an appropriate antibiotic if there is a concern for a dental abscess or streptococcal pharyngitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis should be considered in a patient who has been on therapy for temporomandibular joint dysfunction and presents with tinnitus?

Reveal Answer:
Salicylate toxicity should be eliminated. Early symptoms of salicylate toxicity include nausea, sweating, vomiting, vertigo, fast respiratory rate, tinnitus, or hyperactivity.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Temporomandibular Joint Disorder

Etiologies: bruxism (teeth grinding), malalignment of upper and lower teeth, joint trauma, poor head and cervical posture
Sx: facial pain, ear dysfunction or discomfort, headache
PE: reduced range of motion of the mandible, clicking or popping with jaw movement, tooth wear
Tx: multimodal
Occlusal splint (for bruxism and nighttime clenching)
Biobehavioral management
PT
NSAIDs
Adjunctive treatments: muscle relaxants, TCAs

question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with his parent for an earache and fever. A week ago, he began reporting ear pain, and he has had no relief with acetaminophen and ibuprofen. This morning, the patient began to describe room-spinning episodes and difficulty hearing out of his right ear. His vital signs include temperature 38.4°C, heart rate 126 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate 26/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The physical exam is notable for a bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane. Neurological testing elicits near complete hearing loss in his right ear but is otherwise normal. What complication is this patient most at risk for, given the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is most consistent with bacterial labyrinthitis, with meningitis as its most common disease sequelae. Risk factors and clinical presentations differ between the three types of labyrinthitis. Each most commonly presents with some form of vertigo, tinnitus, or hearing loss, or a combination of these. Serous labyrinthitis is most commonly due to a preceding viral upper respiratory infection. The presenting symptoms are the mildest of the three types. Toxic labyrinthitis is due to an offending medication causing direct damage to the labyrinth. Offending medications can include aminoglycosides, salicylates, and loop diuretics. The associated symptoms are more severe than serous labyrinthitis. Treatment for serous labyrinthitis is based on the patient's symptoms. The mainstay of treatment for toxic labyrinthitis is to remove all offending medications and provide close follow-up, though a full resolution is not assured.

In this case, the patient’s bacterial labyrinthitis is due to his acute otitis media, as noted by his bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane and fever. Bacterial labyrinthitis has the most severe symptoms of the three types, with patients appearing the most toxic. This infection can spread via a contiguous route into the meninges. Thus, antibiotics should be started, and an otolaryngology consult called. These patients should be admitted for continued monitoring and possible surgical drainage.



Brain abscesses (A) are not as commonly associated with bacterial labyrinthitis as meningitis. While they can form due to the direct contiguous spread of an acute otitis media, this patient’s presentation is most consistent with bacterial labyrinthitis. Thus, he is most at risk for meningitis.

Herpes zoster oticus (B), or Ramsay Hunt syndrome, is a type of vestibular ganglionitis caused by the reactivation of a previously dormant varicella zoster infection. It presents as grouped vesicles on erythematous bases within the auditory canal with subsequent vertigo, deafness, and ipsilateral partial or complete facial nerve palsy. Known risk factors include previous varicella infection, immunosuppression, extremes of age, and pregnancy. Although herpes zoster can lead to symptoms of labyrinthitis, it would not be a complication of this patient's current bacterial illness.

Ipsilateral facial paresis (C) can be a complication of many disease processes that cause vertigo, ranging from herpes zoster oticus, vestibular ganglionitis, strokes, and trauma to brain abscesses and tumors. Labyrinthitis is not associated with an increased risk of facial paresis.

One Step Further
Question:
What two primarily childhood viruses can cause viral labyrinthitis?

Reveal Answer:
Rubella and rubeola viruses.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Labyrinthitis

Inflammatory process involving the inner ear membranous labyrinth
Sx: vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus
Vestibular neuritis + unilateral hearing loss = labyrinthitis
Can last days to 1 week
Risks: recent upper respiratory infection (most common)
Medications
Concurrent otitis media
PE: spontaneous horizontal nystagmus
Dx: clinical
Tx: corticosteroids, symptomatic care, vestibular rehabilitation
Remove any offending agents
Bacterial cause requires antibiotics and possibly surgical drainage

question: Which of the following can be appropriately managed in the ED without consultation with an ophthalmologist?
englishExplanation:
Superficial corneal foreign bodies can be removed in the ED without emergent consultation with an ophthalmologist. Corneal foreign bodies are commonly seen in the ED. Patients often report a foreign body sensation, photophobia, and tearing. Slit lamp examination aids in the visualization of the foreign body under magnification and is helpful for removal. Superficial foreign bodies can be removed with the aid of a cotton-tipped swab, a small needle, or even an ophthalmologic burr. Metallic foreign bodies will often have an associated rust ring. The patient should be given a tetanus booster and topical antibiotics as indicated and provided with ophthalmology follow-up for repeat evaluation and rust ring removal as necessary.



Globe perforation (A) is an ophthalmologic emergency and requires emergent consultation for surgical repair. Lacerations that involve the eyelid margin (B) or the canalicular system (C) should be repaired surgically by an ophthalmologist to prevent a poor cosmetic result and functional outcome.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the Seidel test?

Reveal Answer:
Test for globe perforation in which fluorescein dye is placed in the eye, and the eye is examined under cobalt blue light. A positive test shows a stream as aqueous fluid leaks across the cornea.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Foreign Bodies

Apply topical anesthesia
Use cotton-tipped applicator, needle with the slit lamp, or Alger brush to dislodge
If metallic object, remove rust rings in 24–48 hours
Consult ophthalmology for large or deep foreign bodies
Postprocedure topical antibiotics

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with 4 days of gradually progressive monocular loss of central vision with associated right eye pain, which worsens with eye movement. She also notes difficulty with color perception. A right afferent pupillary defect is noted on examination and the optic disk appears edematous. Examination of the left eye is unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.text: Inhibition of outflow of aqueous humor
Occlusion of the central retinal artery
Occlusion of the central retinal vein

englishExplanation:
Optic neuritis is the result of an inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve. It is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS), with half of patients with MS having optic neuritis at some point during the course of illness. It can also be the result of infection (e.g., syphilis, herpes simplex) and other autoimmune disorders such as lupus or sarcoidosis. Patients present with monocular vision loss, which typically progresses over hours to days, with a peak in symptoms at 1–2 weeks. Eye pain, often worse with eye movement, is also seen in most patients. A central scotoma is the most frequently described visual field defect, although almost all types of defects can be seen. A finding specific to optic nerve pathology is the loss of color vision out of proportion to the loss of visual acuity. In addition to decreased visual acuity and visual field defects, the optic disk will appear edematous and hyperemic and an afferent pupillary defect is usually present. Diagnosis is made clinically based on the history and physical examination findings. Magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium can confirm the diagnosis and is helpful in determining the diagnosis in patients without a known history. Intravenous glucocorticoids are typically indicated as there is some evidence that they delay the onset of multiple sclerosis and may hasten visual recovery. Glucocorticoids have not been shown to alter long-term visual outcomes.



Acute angle closure glaucoma results from anterior chamber angle closure, which inhibits the outflow of aqueous humor (B) and increases intraocular pressure. Patients present with sudden onset of eye pain, decreased visual acuity with halos, nausea, vomiting, and headache. The pupil is often mid-range in size and the cornea appears hazy. Patients with acute angle closure glaucoma do not typically have visual field defects or changes in color perception.

Occlusion of the central retinal artery (C) presents with sudden, painless, monocular loss of vision. The retina will appear pale with a cherry red spot on the fovea.

Occlusion of the central retinal vein (D) also presents with painless, monocular loss of vision. Intraretinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and dilated tortuous retinal veins are seen on funduscopic exam described as “blood and thunder.”

One Step Further
Question:
What medications are used to decrease production of aqueous humor in patients with acute angle closure glaucoma?

Reveal Answer:
Topical beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide), and systemic osmotic agents (e.g., mannitol).

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Optic Neuritis

Most commonly caused by multiple sclerosis
Sx: acute monocular vision loss, pain worse with eye movements, loss of color (red) vision, and transient worsening of vision with increased body temperature (Uhthoff phenomenon)
Dx: made clinically
Bedside US might be helpful, MRI will confirm demyelination
Tx: IV methylprednisolone

question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with her parent for evaluation of mouth pain. On physical exam, you see 2–3 mm grey, irregular, ovoid ulcerations on her lower lip and gingival mucosa with a surrounding erythematous halo. These lesions are found only over her anterior oral mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s examination findings are consistent with aphthous ulcers. These are characterized by 2–3 mm, grey, irregular mucosal ulcerations with erythematous halos. The lesions most commonly involve the anterior mucosa (buccal and lingual). While the etiology of these lesions is unknown, they are thought to be related to stress, diet, and genetic factors. Up to one-third of the general population develops these idiopathic ulcers. Treatment consists of pain control with oral mouthwashes, as antiviral and antibiotic treatments have not shown improvement in healing time or recurrence. The lesions commonly resolve spontaneously within 7–10 days.



Herpangina (B), oral candidiasis (C), and viral pharyngitis (D) most commonly present as posterior lesions, not anterior lesions, as seen in this patient. Early in the course of illness, coxsackie lesions appear as erythematous macules that later turn into vesicles and ulcers. Herpangina lesions are papules and vesicles with surrounding erythematous halos. The treatment for both is primarily symptomatic with antipyretics and oral analgesics. Oral candidiasis, most commonly due to Candida albicans, presents as white patches across the tongue or posterior oropharynx. When scraped, the white patches leave erythematous bases that may bleed. Treatment is with oral nystatin.

One Step Further
Question:
What syndrome can cause recurrent viral-like illnesses and aphthous ulcers in children?

Reveal Answer:
Periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis syndrome.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Aphthous Ulcers

Recurrent
Clinical: yellow centers surrounded by red halo, 3–5 mm, round or oval
Location
Buccal or lip mucosa
Rarely labia minora (aka Lipschütz ulcer)
Dx: clinical, do not biopsy
Treatment: supportive, viscous lidocaine, diphenhydramine liquid, topical corticosteroids

question: A 39-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department with dizziness over the past few months. She describes intermittent episodes of feeling like the room is spinning with associated nausea and vomiting. Initially, these episodes occurred only one or two times a month. However, she is seeking care now as they are occurring almost every other day. She reports no fevers, chills, or changes in her vision or speech. Her physical exam is notable for mild right-sided hearing loss but is otherwise grossly normal. What is the underlying cause of this patient’s symptoms?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is most consistent with Ménière disease, a type of peripheral vertigo presumed to be due to increased endolymph within the labyrinth and cochlea. The exact pathogenesis is speculative, with some evidence pointing toward an inability to properly regulate the volume and flow of endolymph. Most commonly, symptoms begin between ages 20 and 40, and patients will describe acute clusters of vertiginous symptoms with nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, hearing loss, ear fullness, or any combination of these. Between attacks, patients are usually asymptomatic. Diagnosis is clinical. While the pathogenesis is not confirmed, treatment has been achieved with antihistamines, betahistine, and calcium channel blockers. Conservative treatment with low-salt diets and avoidance of caffeine and tobacco have shown benefits. Despite treatment, hearing loss and tinnitus may be permanent. If severe, refractory symptoms remain, then vestibular function ablation via intratympanic gentamicin or streptomycin may be appropriate.



Cerebellopontine angle tumors (A) are most commonly vestibular schwannomas. They present as gradual hearing loss followed by gradual and constant mild vertigo. Physical exam may elicit neurologic changes, such as ataxia, ipsilateral abducens nerve palsy, ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and ipsilateral facial weakness. Treatment is with direct neurosurgical intervention.

Infection of the membranous labyrinth (C), or labyrinthitis, presents as acute intermittent vertigo and associated hearing loss in the setting of an ear, nose, or throat infection. Treatment for viral labyrinthitis is supportive, whereas bacterial labyrinthitis requires antibiotics and an otolaryngology referral.

Infection of the vestibular nerve (D), or vestibular neuronitis, is a viral infection that presents as acute-onset constant vertigo that persists for days to months. It does not tend to recur and is not associated with hearing changes. Treatment is with symptomatic support until spontaneous resolution.

One Step Further
Question:
In order, what are the two most common causes of peripheral vertigo?

Reveal Answer:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo and vestibular neuronitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: A 55-year-old woman with a medical history of tracheomalacia with a tracheostomy presents to the emergency department with minor bleeding surrounding the site of her tracheostomy. Her symptoms started 1 hour ago. Her temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 107/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 90 bpm, respiratory rate is 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. Physical exam is notable for erythema surrounding the tracheostomy site. Several minutes later, the patient is noted to have a large amount of blood coming from her tracheostomy tube. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Tracheoarterial fistulas can present with massive hemorrhage and are a devastating complication of a tracheostomy with high mortality. They occur secondary to erosion of the tube tip or cuff into the anterior wall of the trachea, subsequently causing fistulous communication with the innominate artery. Patients may develop an initial bleed followed by massive hemoptysis. When this diagnosis is suspected, patients should undergo immediate interventions to stop the bleeding including overinflation of the cuff to tamponade the bleeding, placement of an endotracheal tube with distal inflation of the cuff, and direct compression with the clinician's finger while the surgical team is contacted to offer definitive care. Diagnostic imaging to confirm this diagnosis is not indicated, as the time it takes to perform angiography or bronchoscopy could result in death from the high rate of bleeding.



Cellulitis with abscess (A) would present with erythema and purulent drainage around the site of the tracheostomy and is unlikely to cause hemorrhage. A significant infection could lead to septic shock, which would present with tachycardia and hypotension but not large bleeding. Pneumothorax (B), with associated subcutaneous emphysema, is a possible complication of a tracheostomy and could present with crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema), or an absence of breath sounds on one side with a chest radiograph demonstrating pulmonary markings that do not extend out to the periphery. Pulmonary embolism (C) could present with tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, and hemoptysis. However, the volume of this patient’s hemoptysis and rapidly declining course in the setting of a tracheostomy suggests that a tracheoarterial fistula is more likely.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnostic test can be ordered in a low-risk patient to rule out a pulmonary embolism?

Reveal Answer:
D-dimer.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tracheostomy Complications

Accidental decannulation
Obstruction
Infection
Fistulas
Bleeding
Tracheoinnominate artery fistula: usually within the first 3 weeks, with the peak incidence between the first and second week
Sentinel bleed followed by massive bleeding
Digital pressure, hyperinflate cuff
Emergency consultation

question: A 29-year-old woman presents with jaw pain and swelling. She noticed painful swelling under the left mandible and pain on the floor of her mouth 2 days ago. She reports no fevers, neck pain, odynophagia, or dysphonia. She has a history of seasonal allergies for which she takes diphenhydramine. On physical examination, there is an area of edema under her left mandible that is firm without overlying skin changes. Her oropharynx is notable for a palpable hard nodule just lateral to the frenulum on the floor of the mouth. Dentition is normal, and there is no trismus. Which of the following is the best next step in care?

options.text: CT of the face with contrast
Gentle massage, tart candy, and analgesia

correctAnswer: Gentle massage, tart candy, and analgesia
englishExplanation:
This patient has sialolithiasis, a condition in which calcium stones form in stagnant salivary ducts. The most common location for stone formation is in the submandibular gland (Wharton duct), followed by the parotid gland (Stensen duct). The diagnosis is usually clinical. Patients present with unilateral colicky pain worsened with eating. It may be possible to palpate a stone in the duct. Glands will be firm and tender. Diagnostic tools include radiographs and thin-cut CT, but these are rarely necessary unless abscess or malignancy is high on the differential.

Treatment is supportive with gentle massage, tart candy (or sialagogues), and analgesia to promote salivary flow. Antibiotics, preferably with antistaphylococcal activity, are only advised if secondary infection is present. Palpable stones may be able to be “milked” or massaged from the duct. Parotitis, viral or bacterial, may mimic sialolithiasis and exists concurrently but usually demonstrates obvious signs of infection, such as purulent drainage and fever, and can rapidly worsen.



CT of the face with contrast (A) should be reserved for cases in which sialolithiasis is not clinically apparent, or there are concerns for an abscess or tumor, which is not the case in this patient.

Emergent otolaryngology consultation (B) is necessary for deep space neck and facial infections, including Ludwig angina, which presents with significant swelling to the upper neck and floor of the mouth as well as odynophagia and trismus that can rapidly compromise a patient’s airway. This patient appears well clinically without any of these signs.

Oral antibiotics (D) would be appropriate in patients with sialadenitis, infection of the gland, or secondary infection from sialolithiasis. This patient likely has uncomplicated sialolithiasis with no fever or overlying cellulitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the common viral cause of parotitis?

Reveal Answer:
Paramyxovirus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Sialolithiasis

Salivary gland stone causing duct obstruction
Sx: recurrent mouth swelling and pain, worse with meals
Common sites: submandibular gland (most common), parotid gland
Tx: gland massage, warm compresses, sialagogues (e.g., lemon drops)
Severe cases: stone removal (manual or surgical)

question: A 7-year-old girl who is unvaccinated presents to the ED in acute respiratory distress. On physical exam, she exhibits stridor and is tripoding. Vital signs are a BP of 105/65 mm Hg, HR of 130 bpm, RR of 30/min, and T of 103.4°F. What is the most likely causative organism in this disease process?
englishExplanation:
This child is exhibiting signs and symptoms of epiglottitis. Typical symptoms include rapid onset of fever, dysphagia, dysphonia, and stridor. Children will often present in the tripod position and should not be disrupted or removed from their position of comfort. Diagnosis of epiglottitis is often clinical, but if the diagnosis is not clear, a lateral soft tissue X-ray of the neck may be obtained and classically reveals a thumbprint sign. X-rays should be done at the bedside, given the risk of losing the patient’s airway in radiology.

Historically, this was most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib). Following the advent of the Hib vaccine, the incidence has decreased, but this bacteria still remains an important cause, especially in unvaccinated or incompletely immunized children. Other important causes include Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species.

Management of epiglottitis should focus on close airway monitoring, keeping the patient in a position of comfort, and scheduling consultations with otolaryngology and anesthesia. Definitive airway management should preferably be performed in the operating room. Intravenous antibiotics, which should include a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) and an antistaphylococcal agent (vancomycin), should be initiated after securing the airway so as not to agitate the child and cause airway compromise.



Klebsiella pneumoniae (B) is not a common cause of epiglottitis.

Staphylococcus aureus (C) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (D) are becoming more common causes of epiglottitis in adults and children due to vaccination against Hib.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the pathognomonic feature of a Klebsiella pneumoniae respiratory infection?

Reveal Answer:
Currant jelly sputum.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epiglottitis

Most commonly caused by H. influenzae (decrease since Hib vaccine), Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species
Sx: rapid onset of fever, muffled voice, dysphagia, respiratory distress
PE: sore throat, stridor, leaning forward, drooling, red swollen epiglottis on direct visualization
Imaging: enlarged epiglottis (thumbprint sign) on lateral neck X-ray
Tx: airway management and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin AND antistaphylococcal)

question: A young man presents to the emergency department with eye pain. Fluorescein staining and Wood lamp examination show the finding above. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
englishExplanation:
The patient is presenting with a corneal abrasion, as seen on Wood lamp examination. Corneal abrasions are a common cause of red or painful eyes. They are usually caused by direct trauma but can also be caused by contact lens irritation, ultraviolet light exposure, or wind exposure. Patients usually report a foreign body sensation, pain, and photophobia. Corneal abrasions can be diagnosed by a careful eye examination with fluorescein staining, as it can help identify a corneal epithelial defect. When visualized under a cobalt blue filter on a slit lamp or under a Wood lamp, there will be uptake of the fluorescein dye in the corneal defect, causing it to appear green.

The majority of corneal abrasions heal spontaneously. Thus, treatment involves providing symptomatic control and preventing superinfection. Small abrasions may not require further treatment, but either erythromycin ointment or polymyxin solution can be used if antibiotics are given. If the patient wears contact lenses, ciprofloxacin or another agent that can cover Pseudomonas infections should be used. If an abrasion is > 2 mm or very painful, an additional cycloplegic agent can be prescribed to provide more symptomatic relief. Small abrasions can be reexamined within 48–72 hours. Large abrasions or abrasions involving the central visual axis should be reexamined by an ophthalmologist within 24 hours. Of note, topical anesthetics should not be prescribed, as they can inhibit corneal healing and suppress the blinking reflex, which is protective of the eye.



Neomycin ointments (B) should be avoided in corneal abrasions to prevent hypersensitivity reactions.

Prednisolone eye drops (C) can be effective in treating traumatic iritis, which is another common cause of eye pain but would be inappropriate in the setting of an isolated corneal abrasion.

Timolol eye drops (D) can be used to treat acute angle-closure glaucoma to lower intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production but would have little utility in treating corneal abrasions.

One Step Further
Question:
What type of injury does a positive Seidel test imply?

Reveal Answer:
Full-thickness corneal injury.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Abrasion

Sx: pain, photophobia, tearing, or foreign body sensation
Uncontrollable crying in infants
Dx: fluorescein stain
Tx
Most are self-limiting
Topical antibiotics to prevent superinfection is common practice
Add antipseudomonal coverage for those who wear contact lenses

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department for left ear pain. On exam, his left ear canal is impacted with cerumen. During irrigation, he begins screaming in pain. You are now able to visualize a portion of his tympanic membrane and find it has been ruptured without surrounding erythema or purulence. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Placement of a ciprofloxacin-instilled ear wick

englishExplanation:
This patient has sustained a tympanic membrane rupture due to increased pressure during irrigation. Tympanic membrane rupture can occur during a wide range of situations: underlying otitis media, direct trauma during ear irrigation, and barotrauma from diving and blast events. Most isolated tympanic membrane perforations due to direct trauma will heal without intervention. Thus, this patient can be discharged home with close follow-up. If there is an infection associated with the tympanic membrane rupture, oral antibiotics, like amoxicillin, should be given. If there is a contaminated penetrating injury, topical antibiotics, like ofloxacin, should be given. Care should be taken to avoid otic steroids as they can slow membrane healing. All tympanic membrane perforations should be followed closely.



Traumatic tympanic membrane ruptures without contamination do not require antibiotic treatment like oral amoxicillin (B), otic amoxicillin (C), and placement of a ciprofloxacin-instilled ear wick (D). If an underlying infection is suspected, oral amoxicillin should be prescribed.

One Step Further
Question:
What characteristics of a perforated tympanic membrane increase the risk of ossicle damage?

Reveal Answer:
Perforation due to penetrating trauma or perforation involving the posterosuperior quadrant.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tympanic Membrane Perforation

Foreign body, infection, blast, ↑ barometric pressure
Pars tensa most commonly perforated
Sx: pain, ↓ hearing, bleeding
​Tx: keep ear dry, analgesics, antibiotics for contaminated injuries
90% heal in a few months

question: A 20-year-old man presents with a sore throat, dysphagia, and drooling. He was seen 2 days ago for the same concern, but the pain is now worse. His vital signs include a blood pressure of 135/85 mm Hg, heart rate of 98 bpm, respiratory rate of 20/min, oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, and temperature of 99.9°F. On examination, there is no pharyngeal erythema or tonsillar exudate. You obtain the soft tissue neck radiograph, as seen above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient has epiglottitis, a disease that is now more common in adults than in children since the development of the conjugate Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccine. Patients typically present with a severe sore throat but have an unremarkable oropharyngeal exam. They may position themselves sitting up, leaning forward, mouth open, head extended, and panting. Often, there will be pain with movement of the thyroid cartilage.

The clinical triad associated with epiglottitis is drooling, dysphagia, and distress (referred to as the three Ds), but these findings are not found as often in adults. A lateral soft tissue neck radiograph may demonstrate an enlarged epiglottis that is thumb shaped. This is referred to as the thumbprint sign.



Bacterial tracheitis (A) is a rare, life-threatening disease that most commonly occurs in children 5–8 years of age. It can mimic croup, but patients appear more toxic. Clinically, this can present similar to epiglottitis.

Diphtheria (B), caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, classically presents with sore throat, low-grade fever, malaise, and a grayish pseudomembrane on the tonsils, pharynx, or nasal tissues. Symptoms typically have a gradual onset.

A peritonsillar abscess (D) is the most common deep facial infection in adults. Patients present with fever, sore throat, trismus, and a peritonsillar mass that displaces the soft palate and uvula.

A retropharyngeal abscess (E) is mostly a condition in infants and children, although it has been described in adults. Patients present with fever, neck pain, and difficulty talking (termed cri du canard or a duck-like voice), swallowing, and breathing. The oropharyngeal exam shows anterior displacement of the posterior pharyngeal wall. The neck radiograph may show prevertebral soft tissue swelling.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the recommended technique to establish a definitive airway in patients with severe epiglottitis?

Reveal Answer:
Awake fiberoptic intubation in the operating room with the patient sitting up.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epiglottitis

Most commonly caused by H. influenzae (decrease since Hib vaccine), Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species
Sx: rapid onset of fever, muffled voice, dysphagia, respiratory distress
PE: sore throat, stridor, leaning forward, drooling, red swollen epiglottis on direct visualization
Imaging: enlarged epiglottis (thumbprint sign) on lateral neck X-ray
Tx: airway management and IV antibiotics (third-generation cephalosporin AND antistaphylococcal)

question: A 77-year-old man presents to the emergency department with blurry vision in his right eye and a foreign body sensation. He wears contact lenses but has forgotten to change them for nearly 1 week. He had a few days of extreme pain on his right forehead 3 weeks ago, followed by a rash that has since gone away. On exam, his right eye is red, and there is a dendritic structure that appears stuck on and that stains poorly with fluorescein. There is a watery discharge from the eye. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Keratitis refers to corneal inflammation and can lead to corneal scarring or perforation, which can be vision threatening. Signs and symptoms of infectious keratitis include ocular pain, foreign body sensation, and ciliary flush. There is often an ulcer visible on examination. This patient presents with the signs and symptoms of keratitis 3 weeks after an untreated episode of herpes zoster, or shingles, that affected the distribution of the first division of the trigeminal nerve, which is consistent with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus is caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus in the trigeminal ganglion, causing paresthesias and hyperesthesias and, subsequently, a rash that progresses from maculopapular to vesicular. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus can progress to involve any part of the eye, including the cornea, and ocular symptoms can be delayed up to a month. When vesicles are seen on the side of the nose, there is an extremely high likelihood of ocular involvement.

Herpes zoster ophthalmicus can manifest in a number of different ways on exam, including pseudodendrites that are easy to mistake for the dendrites that are often considered pathognomonic for herpes simplex keratitis. The pseudodendrites in herpes zoster ophthalmicus are poorly adherent epithelial cells that appear stuck on, lack bulbs at the end of the dendrites, and stain poorly with fluorescein. In contrast, the dendrites seen in herpes simplex keratitis have terminal bulbs and stain brightly with fluorescein. Both herpes zoster ophthalmicus and herpes simplex keratitis can be treated with oral antivirals, including acyclovir and valacyclovir, though higher doses are used in herpes zoster keratitis. Topical antivirals, including acyclovir and ganciclovir, are equally efficacious as oral therapy in herpes simplex keratitis but have no role in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Topical steroids are controversial in herpes zoster ophthalmicus but can exacerbate herpes simplex keratitis, so they are best not prescribed in the ED without ophthalmology consultation.



Adenoviral keratitis (A) can be associated with the more common adenoviral conjunctivitis. Patients have typical symptoms of viral conjunctivitis, followed by foreign body sensations, suggesting corneal involvement. Fluorescein staining demonstrates punctate lesions, not dendritic lesions.

Bacterial keratitis (B) presents with photophobia, foreign body sensation, ciliary flush, mucopurulent discharge, and an ulcer on exam. The ulcer is often visible on penlight exam, even without fluorescein staining. The biggest risk factor for bacterial keratitis is prolonged or improper contact lens use, which this patient has. However, his presentation is otherwise inconsistent with the bacterial cause of his keratitis. Treatment is with topical antibiotics.

Herpes simplex keratitis (C) presents with an acute onset of monocular pain, blurry vision, watery discharge, and ciliary flush. On examination, dendritic ulcers are seen. As described above, the dendritic ulcers in herpes simplex keratitis have terminal bulbs and stain brightly with fluorescein, unlike the pseudodendrites seen in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Treatment is either topical or oral antivirals. Topical steroids should be avoided.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the three most important indications for a patient to see an ophthalmologist within 24 hours when they present to the ED with a red eye?

Reveal Answer:
Decreased vision with a corneal opacity or infiltrate, especially in a contact lens wearer, hyphema or hypopyon, and unilateral red eye with headache, nausea, vomiting, and severe eye pain.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus

Reactivation of latent VZV in CN V1 distribution
Sx: eye pain, redness, tearing,
PE: vesicular rash in CN V1 distribution
Hutchinson sign
Punctate epithelial keratitis, pseudodendrites
Tx: ophthalmology consultation and oral or IV acyclovir (or similar agent)
Complication is acute angle-closure glaucoma

question: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sore throat for 1 day. He also has a cough, runny nose, aches, and fatigue. His children recently had similar symptoms. His T is 97°F (36.1°C), BP is 125/72 mm Hg, HR is 90 bpm, RR is 14/min, and SpO2 is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals the finding above. There is no tender adenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient’s symptoms?
englishExplanation:
When evaluating pharyngitis, the emergency clinician must determine whether it is caused by a bacterial or viral etiology. Bacterial pharyngitis more commonly presents with a fever > 38°C, exudates, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and the absence of cough. Viral pharyngitis typically presents with other symptoms not localized to the oropharynx, including cough, runny nose, and a history of others with the same symptoms, as viral causes of pharyngitis are more easily spread when compared to bacterial causes. Viral pharyngitis is most commonly caused by viruses such as rhinovirus. If a patient has a classic presentation of viral pharyngitis, management is symptom control only. It is generally advisable not to perform a rapid Streptococcus test in patients with a clear viral picture, as false positives will lead to unnecessary antibiotic treatment.



Allergic rhinitis (A) presents with rhinorrhea and red, itchy eyes. Symptoms more commonly occur in a seasonal pattern that is worse in the spring. Treatment is focused on avoidance of causative agents and symptom control with antihistamines. Staphylococcus aureus (C) can cause bacterial tracheitis. This condition is more common after viral infections and is commonly confused with croup. Patients with bacterial tracheitis are much more ill than those with croup and present with high fever, purulent secretions, a hoarse and barking cough, tracheal tenderness, and possible airway loss. Streptococcus pyogenes (D) may cause bacterial pharyngitis. This patient does not have a high fever, exudates, or tender adenopathy, and he has a cough, making the diagnosis of bacterial pharyngitis less likely.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common infectious etiology of croup?

Reveal Answer:
Parainfluenza virus.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Pharyngitis

Most commonly caused by viral > bacteria (GAS, S. pyogenes)
Centor criteria: estimates probability pharyngitis is streptococcal based on PE and Sx
Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate or swelling, fever, absence of cough, age 3–14 years
Modified Centor criteria: +1 for age < 15 years, −1 for age > 45 years
Treatment
Viral: supportive
Bacterial
Penicillin or amoxicillin is first line
Patients with penicillin allergy: cephalexin, cefadroxil (avoid in individuals with immediate-type hypersensitivity to penicillin), clindamycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin (resistance of GAS to these agents is known well and varies geographically and temporally)

question: A 32-year-old man with no significant medical history presents with eye pain. He was struck by a football while playing catch. He notes left eye pain and blurred vision. Physical exam reveals visual acuity of 20/35 in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye with intraocular pressures of 17 mm Hg and 25 mm Hg, respectively. Fluorescein exam reveals no abrasion or uptake. Slit lamp exam shows red blood cells in the anterior chamber. The presence of which of the following factors is most indicative of a need for admission?
englishExplanation:
Hyphema is the presence of red blood cells in the eye's anterior chamber. It can happen spontaneously in patients with blood diathesis (e.g., anticoagulation, leukemia, and von Willebrand disease) and those with underlying ocular pathology (e.g., diabetes mellitus, neoplasm, and keratouveitis). However, most hyphemas seen in the emergency department are due to trauma. Patients may report blurry vision, loss of the lower visual field, pain, and photophobia. Examination with a slit lamp can readily diagnose the presence of hyphema with the finding of layering red blood cells in the anterior chamber. Special attention should be paid to the level of the hyphema at presentation, as any subsequent elevation is a sign of rebleeding. A complete ocular exam, including visual acuity, fluorescein staining, and ocular pressure, should be undertaken except in cases of suspected globe injury in which manipulation of the eye is strictly contraindicated. Intraocular pressure (IOP) must be closely monitored and treated to prevent glaucoma and vision loss. Most patients can be cared for conservatively in the outpatient setting using an eye shield and agents to lower IOP. However, patients at high risk for rebleeding or significant injury, such as a concurrent orbital injury, may require hospitalization for close monitoring. Patients with sickle cell trait or disease are at significant risk of vision loss and also require close monitoring, as sickled cells can block the trabecular meshwork, preventing drainage of aqueous humor and worsening IOP. Moreover, intravascular sickling in the presence of elevated IOP can result in ischemic optic neuropathy. Topical treatment with beta-blockers and alpha-agonists is the first line for elevated IOP. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are the second line but should be avoided in patients with sickle cell disease, as these medications can cause sickling. Surgery is indicated when IOP is not well controlled, which is defined as IOP ≥ 25 mm Hg after 24 hours in patients with sickle trait or disease and IOP ≥ 50 mm Hg for 6 days in other patients. Surgery is also indicated in pediatric patients with grade IV hyphema, as this can result in amblyopia.



Grade II hyphema (A) is defined as red cells filling 33–50% of the anterior chamber. Patients with > 50% coverage of the anterior chamber of grade III hyphema should be admitted for further care.

Hypertension (B) is a risk factor for rebleeding but is not an indication for admission.

Pseudophakia (C), or the presence of an artificial lens, causes no significant complications in hyphema.

One Step Further
Question:
What effect do antifibrinolytic agents (e.g., aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid) have on visual acuity outcomes in patients with hyphema?

Reveal Answer:
No effect.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Hyphema

Often history of blunt or penetrating trauma
Sx: blurry vision
PE: decreased visual acuity and blood in anterior chamber
Tx: gentle ambulation, head elevation of 30–45° for large hyphemas
> 50% hyphema, those with sickle cell disease, and those taking anticoagulants should be admitted
Topical or oral agents to lower IOP
Urgent ophthalmology follow-up or consult in the hospital

question: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with right eye swelling. She is a previously healthy, fully immunized girl with no medications and no known allergies. Her parent states the symptoms started 2 days ago with mild periorbital erythema and edema. The patient has been battling an upper respiratory infection with nasal congestion and discharge, which recently changed in color and became thick. Vital signs are remarkable for T of 38.9°C, HR of 130 bpm, and RR of 18/min. Physical examination is remarkable for significant right periorbital erythema and edema, tachycardia, and equally responsive pupils. Examination is negative for proptosis and pain with extraocular muscle testing. Which clinical feature helps rule out the more emergent process when diagnosing this patient?

options.text: Lack of pain with extraocular movements

correctAnswer: Lack of pain with extraocular movements
englishExplanation:
Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of the anterior portion of the eyelid and periorbital tissues. Postseptal, or orbital, cellulitis is an infection involving the orbit's content (adipose tissue and muscles). Differentiating the two is crucial, as management is significantly different and the outcomes can be catastrophic if postseptal cellulitis is missed. The clinical features of both pre- and postseptal cellulitis are nearly identical, with both demonstrating erythema, warmth, and tenderness to palpation. Visual acuities and pupillary responses are both normal with preseptal cellulitis, and there is a lack of pain with extraocular movements, no proptosis, and no diplopia. If any of these clinical features are present or if the clinician has a high enough suspicion for postseptal cellulitis, a CT scan of the orbit should be obtained to evaluate and rule out postseptal cellulitis. Patients with preseptal cellulitis who appear nontoxic can be treated as an outpatient with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 24-hour ophthalmology follow-up. Patients < 5 years of age or those with significant comorbidities with preseptal cellulitis should be admitted for intravenous antibiotic therapies, including cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam. All patients with postseptal cellulitis require admission with emergent ophthalmology consultation and intravenous antibiotics. Vancomycin is added if methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is suspected.



Afferent pupillary defect (A) and proptosis (D) are both clinical features concerning for postseptal cellulitis. If either of these is present, further evaluation with a CT scan of the orbits would be warranted to evaluate and rule out postseptal cellulitis. If present, the patient would require admission with emergent ophthalmology consultation and intravenous antibiotics, including cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, or ampicillin-sulbactam. Vancomycin is added if MRSA is suspected.

Erythema (B) can be present in both preseptal and postseptal infections and is not a clinical feature that can help differentiate between the two disease processes.

One Step Further
Question:
What age group is most affected by both pre- and postseptal cellulitis?

Reveal Answer:
< 10 years of age.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Preseptal Cellulitis (Periorbital Cellulitis)

Anterior to the orbital septum, does NOT involve the globe or orbital septum
More common in children
Risks: trauma, bites, other facial infection (e.g., dacryocystitis)
Sx: periorbital pain, swelling, erythema
Dx: clinical diagnosis, consider CT if unsure of orbital involvement
Tx: usually oral antibiotics are sufficient

question: An 18-month-old healthy girl without previous episodes of ear infections presents to the emergency department with a fever for 3 days, up to T 38.8°C. On physical examination, the left tympanic membrane lacks mobility and is retracted with overlying erythema. There is auricular protrusion with erythema and tenderness to palpation over the mastoid process. What is the most appropriate initial empiric antimicrobial therapy?
englishExplanation:
Otitis media describes the bacterial infection of middle ear fluid between the external ear canal and the inner ear, including the ossicular chain. The most common bacterial causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Otalgia, fever, otorrhea, hearing changes, and upper respiratory infection symptoms (e.g., rhinorrhea, cough) are common symptoms. The tympanic membrane may appear retracted or bulging with decreased mobility and with redness when inflamed or opaque and yellow-white if an effusion is present. Indications to observe prior to antibiotic treatment include an age of 6 months to 2 years with unilateral otitis media and no otorrhea or severe disease or an age > 2 years with unilateral or bilateral otitis media and no otorrhea or severe disease. Oral antibiotic therapies are otherwise indicated, with amoxicillin as the first-line agent, and alternatives including amoxicillin-clavulanate, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and cefdinir.

Intravenous antibiotics are indicated if complications are present, such as sepsis, intratemporal and intracranial extension (developing mastoiditis like in this patient), or sinus thrombosis or if patients are immunosuppressed. In patients who have not recently had otitis media (< 6 months) and have not recently been taking antibiotics, example empiric regimens should cover streptoccoal and staphylococcal species and include intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam, levofloxacin, or a cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone, cefotaxime). If patients have had recurrent otitis media, chronic ear drainage, or recent antibiotic use, the empiric antibiotic regimen should include coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime). If methicillin-resistant S. aureus risk factors are present, metronidazole with either vancomycin or linezolid should be used.



Intravenous cefepime (B) would be indicated if the patient had a history of recurrent otitis media, chronic ear drainage, or recent antibiotic use.

Oral amoxicillin (C) is indicated as first-line therapy in uncomplicated acute otitis media without recent antibiotic use.

Oral levofloxacin (D) is indicated if patients have had 72 hours of amoxicillin without improvement or a recent failure in antibiotics.

One Step Further
Question:
In acute otitis media, what nerve function should be assessed due to its proximity to the tympanic membrane?

Reveal Answer:
Facial nerve.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Mastoiditis

Most commonly caused by a complication from preceding acute otitis media
Sx: fever, otalgia, and retroauricular swelling and tenderness
PE: erythema and protrusion of the external ear
Dx: clinical, CT can confirm the diagnosis
Tx: admission and IV antibiotics

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of left ventricular assist device placement is presenting for epistaxis. For the past hour, he has experienced a right-sided nosebleed that did not stop with continuous direct pressure from a nasal clamp at home. The patient has a MAP of 75 mm Hg. On exam, the patient has slow bleeding from the right nare, with clots present in the posterior oropharynx. Right-sided anterior nasal packing is placed but needs to be removed due to the patient repeatedly coughing, resulting in blood being expelled from the left nare and the oropharynx. What is the best next step in the treatment of this patient’s epistaxis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with epistaxis in the setting of anticoagulation based on his history of left ventricular assist device (LVAD) dependence. He appears hemodynamically stable. The ideal MAP for patients with an LVAD is typically between 60 and 80 mm Hg to ensure adequate perfusion without overloading the device. Epistaxis in hemodynamically stable patients is initially managed with external compression. Failure of external compression should prompt anterior packing. In nontraumatic cases of epistaxis, bilateral bleeding or bleeding that persists despite anterior packing is concerning for a possible posterior bleed.

Posterior bleeding is most common in older adults with multiple comorbidities and is seen in approximately 10% of cases that present to the emergency department. Posterior packing is valuable for both diagnosis and treatment. Ideally, it should be attempted before otolaryngology consultation, as ongoing bleeding can lead to aspiration, respiratory compromise, and, in extreme cases, hemorrhagic shock. Many cases of posterior bleeding can be stopped with posterior packing, avoiding unnecessary embolization or operative management procedures. Following posterior packing, patients should be admitted for otolaryngology consultation and repeat assessments to determine if hemostasis has been achieved.



Bilateral anterior packing (A) is unlikely to resolve bleeding in this patient with epistaxis. Bilateral anterior bleeds are uncommon in atraumatic epistaxis.

Most posterior bleeding can be stopped with posterior packing. Thus, embolization or operative management (B) is not indicated at this time.

Reversal of anticoagulation (D) should be a last resort in any patient with an LVAD, as this can lead to pump thrombosis.

Silver nitrate cautery (E) is typically unsuccessful in the setting of ongoing bleeding but should be attempted when an anterior site of bleeding has been identified and hemostasis has been achieved.

One Step Further
Question:
Which medication has been shown to safely promote more rapid hemostasis with soaking nasal packing?

Reveal Answer:
Tranexamic acid.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Epistaxis

Most common source
Anterior bleeds: Kiesselbach plexus
Posterior bleeds: sphenopalatine artery
Treatment
Anterior bleeding: direct pressure, topical vasoconstriction (oxymetazoline), chemicalcautery with silver nitrate (if vessel visualized), packing
Posterior bleeding: packing (nasal balloon or Foley catheter)
Admit patients with posterior packing to a monitored bed
Possible complications: septal necrosis (if both sides of septum cauterized), toxic shock syndrome (prolonged packing), infection

question: Which of the following pediatric intranasal foreign bodies needs to be removed expeditiously in the emergency department?

options.text: A posterior foreign body that is barely visible

englishExplanation:
Intranasal foreign body insertion is found, almost exclusively, in pediatric patients. Most children are asymptomatic, but they may present with pain, nasal discharge, bleeding, or simply visualization of the foreign body in the nose. The majority of intranasal foreign bodies are in the right nare, can be visualized in the anterior nasal passage, and are appropriate for removal by an emergency clinician. Otolaryngology referral is warranted for patients with posterior foreign bodies that cannot be visualized, impacted foreign bodies with significant swelling and inflammation, penetrating foreign bodies, and any foreign body that cannot be removed due to poor cooperation or bleeding. However, a few types of foreign bodies that need to be removed expeditiously in the emergency department are button batteries, paired disc magnets inserted into each nostril, and superabsorbent polymer beads. Button batteries can cause alkaline tissue necrosis and result in septal perforation within several hours. Paired magnets inserted into each nostril attach at the nasal septum and can cause perforation from chronic compression. Superabsorbent beads can become lodged over a few days, leading to tissue necrosis. Positive pressure techniques are recommended first-line treatments to remove an intranasal foreign body. If this does not work, several instruments can be used to remove the foreign body, including a suction catheter, a small Foley catheter, or alligator forceps. Pediatric patients will generally need sedation since this procedure is often only successful if the patient remains still.



A posterior foreign body that is barely visible (B) should not be removed by the emergency clinician since it is prone to complications. Patients with a posterior foreign body can be given an urgent otolaryngology referral.

Similarly, a single magnet (C) does not necessarily need to be removed in the emergency department. If it is easily visualized, it may be simple for the emergency clinician to remove, but a single magnet does not pose a risk for septal perforation.

A sponge (D) can also be removed by the emergency clinician, but it does not need to be done expeditiously. A patient with a sponge in the nose should try to avoid getting the area wet or moist since the sponge will expand and then be more difficult to remove.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common complication of a chronic intranasal foreign body?

Reveal Answer:
Bacterial sinusitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Nasal Foreign Body

Most often in children
Unilateral mucopurulent and foul-smelling nasal discharge
Tx: big kiss (positive pressure in mouth by parent while occluding unaffected nares)

question: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ED by his parent due to ear pain and the parent believes that there is a button battery in the child's ear that has been there for at least 24 hours. Physical exam reveals what appears to be a button battery lodged in the right external auditory canal with surrounding edema and erythema. Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.text: Attempt to remove the foreign body using alligator forceps
Attempt to remove the foreign body using irrigation
Discharge the patient for next-day otolaryngology follow-up

englishExplanation:
Foreign bodies of the external auditory canal are most commonly found in young children and most often include beads, pebbles, tissue paper, small toys, popcorn kernels, and insects. Patients with external auditory canal foreign bodies are often asymptomatic but may present with decreased hearing or ear pain. The diagnosis is confirmed by visualizing the foreign body in the external auditory canal on otoscopy.

Most otic foreign bodies can be removed in the ED. However, button batteries in the external auditory canal can cause destruction due to strong electrical currents and pressure necrosis, which is likely occurring in this patient due to his prolonged duration of foreign body in the ear and noticeable canal edema and erythema. Otolaryngology should be consulted before any removal attempts for button batteries, potentially penetrating foreign bodies, or foreign bodies with evidence of injury to the external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, or middle ear. For other foreign bodies, removal using irrigation or direct visualization and forceps may be attempted.



Attempting to remove the foreign body using alligator forceps (A) would not be wise in this case of a button battery in the external auditory canal particularly with surrounding inflammatory changes. Otolaryngology should be consulted prior to any attempts at removal.

Attempting to remove the foreign body using irrigation (B) is contraindicated in the removal of a button battery because irrigation of a button battery enhances current flow and increases the potential for caustic injury.

Discharging the patient for next-day otolaryngology follow-up (D) is inappropriate as this patient requires urgent otolaryngology consultation.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common complication of otic foreign body removal?

Reveal Answer:
External auditory canal abrasion or laceration.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ear Foreign Body

Removal via curette, forceps, or irrigation
Removal requires a cooperative or restrained patient
Irrigation is contraindicated if tympanic membrane may be violated
Irrigation is contraindicated if the material is organic and can swell
Prior to removal, any live insects should be killed with alcohol, mineral oil, or lidocaine
Otitis externa prophylaxis with ototopical antibiotics is indicated if the external auditory canal or tympanic membrane has been excoriated during the foreign body removal

question: A 5-year-old boy with a tracheostomy tube is brought to the ED with a fever and a change in his behavior. His T is 102°F (38.9°C), BP is 85/40 mm Hg, HR is 132 bpm, RR is 30/min, and SpO2 is 92% on room air. The patient is coughing with purulent secretions coming from the tracheostomy tube. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
Tracheostomy tubes increase the risk of infection in the trachea and airway. It is thought that the foreign material and stoma become colonized with bacteria, increasing the risk of infection. Tracheitis, tracheobronchitis, and pneumonia are all more common in patients with tracheostomy tubes. Tracheobronchitis in children with tracheostomies or other artificial airways presents a diagnostic challenge due to its imprecisely defined clinical criteria. There is no singular diagnostic test that conclusively identifies tracheobronchitis. In children who rely on a tracheostomy for prolonged periods, the condition is often identified based on clinical symptoms such as fever and new, purulent tracheal secretions, particularly when no other causes for these symptoms are evident. While sputum cultures can play a role in managing the condition, they alone do not suffice for a definitive diagnosis, underscoring the need for a comprehensive clinical evaluation to accurately identify tracheobronchitis.

Tracheitis refers specifically to inflammation and infection of the trachea. Presenting symptoms may include fever, cough, increased sputum production, odynophagia or difficulty swallowing, drooling, changes in the voice or hoarseness, and respiratory distress. The diagnosis of bacterial tracheitis necessitates the direct observation of the airway through laryngoscopy and tracheobronchoscopy. Imaging of the chest to work up a possible pneumonia is common practice. Management of tracheitis involves obtaining cultures of the sputum and providing broad-spectrum antibiotics, including coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and anaerobes. Common antibiotics can include combinations such as vancomycin, cefepime, and metronidazole, or vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. Suctioning the tracheostomy tube can improve respiratory symptoms in the emergency department. Changing out the tracheostomy tube for source control is also often done on the inpatient side.



Although the combination of ampicillin and gentamicin (A) provides broad coverage, including against some gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, it may not be sufficiently broad for severe infections associated with health care settings, particularly against MRSA or resistant gram-negative bacteria that may be present in this patient with a tracheostomy in place.
