Flucloxacillin (B) is mainly effective against penicillinase-producing staphylococci. Flucloxacillin is a narrow-spectrum choice and might not cover the range of potential pathogens in a tracheostomy-associated respiratory infection, especially in the context of fever and purulent secretions that suggest a more complex bacterial involvement.

The combination of metronidazole and gentamicin (C) is not the first choice regimen for respiratory infections, as metronidazole primarily targets anaerobic bacteria, while gentamicin covers some gram-negative bacteria. This pairing might miss key respiratory pathogens, especially gram-positive organisms.

One Step Further
Question:
What common infection or condition predisposes patients to bacterial tracheitis?

Reveal Answer:
Croup.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tracheostomy Complications

Accidental decannulation
Obstruction
Infection
Fistulas
Bleeding
Tracheoinnominate artery fistula: usually within the first 3 weeks, with the peak incidence between the first and second week
Sentinel bleed followed by massive bleeding
Digital pressure, hyperinflate cuff
Emergency consultation

question: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dentalgia for 3 days. Examination is significant for normal vital signs and pain to percussion of the right upper molar with a small pustule near the base of the same tooth. His airway is grossly patent, and he is able to tolerate his oral secretions. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Emergent dental or oral surgery consult in the emergency department
Oral amoxicillin and dental follow-up in 48 hours
Pain control with oral narcotic medications and discharge

correctAnswer: Oral amoxicillin and dental follow-up in 48 hours
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with a periapical abscess, an acute dental infection commonly seen in patients with poor dentition and associated with dental caries. Patients will present with acute focal dentalgia with severe pain on percussion of the affected tooth and visualization of a parulis (small fistula tract from the abscess to the gingival surface that appears as a pustule near the base of the tooth). Diagnosis can be confirmed with panorex or dental X-rays showing lucency around the periodontal ligament. However, this is not required for diagnosis. Treatment involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral antibiotics including amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or doxycycline, and dental follow-up for definitive treatment. Attempts to drain the abscess may be made depending on clinician comfort. However, all patients require follow-up, and many will need further management, including extraction, for definitive treatment.



An oral chlorhexidine rinse (A) is not used for periapical abscesses. It may be used for acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, in addition to professional descaling, or for alveolar osteitis to rinse loose debris and control bacterial overgrowth.

Emergent dental or oral surgery consultation (B) would be required if the patient had significant swelling of the facial spaces. Odontogenic infections can spread to the submandibular and lingual spaces (Ludwig angina), which would require intravenous antibiotics and emergent specialist consultation.

Oral narcotics (D) are not recommended by the American Dental Association for the control of dentalgia.

One Step Further
Question:
Blocking which nerve will provide analgesia to the right mandibular molars?

Reveal Answer:
Right inferior alveolar nerve block will provide analgesia to all of the right-sided mandibular teeth.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Periapical Abscess

Risk: dental caries
PE: pain on tooth percussion, erythematous and fluctuant swelling of the gingiva
Tx: consider I&D, antibiotics, urgent dental referral

question: A 35-year-old healthy man presents to the emergency department for eye pain and swelling. He reports a recent upper respiratory infection preceding right eye swelling, blurry vision, and pain. Examination is significant for a fever of 101°F (38.3ºC), mild proptosis of the right eye, pain on inward gaze, normal visual acuity, and intraocular pressure of 18 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone and bedside lateral canthotomy
Intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone and emergent ophthalmology consult

correctAnswer: Intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone and emergent ophthalmology consult
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation is consistent with postseptal (or orbital) cellulitis, an ocular emergency. Commonly, postseptal cellulitis will follow upper respiratory infections as translocation of bacteria from the ethmoid sinus allows for bacterial seeding, most commonly due to Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae. In orbital cellulitis, patients may experience diplopia or blurry vision, and examination may reveal limited or painful extraocular movement, chemosis, proptosis, or abnormal pupillary response. If any of these findings are present, the patient should be presumed to have postseptal cellulitis and be given intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone and emergent ophthalmology consult, as this is a vision-threatening emergency. In mild or early cases, it may be difficult to differentiate from preseptal cellulitis, which typically presents with eyelid swelling without vision changes or difficulty with extraocular movement. However, computed tomography with contrast may be used in these equivocal cases.



Lateral canthotomy (A) can be considered in patients with orbital cellulitis who present with either elevated intraocular pressure (> 40 mm Hg) or optic neuropathy.

Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (C) is appropriate for preseptal cellulitis, which is most likely caused by extension from a sinus infection. Patients with preseptal cellulitis should not have proptosis, pain with extraocular movements, or visual changes.

Topical levofloxacin (D) is used for corneal abrasions and bacterial conjunctivitis in those who wear contact lenses.

One Step Further
Question:
In what age group is preseptal cellulitis most common?

Reveal Answer:
Children < 10 years of age.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Orbital Cellulitis

Infection that involves orbital fat and ocular muscles
Most commonly caused by S. aureus, streptococci
Risks: sinusitis, orbital trauma or surgery, odontogenic infection
Sx: eyelid swelling, pain with eye movement
PE: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, decreased vision
Dx: clinically and confirmed with CT scan
Tx: ophthalmology evaluation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, hospital admission
Complications: orbital abscess, vision loss, intracranial infection

question: A 43-year-old man with a history of HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents to the emergency department with concerns about a muffled voice and intermittent stridor that began when he awoke today. Last week he underwent the drainage of a periapical abscess and extraction of the associated molar. Yesterday he developed a sore throat, odynophagia, and neck pain. His physical exam is notable for faint stridor, a muffled voice, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, 1+ tonsils without exudates bilaterally, and no tenderness of the floor of the mouth. What imaging modality is indicated to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Computed tomography of the neck soft tissues
Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck soft tissues
Radiography of the lateral neck soft tissue
Ultrasonography of the neck soft tissues

correctAnswer: Computed tomography of the neck soft tissues
englishExplanation:
A retropharyngeal abscess is a collection of purulent material within the retropharyngeal potential space that lies anterior to the prevertebral fascia and posterior to the pharynx. This space extends caudally from the base of the skull to the level of the carina. Patients with recent intraoral procedures, trauma, foreign body, immunocompromised state, or extension from odontogenic infection are at a higher risk. They may present with odynophagia, dysphagia, neck pain, lymphadenopathy, vocal changes (e.g., muffled voice), and even stridor that leads to respiratory distress. Contrast CT of the soft tissues of the neck is the most sensitive testing modality for determining the diagnosis of retropharyngeal abscess. Imaging hallmarks include a ring-enhancing fluid collection in the retropharyngeal space, though more subtle or earlier findings include fat stranding, reactive edema, fluid tracking between tissue planes, and even mass effect. Early otolaryngology consultation for surgical intervention is key. Most infections are polymicrobial and often involve Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and anaerobes, which can be covered by empiric antimicrobial regimens such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, and clindamycin plus metronidazole. Vancomycin or linezolid may be added for patients at risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The progression of infection can lead to extension into the mediastinum, airway mass effect and compromise, and aspiration secondary to abscess rupture.



Barium esophagography (A) is helpful in the characterization of dysphagia, as it may reveal a diagnosis such as an esophageal stricture, an esophageal diverticulum, or achalasia, but it is less sensitive in characterizing retropharyngeal and prevertebral tissue. MRI (C) provides greater detail but is unnecessary given the increased resources required when there is widespread availability of computed tomography. Radiography (D) may demonstrate thickening and anterior displacement of the retropharyngeal wall, leading to prevertebral widening. This modality is less sensitive for characterizing the size and impact on nearby structures, which are critical to know with a suspected retropharyngeal abscess. Ultrasonography (E) is insufficient for characterizing deeper structures of the neck. This modality would be helpful for identifying superficial areas of soft tissue swelling, such as a cutaneous abscess or phlegmon, and in cases of suspected lymphadenitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis should be suspected in a patient with a recent upper respiratory infection, fever, unilateral neck swelling and pain, and variable cranial nerve deficits (e.g., abducens nerve palsy)?

Reveal Answer:
Lemierre syndrome.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retropharyngeal Abscess

Risks: trauma or URI
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, respiratory anaerobes, foreign body
Sx: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, neck pain
PE: trismus, stridor, nuchal rigidity, muffled voice, cri du canard (duck quack)
Toxic-appearing child, 3–5 years old
X-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space twice the size of the vertebral body
Dx: CT imaging, if patient is stable
Tx: airway control as needed, intravenous antibiotics, surgery for I&D

question: A 54-year-old man presents to the emergency department for sudden onset of flashes in his left eye. There is no associated pain. His ocular ultrasound is shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient’s presentation and ultrasound are most consistent with retinal detachment. Retinal detachment may present with monocular flashes, floaters, a curtain in the visual field, or loss of visual acuity. It is typically diagnosed with dilated ophthalmoscope exam but may also be detected with point-of-care ultrasound. Ocular ultrasound will demonstrate the hyperechoic retinal membrane within the vitreous, which will move with ocular movements. It adheres to the optic disc, as seen in the image above. Retinal detachment requires urgent evaluation by a retina specialist.



Intraocular foreign body (A) is typically associated with eye pain or discomfort. Some foreign bodies may be visualized on ultrasound, depending on their echogenicity. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with a foreign body. Vitreous hemorrhage (D) commonly causes floaters and produces a snow globe appearance on ultrasound, with multiple echoes within the posterior chamber of the vitreous. Posterior vitreous detachment (B) appears as a swaying linear structure in the posterior chamber on ultrasound. In contrast with retinal detachment, it is not tethered to the optic disc.

One Step Further
Question:
What optic nerve sheath diameter is suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure?

Reveal Answer:
Diameter > 5.7–6.0 mm, measured at 3 mm posterior to the globe.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retinal Detachment

Sx: painless loss of vision, floaters, flashing lights, curtain-lowering sensation
PE: retina appears hazy gray with white folds
Dx: ultrasound with hyperechoic floating membrane attached to the optic disc
Tx: stat ophthalmology consult

question: A 15-year-old boy presents with decreased hearing and otorrhea. On examination of the ear, you see the image above. Which of the following is safe?
englishExplanation:
Tympanic membrane perforations occur most commonly from infections as pressure builds up behind the membrane causing it to rupture. Perforation may also result from trauma, including direct ear trauma, explosions, severe pressure (diving), and direct injury from ear cleaning or other instrumentation. In the setting of infection, copious purulent drainage in the external canal is often present. Most perforated membranes heal spontaneously without intervention. Antibiotics may be considered in the presence of an active infection or contamination. Typically, the suspension form is used rather than a solution due to increased viscosity and less likelihood of entering the inner ear. This may be given in combination with antibiotic drops, although prophylactic antibiotics for an isolated perforation are not always required. Rarely, otolaryngology physicians may place a patch over the eardrum if healing is prolonged or ultimately repair the perforation surgically. In children with a perforated tympanic membrane after otitis media, systemic oral therapy is preferred over topical agents. The quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin) are not toxic and can be administered to patients with perforated tympanic membranes.



Antipyrine-benzocaine drops (A) are used for pain control in patients with otitis media. However, when the tympanic membrane is perforated, the benzocaine portion is ototoxic and should be avoided.

Gentamicin drops (B) are a member of the aminoglycoside family of antibiotics and similarly have ototoxic effects and are contraindicated.

One of the most important components of perforation treatment is keeping the ear canal dry. Therefore, swimming (D) should be avoided. Additionally, patients should be advised to wear a shower cap when showering to prevent water from entering the canal.

One Step Further
Question:
What environmental event is associated with tympanic membrane perforation?

Reveal Answer:
Lightning strike.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Tympanic Membrane Perforation

Foreign body, infection, blast, ↑ barometric pressure
Pars tensa most commonly perforated
Sx: pain, ↓ hearing, bleeding
​Tx: keep ear dry, analgesics, antibiotics for contaminated injuries
90% heal in a few months

question: A patient presents after a chemical splash to the eye. What management is immediately indicated?

options.text: Pupil dilation and slit lamp examination

englishExplanation:
Patients who present with chemical exposure to the eye should undergo immediate irrigation with normal saline prior to the initiation of any other management. A rapid measurement of the ocular pH with pH paper, removal of eye contacts, and a gross inspection of the eye should be done quickly prior to irrigation. While application of a topical anesthetic may be rapidly performed prior to initiation of irrigation, it should not delay irrigation of the eye. Irrigation should continue for a minimum of 15–30 minutes, followed by a check of the pH. Irrigation should be continued until the pH normalizes. Once the pH normalizes, the application of cycloplegics and a complete ocular assessment should be performed.

After immediate management, focus should be placed on identifying the substance the patient was exposed to and obtaining ophthalmologic consultation for any significant injuries. Typically, alkaline substances with a pH < 12 and acidic substances with a pH > 2 are not thought to cause significant injury. This may be altered if the duration of contact was prolonged. Long-term complications include perforation, scarring, and neovascularization of the cornea. Glaucoma and cataracts can also occur.



A pressure patch (A) does not remove the chemical agent from the eye and could actually hinder the initial and crucial decontamination process. The priority is urgently removing the chemical agent through irrigation, not immobilizing the eye.

Pupil dilation and slit lamp examination (C) is time-consuming and should be deferred until irrigation is completed. Any exhaustive eye examination should only be performed after irrigation.

Although an ophthalmology assessment (D) is necessary, it should not delay irrigation and normalization of pH, as this is the most vital intervention to prevent further damage.

Topical antibiotics (E) will likely be needed if there is a corneal abrasion or ulceration but should not be applied until irrigation has been completed and the pH is normalized.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the normal ocular pH?

Reveal Answer:
A pH of 6.5–7.5 is normal for the eye.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Chemical Burns

Acidic burns
Coagulative necrosis
Corneal ulceration with limited depth of injury
Tend to be self-limited
Alkali burns
Liquefactive necrosis that leads to deeper damage (cornea, iris, lens)
Penetrates faster and deeper than acidic burns
Irreversible blindness within minutes if untreated
Glaucoma complication
Irrigate until pH 7.0–7.4
Do not delay to perform a comprehensive eye exam

question: A 55-year-old woman with a history of chronic bronchitis presents with redness in her left eye. She reports no change in vision, no trauma, and no pain. Evaluation of the patient demonstrates intact extraocular muscles and equal pupils that are round and reactive to light. Visual acuity is 20/30 in each eye. Which of the following is the best next step in the evaluation and management of her condition?

options.text: CT scan of the orbit and facial bones to evaluate for globe injury
Measure intraocular pressure to rule out a retrobulbar hematoma
Reassure the patient and discharge her home
Stain with fluorescein dye and assess for a corneal abrasion

correctAnswer: Reassure the patient and discharge her home
englishExplanation:
A subconjunctival hemorrhage usually occurs with trivial events such as coughing or sneezing, Valsalva maneuver, or minor blunt trauma. The hemorrhage appears flat and is limited to the bulbar conjunctiva and stops abruptly at the limbus. This appearance is important to differentiate it from bloody chemosis, which can occur with scleral rupture, coagulopathy, or cavernous sinus thrombosis.

A subconjunctival hemorrhage does not cause the patient any pain or change in visual acuity. It generally heals within 14 days. The patient in this scenario has a history of bronchitis and likely developed the subconjunctival hemorrhage from coughing. No further intervention is necessary, and the patient should be reassured and discharged home.



CT scan (A) is a valuable tool when there is concern for injury to the orbit or globe. It helps in the evaluation of a foreign body, orbital cellulitis, fracture, globe rupture, or retinal detachment.

Intraocular pressure (B) is a valuable measurement when the differential includes acute glaucoma, hyphema, lens dislocation or swelling, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, or retrobulbar hemorrhage. Although it can be considered in individuals at risk for these conditions, it has a limited role in the diagnosis or management of subconjunctival hemorrhage.

Indications for ophthalmologic consultation (C) include globe penetration, complex eyelid lacerations, penetrating foreign bodies, injuries to the anterior chamber, hyphema involving > 25% of the anterior chamber, and orbital compartment syndrome. Ophthalmology consultation is not necessary for the management of a subconjunctival hemorrhage.

Fluorescein staining (E) an eye helps to diagnose a corneal abrasion or ulcer. Patients with corneal injury often report light sensitivity with pain and a foreign-body sensation in their eye. This patient may have sustained minor trauma causing her subconjunctival hemorrhage. But absent discomfort, there is limited reason to suspect corneal injury.

One Step Further
Question:
What injury can occur if Hemoccult drops are instilled in the eye?

Reveal Answer:
Severe alkali burns can occur.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Subconjunctival Hemorrhage

Blood in the eye
Most commonly caused by coughing, sneezing, minor trauma
PE: blood under the conjunctiva that stops at the limbus
Tx: reassurance

question: A previously healthy 45-year-old woman presents with dizziness for the past day, especially when she rolls over in bed. She feels a spinning sensation and intense nausea. This lasts for a short period of time and resolves with a position change. Which of the following is the most effective management for the most likely condition?
englishExplanation:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common type of vertigo in the United States. It is caused by loose calcium debris in the posterior semicircular canal of the ear. BPPV is more common in older individuals and affects women more than men. A history of head trauma is a risk factor.

Clinical manifestations include recurrent episodes of vertigo that last < 1 minute and resolve with positional changes of the head. Patients with severe symptoms may also experience nausea and vomiting. Diagnosis is clinical and based on history and physical exam findings showing nystagmus during provoking maneuvers. The first choice of treatment is canalith repositioning maneuvers. There are two maneuvers that may be used, the more commonly used Epley maneuver and the Semont maneuver.



Corticosteroids (A) are used in the treatment of Ménière disease, which is a part of the differential diagnosis of BPPV but are not effective in treating BPPV.

Vestibular suppressant medications (C) do not stop the vertigo symptoms. It may provide minimal relief of symptoms, but only masks the problem and generally has unpleasant side effects, including drowsiness.

BPPV is a benign condition that resolves spontaneously. Watchful waiting (D) may be considered. However, it is not the first choice of treatment because patients will experience weeks or months of uncomfortable vertigo symptoms without intervention.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the name of the provocative maneuver used to diagnose benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?

Reveal Answer:
Dix-Hallpike maneuver.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

Presents with the sudden sensation of room spinning with positional changes of the head
Episodes last seconds to minutes
Most often caused by the presence of displaced otoconia within the semicircular canals
Posterior canal most commonly affected
Dx: Dix-Hallpike maneuver (posterior canal BPPV)
Tx: particle positioning maneuver (e.g., Epley maneuver)

question: A 25-year-old metal construction worker presents to the emergency department with eye pain. At work, he experienced sudden right eye pain that worsened with blinking. Physical exam reveals the finding above. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Erythromycin eye ointment and discharge with primary care follow-up
Ophthalmology consult for emergent debridement and moxifloxacin eye drops
Removal of the foreign body and discharge with primary care follow-up
Removal of the foreign body, erythromycin eye ointment, and ophthalmology follow-up

correctAnswer: Removal of the foreign body, erythromycin eye ointment, and ophthalmology follow-up
englishExplanation:
A corneal foreign body can cause significant pain and result in permanent vision loss if not managed appropriately. Patients will often present with eye pain, tearing, and possible vision change, with pain worsened by blinking. Management first centers on a thorough physical exam, including inverting the eyelids and performing irrigation to remove debris or easily dislodged foreign bodies. If a foreign body is found, a fluorescein stain should be performed, and the clinician must ascertain that this foreign body has not fully penetrated the globe. Once the foreign body is localized and an open globe is ruled out, the foreign body should be removed. The body can be removed with a cotton swab or a blunt needle. Exam afterward with fluorescein should occur to ensure removal and to visualize the likely resultant abrasion (unless it is clearly a very superficial injury). Patients should then be given topical antibiotics (erythromycin for most patients, fluoroquinolone drops for contact lens wearers). Follow-up requirements are determined by symptoms and severity of injury. Those with large abrasions, change in vision, prolonged healing time, or persistent pain should follow up with an ophthalmologist to ensure appropriate healing and to be certain that further care is not needed, such as debridement or removal of a rust ring (if the foreign body was metal like is likely in this patient).



Erythromycin eye ointment and discharge with primary care follow-up (A) is the appropriate management of a corneal abrasion that does not impair vision (not over the pupil). This condition would present on fluorescein stain with focal uptake of fluorescein where the abrasion occurred.

Ophthalmology consult for emergent debridement and moxifloxacin eye drops (B) is appropriate management of a corneal ulcer that presents with eye pain, photophobia, tearing, and impaired vision. Fluorescein stain will reveal a ragged ulcer on the cornea. This condition is associated with previous trauma and prolonged contact lens use.

Removal of the foreign body and discharge with primary care follow-up (C) is not appropriate for this foreign body as it is likely a metallic foreign body, based on the history. Furthermore, topical antibiotic therapy is indicated.

One Step Further
Question:
What ophthalmologic condition presents with dendritic ulcers on fluorescein stain?

Reveal Answer:
Herpes keratitis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Foreign Bodies

Apply topical anesthesia
Use cotton-tipped applicator, needle with the slit lamp, or Alger brush to dislodge
If metallic object, remove rust rings in 24–48 hours
Consult ophthalmology for large or deep foreign bodies
Postprocedure topical antibiotics

question: A 48-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for 1 week of vertigo. The vertigo is nonpositional and episodic, typically lasting 1–2 hours per episode. She also notes nausea and a sensation of fullness and ringing in her left ear. She has a history of nephrotic syndrome and takes furosemide daily. She reports no headaches, fevers, ear pain, or ear drainage. Her cranial nerve exam is notable for diminished hearing on the left. Otoscopic examination of the ear is normal. There is no nystagmus. She has equal strength and sensation in all extremities. She is reluctant to ambulate due to her symptoms but is able to stand and walk without assistance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with the classic triad of symptoms associated with Ménière disease: hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. The pathophysiology is poorly understood, but it is thought to be the result of increased endolymph in the labyrinthine system. Symptoms are usually unilateral but can be bilateral. The onset of vertigo is sudden and occurs in episodes that last between 20 minutes to several hours. Hearing loss is sensorineural and may persist between episodes of vertigo. There may also be associated nausea, vomiting, or aural fullness. Imaging is not required for the diagnosis of Ménière disease. However, the presence of any acute neurologic signs or symptoms should prompt evaluation for a central etiology of vertigo in the emergency department. Central causes of vertigo include cerebellar or brainstem stroke, cerebellar hemorrhage, and posterior circulation transient ischemic attack. The presence of focal weakness, persistent headache or neck pain, dysmetria, speech disturbance, acute hearing loss, visual deficits, spontaneous vertical nystagmus, or gait disturbance should prompt neuroimaging. Treatment of Ménière disease can include antihistamines, combination therapy with triamterene and hydrochlorothiazide, or calcium channel blockers. Patients with symptoms of Ménière disease should follow up with otolaryngology.



Benign paroxysmal peripheral vertigo (BPPV) (A) is the most common cause of vertigo and is due to dislodged otoconia in the semicircular canals. It presents as short episodes of vertigo and nystagmus that are < 2 minutes and worsened with positional change. The presence of vertical upward and rotary nystagmus with Dix-Hallpike testing confirms the diagnosis of BPPV. Treatment involves bedside maneuvers that reposition otoconia, such as the Epley maneuver.

Labyrinthitis (B) is a complication of otitis media, viral or bacterial. It may also present with vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus. However, it presents with constant, nonepisodic vertigo that can last several days. This patient’s symptoms are episodic, and she does not have signs or symptoms of an ear infection, which makes labyrinthitis unlikely.

Ototoxicity may be caused by various medications, including loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, and cytotoxic drugs. This patient is taking furosemide, a loop diuretic. Typically, ototoxicity will present with sensorineural hearing loss. While ototoxic medications can sometimes cause tinnitus, vertigo is rare, which makes a medication side effect (C) less likely.

Vestibular neuritis (E) is the second most common cause of vertigo. It presents as continuous vertigo that lasts for days but does not cause hearing loss or tinnitus, which makes it unlikely in this patient. Treatment is symptomatic, and it will spontaneously resolve within days to weeks.

One Step Further
Question:
Which bedside test can distinguish peripheral versus central causes of vertigo in patients with persistent vertigo and nystagmus?

Reveal Answer:
Head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (HINTS) exam.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: A 37-year-old woman presents to the emergency department for worsening chronic headaches. The results of her funduscopic exam are shown above. She has a normal noncontrast head CT. Which of the following is most likely associated with this presentation?

options.text: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure 31 cm H2O

correctAnswer: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure 31 cm H2O
englishExplanation:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, previously known as pseudotumor cerebri, typically presents as a persistent headache, most in female patients of reproductive age who have a history of obesity and who are found to have papilledema on examination with an otherwise normal neurologic exam. Patients may also have visual disturbances and pulsatile tinnitus. Papilledema presents as elevation of the optic disk with a blurring of the disk margins on the funduscopic exam. Retinal venous engorgement may be seen as well. All patients with papilledema should receive neuroimaging with either a head CT or brain magnetic resonance imaging to rule out mass lesions. However, patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension will typically have normal neuroimaging. When the diagnosis is suspected, a lumbar puncture should be performed in the lateral decubitus position. Opening pressures will be elevated, > 25 cm H2O. The first-line treatment is with acetazolamide to decrease cerebrospinal fluid production. Weight loss should also be encouraged.



Aura preceding headache (A) is associated with a migraine. While migraines are common in young women, and patients will have normal neuroimaging if it is done, the retinal exam will also be unremarkable. A normal retinal exam will show branching dark red lines (venules) and slightly thinner bright red lines (arterioles) that converge on the optic disk. The optic disk is normally pale, with sharp, flat margins, and contains the cup, which is about half the diameter of the disk. You may be able to see the macula, which is a slightly darker area of the retina lateral to the disk.

Jaw claudication (B) is associated with temporal arteritis and can result in central retinal artery occlusion. Funduscopic findings for central retinal artery occlusion include a pale fundus with a cherry red macular spot. Temporal arteritis is rare in patients < 50 years old.

Left ventricular hypertrophy (C) is associated with chronic severe hypertension, which can cause hypertensive retinopathy. This is characterized by hard exudates, sausage-shaped venules, and narrowing of arterioles on funduscopy. Chronic hypertension can also cause papilledema and should be considered in the differential diagnosis. However, this is less likely to be present in this young of a patient.

One Step Further
Question:
How can you diagnose papilledema with ultrasound?

Reveal Answer:
Optic nerve sheath diameter > 5 mm, measured 3 mm posterior to the globe.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Papilledema

Cause: most commonly due to increased intracranial pressure (e.g., mass effect, hydrocephalus)
Sx: acute onset of intermittent headaches and blurred vision
PE: optic disc swelling
Tx: find and treat underlying cause

question: A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department for left throat and ear pain that began 4 days ago. He was seen by his primary care clinician 3 days ago and started on a course of oral amoxicillin. On waking this morning, his voice was muffled, and he had new difficulty and pain with swallowing. Vital signs include a temperature of 37.8°C, HR of 90 bpm, BP of 125/80 mm Hg, and SpO2 of 98% on room air. His physical examination is significant for an intact airway, with left lateral neck tenderness and lymphadenopathy, as well as the oropharyngeal findings shown above. He is speaking in full sentences and has no drooling or trismus. What is the definitive management for this patient’s condition?

options.text: Needle aspiration of the involved site
Outpatient referral to otolaryngology for tonsillectomy
Urgent transfer to the operating room

correctAnswer: Needle aspiration of the involved site
englishExplanation:
A peritonsillar abscess is a fluid collection between the tonsillar capsule, the superior pharyngeal constrictor, and the palatopharyngeus muscles. These abscesses often arise secondary to tonsillitis, pharyngitis, or as a complication from a recent dental procedure. Broad risk factors include odontogenic infection, periodontal disease, mucosal trauma, immunocompromised state, and diabetes mellitus. Patients will often present at a younger age with symptoms such as fever, a sore throat worse on one side, ipsilateral ear pain, trismus, drooling, dysphagia, odynophagia, and a muffled voice. The physical examination will change with the severity and size of the abscess. In the early stages, the tonsil and anterior pillar may appear erythematous and edematous and may exhibit a medial shift. As the abscess enlarges, the uvula and soft palate may shift toward the contralateral side, and the tonsil may be tender with palpable fluctuance. Definitive treatment involves drainage of the abscess, which can be achieved by needle aspiration in the emergency department when the patient is well appearing and there is no concern for airway compromise. Adjunctive antibiotics should cover Streptococcus and anaerobic oral flora (e.g., Fusobacterium). Up to 90% of patients will be effectively treated with a single needle aspiration and can be discharged. Indications for admission for parenteral antibiotics include toxic appearance, immunocompromised state, inability to tolerate sufficient oral intake to remain hydrated, and concern for airway involvement.



Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam (A) is appropriate for patients whose symptoms have worsened despite outpatient antibiotics and drainage or who are immunocompromised, are toxic-appearing, have airway involvement, or are otherwise unable to tolerate oral antibiotics. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate (C) would be an appropriate next step for a patient with Streptococcus tonsillitis who has not experienced relief with amoxicillin alone. However, the associated abscess requires more than antibiotic therapy for source control. Outpatient referral to otolaryngology for a tonsillectomy (D) may be indicated for patients with recurrent tonsillitis or peritonsillar abscesses. Urgent transfer to the operating room (E) for incision and drainage may be indicated if patients appear toxic, have airway involvement, or cannot tolerate the procedure in the emergency department.

One Step Further
Question:
What deep neck space infection presents with submandibular, sublingual, and submental space infection?

Reveal Answer:
Ludwig angina.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Peritonsillar Abscess

Risks: streptococcal tonsillitis, mononucleosis, smoking, dental or periodontal disease
Occurs in patients < 40 years old
Young adults and adolescents are most common
Cause: polymicrobial, group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and respiratory anaerobes
Sx: severe sore throat and fever
PE: dysphagia, drooling, trismus, hot potato voice, and a uvula displaced away from abscess
Tx: antibiotics ± I&D or needle aspiration based on abscess size
Inpatient care for toxic appearance, need for IV hydration and analgesia, signs of parapharyngeal extension on CT scan, or immunocompromise with multiple comorbidities

question: A 3-year-old presents to your emergency department with fever, new-onset torticollis, and difficulty swallowing. Concerned about a retropharyngeal abscess, you obtain X-rays of the neck to evaluate the soft tissues anterior to the spine. Which of the following is the appropriate method to tell the X-ray technologist to obtain the films?
englishExplanation:
Retropharyngeal abscesses are most often seen in children < 5 years of age and are commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Patients typically present with fever, odynophagia, stridor, drooling, and torticollis. Both breathing and positioning have an effect on the apparent thickness of prevertebral soft tissues on X-ray, making proper technique essential in obtaining an accurate diagnosis. At the end of expiration with the neck in flexion, the upper airway and the prevertebral soft tissues relax, causing variability in the measured thickness. This makes it difficult to distinguish the abnormal swelling associated with an abscess.

Thus, an X-ray on inspiration (ideally end-inspiration) with neck extension is the appropriate technique. The measurement of prevertebral soft tissues that is considered pathologically widened in children on X-ray is 7 mm at C2 or 14 mm at C6. CT of the neck with contrast to evaluate for a retropharyngeal abscess should be obtained instead of X-ray if you have high suspicion or should be obtained if the X-ray is positive. Children with a retropharyngeal abscess require hospitalization and consultation with an otolaryngologist. Current intravenous antibiotic recommendations are ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin but should be tailored to local susceptibility patterns.



An X-ray on expiration with neck extension (A) or on expiration with neck flexion (B) is inappropriate as the X-ray should be done on inspiration.

An X-ray on inspiration with neck flexion (D) or hyperflexion (E) is inappropriate, as the X-ray should be done with neck extension.

One Step Further
Question:
What are the anatomic boundaries of the retropharyngeal space?

Reveal Answer:
It extends from the base of the skull to the posterior mediastinum. The middle layer of the deep cervical fascia is the anterior boundary, and the deep layer of the deep cervical fascia is the posterior boundary.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retropharyngeal Abscess

Risks: trauma or URI
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, respiratory anaerobes, foreign body
Sx: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, neck pain
PE: trismus, stridor, nuchal rigidity, muffled voice, cri du canard (duck quack)
Toxic-appearing child, 3–5 years old
X-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space twice the size of the vertebral body
Dx: CT imaging, if patient is stable
Tx: airway control as needed, intravenous antibiotics, surgery for I&D

question: A 44-year-old woman presents with a sensation that the room is moving. The symptoms started 1 hour ago. She states that when she turns her head to the left, she feels the spinning sensation, and when she holds her head still, it subsides. The episodes are accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Her neurologic exam is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient’s condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient has benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and should be treated with the Epley maneuver. Vertigo can either be of peripheral or central origin. Peripheral causes of vertigo are typically benign and include otitis media, labyrinthitis, Ménière disease, vestibular neuronitis, and BPPV. Central causes of vertigo are generally dangerous and include CNS infections, vertebral basilar artery insufficiency, cerebellar hemorrhage or infarction, and temporal lobe epilepsy.

Differentiating central from peripheral vertigo is vital in determining the etiology and course of action. Peripheral vertigo tends to be sudden and severe in onset, lasting for seconds to minutes at a time. Nystagmus should be unidirectional, and head position worsens symptoms. Central vertigo may be sudden or gradual in onset and can last for weeks or months. Nystagmus may be horizontal, vertical, rotatory, or bidirectional. Head position does not affect the vertigo, and there are usually associated neurological findings. BPPV is typically described as a severe onset of room spinning, nausea, and vomiting associated with a specific head movement.

The symptoms improve with immobilization. BPPV is typically caused by the presence of an otolith in one of the semicircular canals. In patients with suspected BPPV, a Dix-Hallpike maneuver can be performed to aid in diagnosis, and an Epley maneuver can be performed to reposition or expel the otolith from the semicircular canal.



CT scan of the head (A) may be helpful if a central cause of vertigo is suspected, although CT scan usually does not provide adequate imaging of the posterior fossae. This patient most likely has a peripheral cause of vertigo based on the acute onset of vertigo, nausea, and vomiting, which is worsened with specific head positions.

Meclizine (C) is an antihistamine that may be useful in the treatment of continuous vertigo symptoms or to relieve nausea associated with motion sickness, but it is not used for brief episodic symptoms such as those associated with BPPV.

MRI of the brain (D) is more useful than CT for assessing patients for central causes. MRI would be more suitable if there were concerns for a central cause of vertigo such as a cerebrovascular accident or tumor, which is not suggested by this patient’s presentation and neurologic exam.

Vestibular rehabilitation (E) is a series of exercises designed to improve balance and reduce dizziness-related problems. While it can be beneficial for patients with persistent dizziness or balance disorders, its role is limited to the management of BPPV, which responds well to repositioning maneuvers such as the Epley maneuver.

One Step Further
Question:
What diagnosis does a positive head impulse test point to in a patient with continuous vertigo?

Reveal Answer:
Vestibular neuritis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)

Presents with the sudden sensation of room spinning with positional changes of the head
Episodes last seconds to minutes
Most often caused by the presence of displaced otoconia within the semicircular canals
Posterior canal most commonly affected
Dx: Dix-Hallpike maneuver (posterior canal BPPV)
Tx: particle positioning maneuver (e.g., Epley maneuver)

question: A 49-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis presents to the emergency department stating that she feels like the room around her is spinning. She reports a similar episode 3 weeks ago and, since then, has had an intermittent ringing sound in her ears. Her spouse adds that, over the same time frame, she also has developed some difficulty hearing from the left ear. During your exam, the patient has an episode of nonbilious vomiting and states that the room is spinning again. Vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
This patient likely has Ménière disease. This disorder is associated with increased endolymph within the cochlea and labyrinth. The common triad is tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss (sensorineural, more often unilateral than bilateral). A key finding in Ménière disease is fluctuating hearing loss. Episodes are abrupt in onset and associated with nausea and vomiting. There are often long, symptom-free intervals between attacks.



Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) (A) is sudden in onset, short-lived, and positional in nature. It is not associated with tinnitus or hearing loss.

While cerumen impaction (B) may be associated with hearing loss, it is typically not associated with ringing and dizziness.

Salicylate (aspirin) toxicity (C) is associated with tinnitus and reversible hearing loss. This patient has a history of osteoarthritis and may be using aspirin for her pain. However, salicylate toxicity is usually associated with bilateral hearing loss. Symptoms of vertigo are also uncommon in such patients.

Vestibular neuronitis (D) manifests with severe vertigo positional in nature but is not associated with hearing loss. It is usually preceded by a viral upper respiratory infection.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the most common cause of unilateral hearing loss?

Reveal Answer:
Cerumen impaction.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: A 4-year-old boy presents to the urgent care with his parent due to 2 days of severe right ear pain. His vital signs are within normal limits. Otoscopy reveals a bulging tympanic membrane with a middle ear effusion. Upon discussing antibiotic treatment options, the parent notes that the patient developed a diffuse rash several days after treatment with penicillin in the past. Which of the following is the best antibiotic choice for treating this patient’s suspected diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Acute otitis media (AOM) is a common pediatric infection characterized by inflammation of the middle ear space accompanied by signs of acute illness. It typically affects children between 6 months and 3 years of age and remains a frequent cause of antibiotic prescriptions in the emergency department. The condition is most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Risk factors include exposure to tobacco smoke, bottle-feeding while supine, daycare attendance, and lack of immunization against S. pneumoniae and influenza.

Diagnosis is clinical and relies on the presence of a bulging tympanic membrane, middle ear effusion, and signs of middle ear inflammation. This patient's presentation with ear pain, normal vital signs, and a bulging tympanic membrane with effusion is classic for uncomplicated AOM. While observation is reasonable for selected cases, such as children ≥ 2 years with mild symptoms, antibiotic therapy is typically recommended for children younger than 6 years with moderate to severe symptoms, bilateral disease, or otorrhea.

Amoxicillin remains the first-line treatment for AOM due to its efficacy, safety profile, and narrow spectrum of activity. However, in children with a history of a hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin, second- or third-generation oral cephalosporins (e.g., cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime) are appropriate alternatives. Cefpodoxime, a third-generation oral cephalosporin, provides adequate coverage for common bacterial pathogens and has favorable pharmacokinetics in pediatric patients. It is well tolerated and avoids broader-spectrum or less effective alternatives such as macrolides or fluoroquinolones.



Macrolides, such as azithromycin (A), and lincosamides, such as clindamycin (D), are used to treat AOM in patients with hypersensitivity or serious delayed reactions to penicillins. However, they are not preferred in this case as azithromycin has increasing macrolide resistance among S. pneumoniae and limited activity against nontypeable H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis. Similarly, clindamycin has limited coverage for H. influenza and M. catarrhalis and has more side effects than cefpodoxime.

First-generation cephalosporins such as cephalexin (C) and cefazolin are commonly used to treat Staphylococcus aureus skin and wound infections and urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Cephalexin lacks sufficient activity against H. influenza, one of the more common bacterial causes of AOM.

One Step Further
Question:
What type of hypersensitivity reaction is serum sickness?

Reveal Answer:
Type III hypersensitivity.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Acute Otitis Media in Pediatrics

Most often infant or young child
Most common bacteria isolated include H. influenzae (nontypable), S. pneumoniae, and M. catarrhalis (there is decreased incidence of S. pneumoniae due to PCV13 vaccination)
Sx: ear pain, middle ear effusion + signs of infection or inflammation (fever, otorrhea, pus)
PE: erythema, bulge and decreased mobility of TM, purulent fluid
Tx: amoxicillin, consider amoxicillin-clavulanate in otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome
Consider period of observation if patient ≥ 2 years old and immunocompetent with mild symptoms

question: A neonate presents to the ED with purulent conjunctivitis with profuse exudate and swelling of the eyelids. Gram stain of the drainage reveals gram-negative diplococci. What is the most common age of presentation for this disease process?
englishExplanation:
This patient is presenting with signs and Gram stain findings consistent with gonorrheal neonatal conjunctivitis. Gonorrheal neonatal conjunctivitis typically presents 2–5 days after birth. It presents with bilateral copious purulent discharge and is often accompanied by systemic symptoms. It is potentially life-threatening. Diagnosis of gonorrheal neonatal conjunctivitis is made on Gram stain as it reveals gram-negative diplococci. A full sepsis workup should also be initiated due to the high risk of systemic disease. Septic arthritis is the most common manifestation of disseminated disease in this age group. Management of gonorrheal neonatal conjunctivitis is with intravenous ceftriaxone or cefotaxime and admission. The eyes should also be frequently and copiously irrigated with saline.



Age of 2–14 days (B) is typical for presentation of herpes simplex virus neonatal conjunctivitis.

Age of 5–14 days (D) is typical for presentation of chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis.

Age of 14–28 days (A) is outside the typical window of presentation of neonatal conjunctivitis.

One Step Further
Question:
What organism is associated with conjunctivitis and corneal ulcers in contact lens wearers?

Reveal Answer:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Neisseria gonorrhoeae Conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)

Risks: sexually active adults, vaginal birth in a mother infected with Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Most common in neonates 2–5 days old
PE: hypermucopurulent ocular discharge, eyelid swelling, and erythematous and thickened conjunctivae
Untreated → corneal ulceration, scarring, blindness
Tx
Admission to hospital
Rule out disseminated disease (sepsis, arthritis, meningitis)
Rule out Chlamydia trachomatis coinfection and treat for possible coinfection
Ceftriaxone (unless neonate is receiving calcium-containing intravenous fluids or has clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia)
Prevention: erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment applied shortly after birth

question: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a persistent sore throat and progressive voice changes over the past 4 weeks. He was initially evaluated for this concern 3 weeks ago and was treated with antibiotics for presumptive bacterial pharyngitis. At that time, he reported a sore throat without fever and did not have any voice changes. However, since then, his symptoms have progressed, and now he has difficulty swallowing and voice changes. He is afebrile, and his vital signs are within normal limits. On physical exam, there is nontender cervical lymphadenopathy on the right side of his neck and a fullness in the right oropharynx, deviating the uvula to the left. He does not have any exudates or drainage. Computed tomography imaging shows an exophytic lesion on the right side of the oropharynx extending to the base of the tongue without a discrete fluid collection. What virus is most often associated with this type of lesion?
englishExplanation:
Head and neck cancers account for approximately 3% of all malignancies. The most common type of cancer of the head and neck is squamous cell carcinoma, but other varieties include lymphomas, adenocarcinomas, and sarcomas. These tumors can be located in the mouth, on the tongue, in the nasopharynx, larynx, oropharynx, or the salivary glands. Certain factors put patients at risk for each type of cancer and tobacco use is one of the most important risk factors. However, other risk factors include alcohol use, opium use, betel nut chewing, certain industrial exposures, viral infections, a poor diet, and prior radiation therapy for another cancer.

This patient is presenting with symptoms characteristic of oropharyngeal cancer, and he was found to have a concerning mass on computed tomography imaging. Oropharyngeal tumors, particularly those that involve the base of the tongue or the tonsils, are most commonly associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, specifically type 16. HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States. The incidence of laryngeal and oral cancers has declined over 30 years coinciding with the decline in tobacco use. However, the incidence of oropharyngeal cancer has remained constant, likely because of its association with HPV. Patients usually do not develop the cancer until 10 years after exposure to HPV. Determining whether a particular oropharyngeal tumor is HPV-related helps determine the patient’s prognosis. Patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer have a better prognosis than those with HPV-negative cancer. However, treatment is the same for both types of cancers and includes chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and surgery.



Infection with Epstein-Barr virus (A) is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a rare malignancy.

Hepatitis C virus (B) is more strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma. However, it has also been associated with esophageal and other head and neck cancers.

Herpes simplex virus (C) is less strongly correlated with head and neck cancers than Epstein-Barr virus and human papillomavirus but the virus can lead to malignant transformation in head and neck cancers.

One Step Further
Question:
In those who use mouthwash, what factors show a slight increase in the risk of developing oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancer?

Reveal Answer:
Using an alcohol-based mouthwash for > 35 years on a daily basis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
HPV-Related Oropharyngeal Carcinoma

Most commonly caused by HPV type 16
Prevalence of oral HPV infection decreases with HPV vaccine
Common locations: tongue base, soft palate, tonsils
TNM staging
Tx options based on various factors (e.g., staging) may include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy

question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the ED with fever and headache. She was recently treated for sinusitis. However, her headache has since worsened. On physical exam, you note a unilateral lateral gaze palsy and periorbital edema. Which of the following is the most definitive diagnostic imaging study for this condition?
englishExplanation:
This patient is exhibiting signs and symptoms consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a clinical diagnosis, although imaging is often used in cases of diagnostic uncertainty or to confirm the diagnosis. CT angiography is often used as a screening imaging study. However, a negative CT scan cannot rule out cavernous sinus thrombosis reliably when the clinical suspicion is high. Magnetic resonance imaging with venography (MRV) is the preferred imaging choice as the MRV will show the absence of venous flow in the affected cavernous sinus.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is usually a late complication of an infection of the paranasal sinuses. It is more rarely caused by bacteremia or infections of the maxillary teeth or other facial areas. The cavernous sinuses are the most centrally located of the dural sinuses and lie on either side of the sella turcica and adjacent to the sphenoid sinus. Thus, cavernous sinus thrombosis is more commonly seen with sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis. The internal carotid artery passes through the cavernous sinus. The third, fourth, sixth, and portions of the fifth cranial nerves also course through the sinus. This close proximity of veins, arteries, nerves, and paranasal sinuses accounts for the classic presentation of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The clinical presentation is usually due to the venous obstruction as well as impairment of the cranial nerves that are near the cavernous sinus. Headache is the most common presenting symptom and is usually followed by fevers, periorbital edema, and cranial nerve signs. Lateral gaze palsy due to an isolated cranial nerve VI palsy is usually seen first as CN VI lies freely within the sinus, while the others course within the lateral walls of the sinus. As the infection tracks posteriorly, patients develop visual disturbances and proptosis. Periorbital edema and vision changes rapidly become bilateral due to the communicating veins bridging the cavernous sinuses. Appearance of signs and symptoms in the contralateral eye is diagnostic of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Systemic signs indicative of sepsis are late findings. Cavernous sinus thrombosis should be considered in all patients with a headache and cranial nerve abnormalities.

Cavernous sinus thrombosis is generally a fulminant process with high rates of morbidity and mortality. Fortunately, the incidence of cavernous sinus thrombosis has decreased greatly with the advent of effective antimicrobial agents. Staphylococcus aureus accounts for most infections. Streptococcus pneumoniae, gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes can also be seen. The generally accepted antibiotic regimen includes vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and metronidazole. Otolaryngology should be consulted, and the patient should be admitted to the ICU for further care.



While CT of the head (A) is often the first test used in patients with suspected cavernous sinus thrombosis, it is not the most definitive diagnostic test as it may miss cases usually caught by MRI with MR venography.

Invasive cerebral arteriography (B) would be the most definitive test for arterial blockage within the cerebral vasculature (although rarely done unless for interventional purposes), but does not image the venous system as well as the arterial system and is highly invasive.

Radiographs of the paranasal sinuses (D) may show air-fluid levels or opacification in sinusitis, but are not indicated in patients with cavernous sinus thrombosis.

One Step Further
Question:
What other serious neurologic condition is most often diagnosed using MRI with venography besides cavernous sinus thrombosis?

Reveal Answer:
Dural venous sinus thrombosis.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis

Life-threatening condition
Caused by infection, often S. aureus
Presentation: fever, periorbital edema, chemosis
CN VI dysfunction (lateral gaze palsy)
Dx: MRI, CT
Tx: antibiotics, heparin

question: A 60-year-old woman with a history of diabetes mellitus presents to the ED with severe left ear pain and low-grade fever. Examination of her auditory canal is shown above. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
englishExplanation:
Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is a life-threatening invasive infection of the external auditory canal and can spread to involve the base of the skull. Malignant otitis externa is overwhelmingly seen in older patients with diabetes mellitus. The most common contributing organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which has been implicated in most cases. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative organism capable of growing in distilled water. A patient with suspected malignant otitis externa may have a history of ear irrigation. Clinical manifestations include otalgia and otorrhea. The pain is generally more severe than that found in simple otitis externa, although the two may be difficult to distinguish, especially early on in the disease process. The classic physical exam finding is granulation tissue in the inferior portion of the external auditory canal.

As the infection progresses, osteomyelitis of the skull base and temporomandibular joint can develop. Disease progression to osteomyelitis can manifest as cranial nerve deficits, with the facial nerve being the most likely to be affected. Other central nervous system complications include meningitis, brain abscess, and dural sinus thrombophlebitis. The diagnosis of malignant otitis externa is based on clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings. A markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein can support the diagnosis and is the most characteristic lab abnormality.

Computed tomography showing bone erosion and soft tissue changes in the subtemporal region may strongly suggest the diagnosis. The recommended treatment for malignant otitis externa is ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 8 hours, although mild cases can be treated with oral therapy. Other antipseudomonal antibiotics such as cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, and ceftazidime are also appropriate.



Cephalexin (A) is a beta-lactam antibiotic used to treat gram-positive bacterial infections.

Clindamycin (C) is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that is used to treat gram-positive and anaerobic bacterial infections.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (D) and vancomycin (E) are used to treat gram-positive bacterial infection secondary to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also cover some gram-negative and protozoa. None of these antibiotics have activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

One Step Further
Question:
What is the treatment for malignant otitis externa secondary to Aspergillus species?

Reveal Answer:
Voriconazole.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Otitis Externa

Most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Risks: swimming or moisture exposure
Sx: malodorous discharge, pruritus, otalgia
PE: erythematous, edematous canal with pain with palpation of tragus or pinna
Tx: topical antimicrobials with or without steroids
Necrotizing otitis externa
Complication seen in those with diabetes or immunocompromised
Sx: otorrhea unresponsive to treatment, periauricular pain, swelling
Tx: fluoroquinolone (often IV therapy needed)

question: A 21-year-old man presents after a chemical exposure to the eye. He was emptying a bottle when the liquid splashed into his right eye. The bottle is not available. Irrigation is started with normal saline. Which of the following is the most proper endpoint of irrigation?
englishExplanation:
Chemical exposures to the eye cause severe pain and irritation. Without quick intervention, depending on the nature of the irritant (acidic or alkali), burns will occur. Alkali burns are more common than acidic burns and also potentially more dangerous due to the interaction with lipids in the cornea and concern for deep liquefactive necrosis. Treatment of all chemical burns to the eye is with copious irrigation. If only one eye is involved, care is taken to avoid spilling any of the fluid into the opposite eye. Water can be used immediately and then switched to normal saline or lactated Ringers. The use of a topical anesthetic facilitates irrigation and helps to ease the pain of the burn. Initial irrigation should consist of 2 L of liquid. However, the goal is to achieve a pH that is as close to neutral at 7.0–7.4 as possible. This is measured with litmus paper. If this is not available, a urine dipstick can also be used for pH ranges. It is more common for alkali burns to require more irrigation than acidic burns.



2 L (A) of fluid is the starting volume of irrigation but additional fluid may be necessary if normal pH has not been achieved with 2 L. After irrigation, the cornea must be examined with a slit lamp. The absence of fluorescein uptake (B) may not be achieved if a corneal abrasion has occurred during the burn. Therefore, this is not an endpoint of therapy. Normal intraocular pressure (C) is seen in most chemical burns because there is no involvement of the intraocular portion of the eye if treated rapidly.

One Step Further
Question:
What is a potential danger of using a plastic "contact lens" device for an ocular chemical burn?

Reveal Answer:
Trapping some of the original chemical under the lens.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Corneal Chemical Burns

Acidic burns
Coagulative necrosis
Corneal ulceration with limited depth of injury
Tend to be self-limited
Alkali burns
Liquefactive necrosis that leads to deeper damage (cornea, iris, lens)
Penetrates faster and deeper than acidic burns
Irreversible blindness within minutes if untreated
Glaucoma complication
Irrigate until pH 7.0–7.4
Do not delay to perform a comprehensive eye exam

question: A 67-year-old woman with a history of COPD, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus presents to the ED with vertigo that began 2 hours ago. She has a history of similar episodes in the past. She also has tinnitus, which is new today. Her home medications include metformin, losartan, spironolactone, tiotropium, and albuterol. On examination, her cranial nerves are intact. Weber testing localizes to the right ear. Her strength is 5/5 throughout her bilateral upper and lower extremities. Findings on finger-nose-finger and heel-to-shin testing are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Ménière disease often presents with a triad of vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. However, there is significant variability in the presentation, and a diagnosis is difficult to achieve due to overlap with other syndromes causing vertigo and tinnitus. Ménière disease is thought to arise from increased endolymphatic production within the membranous labyrinth resulting in endolymphatic hydrops, which leads to endolymphatic duct distension.

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery recently established a set of diagnostic guidelines to assist clinicians. A definitive diagnosis of Ménière disease can be established if specific criteria are met. First, patients must experience two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours. There must also be documented low to midfrequency sensorineural hearing loss before, during, or following an episode of vertigo. Associated aural symptoms (e.g., hearing loss, tinnitus, or fullness) should be present in the affected ear. And lastly, other etiologies should be excluded.

The traditional approach to management includes lifestyle and dietary modifications (e.g., low sodium intake). Medical adjuvants can include vertigo suppressants (e.g., meclizine), diuretics, or betahistine. More invasive measures, such as intratympanic steroids, intratympanic gentamicin, ablation, and labyrinthectomy, can be considered in patients with debilitating, chronic symptoms.



Cerebellar stroke (A) is a central cause of vertigo arising from the disruption of the posterior circulation. The head impulse, nystagmus, and test of skew (HINTS) exam assists in differentiating peripheral and central causes of vertigo. The head impulse test evaluates for an abnormal vestibulo-ocular reflex. The presence of a catch-up saccade indicates peripheral vestibular neuropathy. A normal vestibulo-ocular reflex is concerning for a central etiology, as central causes of vertigo do not lead to vestibular nerve dysfunction. Nystagmus seen in peripheral causes is typically horizontal, while spontaneous vertical nystagmus should raise concern for a central etiology. Test of skew through the cover-uncover test is suspicious for a central cause of vertigo if there is vertical or diagonal movement of the eyes after being uncovered.

Ototoxic agents (C), such as aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cytotoxic agents (e.g., vinblastine, cisplatin), and antidysrhythmic agents (e.g., quinidine), can lead to hearing loss and peripheral vestibular dysfunction. A patient with no recent exposures to an ototoxic agent should be evaluated for alternative causes of symptoms.

Vestibular neuritis (D) may present with vertigo and should demonstrate nystagmus (e.g., spontaneous or gaze-evoked), an abnormal head impulse test, absence of vertical skew deviation, and absence of new hearing loss. The diagnosis should be suspected in a patient with concurrent or recent viral illness, as vestibular neuritis is thought to result from viral or postviral inflammation of the vestibular fibers of CN VIII.

One Step Further
Question:
What maneuver can help diagnose horizontal canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?

Reveal Answer:
The supine roll test.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Ménière Disease

Commonly presents with low-frequency hearing loss, episodic vertigo, fluctuating tinnitus or aural symptoms
Most often caused by too much inner ear endolymph and increased pressure within the inner ear
Dx: clinical
Tx options may include lifestyle changes (e.g., low-salt diet), pharmacologic therapy (e.g., diuretics, betahistine)

question: A 5-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a sore throat. His T is 102°F (38.9°C), BP is 105/60 mm Hg, HR is 132 bpm, RR is 25/min, and SpO2 is 97% on room air. Physical exam reveals a child with a hoarse voice and trismus, with erythema of the posterior oropharynx. He is drooling currently. Which of the following is the most important next step in management?

options.text: Bedside incision and drainage of abscess
Transfer to the operating room for intubation

correctAnswer: Transfer to the operating room for intubation
englishExplanation:
Retropharyngeal abscess is a life-threatening diagnosis that presents most commonly in pediatric patients aged 3–5 years. Patients will appear unwell and have a fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing. Trismus may be noted, as well as stridor, meningeal signs, and voice changes. Patients may be drooling and have trouble managing their secretions.

Management is first centered on securing the patient’s airway. Given that this can be a challenging intubation, it is preferable to transfer the patient to the operating room for intubation in a more controlled environment. Other critical steps include administering broad-spectrum antibiotics, performing a CT of the neck with contrast, and surgical drainage by otolaryngology.



Bedside incision and drainage of the abscess (A) is the appropriate treatment for a peritonsillar abscess in addition to antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate) and possibly dexamethasone. A peritonsillar abscess may present with voice changes and trismus but would also demonstrate a large abscess with deviation of the uvula away from the infection.

Intubation in the emergency department (B) is plausible if the patient is imminently going to lose their airway. Given how challenging intubation can be in these patients, it is more appropriate to promptly transfer them to the operating room for intubation (possibly fiber optic intubation).

Piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin administration (C) is the appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage for this patient’s condition. However, this patient appears ill, and their airway is threatened. It is important to avoid perturbing the patient by starting an IV until their airway can be secured.

One Step Further
Question:
If a peritonsillar abscess is incised without optimal drainage, is a repeat incision mandatory?

Reveal Answer:
Generally, it is not. Patients seem to have similar outcomes whether significant purulent material is released or not.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Retropharyngeal Abscess

Risks: trauma or URI
Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, group A Streptococcus, respiratory anaerobes, foreign body
Sx: fever, sore throat, dysphagia, neck pain
PE: trismus, stridor, nuchal rigidity, muffled voice, cri du canard (duck quack)
Toxic-appearing child, 3–5 years old
X-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral) space twice the size of the vertebral body
Dx: CT imaging, if patient is stable
Tx: airway control as needed, intravenous antibiotics, surgery for I&D

question: A 5-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parent due to copious eye discharge. The parent reports it began the day prior and has worsened since onset. She was born via an uncomplicated, full-term vaginal delivery. Vital signs show a T of 102.3°F (39.1°C), HR of 170 bpm, RR of 60/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air. Physical examination shows significant, purulent drainage from the eyes bilaterally with erythema and swelling of the bulbar conjunctiva. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient’s condition?

options.text: Combination therapy with topical and oral erythromycin and ophthalmology consultation
Discharge with close pediatrics follow-up and warm compresses
Intravenous cefotaxime, topical erythromycin, oral erythromycin, and ophthalmology evaluation
Single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone and discharge with pediatrics follow-up

correctAnswer: Intravenous cefotaxime, topical erythromycin, oral erythromycin, and ophthalmology evaluation
englishExplanation:
Ophthalmia neonatorum specifically refers to conjunctivitis in infants < 30 days old. The five primary etiologies are chemical, gonococcal, chlamydial, other bacterial, and viral. These etiologies are differentiated by the timing of symptom onset and specific clinical presentation, and the treatment varies between them. The most likely etiology in this patient is gonococcal conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The incidence of such infections is related to the prevalence of N. gonorrhoeae in women of reproductive age within a population, as it occurs due to preexisting genitourinary gonorrheal infection of the mother. Incidence in resource-limited settings is significantly higher than in resource-rich settings.

Gonococcal conjunctivitis typically presents at 2–5 days of life with copious, purulent eye discharge with bulbar conjunctival erythema and chemosis. While these particular features can suggest gonococcal conjunctivitis, Gram stain showing gram-negative diplococci or a positive culture solidifies the diagnosis. Determining appropriate therapy for this condition requires identifying signs of systemic involvement with further diagnostic evaluation of the blood, urine, and CSF as indicated. This patient’s fever suggests systemic infection and warrants treatment with intravenous cefotaxime (50 mg/kg every 8 hours). Patients should also be treated for potential concomitant chlamydial conjunctivitis with both oral and topical erythromycin. Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually occurs later in infancy but can still be the causative organism at 5 days of life. Patients with isolated conjunctivitis and no signs of systemic infection can be treated with intramuscular ceftriaxone. Ophthalmology evaluation is appropriate in all cases of infectious ophthalmia neonatorum. Improperly treated cases of gonococcal neonatal conjunctivitis can progress to corneal ulceration, perforation, and dissemination of infection if not already present.



A combination of both topical and oral erythromycin (A) is used in the treatment of chlamydial conjunctivitis but would not be sufficient in treating gonorrheal conjunctivitis, which is more likely in this patient.

Chemical conjunctivitis presents with eye discharge and erythema within 24 hours of delivery and is typically treated with close observation (B), but the time course and severity of this patient’s symptoms suggest gonococcal conjunctivitis.

Conjunctivitis due to herpes simplex virus infection typically presents at 14–28 days of life and should be treated with intravenous acyclovir as well as lumbar puncture (C) to rule out central nervous system involvement.

A single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone and close follow-up (E) is appropriate for patients with isolated gonococcal conjunctivitis without systemic involvement. However, this patient’s fever suggests systemic involvement and requires a higher level of care.

One Step Further
Question:
Which pathogen is associated with conjunctivitis and corneal ulceration in patients who wear contact lenses?

Reveal Answer:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Rapid Review
Rapid Review
Neisseria gonorrhoeae Conjunctivitis (Ophthalmia Neonatorum)

Risks: sexually active adults, vaginal birth in a mother infected with Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Most common in neonates 2–5 days old
PE: hypermucopurulent ocular discharge, eyelid swelling, and erythematous and thickened conjunctivae
Untreated → corneal ulceration, scarring, blindness
Tx
Admission to hospital
Rule out disseminated disease (sepsis, arthritis, meningitis)
Rule out Chlamydia trachomatis coinfection and treat for possible coinfection
Ceftriaxone (unless neonate is receiving calcium-containing intravenous fluids or has clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia)
Prevention: erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment applied shortly after birth

question: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right eye vision loss. His vision was initially blurry but has progressed, and he is now unable to see anything other than light and some movement. Funduscopy reveals the finding above. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation:
Central retinal vein occlusion presents with sudden-onset painless vision loss, which may include blurry vision all the way to complete blindness. Patients at high risk have conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and hypercoagulable states.
